instructions: Take a concrete task from your work that you plan to give to AI.
Run it through the four D's in turn: write one sentence each for Delegation, Description, Discernment and Diligence.
Turn the questions into a 30-second checklist: am I delegating the right work, is the prompt specific, did I verify the output, is the iteration ready.
Note which of the four stages you usually rush — that is your risk zone.
s4.validate: You have a completed 4D checklist for a real task and know which D you most often skip.
s4.tip: The checklist takes 30 seconds and saves hours of rework. Checking the input and output is cheaper than redoing everything.

s5.title: End-to-end example: from delegation to finished result
s5.why: Seeing 4D in action across one continuous example matters more than knowing the definitions separately: it shows how the stages connect into a loop.
instructions: Delegation — decide: 'synthesizing five research articles is suitable for AI; the final decision stays with me'.
Description — phrase it: 'summarize these 5 articles into 3 key themes for a non-technical audience, max 200 words per theme'.
Discernment — evaluate the output: 'Claude cited a statistic I cannot verify — flag it and don't use it as fact'.
Diligence — iterate: 'revise theme 2, it misses the regulatory angle from article 3', and repeat until the result is reliable.
s5.validate: You can reproduce this loop on your own task, saying all four steps out loud as one process.
s5.tip: Notice: Diligence loops back to Description — a good edit is a new, small, precise prompt.

s6.title: Common mistakes and a final check
s6.why: Knowing the framework and avoiding the usual traps are different things. This step locks in 4D through anti-patterns and self-checking.
instructions: Delegation: don't give AI tasks that require human judgment — ethical decisions and sensitive communications stay with you.
Discernment: don't publish AI output without fact-checking, however convincing it looks.
Diligence: don't stop at one iteration — it's about feedback loops, not a single send.
Run a final self-check: take your last AI result, run all four D's, and find at least one stage you could have done better.
s6.validate: You can list one mistake for each of the four D's and apply the 4D checklist by default before significant tasks.
s6.tip: If it's hard to remember, post the four questions where you can see them. After a couple of weeks they become automatic.

prompt-principles.title: Core Prompt Principles
prompt-principles.subtitle: Context, then Role, then Task, then Format, then Constraints — the framework that works almost always
prompt-principles.whatItIs:
Five elements that turn a vague request into a precise one: context (what's the situation), role (who the model should be), task (what exactly to do), format (how to deliver), and constraints (what to avoid). It's not "prompt magic" but a simple habit: 30 seconds of structure save 15 minutes of back-and-forth.

The course walks through each principle in turn with live examples, and at the end you assemble everything into one working prompt and test it. Related nodes: [[node:prompting|prompting]] as the overall discipline, [[node:pr-role|role]], [[node:pr-4d|4D task]], and [[node:pr-xml|XML tags]] for format.
prompt-principles.approach: Don't memorize — apply it right away to your real task. After each step, add one more element to your own prompt, and at the end send it to Claude and compare it with what you'd get without structure.
outcomes: You understand why structure yields an answer you don't have to rewrite
You can set context so the model doesn't have to guess
You assign role and format deliberately, not at random
You phrase the task as one clear action instead of a vague wish
You assemble a full prompt from five blocks in a minute

applyIn.title: Work emails and texts
applyIn.description: Any draft of an email, post, or report goes through the framework — and comes out ready on the first try, not after three rounds of edits.

applyIn.title: Analysis and decisions
applyIn.description: When you need solution options or data analysis, an expert role plus a table format gives a structured, comparable answer.

applyIn.title: Training the team
applyIn.description: The same framework is a shared language for the whole team: prompts become repeatable and easy to hand off.

pitfalls: Writing the task right away without context and role — the model guesses and errs more often.
Specifying format as "make it nicer" instead of specifics ("table: columns A, B, C").
Overloading with constraints — keep 2–3 that truly matter.
Confusing role with task: "be a marketer" is a role, "write 5 headlines" is a task.
Assuming one perfect prompt solves everything — structure sets the foundation, then refine iteratively.

exercises.question: Take your usual one-line request to Claude and add context and a role. Send both versions and compare.
exercises.hint: If there's barely any difference, the context was too generic. Add specifics: who you are, who the result is for.

exercises.question: Phrase the task so it has exactly one action and an explicit output format (list / table / paragraph).
exercises.hint: Check: can you tell unambiguously from your wording what counts as a finished result?

exercises.question: Assemble a full prompt from the five blocks for a real task and run it in Claude.
exercises.hint: If the answer is off, it's almost always one missing block. Find which one.

s1.title: Why structure at all: before and after
s1.why: Until you see the contrast between a vague and a structured request with your own eyes, the principles stay abstract.
instructions: Open Claude and send a short request for a real task, e.g. "Help me with a client email".
Save the answer — this is your "draft without structure".
Don't fix it yet: in the next steps you'll add one element at a time and compare at the end.
Remember the feeling: a generic answer needs clarifications, and each clarification is another round of back-and-forth.
s1.validate: You have one "raw" Claude answer to an unstructured request — a baseline for comparison.
s1.tip: The [[node:prompting|prompting]] framework isn't about length but order. A short but structured prompt almost always beats a long but chaotic one.

s2.title: Context: give the model the picture
s2.why: Without context the model guesses the circumstances and misses more often — and guessing costs you extra edits.
instructions: Add 1–2 sentences to the request: who you are, who the result is for, what the situation is.
Example: "I'm a manager at a B2B service, the client is a month late on payment, and I want to keep the relationship."
Avoid extra detail — only facts that change the answer.
Send the updated request and compare it with the draft from step 1.
s2.validate: The answer is noticeably closer to your situation — the generic "depending on circumstances" phrases are gone.
s2.tip: A good context test: mentally remove it — if the model's answer would change a lot, the context matters and is needed.

s3.title: Role: set the point of view
s3.why: A role tunes the tone, depth, and priorities of the answer: a "lawyer" and a "copywriter" will write the same email very differently.
instructions: Add a role line at the start: "You are an experienced account manager who values long-term client relationships."
Pick a role for the goal, not a "universal expert" — the more precise, the more useful.
Don't confuse role with task: role is "who to be", task is "what to do".
Send it and see how the tone of the answer has shifted.
s3.validate: The tone and emphasis of the answer match the chosen role (e.g. more diplomatic, or conversely firmer).
s3.tip: More on this technique — the [[node:pr-role|role in a prompt]] node: one precise role often replaces a paragraph of instructions.

s4.title: Task: one clear action
s4.why: A vague task ("do it well") gives a vague answer. A clear action verb sets a concrete goal for the model.
instructions: Reframe the essence into one action: "Write an email", "Suggest 3 wording options", "Draft a 5-point plan".
If there are several actions, split them into numbered subtasks rather than piling them up.
Drop the polite "could you possibly" — it doesn't hurt, but the action verb's specificity matters more.
Send the updated prompt.
s4.validate: From the task wording you can unambiguously tell what counts as a finished result.
s4.tip: The task framework is covered in the [[node:pr-4d|4D task]] node: the more concrete the action and scope, the fewer iterations.

s5.title: Format and constraints: how to deliver and what to avoid
s5.why: Format makes the answer ready to use, and constraints cut out what you definitely don't need.
instructions: Specify the format explicitly: "a table with columns Tone / Text / Risk", "a bulleted list", "no longer than 150 words".
Add 2–3 constraints: "no jargon", "don't mention the amount", "tone friendly but firm".
Don't overload — extra constraints contradict each other and confuse the model.
For complex formats use separator tags (see [[node:pr-xml|XML tags]]) so the model doesn't blend blocks.
s5.validate: The answer arrived in exactly the requested format and without what you forbade.
s5.tip: If the format is complex, show the model a 2-line mini-sample. An example beats any description.

s6.title: Assemble it into one prompt and test
s6.why: The power of the framework shows only when all five elements work together — and that's easy to verify by comparison.
instructions: Assemble the final prompt in order: Context, then Role, then Task, then Format, then Constraints.
Send it to Claude in a fresh chat — without the history of past attempts.
Compare the result with the "raw" draft from step 1.
If something is off, find the missing or weak block and strengthen just that one instead of rewriting everything.
s6.validate: The final answer is usable with almost no edits and is noticeably better than the draft from step 1.
s6.tip: Save a successful prompt as a template with placeholders — the [[node:prompting|prompting]] framework gets reused across dozens of tasks.

prompt-xml.title: XML tags in prompts for Claude
prompt-xml.subtitle: Mark up your prompts with tags so Claude doesn't confuse data with instructions
prompt-xml.whatItIs: Claude is trained to understand XML-like markup especially well: blocks such as <context>, <task>, <example>, <constraints>. Tags turn a wall of text into a structure where the model can see where the data is, where the task is, where the example is, and where the constraints are. It's not magic — just explicit signaling of the boundaries between meaningful blocks.
prompt-xml.approach: We move from motivation to practice: first why mark up a prompt at all, then the basic tag set, then marking up a long prompt, a before/after example walkthrough, nesting and referencing tags inside the instruction — and finally common mistakes with a validation checklist. XML tags in this course are kept as-is and never replaced with emoji or markdown.
outcomes: You understand why Claude works more stably with XML markup on long prompts
You use the basic tag set <context>, <task>, <example>, <constraints>
You can mark up a long prompt so data doesn't blend into instructions
You apply nested tags and reference them in the instruction text
You avoid typical mistakes: extra tags, unclosed blocks, marking up simple requests

applyIn.title: Long prompts with data
applyIn.description: When you paste a large document, log, or code into a prompt, you wrap it in <context> or <data>, and keep the task separately in <task>, so Claude doesn't mistake the data for an instruction.

applyIn.title: Few-shot examples
applyIn.description: You wrap each training example in <example> so the model clearly separates samples from the current request. See [[node:pr-fewshot|learning from examples]].

applyIn.title: Complex tasks with constraints
applyIn.description: When a task has many conditions, you move them into <constraints> so Claude doesn't lose requirements in the general flow of text.

pitfalls: Marking up a simple one-line request with tags — that's noise, not value
Forgetting the closing tag (</task>) — block boundaries blur and the model gets confused
Inventing dozens of exotic tags instead of 3-4 clear ones — the structure stops being readable
Putting data and instruction in one block — the whole point of markup is lost
Referencing a tag in the instruction that isn't in the prompt — Claude can't find what you mean

exercises.question: You have a prompt: a long article text, and at the end the phrase "summarize it". How do you tag it so Claude doesn't confuse the article with the instruction?
exercises.hint: Wrap the article itself in <context>...</context>, and the command in a separate <task>summarize it</task>.

exercises.question: You want to give Claude 3 examples of correct answers and 1 new question. Which tags do you use?
exercises.hint: Each sample goes in its own <example>, the current request in <task>. That way the model sees the examples are training, not data to answer.

exercises.question: Why write "use the data from the <context> tag" in the instruction if the data is already in the prompt?
exercises.hint: An explicit tag reference removes ambiguity: Claude knows exactly which block to treat as the source and which to ignore.

s1.title: Why Claude needs XML markup
s1.why: Without structure, a long prompt is a wall of text where the model guesses where the data ends and the task begins. XML tags give explicit boundaries, and on complex tasks the result becomes 2-3 times more stable.
instructions: Take one of your long prompts where data and instruction run as solid text
Visually mark where the "material" is (text, code, log) and where the "command" is — what to do with it
Recognize the problem: without markup Claude may mistake some data for an instruction or vice versa
Remember the idea: a tag is an explicit signal "a separate meaningful block starts here"
Connect this to the basics in [[node:prompting|prompting]] — XML is a structure tool, not a replacement for a clear request
s1.validate: You can explain in one sentence what problem XML markup solves (separating data from instructions).
s1.tip: XML tags in Claude don't have to be "real" valid XML — what matters is a clear pairing of opening and closing tag.

s2.title: Basic tags: <context>, <task>, <example>, <constraints>
s2.why: You don't need to invent your own notation. Four tags cover 90% of tasks, and they're intuitive both to you and the model.
instructions: <context> — put background information, data, a document, or code here
<task> — one clear statement of what needs to be done
<example> — samples of the desired answer, one example per tag
<constraints> — limits: format, length, tone, what to avoid
Remember: tag names in lowercase, every opened tag is closed (</task>)
s2.validate: You can name the purpose of each of the four basic tags without a hint.
s2.tip: A tag name should describe its content: <context>, <data>, <transcript> are better than faceless <block1>, <block2>.

s3.title: How to mark up a long prompt
s3.why: The main benefit of markup shows up precisely on long prompts: when there's a lot of material, without tags the model loses track of what's the source and what's the task.
instructions: Split the prompt into meaningful parts: background, data, task, constraints, examples
Wrap each part in a suitable tag and close it
Place <task> closer to the end — that keeps the instruction "fresh" in context
Never put data and command in one block — those are different tags
Lean on the principles from [[node:pr-principles|prompting principles]]: one task = one clear statement
s3.validate: Your long prompt is split into at least 3 tags, and each block contains only one type of content.
s3.tip: The order "context, then data, then task, then constraints" works best: the model gets the background first, then the command.

s4.title: A worked example: before and after
s4.why: The contrast between "flat text" and a "marked-up prompt" shows what XML structure actually gives you more vividly than any theory.
instructions: BEFORE (flat): "Here's an article about coffee ... at the end make a short summary in 3 points, no fluff"
AFTER: <context>text of the article about coffee...</context>
Add the task separately: <task>make a short summary of the article</task>
Add constraints: <constraints>3 points, no fluff, in English</constraints>
Compare: in the AFTER version Claude knows for sure the article is the source, not part of the instruction
s4.validate: You rewrote one of your real "flat" prompts into a marked-up version with at least three tags.
s4.tip: If the result improved, save the marked-up template and reuse it, changing only the contents of <context>.

s5.title: Nesting and referencing tags in the instruction
s5.why: When structure gets more complex, tags can be nested, and the instruction can explicitly reference them by name. This removes the last bit of ambiguity.
instructions: Nest tags when there's a hierarchy: <examples><example>...</example><example>...</example></examples>
Don't overdo depth — two levels of nesting are almost always enough
In the task text reference a tag by name: "use the data from <context>, take the format from <example>"
That way Claude knows exactly which block is the source and which is the sample
For structured output, connect with [[node:pr-structured|structured output]] — ask for the answer in tags too, e.g. <answer>
s5.validate: You wrote an instruction that references at least one tag from the prompt by name.
s5.tip: Asking to "return the answer inside <answer>...</answer>" makes later automatic parsing of the result easier.

s6.title: Common mistakes and validation
s6.why: XML markup breaks on small things: an unclosed tag, extra markup on a simple request, a reference to a nonexistent block. A final checklist catches this before you send.
instructions: Check pairing: every <tag> has a closing </tag>
Remove markup if the request is short and unambiguous — there tags are noise
Make sure data and instruction sit in different tags, not one
Check that all tags referenced by the instruction actually exist in the prompt
Run the prompt and look: did Claude take the data from where you expected?
s6.validate: You went through the 4-point checklist on your prompt and found no unclosed or extra tags.
s6.tip: Not sure if markup is needed? The rule is simple: a long prompt with different data types — yes; a short question — no.

prompt-fewshot.title: Few-shot: teaching by input-to-output examples
prompt-fewshot.subtitle: Show 1-3 examples — and the model picks up the pattern without long explanations
prompt-fewshot.whatItIs:
Few-shot is a technique where instead of describing a task in words, you show ready input-to-output pairs. The model picks up the pattern from the examples and continues it on new data. It is the strongest way to lock in a format, tone, and style that are hard to put into instructions.

Where zero-shot (just an instruction) gives a vague result, two or three precise examples set a firm frame. Few-shot pairs well with [[node:prompting|basic prompting]] and [[node:pr-xml|XML structure]], which cleanly separates the examples from the request.
prompt-fewshot.approach: Don't explain what's easier to show. Give 1-3 diverse, non-contradictory examples in a single format, wrap them in tags, and end with a real input without an answer — the model will complete the output by pattern. Example quality matters more than quantity.
outcomes: Understand when examples beat verbal instructions
Choose the right number of examples (1-3) and their diversity
Format input-to-output pairs via XML tags so the model doesn't confuse them with the request
Recognize and remove example bias and contradictions
Combine few-shot with other techniques and validate the result

applyIn.title: Non-standard output format
applyIn.description: When you need a specific JSON, table, or markup that's hard to describe in words — show 2 ready examples.

applyIn.title: Subtle tone and style
applyIn.description: When brand voice or a specific intonation matters — examples convey it more precisely than any description.

applyIn.title: Classification and labeling
applyIn.description: When you need to sort texts into categories — a few labeled examples set the class boundaries.

pitfalls: Contradictory examples — the model picks a random pattern and the result drifts.
Example bias: if all examples are from one category, the model leans toward it even where it shouldn't.
Too many examples (5+) — they bloat the prompt and rarely improve accuracy over 2-3.
Examples not separated from the request — the model confuses 'samples' with 'the task to perform'.
All examples are easy, with no edge cases — the model stumbles on atypical input.

exercises.question: Take a task you usually describe in words (e.g. 'summarize in 3 bullets') and rebuild it as few-shot: give 2 input-to-output pairs and one new input. Compare the result to the purely verbal version.
exercises.hint: Wrap examples in <example>...</example> tags so the model doesn't mistake them for the task.

exercises.question: Create deliberately contradictory examples (one output in uppercase, another in lowercase) and see which pattern the model picks on a new input.
exercises.hint: The unpredictable answer is a clear demonstration of why examples must be consistent.

exercises.question: Add one edge-case example (empty input, very long text, atypical case) and check whether the result became more robust.
exercises.hint: An edge example shows the model how to behave in exceptions, not just in ideal cases.

s1.title: What few-shot is and when it beats explanations
s1.why: The key insight: showing a finished result is often more effective than describing it. Few-shot removes ambiguity where words fail — in format, tone, and structure.
instructions: State the task two ways: as a verbal instruction (zero-shot) and as an input-to-output example.
Ask yourself: can you describe the desired format in one precise sentence? If not — that's a signal for few-shot.
Remember the rule: format, tone, and style are almost always better shown; facts and logic are better explained (see [[node:prompting|basic prompting]]).
Few-shot gives roughly +30-80% format accuracy compared to zero-shot.
s1.validate: You can name a concrete task where an example is more precise than any description.
s1.tip: If you catch yourself writing a long paragraph on 'exactly how to format the answer' — almost always it should be replaced by a single example.

s2.title: How many examples (1-3) and which ones
s2.why: The number and diversity of examples directly shape the result. Too few — the model won't catch the pattern; too many — bloat the prompt; too similar — create bias.
instructions: Start with one example (one-shot). If the pattern is unstable — add a second and a third.
Stop at 2-3 examples: beyond that accuracy grows little while prompt length and cost grow noticeably.
Make examples diverse: different inputs, different cases, not three copies of the same thing.
If the task has categories — cover different categories with examples, not just one.
s2.validate: You have 1-3 dissimilar examples covering the typical cases of the task.
s2.tip: Diversity matters more than quantity: two different examples are stronger than five nearly identical ones.

s3.title: How to format examples: input-to-output pairs and XML
s3.why: The model must clearly understand which parts are samples and which is the actual task. Without markup it confuses examples with the request and tries to 'perform' them.
instructions: Format each example as an explicit pair: input and expected output side by side.
Wrap examples in tags, e.g. <example><input>...</input><output>...</output></example> — this is [[node:pr-xml|XML structure]].
Keep a single format across all examples: same tags, same output structure.
At the end, give a new input without an output — the model will complete the answer by pattern.
Don't mix several output formats in one example.
s3.validate: Examples are visually and structurally separated from the final request, and the format is identical across all.
s3.tip: Uniform tags are half the battle: the model copies exactly the structure it sees in the examples.

s4.title: A worked example
s4.why: One worked case cements everything above: the number of examples, their formatting, and the final input in action.
instructions: Task: extract the sentiment of a review. Give two examples: <example><input>Delivery was a week late</input><output>negative</output></example> and <example><input>Everything arrived on time, packaging perfect</input><output>positive</output></example>.
Add an edge example with a mixed case: <example><input>The product is good, but support is silent</input><output>mixed</output></example>.
At the end, give a new input without an answer: <input>The price stings, but the quality is top-notch</input>.
Run it and check that the model returned a single word from the given set, not a long text.
s4.validate: The model answers strictly in the examples' format (a single label word), including the mixed case.
s4.tip: Including an edge example ('mixed') pre-teaches the model not to fall into binary thinking.

s5.title: Common pitfalls: bias and contradictions
s5.why: Most few-shot failures aren't a lack of examples but their poor quality: contradictions and a skew toward one category.
instructions: Check examples for contradictions: the same input type must not produce different output formats.
Check balance: if all examples are one category — the model will lean toward it (example bias).
Make sure the order and frequency of examples don't artificially hint at the 'right' answer.
Remove duplicate examples — they add no signal, only length.
s5.validate: Examples are mutually consistent and balanced across categories, with no duplicates.
s5.tip: If the result 'jumps' from run to run — contradictory examples are almost always to blame, not the model.

s6.title: Validation and combining with other techniques
s6.why: Few-shot isn't an isolated trick. It's amplified by structure and reasoning, and a final check confirms the pattern was truly picked up.
instructions: Run the prompt on 3-5 new inputs and confirm the format stays stable across all.
Combine few-shot with [[node:pr-xml|XML structure]] for a clean separation of examples and request.
For complex tasks add a [[node:pr-cot|chain of thought]]: let examples show both the reasoning and the final output.
If the format is stable — save the prompt as a reusable template.
s6.validate: The format reproduces stably on new inputs, and the prompt is saved as a ready template.
s6.tip: Few-shot + [[node:pr-cot|chain-of-thought]]: examples that show reasoning teach the model not only the answer format but the way to think.

prompt-cot.title: Chain of Thought: reasoning step by step
prompt-cot.subtitle: Make the model think out loud — and get the right answer on hard tasks
prompt-cot.whatItIs:
Chain of Thought (CoT) is a technique where you ask the model not to blurt out an answer, but to first walk through logical steps: unpack the conditions, weigh the options, check itself — and only then give a conclusion. The model literally "thinks out loud."

Why it works: each reasoning step becomes context for the next one. A complex task breaks into small pieces, and the model stumbles less often. On logic, math, and multi-step analysis, CoT adds +20-40% accuracy compared to answering head-on.

This course teaches not just writing "think step by step," but managing the reasoning: where to turn it on, how to separate it from the final answer, and where it only gets in the way.
prompt-cot.approach: Don't memorize phrases. Take one REAL task where Claude errs or answers shallowly (a calculation, comparing options, analyzing a situation). Run it through every step of the course and watch how the answer changes. By the end you'll have a working prompt with controlled reasoning and an understanding of when CoT isn't needed.
outcomes: Recognize tasks where step-by-step reasoning genuinely raises accuracy
Turn on CoT with the right wording ("think step by step," tag markup)
Separate the draft reasoning from a clean final answer
Avoid wasting tokens and time on CoT where it's unnecessary
Understand how CoT relates to extended thinking mode

applyIn.title: Analysis and comparisons
applyIn.description: Evaluate options, weigh pros and cons, draw a conclusion from conditions — CoT stops the model from cutting corners and giving a shallow opinion.

applyIn.title: Math and calculations
applyIn.description: Multi-stage computations, percentages, conversions. Step-by-step reasoning catches arithmetic errors before they reach the answer.

applyIn.title: Multi-step tasks
applyIn.description: When the answer must be "derived" through 3-5 intermediate inferences rather than recalled as a fact. CoT holds the logic together step to step.

pitfalls: Turning on CoT for simple factual questions — you get a long wall of reasoning for a one-word answer.
Not separating reasoning from the conclusion — the user drowns in the draft and can't find the result.
Asking to "think step by step" but giving no step structure on a hard task — the reasoning becomes vague.
Ignoring token cost: long CoT in every request makes work more expensive and slower.
Confusing CoT with extended thinking — they're different: you set the first with a prompt, the second is a model mode.

exercises.question: Take an analytical task (e.g. "which of three options is best and why") and solve it TWICE: once with a plain prompt, once adding "First analyze each option step by step, then conclude." Compare depth and accuracy.
exercises.hint: The effect is clearer on tasks with several criteria and trade-offs.

exercises.question: Take a CoT prompt and add the requirement: "Put reasoning in <reasoning> tags, give the final answer after them as one paragraph." Check that the result is now clean and readable.
exercises.hint: This way the draft of thinking doesn't interfere with using the finished answer.

exercises.question: Find a simple question ("capital of France," "translate a word"), attach "think step by step" to it, and look at the bloated answer. Note why CoT here is an anti-pattern.
exercises.hint: If the answer is a fact, not a derivation, the reasoning only wastes tokens.

s1.title: Understand what CoT is and when it helps
s1.why: CoT isn't "magic for every request" — it's a tool for tasks where the answer must be derived, not recalled. First learn to tell those tasks apart.
instructions: Remember the essence: CoT is asking the model to reason out loud, step by step, before the final answer.
Write down 3 of your own tasks where Claude answered shallowly or made errors: calculations, comparisons, situation analysis.
Note the sign of a "CoT task": the answer can't be given in one phrase — it must be DERIVED from the conditions.
This is a core prompting technique — see [[node:prompting|prompt engineering]] for the broader context.
Pick ONE task from the list — you'll carry it through the whole course.
s1.validate: You have one real task where the answer must be derived by logic, not recalled as a fact.
s1.tip: Marker test: if you'd solve the task on paper or "by hand," it's a candidate for CoT.

s2.title: Learn how to ask for reasoning
s2.why: The model won't turn on CoT by itself on a short request. You need explicit wording — from a simple trigger to structured steps.
instructions: Simplest way: add "Think step by step before answering" at the end of the prompt.
Stronger: set the step structure — "1) list the data 2) form options 3) check each 4) conclude."
More reliable still: ask to wrap the reasoning in a tag, e.g. "Reason inside <reasoning>...</reasoning>."
Run your task from step 1 with the "think step by step" trigger and save the answer.
Tag markup is an XML-structuring technique — see [[node:pr-xml|XML tags]].
s2.validate: Your answer now contains visible intermediate reasoning steps, not just a conclusion up front.
s2.tip: The harder the task, the more concretely you should set the steps — "think step by step" alone gets vague.

s3.title: Separate reasoning from the final answer
s3.why: Raw reasoning helps the model but hinders the human. The final answer must be separated and readable on its own.
instructions: Ask explicitly: "Put reasoning in <reasoning>, give the final answer after it as a separate block."
Or: "At the end, under the heading SUMMARY, give a clean answer with no reasoning."
Check: can you copy just the final block and use it without the draft.
If the result is still "smeared" across the reasoning, strengthen the instruction: "Summary — max 3 sentences."
Tagging the reasoning relies on [[node:pr-xml|XML tags]] for block boundaries.
s3.validate: The answer clearly shows two blocks: reasoning and a separate clean summary usable on its own.
s3.tip: The final answer should make sense to someone who did NOT read the reasoning — that's the test of good separation.

s4.title: Work through a detailed example
s4.why: Theory sticks on a full example. Walk a task end to end — from conditions to a clean conclusion — and see the technique at work.
instructions: Take the task: "A team has 3 tools (A — $20/mo, B — $35/mo, C — free but weaker). Budget is $50, integrations and support are needed. Which to choose?"
Prompt: "Solve step by step in <reasoning>: 1) list criteria 2) rate each tool 3) match against budget 4) conclude. Then under the heading RECOMMENDATION — a clean answer."
Watch how the model, in reasoning, runs through the options, catches the budget constraint, and justifies the choice.
Compare: the same question without CoT usually gives "take B, it's popular" — with no criteria analysis.
Transfer this structure to your own task from step 1.
s4.validate: You see how step-by-step reasoning leads to a justified conclusion, and you've repeated the structure on your task.
s4.tip: A good CoT example always shows WHY alternatives were rejected, not just what was chosen.

s5.title: Understand when CoT is unnecessary
s5.why: CoT costs tokens and time. On simple tasks it doesn't raise accuracy, only bloats the answer. Knowing the boundary matters.
instructions: Don't apply CoT to factual questions ("capital of...," "translate a word," "release date") — the answer is recalled, not derived.
Don't apply it to simple single-step tasks — the reasoning there is longer than the answer itself.
Mind the cost: long CoT in every request is more expensive and slower, especially at scale.
For genuinely hard tasks there's a separate mode — [[node:cap-thinking|extended thinking]], where the model thinks longer without a manual CoT prompt.
Distinguish: you set CoT in words in the prompt; extended thinking is a model mode enabled by a setting.
s5.validate: You can explain with an example why CoT on a simple question is an anti-pattern, and you know about extended thinking as an alternative.
s5.tip: Rule: no derivation from conditions, no CoT. A fact or a single operation — answer directly.

s6.title: Verify the result
s6.why: A final check cements the skill: you should be able both to turn CoT on where it's needed and off where it isn't.
instructions: Take your task from step 1 and confirm: the answer with CoT is more accurate and better justified than without it.
Check that the final summary is separated and readable without the reasoning draft.
Take a simple question and confirm you do NOT force CoT onto it.
Formulate a one-line rule for yourself: "when I turn on step-by-step reasoning."
Save the working prompt template with the <reasoning> tag to your notes for reuse.
s6.validate: You have a ready CoT prompt template and a clear rule for which tasks to apply it to and which not.
s6.tip: The best check is to give your final answer to a colleague: did they grasp the conclusion without reading the reasoning?

prompt-role.title: Role and context
prompt-role.subtitle: How to give the model an expert persona: "You're an expert in X with a focus on Y for audience Z"
prompt-role.whatItIs: A course on one of the most powerful techniques in [[node:prompting|prompting]]: you assign the model a role and context up front. A phrase like "You're a web application security expert with a focus on the OWASP Top 10" sets the depth, vocabulary, and angle of the answer before you've even stated the task itself.
prompt-role.approach: We move from meaning to practice: first we unpack why a role changes the answer at all, then we learn to phrase a concrete role instead of a vague "you're an expert", add context and audience, work through a before/after example, decide where the role should live — in [[node:instructions|Custom Instructions]] or in chat — and close with common mistakes and a validation checklist.
outcomes: You understand why a role raises answer depth by 1-2 levels
You phrase a concrete role using the "X with a focus on Y for audience Z" formula
You add context to the role: constraints, format, point of view
You distinguish when a role goes in the system prompt versus a regular message
You catch and fix vague and contradictory roles with a checklist

applyIn.title: Code review and security
applyIn.description: The role "security expert focused on injections" makes the model hunt for vulnerabilities systematically instead of praising the code.

applyIn.title: Copy for an audience
applyIn.description: The role "editor who writes for busy executives" changes the length, tone, and structure of the output for a specific reader.

applyIn.title: Teaching and explanations
applyIn.description: The role "teacher explaining to a beginner without jargon" sets the level of simplification and the number of examples.

pitfalls: An empty role like "you're an expert" or "you're an assistant" — the model already knows this, zero benefit
The role contradicts the task: you assigned a "poet" but ask for legal analysis
Too many roles at once — "you're a lawyer, marketer, and designer" blurs the focus
There's a role but no audience or context — the answer is expert-level but aimed wrong
The role is typed manually in chat every time when it's needed constantly — it belongs in Custom Instructions

exercises.question: Turn the vague role "You're an expert, help me with text" into a concrete one using the X / Y / Z formula.
exercises.hint: Name the area (X), the narrow focus (Y), and who you're writing for (Z). For example: "business-copy editor focused on brevity for top managers".

exercises.question: You need to find bugs in a SQL query. Write a role and immediately add context to it (one constraint and the desired format).
exercises.hint: A database role + focus on performance, plus context: "PostgreSQL database, answer as a list of issues in descending order of importance".

exercises.question: Every day you ask the model to answer as your personal technical mentor. Where should this role go and why?
exercises.hint: If the role is always the same, it belongs in Custom Instructions so you don't repeat it in every chat.

s1.title: Why a role at all: level and focus of the answer
s1.why: Without a role the model answers "on average" — at the level of a broad audience. A role pulls in the relevant persona: depth, vocabulary, and angle all change. It's the cheapest way to raise answer quality.
instructions: Take one of your usual queries with no role and mentally judge what expert level the answer arrived at.
Remember the effect formula: a good role = +1-2 levels of answer depth.
Understand that a role affects TWO parameters: level (beginner ↔ expert) and focus (general overview ↔ narrow angle).
s1.validate: You can explain in one sentence what a role actually changes in the answer — depth and angle, not "makes the answer better in general".
s1.tip: A role isn't politeness magic. It works because it narrows the answer space to the slice relevant to an expert.

s2.title: A concrete role: not "expert" but X with a focus on Y for audience Z
s2.why: "You're an expert in everything" gives the model nothing — it already knows a bit of everything. The power is in narrowing. The "X with a focus on Y for audience Z" formula turns an abstract role into a working tool.
instructions: X — the area of expertise: "web application security", not "technology".
Y — the narrow focus within the area: "with a focus on the OWASP Top 10 and injections".
Z — the audience for the answer: "for a junior developer with no security experience".
Assemble it all into one phrase and read it aloud — it should sound like a description of a specific person.
Check: can this role decline part of the topics? If yes, the focus is set.
s2.validate: Your role has all three parts (area, focus, audience), and none can be dropped without losing meaning.
s2.tip: If the role fits any task in the world, it's too broad. A good role excludes the irrelevant.

s3.title: Add context to the role
s3.why: The role sets "who answers", the context sets "under what conditions". Without context an expert role produces a correct but inappropriate answer: wrong format, wrong constraints, wrong situation.
instructions: Add the situation to the role: "we're a 5-person startup", "the code is in production", "deadline is tomorrow".
Add constraints: budget, stack, prohibitions ("no third-party libraries").
Specify the desired output format: list, table, step-by-step plan.
Link the context to the role's focus — they must not contradict each other.
s3.validate: At minimum the situation and answer format are added to the role, and they agree with the role's focus.
s3.tip: Context is everything you hold in your head but didn't say. Dump it: the model can't see your screen.

s4.title: Before / after example
s4.why: The difference between a vague and a worked-out role is only visible by contrast. The same question yields fundamentally different answers.
instructions: BEFORE: "You're an expert. Look at my code and tell me what's wrong." — the model replies with generic style advice.

AFTER: "You're a security engineer focused on injections and authentication, reviewing for a team with no security experience. The code is in production, the stack is Node.js. Find vulnerabilities, rank by criticality, give a fix for each."
Compare: the second case sets area, focus, audience, situation, and format.
Rewrite one of your own recent real queries using this model.
s4.validate: You have a before/after pair on your own query, and in the "after" version X, Y, Z, context, and format are visible.
s4.tip: Lean on the general [[node:pr-principles|prompting principles]]: a role is specificity, and specificity always beats abstraction.

s5.title: Role in the system prompt / Custom Instructions vs in chat
s5.why: The same role can be set once in a message or pinned permanently. Choosing the location saves time and keeps the model's behavior stable.
instructions: A one-off role for a specific task — write it right in the chat message.
A permanent role that's needed almost always (your style, your area) — move it to [[node:instructions|Custom Instructions]] or the system prompt.
Don't duplicate: if the role is already in Custom Instructions, don't repeat it in every message.
The system prompt has priority — a role there affects the whole dialogue, not just one message.
s5.validate: For your role you can say where it belongs — in chat or in Custom Instructions — and justify the choice by frequency of use.
s5.tip: The rule is simple: repeats every time, then Custom Instructions; unique to the task, then chat.

s6.title: Common mistakes and validation
s6.why: Most role failures come down to two mistakes: an empty role and a role that contradicts the task. The checklist catches them 20 seconds before sending.
instructions: Empty role: "you're an expert" / "you're an assistant" — cross it out, zero benefit.
Contradiction: the role "creative copywriter" with the task "review a legal contract" is a mismatch, rephrase it.
Overload: three or four roles in one — keep one, the most relevant.
Run the final checklist: is there an X? a Y? a Z? context? does the role not argue with the task?
If any item is "no", refine it before sending.
s6.validate: Your role passes all five checklist items: area, focus, audience, context, and no contradiction with the task.
s6.tip: Not sure if you even need a role? Ask: will the answer change noticeably? If not, you don't need a role — don't overcomplicate.

prompt-prefill.title: Prefill: setting the start of Claude's response
prompt-prefill.subtitle: How to lock the first characters of the response in advance to get the exact format and tone
prompt-prefill.whatItIs: Prefill is a technique where you set the start of Claude's response in advance, and the model continues from exactly that point. In the API it's the `assistant` field at the end of the message list; in the Workbench you can type it right in the editor. This locks format and tone from the first character instead of "hoping the model follows the instruction".
prompt-prefill.approach: We move from the mechanics (what the assistant role is and where prefill is available) to the motivation (why anchor the start), then to practice and a worked example producing clean JSON. Next we connect prefill to [[node:pr-structured|structured output]] and close with limitations and common mistakes plus a final check.
outcomes: You understand that prefill is an assistant-role message started for the model, and where it's available (API, Workbench)
You can use a short anchor (e.g. `{`) to make Claude return clean JSON with no preamble
You can tell when prefill is stronger than a verbal instruction or Few-shot
You connect prefill to [[node:pr-structured|structured output]] for reliable parsing
You avoid the main mistake — an overly long prefill — and verify the result

applyIn.title: JSON responses for parsing
applyIn.description: Prefill `{` guarantees the response begins right with the object, no "Here's your JSON:" — your program parses without cleanup.

applyIn.title: Locking tone and format
applyIn.description: Prefilling the first line ("Dear customer," or "## Summary") sets style and structure from the first character.

applyIn.title: Bypassing openers
applyIn.description: When the model likes to start with "Sure! Here's...", prefilling the right beginning simply removes the preamble.

pitfalls: Overly long prefill: the model "reaches" for it and loses quality — 1-3 anchor tokens are enough
Prefill with a trailing space: in the API this causes an error — strip trailing whitespace
Forgetting that prefill is not available as a separate role in the regular Claude web chat — there it's only a "start like this" phrase
Prefill `{` but with no schema description: the model generates arbitrary JSON — you still must specify the format
Expecting prefill to close the opening brace: you get JSON without the leading `{`, which you must add when parsing

exercises.question: You need a response strictly in JSON for automatic processing. What prefill do you put in the assistant role and what must you also add to the instruction?
exercises.hint: The anchor is a single `{`. In the instruction, describe the field schema, otherwise the model invents the structure itself.

exercises.question: The model stubbornly starts the response with "Sure, here's the result:". How do you remove the preamble via prefill?
exercises.hint: Set the first line to exactly the beginning you need — e.g. `## Result` or `{`.

exercises.question: Why does a 200-word "correct beginning" prefill often degrade the answer?
exercises.hint: The model spends effort reconciling with the long text instead of solving the task. The anchor must be short.

s1.title: What prefill is and where it's available
s1.why: Without understanding the mechanics, prefill seems like magic. In reality it's just an assistant-role message started for the model, which it must continue.
instructions: Remember: a conversation with the model is a list of messages with user and assistant roles
Prefill is when you write the start of the assistant message yourself and the model finishes the rest
In the API: add a final element to the `messages` array with the `assistant` role and the desired text
In the Workbench (Anthropic Console): type the start of the response directly in the assistant field
In the regular web chat there's no separate role — there prefill is imitated by the phrase "Start the response like this: ..."
s1.validate: You can explain in your own words: prefill is an unfinished assistant message that the model continues.
s1.tip: A related topic is [[node:prompting|prompting]]: prefill is one of the techniques for steering the response, not a separate technology.

s2.title: Why lock the start of the response
s2.why: A verbal instruction "answer in JSON" is a request; prefill `{` is already-started JSON that the model physically continues. This locks the format more reliably.
instructions: Formulate which start of the response is critical for you: a `{`, a heading, a tone, a refusal of openers
Compare two paths: describe the format in words or start it for the model via prefill
Remember the effect: prefill gives roughly +50-100% format adherence compared to words
Note the bonus: prefill saves context where Few-shot examples overload it
Decide what exactly to anchor — usually 1-3 tokens at the very start
s2.validate: You can name at least two tasks where prefill is more reliable than a verbal instruction (JSON, fixed tone).
s2.tip: Prefill doesn't cancel the instruction in the user message — it reinforces it by setting the start.

s3.title: How to apply prefill in practice
s3.why: Knowing the mechanics isn't enough — it matters to assemble the request correctly: instruction in user, short anchor in assistant, no trailing spaces.
instructions: In the user message, give the task and describe the desired format (e.g. the JSON schema)
Add a message with the `assistant` role containing only the start of the response — a short anchor
Remove trailing spaces in the prefill: a trailing space in the API causes an error
Send the request — the model continues from exactly your anchor
When assembling the final text, remember that your prefill is part of the response (it must be prepended)
s3.validate: You assembled a request where user gives the task and the assistant message contains a short anchor with no trailing spaces.
s3.tip: The Workbench is convenient for experimenting: you change the anchor and immediately see how the start of the response changes.

s4.title: Worked example: prefill `{`, then clean JSON
s4.why: The most common scenario is getting JSON that a program parses without cleanup. Prefill `{` solves this with a single character.
instructions: User message: "Return product data per the schema: {\"name\": string, \"price\": number, \"in_stock\": boolean}"
Assistant prefill: exactly one character `{`
Result: the model continues with `"name": ...}` — no "Here's your JSON:" and no markdown wrapper
Note: the finished response has no leading `{` (it's in the prefill) — prepend it before parsing
Check that the result parses: concatenate prefill + response and run it through a JSON parser
s4.validate: Your concatenated text (`{` + the model's response) successfully passes through a JSON parser with no manual cleanup.
s4.tip: If you want an array — prefill `[`; if a markdown table — prefill the header row starting with `|`.

s5.title: Connection to structured output
s5.why: Prefill is a tool, and the goal is most often a reliable machine-readable response. So prefill almost always works in tandem with [[node:pr-structured|structured output]].
instructions: Treat prefill as one of the ways to achieve [[node:pr-structured|structured output]]
Combine: a clear schema in the user message + a `{` anchor in the assistant prefill
Remember the difference: the schema describes WHAT is inside, the prefill guarantees the response STARTS correctly
If you work through the [[node:pl-api|API]], prefill is just an extra element of the messages array
For complex schemas, first describe the format in words, then reinforce with an anchor
s5.validate: You understand that prefill sets the start while [[node:pr-structured|structured output]] sets the content of the format; together they yield reliable JSON.
s5.tip: Don't rely on prefill alone: without a schema description in the user message, the model invents the fields itself.

s6.title: Limitations, mistakes and verification
s6.why: Prefill is powerful, but it has boundaries. Knowing the traps saves hours of debugging confusing responses.
instructions: Don't make the prefill long: the model "reaches" the response toward it and loses quality — 1-3 tokens are enough
Don't leave a trailing space in the prefill — in the API this is an error
Remember: the regular web chat has no separate assistant role — there prefill is only imitated by a phrase
Account for the fact that prefill doesn't close brackets automatically — the leading character stays in your text
Final check: concatenate prefill + response and make sure the result is in the needed format (parses, starts correctly)
s6.validate: You can list at least three prefill limitations and you verify the result by concatenating prefill + response.
s6.tip: If the response still "drifts" — shorten the prefill to a single anchor character and move the details into the user instruction.

prompt-structured.title: Structured output
prompt-structured.subtitle: JSON, XML, table, and CSV by a strict schema — so the answer is read by a machine, not just a human
prompt-structured.whatItIs: A set of techniques that make Claude return the answer in a strict structure: JSON by a given schema, XML, a markdown table, or CSV. Achieved by describing the schema right in the prompt, giving an explicit output example, and using prefill, which removes extra wrappers and preamble.
prompt-structured.approach: We move from motivation to reliability: first we figure out why a strict structure is needed and where it fits into a pipeline, then we learn to define the schema explicitly (fields, types, example), choose the right format for the task (JSON vs table vs CSV), assemble a full working example with a schema description, achieve reliable parsing via prefill and validation, and finish by reviewing common mistakes and checking the result.
outcomes: You understand when a strict structure is mandatory and when it is overkill
You can describe a schema explicitly: fields, types, constraints, output example
You choose the format (JSON / table / CSV / XML) deliberately for the task
You get clean parsing via prefill and strip away extra text
You validate the answer and know what to do with deviations from the schema

applyIn.title: Pipeline integration
applyIn.description: When a code parser follows Claude: the answer must be valid JSON or CSV so it can be passed on without manual fixing.

applyIn.title: Batch processing
applyIn.description: Thousands of uniform requests (ticket classification, field extraction) — structure guarantees that every answer fits the table the same way.

applyIn.title: Reports and tables
applyIn.description: Summaries, risk registers, option comparisons — a markdown table or CSV is immediately ready to paste into a document or import into Excel.

pitfalls: Asking to "return JSON" without a schema and example — Claude will invent the field names and set itself
Not using prefill — the answer gets wrapped in ```json or starts with a phrase like "Sure, here is your JSON"
Not setting types and constraints (length, enum) — numbers come back as strings, severity gets arbitrary values
Choosing JSON where the data is flat and tabular — CSV or a table would be simpler and more reliable
Not validating the answer in code and blindly trusting that the structure is always correct

exercises.question: Describe a JSON schema for extracting data from a review: sentiment (one of positive/neutral/negative), a 1–5 score, and a list of mentioned topics. Include types and an example.
exercises.hint: Use an enum for sentiment, a number for the score, an array of strings for topics. Add one filled-in example object right in the prompt.

exercises.question: Rewrite the request "give me a comparison of three plans" so the answer comes as a markdown table with fixed columns.
exercises.hint: Explicitly list the column names and order, define one row per plan, and ask for no text before or after the table.

exercises.question: Formulate a prefill and instruction so the answer starts strictly with the { character and contains no preamble.
exercises.hint: In the instruction — "no preamble, start with {"; in the prefill put the opening brace as the first character of the model's answer.

s1.title: Why a strict structure is needed
s1.why: Free text is convenient for a human but unreliable for a machine: a parser breaks on an extra phrase or a different field order. A strict structure turns a text model into a predictable pipeline component.
instructions: Determine who reads the answer: a human (then structure is optional) or a code parser / another system
If automatic processing follows Claude — structure is mandatory
State exactly where the answer will land: a table row, an object for an API, a database record
Fix the goal of the step: the answer should parse in ~99% of cases, not ~70% as with free text
s1.validate: You can name the specific system or code that will read the answer and the format it needs.
s1.tip: If only a human reads the answer — don't overcomplicate: a strict schema is extra load here. Structure is needed where there is a machine recipient.

s2.title: Define the schema explicitly
s2.why: Without an explicit schema Claude guesses the names and set of fields, and they change from request to request. An explicit description of fields, types, and constraints makes the output stable. This is the foundation of the whole [[node:prompting|prompting]] approach for structured tasks.
instructions: List all fields with their purpose
Specify the type of each field: string, number, boolean, array, object
Set constraints: string length, number range, enum of allowed values
Add one fully filled-in output example right in the prompt
Clarify whether fields are required and what to do when data is missing (null or omit)
s2.validate: The prompt has a list of fields, types, constraints, and at least one example of a filled-in object.
s2.tip: An output example works more strongly than a verbal description: Claude copies the example's shape more precisely than it interprets abstract rules.

s3.title: JSON vs table vs CSV — what when
s3.why: The format is chosen for the recipient and the shape of the data. The wrong choice complicates parsing: nested JSON where CSV would suffice, or a table where nested objects are needed.
instructions: JSON — when the data is nested (objects inside arrays) and goes to an API or code
CSV — when the data is flat, uniform rows, and an import into a table/Excel is needed
Markdown table — when a human reads the answer in chat or it is pasted into a document
XML — when the target system requires it or you need explicit block boundaries; see [[node:pr-xml|XML tags]]
For CSV and tables fix the order and names of columns, for JSON — the exact object shape
s3.validate: You can justify the format choice based on the recipient (human/code) and the data shape (flat/nested).
s3.tip: Flat tabular data is almost always simpler and more reliable in CSV or a table than in JSON — less syntax for the model to break.

s4.title: A worked example with a schema description
s4.why: Separate rules work more weakly than one assembled prompt where the schema, types, and example go together. A full example shows Claude the exact goal and sharply reduces answer variance.
instructions: Assemble in one prompt: the task, the list of fields with types, the constraints, and the output example
For example: return JSON {"summary": string (≤200 chars), "risks": [{"id": string, "severity": "low"|"med"|"high"}]}
Show one fully filled-in example of this JSON with values
Add the output instruction: "no preamble, start with {"
Check that the example itself is valid — the model will copy its shape, including mistakes
s4.validate: The prompt contains the task, the schema with types, a filled-in example, and the output format instruction — all in one place.
s4.tip: Before sending, run your reference example through a parser yourself: if it doesn't parse for you, the model's answer won't parse either.

s5.title: Reliability: prefill, validation, extra text
s5.why: Even with a good schema the model adds a ```json wrapper or a phrase like "Sure, here is the answer". Prefill removes the preamble, and validation catches deviations before they reach the system. More on the technique — [[node:pr-prefill|prefill]].
instructions: Use prefill: put the opening character ({ or [) as the start of the model's answer
In the instruction explicitly forbid preamble and a markdown wrapper
After receiving the answer, validate it in code (JSON.parse, schema check)
If extra text arrives — cut to the first { and after the last }, or tighten the prefill
On repeated failures add a counter-example: "don't wrap in ```, don't write an intro"
s5.validate: The answer starts straight with the structure, without a wrapper or preamble, and passes the parser/validator successfully.
s5.tip: Prefill is the cheapest way to remove chatter: the model physically continues from the inserted brace and cannot start with an intro phrase.

s6.title: Mistakes and checking
s6.why: Structured output seems ready until you hit an edge case: empty data, a non-standard value, long text. A final check catches this before production.
instructions: Run the prompt on 5–10 different inputs, including empty and anomalous ones
Check that types and enums are respected always, not only on convenient examples
Make sure missing data is handled as you defined (null/omit)
Check boundary constraints: string length, a number out of range
Record the failed cases and refine the schema or prefill for them
s6.validate: On a set of varied and edge inputs the answers stably pass the validator without manual fixing.
s6.tip: Deliberately feed a "bad" input (empty, very long, missing the needed data) — that's exactly where the holes in the schema surface, invisible on perfect examples.

prompt-iterate.title: Prompt iteration
prompt-iterate.subtitle: Run, then find one failure, then one edit, then repeat
prompt-iterate.whatItIs:
A systematic way to get a prompt to the result without rewriting it from scratch. Instead of "I'll redo it all", you treat the prompt as a hypothesis: you run it, find ONE concrete failure, make ONE edit (role / example / constraint), compare — and repeat the cycle.

Most "bad" prompts turn into "great" ones after 3-5 targeted iterations. This course gives you the method: how to lock in a baseline, how to find a real failure, how to change one thing at a time and know exactly what helped. It builds on [[node:prompting|basic prompting]] and works together with [[node:pr-fewshot|few-shot examples]].
prompt-iterate.approach: The key rule: one edit per iteration. If you change five things at once, it's impossible to tell what worked. Don't rewrite the working parts: fix a specific failure, not a "general feeling". And always compare with the previous version on the same inputs.
outcomes: You understand when iteration beats rewriting from scratch
You can lock in a baseline and define a criterion for "good"
You find ONE concrete failure instead of a vague "I don't like it"
You make one edit at a time and see its effect
You know when to stop and save the prompt as a template

applyIn.title: A working prompt that's "almost there"
applyIn.description: The prompt gives ~70% of the result. Instead of rewriting, you finish it off in 2-3 iterations.

applyIn.title: A prompt for the team
applyIn.description: You bring the prompt to stable quality and save it as a template, so the whole team gets the same result.

applyIn.title: Automation and recurring tasks
applyIn.description: A prompt that runs every day is worth polishing once with iterations — the savings compound.

pitfalls: Changing several things in one iteration — afterwards it's unclear what actually helped
No criterion for "good" — iterations run on gut feeling and never end
Rewriting the whole prompt and losing the working parts
Testing on a single input — an edit "fixes" one case and breaks the rest
Not stopping in time: polishing something that's already good enough

exercises.question: Take a prompt you're "almost happy" with. Run it on 3 different inputs and write down one concrete failure for each. Which failure is common across them?
exercises.hint: Look for a pattern, not a one-off glitch. A failure common to all 3 inputs is the best candidate for the first edit.

exercises.question: Define a criterion for "good" for your prompt in one verifiable sentence (not "high quality", but "answer ≤ 5 bullets, each with an example").
exercises.hint: If the criterion can't be checked yes/no, it's too vague — reformulate it.

exercises.question: Make ONE edit (add a role OR one example OR one constraint) and compare the new answer with the old one on the same inputs. Did it get better against your criterion?
exercises.hint: If it got worse, roll the edit back — that's a normal part of the cycle. The hypothesis wasn't confirmed.

s1.title: Why systematic iteration, not rewriting from scratch
s1.why: Rewriting a prompt from scratch throws away the working parts and starts over every time. Iteration keeps what already works and fixes only the problem — it's many times faster and clearer.
instructions: Adopt the mindset: a prompt is a hypothesis, not a final text. You improve it in cycles, not in one heroic rewrite.
Memorize the four-step cycle: run, then find one failure, then one edit, then compare.
Don't throw away the old version: working parts (format, good phrasing) should be preserved, not lost in a rewrite.
Set the course goal: learn to change ONE thing at a time and know exactly what helped.
s1.validate: You can explain in your own words why "3-5 targeted edits" is usually better than "rewrite everything from scratch".
s1.tip: If you feel like rewriting everything, that's a sign you haven't found a concrete failure yet. Find the failure first.

s2.title: Lock in a baseline and a criterion for "good"
s2.why: Without a starting point and a success criterion, you can't tell whether an edit helped. Iteration without a criterion turns into endless polishing on gut feeling.
instructions: Save the current version of the prompt as the baseline (version 0) — this is what you'll compare against.
Run the baseline on 3 fixed inputs and save all three answers — this is your reference for comparison.
Define a criterion for "good" in one verifiable sentence: what specifically must be in the answer (format, length, tone, presence of examples).
Check the criterion as yes/no: can you say unambiguously from the answer whether it's met? If not, reformulate it.
s2.validate: You have a saved baseline, three reference answers, and one verifiable criterion for "good".
s2.tip: Use the same 3 inputs throughout the course — otherwise comparing versions loses its meaning.

s3.title: Find ONE concrete failure
s3.why: "I don't like the result" isn't a failure, it's a feeling. An edit can only target a concrete problem. One clear failure = one clear hypothesis for an edit.
instructions: Compare the three reference answers against your criterion for "good" and write down what exactly is wrong in each.
Find a common pattern: which failure repeats across several inputs — it matters more than a one-off glitch.
State the failure concretely: not "too long", but "the answer is a solid paragraph instead of a list of ≤5 bullets".
Pick ONE failure for this iteration — the most frequent or most painful. Note the rest for later.
s3.validate: You have one concrete, verifiable failure stated as "it should be X, but it comes out as Y".
s3.tip: If there are many failures, start with the one that breaks the most answers. Fix them one at a time.

s4.title: Make ONE edit and compare
s4.why: One edit per iteration is the only way to know exactly what worked. If you change several things at once, the result may improve, but you won't know why and you won't be able to reproduce it.
instructions: Pick ONE type of edit for your failure: clarify the role, add one [[node:pr-fewshot|few-shot example]], or add one constraint.
Make only that edit — don't touch anything else in the prompt.
Run the new version on the same 3 inputs as the baseline.
Compare the new answers with the old ones against the criterion for "good": better, worse, or no change?
If it's worse or unchanged, roll the edit back and formulate a different hypothesis. That's a normal part of the cycle.
s4.validate: You made exactly one edit, ran it on the same inputs, and can say whether it helped or not.
s4.tip: Keep a short log: "edit, then effect". After 3-4 iterations you'll see which techniques really work for your task.

s5.title: When to stop and save as a template
s5.why: Iteration can go on forever. The criterion for "good" from step 2 is your stop signal. Once the prompt reliably passes the criterion, further polishing spends time without payoff.
instructions: Stop when the prompt passes your criterion for "good" on all 3 inputs — the goal is reached.
Check stability: run the final version on 1-2 new inputs too, to make sure the edits didn't overfit to the three test cases.
Save the final prompt as a template with placeholders for the variable parts — add it to your library of [[node:ready-prompts|ready prompts]].
Write down the criterion for "good" and 1-2 example inputs next to it — so the next time you edit, you know what to compare against.
s5.validate: You have a final prompt template that passes the criterion, and it's saved for reuse.
s5.tip: "Good enough" is usually reachable in 3-5 iterations. If you've gone past 8, the criterion is probably vague — go back to step 2.

s6.title: Common mistakes and a final check
s6.why: Two mistakes kill iteration: changing everything at once (unclear what helped) and working without a criterion (unclear when to stop). The final check catches them before you waste time.
instructions: Mistake "change everything at once": the rule is one edit per iteration. If you changed three things, you don't know which worked.
Mistake "no criterion": without a verifiable "good", iterations never end. The criterion is set in step 2, before any edits.
Mistake "single input": an edit tuned to one example breaks the rest. Test on at least 3 inputs.
Final check: run the checklist — got a baseline? got a verifiable criterion? changed one thing at a time? tested on 3 inputs? saved as a template?
s6.validate: You pass the whole checklist for your prompt: baseline, criterion, one edit at a time, 3 inputs, saved template.
s6.tip: Print the 5-point checklist and keep it nearby — it turns iteration from intuition into a reproducible process.

agent-principles.title: Agent design principles
agent-principles.subtitle: Narrow purpose, a clear trigger, least-tools, and a verifiable output
agent-principles.whatItIs: A course on the six properties that separate a reliable [[node:agents|agent]] from a long prompt: narrow purpose, a single clear trigger, a limited tool set, a verifiable structured output, and explicit boundaries and safety. It's a checklist before launch, not a post-mortem.
agent-principles.approach: We move principle by principle like a filter: at each step you state one property of your future agent and immediately test it against your own example. By the sixth step you have a ready specification you can ship or hand off to a team.
outcomes: State the agent's purpose in one sentence with no "and"
Describe a trigger that makes it clear when the agent fires and when it doesn't
Assemble a minimal tool set for the task (least-tools)
Pin down an output format that can be checked automatically
Describe boundaries: what the agent does NOT do and what needs confirmation

applyIn.title: Before building a subagent
applyIn.description: Run a [[node:cc-subagents|subagent]] idea through the six principles and cut whatever isn't ready before writing the first line.

applyIn.title: Reviewing someone else's agent
applyIn.description: Take an existing agent and check it against the checklist: where the weak spot is, there's the cause of the "weird behavior".

applyIn.title: Handing off to a team
applyIn.description: A principle-based spec is a document another person can use to understand the agent without your verbal explanations.

pitfalls: A purpose with "and": an agent that "reviews PRs and writes tests and deploys" is three agents
A vague trigger: unclear when the agent should fire and when it should stay silent
30 tools "just in case" — the agent picks the wrong ones and behavior drifts
Free-text output that can't be checked automatically
No boundaries: the agent silently performs a dangerous action without confirmation

exercises.question: State the purpose of a spell-checking agent for articles in one sentence with no "and". What stays out of scope?
exercises.hint: If you're tempted to add "and also checks facts" — that's a separate agent. Purpose = one verifiable action.

exercises.question: For a reviewer agent, what is the minimal tool set, and why does it NOT need write access to the repo?
exercises.hint: Review is reading and commenting. Write access widens the risk surface with no benefit to the task.

exercises.question: Design an output format for an email-classifier agent that can be verified automatically.
exercises.hint: Think of a fixed set of labels and a structure like {label, confidence}, not "an answer in its own words".

s1.title: Why design principles matter
s1.why: Most "non-working" agents fail not because of the model but because one of the basic principles was skipped at design time. Principles turn a fuzzy idea into a verifiable specification.
instructions: Write down the agent that "almost works" or that you want to build — in one phrase
Say the six properties out loud: purpose, trigger, tools, output, boundaries, safety
Mark the points you "didn't think about" — that's usually where the agent breaks
Adopt the rule: 2+ skipped points = the agent isn't ready to launch
s1.validate: You have a list of six points and an honest mark of where the gaps are.
s1.tip: Principles are a filter BEFORE launch. It's cheaper to discard a bad idea on paper than to debug it in prod.

s2.title: Narrow purpose and one clear trigger
s2.why: An agent with a broad purpose picks different strategies on similar inputs — behavior becomes unpredictable. A narrow purpose and an explicit trigger make the agent deterministic and understandable.
instructions: State the purpose in one sentence with no "and"
If an "and" appears — split into two agents or choose the main one
Describe the trigger: what event or request fires the agent
Describe the anti-trigger: when the agent must NOT fire
Cross-check the trigger against the purpose — they must point to the same thing
s2.validate: The purpose is one phrase with no "and"; for the trigger it's clear both when it fires and when it stays silent.
s2.tip: A good trigger can be read to an outsider and they'll guess what the agent does. It's like the narrow scope of a [[node:skills|skill]].

s3.title: A limited tool set (least-tools)
s3.why: Every extra tool is an extra behavior path and an extra risk surface. A minimal set makes the agent more reliable and predictable: less choice means fewer mistakes.
instructions: Write down every tool that comes to mind for the task
For each, ask: "can the agent fulfill its purpose without it?" If yes — drop it
Split into read and write: keep write only if it's literally in the purpose
For external data, decide whether an [[node:mcp|MCP]] source is needed or local tools suffice
Keep the minimal set and record a reason for each tool
s3.validate: Every tool in the final list has a written "why" justification.
s3.tip: "Least-tools" is like "least-privilege" in security: grant exactly what one task needs, no more.

s4.title: A verifiable structured output
s4.why: If the agent's output is free text, it can't be checked automatically and can't be reliably passed down the chain. A structured output turns the agent into a dependable building block rather than a paragraph generator.
instructions: Define exactly what the agent should return — data, a label, a list of actions
Pin down the format: the set of fields, allowed values, required keys
Describe at least one auto-check: "the output is valid if field X exists and is from set Y"
Add an explicit format for the "no result" case, not an empty string
Confirm the output can feed the next step with no manual editing
s4.validate: There is a description of the output format and at least one rule by which it can be checked automatically.
s4.tip: Fixed labels beat free text: {label, confidence} is script-checkable, a paragraph is not.

s5.title: Boundaries and safety: what the agent does NOT do
s5.why: Without explicit boundaries an agent will sooner or later take a dangerous action because "it seemed logical". Stated boundaries and confirmation points are insurance against irreversible mistakes.
instructions: Write down the list of forbidden actions: what the agent never does
Mark irreversible actions (deletion, sending, payment) — they need a confirmation request
Describe a fallback: what to do when the task is out of scope or data is missing
Make dangerous actions idempotent or at least visible in the logs
Check that the boundaries don't contradict the purpose from step 2
s5.validate: There is a "the agent does NOT do" list and a confirmation rule for irreversible actions.
s5.tip: The rule is simple: an irreversible action only after an explicit "yes" from a human. This is a baseline safety requirement for any [[node:agents|agent]].

s6.title: A good-agent checklist and the final check
s6.why: The collected principles must be run as a single checklist, otherwise it's easy to miss a gap between steps. The final check is the last filter before launch.
instructions: Walk the checklist: purpose, trigger, tools, output, boundaries, safety
On each point answer "ready / not ready" — no "almost"
If anything is "not ready" — go back to the matching step and finish stating it
Run a mental dry run on one real input: what the agent does step by step
Record the final specification as a document that can be handed off
s6.validate: All six points are marked "ready" and there is one dry run on a real example.
s6.tip: A checklist-based spec reads like a short brief — another person can reproduce the agent from it without your explanations.

agent-code-reviewer.title: Code Reviewer Agent
agent-code-reviewer.subtitle: Auto-review of PRs and commits against a checklist: security, readability, tests, regressions
agent-code-reviewer.whatItIs: A Code Reviewer agent is a specialized [[node:agents|agent]] that reads code changes (diff, PR files) and produces comments against a clear checklist: security, readability, test coverage and regression risk. It doesn't replace the human expert — it lifts the pre-review routine off them: by the time a human looks, the obvious issues are already found and sorted by severity.
agent-code-reviewer.approach: The course builds the agent from boundaries to rollout. First we fix what the agent does and does NOT do, then we write the checklist as the source of truth, set the role and instructions, connect the code context (diff/files), standardize the output format by severity (no style bikeshedding) and embed the agent into the PR process. Every step ends with a check on a real PR.
