s2.why: Two lists decide everything: permissions.allow permits actions without confirmation, permissions.deny forbids them hard. deny always beats allow. Without understanding the syntax you'll either permit too much or permit nothing.
instructions: Write a rule as action type plus pattern: Bash(npm test), Edit(./src/**), Read(./docs/**)
Add a safe command to permissions.allow and confirm the prompt disappears
Add a dangerous command to permissions.deny and verify Claude refuses to run it
Remember the priority: if an action is in both allow and deny — deny wins
Use a :* pattern for a group of commands (e.g. Bash(git push:*)) rather than allowing everything at once
s2.validate: You wrote one working rule in allow and one in deny and verified they behave as expected.
s2.tip: Start with narrow patterns and widen as needed — tightening rules after the fact is harder.

s3.title: Typical safe permissions
s3.why: Reading files, running tests, lint, formatting — actions with no irreversible consequences. It makes sense to put them in allow: they repeat dozens of times per session, and confirming each one breaks your flow.
instructions: Add reading to permissions.allow: Read(./**) — reviewing code breaks nothing
Allow tests and checks: Bash(npm test:*), Bash(npm run lint:*)
Allow safe git status commands: Bash(git status), Bash(git diff:*)
Verify that routine actions then run without questions
Don't add commands here that change things irreversibly — reading and checks only
s3.validate: Routine operations (tests, status, reading) run without confirmation, while mutating commands still ask.
s3.tip: A good sign of an allow candidate: the command can be run ten times in a row with no harm.

s4.title: Dangerous actions: why they go in deny
s4.why: Deleting files, arbitrary network calls, access to secrets — actions with irreversible or leaking consequences. They belong in permissions.deny: even in autonomous mode Claude won't be able to run them.
instructions: Block deletion: Bash(rm -rf:*) in permissions.deny
Block reading secrets: Read(./.env), Read(./**/*.key) — so values never enter the context
Limit arbitrary network: forbid Bash(curl:*) and Bash(wget:*) if the project doesn't need them
Protect critical files: Edit(./package.json), Edit(./.git/**)
Connect this to environment isolation — see [[node:sys-agent-sandbox|sandbox for the agent]]
s4.validate: An attempt to run a forbidden command (e.g. rm -rf) is rejected rather than producing a confirmation prompt.
s4.tip: deny isn't "ask permission" — it's "never allowed". Put here what you don't want to even think about in a rush.

s5.title: Ask / Auto-accept / Plan modes and their link to rules
s5.why: The mode sets the default behavior for actions that are in neither allow nor deny. Ask asks every time, Auto-accept runs without questions, Plan only plans without executing. But deny applies always, in any mode.
instructions: Remember: Ask is the safe default mode — confirmation on every unapproved action
Auto-accept speeds up work but removes confirmations — it relies only on your deny rules
Plan shows a plan without executing — useful to see Claude's intentions in advance
Understand the key point: switching to Auto-accept or Bypass does NOT disable permissions.deny
Before Auto-accept or Bypass, make sure deny covers all dangerous actions
s5.validate: You can explain what happens to an rm -rf command in Auto-accept mode when a deny rule exists (it will be blocked).
s5.tip: Auto-accept without a solid deny is the most common cause of incidents. Deny first, speed second.

s6.title: Safe-configuration checklist and verification
s6.why: Scattered rules easily leave gaps. A checklist turns permissions into deliberate protection: you explicitly verify that the dangerous is blocked and the routine is allowed before trusting Claude with autonomy.
instructions: Check deny: rm -rf, reading secrets (.env, keys), arbitrary network, critical files — all in place
Check allow: reading, tests, lint, safe git commands — routine needs no confirmation
Make sure there are no broad rules like allow: [Bash(*)] — narrow them with patterns
Run a typical session and see where Claude still asks or where something slips through
Commit the configuration in the project (see [[node:cc-config|Claude Code configuration]]) so rules are shared across the team
s6.validate: Your permissions file passes the checklist: dangerous in deny, routine in allow, no broad rules, verified in a real session.
s6.tip: Revisit permissions with every new type of task — the rule set lives alongside the project.

cc-slash.title: Claude Code slash commands
cc-slash.subtitle: /init, /clear, /compact, /agents and your own commands — in one keystroke
cc-slash.whatItIs:
Slash commands are short commands starting with `/` that launch a ready-made scenario instead of a long prompt. In [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] they handle the routine: [[node:cc-cmd-init|/init]] analyzes the project and creates a [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]], /clear resets the context, /compact compresses the history, /agents manages [[node:cc-subagents|subagents]].

There are built-in commands (shipped with Claude Code) and custom ones — which you define yourself as markdown files. Commands work both in the terminal and in claude.ai chats. This is your lever for controlling the session: context, quality, configuration — all through `/`.
cc-slash.approach: Don't memorize the list. Open Claude Code, type `/` and browse the autocomplete — it shows you what's available. Run every command from this course in a real project: the effect is immediate.
outcomes: You invoke commands via `/` and autocomplete, without memorizing them
You know the purpose of the key built-ins: /init, /clear, /compact, /help
You consciously manage session context (when to clear, when to compact)
You apply quality and config commands (/security-review, /config)
You create your own slash command for your routine

applyIn.title: Starting a new project
applyIn.description: First thing — /init: Claude studies the codebase and creates a CLAUDE.md so it can work meaningfully from then on.

applyIn.title: A long session
applyIn.description: Context has gone stale or is overloaded — /compact compresses the history, /clear resets it. Answer quality recovers.

applyIn.title: Repeating routine
applyIn.description: The same scenario every day — wrap it in your own command and launch it with three characters.

pitfalls: Typing commands from memory instead of `/` + autocomplete — one typo and the command won't fire.
Ignoring /clear when context is overloaded — answers degrade and you blame the model.
Confusing /clear (wipes everything) with /compact (compresses, keeps the gist) — losing needed history.
Inventing nonexistent commands — if it's not in autocomplete or /help, it doesn't exist.
Making a custom command for every trifle — files pile up and you can't keep track.

exercises.question: Open Claude Code in any project, type `/` and scroll the list. Run /help and find three commands you didn't know.
exercises.hint: If the list doesn't appear — `/` must be at the very start of the input line, with no space before it.

exercises.question: In a filled-up session run /compact, then compare the behavior with /clear in a new session. Notice the difference in what Claude 'remembers'.
exercises.hint: After /compact the key conclusions remain; after /clear the model starts from a blank slate.

exercises.question: Create your own command for a frequent task (e.g. reviewing the current branch) and invoke it via `/`.
exercises.hint: A custom command is a markdown file in the project's commands folder; the file name becomes the command name.

s1.title: What slash commands are and how to invoke them
s1.why: Without this you'll write long prompts where three characters suffice. Commands are the main way to control a [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] session.
instructions: Open Claude Code in any project.
Place the cursor at the start of the input line and type `/` — a list of available commands with autocomplete appears.
Type a couple of letters (e.g. `/cl`) — the list filters. Pick a command and press Enter.
Remember the principle: don't memorize, invoke via `/` + autocomplete.
s1.validate: Typing `/` shows a dropdown of commands, and filtering by letters narrows it down.
s1.tip: Commands work both in the terminal and in claude.ai chats — the `/` syntax is the same.

s2.title: Key built-in commands: /init, /clear, /compact, /help
s2.why: This is the daily-use core. Without them you explain the project by hand and get lost in an overloaded context.
instructions: In a new project run [[node:cc-cmd-init|/init]] — Claude studies the code and creates a [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] describing the project.
Run /help — review the full list of available commands and their purpose.
Remember /clear — a full reset of the current session's context.
Remember [[node:cc-cmd-compact|/compact]] — compressing the history while keeping the gist, without a full reset.
s2.validate: After /init a CLAUDE.md appears at the project root; /help shows the command list.
s2.tip: /help is your source of truth: if a command isn't there, it doesn't exist — don't invent it.

s3.title: Managing the session and context with commands
s3.why: Context is a limited resource. When it's overloaded or stale, answer quality drops. Commands give you control back.
instructions: Work in a session until answers get worse or the model 'forgets' the beginning.
Run [[node:cc-cmd-compact|/compact]] — the history compresses, key conclusions remain.
If the task changed completely — run /clear to start with fresh context.
Choosing rule: same task but bloated context, use /compact; new task, use /clear.
s3.validate: After /compact Claude still remembers the gist; after /clear it starts from scratch.
s3.tip: Don't wait for full degradation — compact context ahead of time, at logical task boundaries.

s4.title: Quality and config commands: /security-review, /config
s4.why: Some commands are ready-made checks and access to settings. They give you quality and control without manual fuss.
instructions: Run /help and find the quality and configuration commands in the list.
Run /security-review on the current changes — get a structured breakdown of vulnerabilities.
Open /config — review and, if needed, change Claude Code settings.
Use /review (if available) for a structured code review of the current branch.
s4.validate: /security-review produces a report on the changes; /config opens the settings.
s4.tip: The exact command set depends on the version — check /help, not your memory.

s5.title: Creating your own command (custom slash command)
s5.why: A custom command turns a repeating prompt into a single call. It's personal automation of routine inside [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]].
instructions: Create the project commands folder (`.claude/commands/`) if it doesn't exist yet.
Add a markdown file, e.g. `review-branch.md` — the file name becomes the command name (`/review-branch`).
Inside, describe the prompt scenario: goal, what to check, output format.
Save it, type `/` — your command appears in autocomplete. Invoke it.
s5.validate: A command named after your file shows up in the `/` list and runs the defined scenario.
s5.tip: Keep custom commands short and parameterizable — one command = one repeating task.

s6.title: How not to get lost + a check
s6.why: There are many commands and versions change. A few simple habits save you from typos and invented commands.
instructions: Always invoke via `/` + autocomplete, not from memory.
Unsure whether a command exists — check via /help.
For context keep the pair in mind: /compact (compress) vs /clear (reset).
Name your commands by action — so in a month you still know what they do.
Test yourself: run /init, /help, /compact, /clear and one of your own commands in a row.
s6.validate: You invoke any needed command via `/`, tell /compact from /clear, and verify a command's existence via /help.
s6.tip: If a command isn't in autocomplete and not in /help — it doesn't exist in your version, don't invent it.

cc-plan-mode.title: Plan Mode in Claude Code
cc-plan-mode.subtitle: Think first, change later: the model builds a plan with no edits and executes only after your OK
cc-plan-mode.whatItIs: Plan Mode is a [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] mode where the model does not touch files but assembles a change plan as a structured list of steps. You read the plan, edit it, and approve — and only then does execution begin. It is a barrier between the AI's intent and real edits.
cc-plan-mode.approach: The course goes from understanding the point of Plan Mode to practice: enable the mode, let the model think through a hard task, read and fix the plan before a single edit, move to execution, and learn when the mode is overkill. Grounded in real work in the [[node:cc-terminal|Claude Code terminal]].
outcomes: You understand how Plan Mode differs from the normal mode and why thinking and execution are separated
You can enable and disable Plan Mode right in a session
You recognize tasks where a plan is mandatory (large, multi-step, sensitive)
You read the model's plan and fix it before any file is changed
You control the move from plan to execution, including via Auto-accept

applyIn.title: Large refactor
applyIn.description: Before editing 10+ files the plan shows every step in advance — you see if the AI is about to touch something it shouldn't.

applyIn.title: Sensitive areas
applyIn.description: Auth, payments, DB migrations: the plan lets you read the model's intent before it becomes irreversible.

applyIn.title: Unfamiliar code
applyIn.description: In someone else's or legacy project the plan is a map: first you understand what and why, then you allow edits.

pitfalls: Enabling Plan Mode on trivial edits (one line, one file) — overhead without benefit
Approving the plan without reading it — the whole point of the mode is lost, you might as well work without it
Confusing "the model showed a plan" with "the model already did everything": before approval no files are touched
Forgetting to leave Plan Mode and wondering why edits aren't applied
Turning on Auto-accept for a complex plan right away without checking the first steps manually

exercises.question: You need to rename a variable in one file and run a DB schema migration across ten. For which of the two tasks is Plan Mode justified, and why?
exercises.hint: Weigh the cost of a mistake against reversibility. Where is rollback cheap, and where is it not?

exercises.question: The model showed a 7-step plan; step 4 touches a file you didn't want changed. What do you do before approving?
exercises.hint: The plan is edited with words in chat before execution — ask to remove or change the specific step.

exercises.question: After approving a 15-step plan you'd rather not confirm each edit manually. What execution mode gives you that, and what should you watch for?
exercises.hint: Auto-accept speeds things up, but check the first steps before trusting the rest.

s1.title: What Plan Mode is and why
s1.why: Without grasping the point, the mode looks like an extra click. In fact it separates two stages — think and change — and that is exactly what removes the risk of irreversible edits.
instructions: Remember the core: in Plan Mode the model does NOT apply edits but assembles a change plan as a list of steps
Compare with the normal mode where [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] changes files as it answers
Adopt the principle "think first, change later": the plan is a barrier between the AI's intent and real files
Realize the payoff: 5 minutes reviewing the plan saves an hour of rollback when the model goes off-track
s1.validate: You can explain in one sentence how Plan Mode differs from the normal mode, without mentioning UI.
s1.tip: Think of the plan as a surgeon's draft before an operation: the cut is made only after sign-off.

s2.title: How to enable Plan Mode
s2.why: The mode is useless if you can't turn it on at the right moment. Enabling it is a deliberate decision: "let's plan first."
instructions: Open a [[node:cc-terminal|Claude Code session in the terminal]]
Enter Plan Mode via the mode switch in the current session
Or ask in words: "Enter plan mode and propose a plan, no edits until my OK"
Make sure the session shows Plan Mode active before giving the task
s2.validate: You enabled Plan Mode and see the model respond with a plan rather than editing files.
s2.tip: If unsure of the mode state — just ask the model which mode it's in right now.

s3.title: When to use Plan Mode
s3.why: The mode pays off on hard and dangerous tasks, and only slows you down on trivial ones. Choosing the moment matters more than enabling it.
instructions: Turn on the plan before mass changes — a 10+ files guideline
Turn it on before migrations and edits in sensitive places: auth, payments, DB schema
Turn it on in unfamiliar or legacy code where mistake cost and rollback are high
Assess reversibility: the more expensive the rollback, the stronger the need for a plan
s3.validate: From a task description you quickly decide whether Plan Mode is needed and can justify the choice.
s3.tip: Simple rule: "many steps OR a dangerous place" — plan; "one line" — don't.

s4.title: How to read and fix the plan before execution
s4.why: The mode's main value is the chance to step in before edits. A plan approved without reading protects against nothing.
instructions: Read the whole plan: what steps, which files are touched, in what order
Check for extra or dangerous steps — for example, edits where you didn't ask
Fix the plan with words in chat: ask to remove, change, or add a specific step
Let the model update the plan and reread it once more before approval
s4.validate: You made at least one edit to the plan via chat and confirmed the model rebuilt it.
s4.tip: Pay special attention to steps touching config and permissions: cross-check the [[node:cc-cfg-permissions|permission settings]].

s5.title: Moving from plan to execution (Auto-accept)
s5.why: After approval you still pick the pace of execution. Auto-accept speeds things up, but on a complex plan it's better to check the first steps manually first.
instructions: Approve the plan — only then does the model start applying edits
Decide the execution mode: confirm each edit, or enable Auto-accept
Auto-accept makes sense when the plan is already read and the steps are predictable
On a large plan check the first edits manually before trusting the rest
s5.validate: You consciously chose between manual confirmation and Auto-accept and understand the risk of each.
s5.tip: Auto-accept is trust given in advance: grant it only to a carefully read plan.

s6.title: When Plan Mode is overkill + check
s6.why: Applying the plan everywhere is an antipattern: on small edits it adds steps without benefit. The final check cements when the mode fits and when it doesn't.
instructions: Don't enable Plan Mode on trivial work: one line, one file, an obvious edit
Weigh the balance: the plan's benefit must outweigh the time spent reviewing
Re-test yourself on two of your recent tasks: where would a plan fit, where would it be excess
Lock in the choice rule and keep it handy for the next sessions
s6.validate: You can name a task where Plan Mode fits and one where it's overkill, with reasoning.
s6.tip: When in doubt whether a plan is needed, ask yourself: "is rollback expensive if the AI goes off-track?" — if no, you don't need the plan.

cc-ide.title: Claude Code in the IDE: VS Code and JetBrains
cc-ide.subtitle: The same agent, but inside the editor: inline diffs, accept/reject, and sync with open tabs
cc-ide.whatItIs: The [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] extension for VS Code and JetBrains. It is not a separate product but the same agent you use in the terminal, embedded in the editor: edits arrive as inline diffs, changes are accepted or rejected with buttons, and the agent sees your open tabs as visual context. Installed from the marketplace.
cc-ide.approach: We go from "why keep the agent in the editor at all" to installation, linking with the terminal version through shared settings and CLAUDE.md, working with diffs, and consciously choosing between IDE and terminal. We finish with common problems and a quick check that everything works.
outcomes: You understand that the IDE extension and terminal Claude Code are one agent, not two tools
You installed the extension in VS Code or JetBrains and ran your first edit
You linked the IDE with the terminal version through shared settings and CLAUDE.md
You can accept and reject changes via the diff view right in the editor
You consciously choose when the IDE is more convenient and when the terminal is

applyIn.title: Fast edit loop
applyIn.description: You ask for an edit in the current file — you see the diff in the context of the surrounding code and accept or reject it with one button.

applyIn.title: Reviewing the agent's changes
applyIn.description: The agent proposes several edits — you review them visually across tabs instead of reading patches in the terminal.

applyIn.title: Working in your usual editor
applyIn.description: You never leave VS Code or JetBrains: the agent is at hand, not in a separate terminal window.

pitfalls: Using only the IDE extension and not knowing the CLI — you lose sessions, --resume, and plugins
Thinking these are two different products: it is really one agent with shared settings
Not setting up CLAUDE.md — the agent in the IDE works without project rules just as in the terminal
Accepting diffs without looking: the inline view is convenient, but the review is still yours
Expecting capabilities the IDE doesn't have: the extension adds a visual layer, but the logic is the same as in the terminal

exercises.question: How is the Claude Code IDE extension fundamentally different from the terminal version?
exercises.hint: Think about the agent and the presentation layer: what changes and what stays the same.

exercises.question: Why keep CLAUDE.md in the project if you work through the IDE extension?
exercises.hint: Where does the agent get project rules — does it depend on how it is launched?

exercises.question: In what situation is the terminal more convenient than the IDE extension?
exercises.hint: Recall sessions, --resume, and plugins.

s1.title: Why Claude Code in the IDE
s1.why: Before installing the extension, it is important to understand: this is not a new tool but the same agent in a different environment. Otherwise you will look for "IDE-version features" that don't exist.
instructions: Remember: the extension is [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] inside the editor, the same agent as in the terminal
The main benefit is visual context: edits arrive as inline diffs right in the code
Open tabs become context — the agent sees what you are working on
The accept/reject loop speeds up: fewer switches between terminal and editor
s1.validate: You can explain in one sentence why the IDE extension and the CLI are one agent, not two tools.
s1.tip: Don't treat the extension as a replacement for the terminal — it is a second entry point to the same agent.

s2.title: Installing the extension (VS Code / JetBrains)
s2.why: Without the installed extension the agent stays only in the terminal. Installing from the marketplace is the only supported way.
instructions: Open your editor's marketplace: VS Code Marketplace or JetBrains Marketplace
Find the Claude Code extension and install it
Restart the editor if it asks you to
Check that the Claude command appears (in VS Code — via Cmd+Shift+P)
s2.validate: The Claude command is available in the editor's command palette, and the extension is in the installed list.
s2.tip: If the extension isn't listed — make sure your editor version is recent enough; see [[node:cc-install|installing Claude Code]].

s3.title: Linking with terminal Claude Code
s3.why: The IDE extension and [[node:cc-terminal|terminal Claude Code]] share the same settings and project rules. If you don't realize this, you will start duplicating configuration.
instructions: Remember: the extension and the CLI use the same shared settings and account
Put CLAUDE.md in the project root — the agent reads it both in the IDE and in the terminal
Check that project rules from CLAUDE.md work the same in both modes
Don't configure the agent twice — there is one setup per project
s3.validate: A rule written in CLAUDE.md is honored by the agent both in the IDE and in the terminal.
s3.tip: CLAUDE.md is a single source of rules: change it once and the effect shows everywhere.

s4.title: Working with files and diffs in the IDE
s4.why: The main value of the IDE version is visual diffs. Being able to read and apply them is the core working loop.
instructions: Ask for an edit to the current file (in VS Code — Cmd+Shift+P, then Claude: ask in current file)
Wait for the edit — it arrives as an inline diff right in the editor
Review the change in the context of the surrounding code
Accept or reject the change with the button in the diff view
s4.validate: You triggered an edit, saw the inline diff, and consciously accepted or rejected it.
s4.tip: The inline view is convenient, but the review stays with you — don't accept diffs blindly.

s5.title: When the IDE beats the terminal and vice versa
s5.why: It is not either/or. The extension and the [[node:cc-terminal|terminal]] complement each other — the choice depends on the task.
instructions: Choose the IDE when the main work is in the editor and you need a fast edit loop with visual diffs
Choose the terminal when you need sessions, --resume, and plugins
Use the IDE's visual context to review several edits at once
Switch between them freely — it is one agent with shared settings
s5.validate: For a specific task you can justify where it is more convenient to do it — in the IDE or the terminal.
s5.tip: Knowing the CLI doesn't lose value after you install the extension — on the contrary, it remains the foundation.

s6.title: Common problems and a check
s6.why: If the extension doesn't respond or behaves oddly, the cause is usually settings or not realizing it is the same agent. A quick check saves time.
instructions: The extension doesn't see project rules — check that CLAUDE.md is in the root
The Claude command didn't appear — restart the editor and verify the extension is installed
You expect features that don't exist — remember the logic is the same as in the terminal, the IDE only adds a visual layer
Make a test edit to the current file and confirm the diff arrives and can be accepted
s6.validate: The extension is installed, sees CLAUDE.md, and a test edit goes through the diff view without errors.
s6.tip: If something behaves strangely in the IDE — repeat the same task in the terminal: that tells you whether the problem is in the extension or in the request itself.

af-llm-basics.title: What an LLM actually is — plain language
af-llm-basics.subtitle: Six steps from "magic" to "smart word-guesser" — without a single formula
af-llm-basics.whatItIs: An explainer course for anyone who wants to understand what really happens inside Claude, ChatGPT and the like. No math: just clear analogies — your phone's word suggestions, a car versus a horse, guessing. By the end you'll get why AI is brilliant at some things and fails at others.
af-llm-basics.approach: We start from the simplest fact — "the model predicts the next chunk of text" — and build understanding step by step: tokens, training and inference, hallucinations, temperature. Each step is one idea plus a check that it landed. Finally we tie it all to working with Claude in practice.
outcomes: Explain to a friend in a minute what an LLM is, without the word "neural network"
Understand why AI fumbles multiplication but writes great emails
Stop being surprised by hallucinations and learn to catch them
Grasp what "a bigger model" means and why it costs more
Start phrasing requests based on how the model actually works

applyIn.title: Realistic expectations at work
applyIn.description: Before handing AI a task, you'll judge whether it'll guess well or miss — and double-check numbers and facts in advance.

applyIn.title: Team debates and decisions
applyIn.description: When a colleague says "AI should be able to do this", you can calmly explain why it can or can't, with no mysticism.

applyIn.title: Choosing a model and its cost
applyIn.description: Knowing that bigger = smarter, pricier and slower, you'll consciously pick where you need a powerful model and where a light one is enough.

pitfalls: Thinking AI "knows" facts — it actually memorized word patterns, not a database of truths
Trusting a confident tone: the model sounds confident even when making things up
Expecting precise math from something that by nature guesses the next symbol
Assuming the model remembers yesterday's chat or fresh news — that isn't in its training data
Confusing "well written" with "true" — smooth text does not equal a verified fact

exercises.question: A friend asks: "Why did Claude confidently name a book that doesn't exist?" How would you explain it in one sentence using the idea of word prediction?
exercises.hint: Recall the phone suggesting words: the model picks a plausible continuation, it doesn't check whether the thing actually exists.

exercises.question: You need to sum 30 numbers in a report. Would you trust the model to do it "in its head" or give it a tool? Why?
exercises.hint: Think about whether this is guessing or calculating, and revisit the 47×83 multiplication step.

exercises.question: You asked the same question twice and got different answers. Is this a malfunction or normal? Which setting is responsible?
exercises.hint: Look at the variability step — there's a "knob" that controls how predictable answers are.

s1.title: What a language model is: predicting the next word
s1.why: This is the foundation of the whole course. Grasp one idea — "the model just guesses the next chunk of text" — and the rest falls into place, and unrealistic expectations disappear.
instructions: Recall how your phone suggests a word in a text: "I'll be..." becomes "home / late / there soon". The model does the same, just at a different scale.
Replace "word" with "next chunk of text": the model looks at all the prior text and picks the most plausible continuation.
Remember: it wasn't trained on your texts, but on a huge slice of the internet — Wikipedia, books, articles, forums.
Connect the names: Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini are all LLMs (large language models). Different models = different sizes and data.
Check out [[node:ai-fundamentals|the basics of working with AI]] to see how this idea fits the bigger picture.
s1.validate: You can explain to a neighbor in 20 seconds what an LLM does, without using the words "neural network", "algorithm" or "magic".
s1.tip: Keep this image in mind: AI isn't a horse that knows the way on its own — it's a car that you drive.

s2.title: Tokens: why the model "doesn't count letters"
s2.why: The model sees text not as letters and words, but as "tokens" — chunks. This explains the oddities: why it gets confused counting letters in a word, or mangles long numbers.
instructions: Imagine the text is cut into pieces: sometimes a whole word, sometimes part of a word, sometimes a symbol. Such a piece is called a token.
Understand the consequence: the model works with chunks, not individual letters — so "how many r's are in the word…" is unnatural for it.
Notice that digits are also split into chunks, which is why the model easily distorts long numbers.
Tie it to money: the cost of using AI is counted exactly in tokens — the longer the text, the more expensive.
To go deeper into how text turns into meaning-numbers, look at [[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]].
s2.validate: You can explain why "count the letters" is a poor task for the model, drawing on the idea of tokens.
s2.tip: If you need exact letters or digits — ask the model to spell out one symbol at a time, or give it a tool.

s3.title: Training versus inference — in plain words
s3.why: People mix up two different moments: when the model "learned" and when it "answers you". Separate them, and you'll see why it doesn't know fresh news and doesn't remember your conversation forever.
instructions: Training is like long study in the past: the model "read" a giant text once and memorized patterns. That ended before you started talking to it.
Inference is the moment you ask a question and it answers right now, applying what it learned. It isn't learning anything new in that moment.
Conclude: anything that happened after training (yesterday's news, your report) the model doesn't know unless you provide it in the request.
Understand memory: within a single conversation it remembers context, but between different chats nothing is saved by default.
Cross-check with [[node:cap-limitations|capabilities and limitations]] to see Claude's concrete boundaries.
s3.validate: You can explain the difference between "the model learned" and "the model answers", and why this means it doesn't know yesterday's events.
s3.tip: Need fresh data or your files — paste them right into the request; the model won't pull them out of thin air.

s4.title: Why the model confidently makes mistakes (hallucinations)
s4.why: The most dangerous beginner trap is trusting a confident tone. The model always sounds confident, even when it's making things up. Understanding the mechanics means learning not to fall for it.
instructions: Recall step 1: the model picks a plausible continuation. "Plausible" doesn't mean "true".
Name the phenomenon: when the model confidently produces an invented fact, book, quote or number — that's a "hallucination".
Understand why it's confident: the model has no built-in "I'm not sure" sensor — smooth text is generated the same way for truth and for fiction.
Build a habit: facts, numbers, dates, names, links — always double-check against the original source.
Separate style from truth: beautiful and fluent does not equal correct.
s4.validate: You can give one example where the model might confidently lie, and say how you would verify it.
s4.tip: Ask the model to show sources or admit "not sure" — but still verify critical facts yourself.

s5.title: Temperature: where the variability of an answer comes from
s5.why: Sometimes the same question yields different answers — this isn't a bug. A simple setting controls "how predictable answers are". Understanding it, you control the stability of the result.
instructions: Picture a "creativity knob" (it's called temperature): low — the model picks the most likely continuation, answers are similar and predictable.
Turn the knob higher — the model more often takes less obvious options, answers become more varied and unexpected.
Choose per task: for facts, code and instructions you want low temperature; for ideas, copy and brainstorming — higher.
Accept it as normal: with high variability two identical requests will give different answers — that's expected, not a malfunction.
Remember: temperature doesn't make the model "smarter" or "more honest" — it only changes how boldly the model strays from the most likely option.
s5.validate: You can say which temperature to pick for "compute by the instruction" and for "come up with 10 names", and why.
s5.tip: Getting randomness where you need stability — lower the variability and phrase the request more strictly.

s6.title: What this changes in working with Claude + comprehension check
s6.why: Here all five ideas come together into practice. From "AI should know everything" you move to "I understand where it's strong and where to hedge" — and start using Claude deliberately.
instructions: Connect it all: Claude is a smart text-guesser, trained in the past, seeing tokens, sometimes hallucinating, with adjustable variability.
Apply the rule: for exact numbers and calculations, give it a tool or check yourself rather than trusting it "in its head".
Give context: paste fresh data, files and facts right into the request — the model doesn't know what isn't in its training or your message.
Test yourself with a question: why can Claude confidently get a simple fact wrong? (the answer is in steps 1 and 4).
Lock in the route: return to [[node:ai-fundamentals|the basics of working with AI]] and keep [[node:cap-limitations|capabilities and limitations]] handy.
s6.validate: You can explain three things without prompts: why AI errs at math, why it sounds confident while making things up, and why it sometimes answers differently.
s6.tip: Before an important task, ask yourself one question: "is this guessing or calculation/fact?" — and decide whether you need a check or a tool.

af-embeddings.title: Embeddings — how AI understands "by meaning"
af-embeddings.subtitle: How text turns into numbers of meaning, and why close numbers mean close meaning
af-embeddings.whatItIs: An embedding turns a word, phrase, or document into a set of numbers (a vector). Things with similar meaning get similar numbers. That lets AI search "by meaning" instead of by exact word match: "forgot my password" and "how to reset my password" end up close together.
af-embeddings.approach: We move from feel to practice: first an intuition for what a vector of meaning is, then why closeness of numbers equals closeness of meaning, then why business needs it, how it ties to [[node:af-vector-db|vector DBs]] and [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]], where it shows up in real life, and where it breaks. No formulas, no math.
outcomes: Explain in plain words what an embedding is and why text is turned into numbers
Understand why "closeness of vectors" means "closeness of meaning"
Name three real tasks embeddings solve: search, recommendations, clustering
See embeddings, vector DBs, and RAG as one connected chain
Notice the limits: where embeddings get it wrong and why

applyIn.title: Knowledge base search
applyIn.description: An employee types "email not arriving" while the FAQ says "email delivery failures". Embeddings still find the right article despite the different words.

applyIn.title: Similar-item recommendations
applyIn.description: "Similar products", "similar docs", "customers like this one" — all of it is finding the nearest vectors to a chosen one.

applyIn.title: Grouping incoming requests
applyIn.description: Thousands of support tickets sort themselves into topics (clusters) by meaning, with no manual labeling.

pitfalls: Thinking embeddings "understand meaning like a human" — they catch pattern similarity, not understanding
Using embeddings from an old, cheap model — bad numbers produce bad matches
Expecting perfection on rare terms and in-house company slang — the model often misses there
Confusing embeddings with plain keyword search — they are different mechanisms
Assuming embeddings give the answer by themselves — they only find similar items; RAG builds the answer on top

exercises.question: Why does exact-word search miss the article "WiFi problems at home" for the query "internet not working", while embedding search finds it?
exercises.hint: Think about what plain search compares (letters/words) versus what embeddings compare (closeness of number sets = closeness of meaning).

exercises.question: Name one task each for search, recommendations, and clustering. What do they share at the core?
exercises.hint: In all three, things are turned into vectors, and then it all comes down to "how close are these number sets".

exercises.question: Where are embeddings more likely to fail: on the phrase "forgot my password" or on an internal codename like "Project Phoenix-7"? Why?
exercises.hint: The model is strong on common, general phrasing and weak on rare terms and in-house slang it has barely seen.

s1.title: What an embedding is: text becomes a vector of meaning
s1.why: Without the intuition "a word becomes numbers", everything else sounds like magic. This step removes the magic.
instructions: Picture AI assigning a set of numbers to each word or phrase — that set is the vector (embedding)
The core rule: things with similar meaning get similar numbers
Take the pair "cat" and "kitten" — their number sets are close; "cat" and "accounting" — far apart
Say it out loud: "text becomes coordinates of meaning", no formulas needed
s1.validate: You can say in your own words that an embedding is a set of numbers, and that similar things get similar numbers.
s1.tip: Don't try to read the numbers themselves — all that matters is that close meanings give close sets.

s2.title: Closeness of meaning = closeness of vectors
s2.why: This is the heart of the idea: all the "meaning magic" reduces to checking how close two number sets are.
instructions: Picture points on a map: nearby points = phrases close in meaning
"Forgot my password, help" and "how to reset my password" — two points sitting next to each other
"Forgot my password" and "borscht recipe" — two points far apart
AI doesn't "think" — it measures the distance between points and takes the nearest ones
Remember: searching by meaning = finding the nearest points
s2.validate: You can explain why "close vectors" and "close meaning" are the same thing in practice.
s2.tip: A map of cities is a solid analogy: neighboring cities are close, distant ones are not. Phrases work the same way.

s3.title: Why it matters: search, recommendations, clustering
s3.why: The idea becomes valuable once you see three real tasks that are hard to solve well without embeddings.
instructions: Search by meaning: a user's query finds the right article even when the words differ
Recommendations: "similar products / docs / customers" is finding the nearest vectors
Clustering: thousands of requests group themselves into topics by closeness of meaning
Notice the common thread: all three reduce to closeness of number sets
s3.validate: You can name three tasks and explain that the same vector comparison sits at the core of all of them.
s3.tip: If a task sounds like "find similar by meaning", embeddings are almost certainly under the hood.

s4.title: The link with vector DBs and RAG
s4.why: Embeddings rarely work alone — they're part of a chain. Without this picture it's easy to get lost in the terms.
instructions: Embeddings produce numbers — those numbers need to be stored and searched for nearest matches
That's the job of [[node:af-vector-db|vector DBs]]: storage tuned for finding close vectors
On top of that runs [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]]: it finds the relevant chunks and feeds them to the AI for the answer
Assemble the chain: text, then embedding, then vector DB, then RAG finds and answers
All of this is part of [[node:ai-fundamentals|AI fundamentals]], not separate exotica
s4.validate: You can sketch the four-link chain and state what each link is responsible for.
s4.tip: Embeddings are "how to compare", the vector DB is "where to store and search", RAG is "how to use it in the answer".

s5.title: Where it shows up in real life
s5.why: Once you recognize embeddings in products you already use, the idea stops being abstract.
instructions: Google Photos finds "all the cats" with no labels — that's embeddings for photos
Spotify suggests "similar songs" — closeness of track vectors
Support: the query "email not arriving" finds the FAQ "email delivery failures"
Corporate search: a Slack bot answers "forgot my password" by finding the "Password reset" article
Note: Anthropic doesn't ship its own embeddings — for hybrid setups people use Voyage AI, OpenAI text-embedding-3, or open-source models
s5.validate: You can name at least two familiar products and explain that embeddings power them.
s5.tip: Any "similar items" or "smart search" feature in an app is a reason to suspect embeddings.

s6.title: Limits, misunderstandings, and a check
s6.why: Without knowing the limits you'll trust embeddings where they fail and blame a "dumb AI".
instructions: Embeddings catch pattern similarity — they don't understand meaning like a human
On rare terms and in-house company slang, matches are often poor
Quality depends heavily on the model: an old cheap model = bad matches
Solid options today — OpenAI text-embedding-3, Cohere embed, natively in Claude
Check yourself: explain why "found something similar" isn't the same as "found the right thing"
s6.validate: You can name two situations where embeddings get it wrong, and why the choice of model matters.
s6.tip: If search keeps missing on your terms, check the embedding model first, not the search itself.

af-vector-db.title: Vector Database — a library for meanings
af-vector-db.subtitle: Where AI stores knowledge and finds what you need by meaning, not by words
af-vector-db.whatItIs: A vector database stores not texts but their "meaning fingerprints" ([[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]] — number sets). Its superpower: in milliseconds, find among millions of records the ones closest in meaning to a query. Like a library where books are shelved by topic, not alphabetically: grab one on gardening and ten more on gardening sit right beside it.
af-vector-db.approach: We move from "why does it even exist" to how data gets in, how similarity search works, the role it plays in [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]], which solutions exist, and where the limits are. All conceptual, no math and no formulas — just the understanding you need to decide "need it / don't need it".
outcomes: Explain in plain words why a vector database matters and how it differs from a regular one
Understand how data turns into [[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]] and lands in storage
Grasp the principle of similarity search (nearest neighbor) without math
See where the database sits inside a [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]] system
Decide whether you need a vector database and which solution to pick

applyIn.title: Enterprise knowledge search
applyIn.description: Thousands of company documents are searched by meaning: an employee asks in their own words, and the system finds what's relevant even when the exact words aren't in the text.

applyIn.title: Knowledge-base chatbot (RAG)
applyIn.description: The bot first finds the right fragments in the vector database, then hands them to Claude — the answer rests on your data, not the model's guesses.

applyIn.title: Similar-item recommendations
applyIn.description: Similar products, articles, or customers are found through closeness in meaning rather than manual tags and categories.

pitfalls: Grabbing an expensive managed service when pgvector on your existing Postgres would do
Putting a vector database on 50 documents — it's overkill, everything fits in app memory
Thinking the database itself "understands" meaning — meaning comes from embeddings, the database just finds nearest matches fast
Expecting an exact answer from the database — it returns similar items; the final answer is shaped by the model in [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]]
Picking a solution "for fashion" rather than for real scale and speed requirements

exercises.question: How does search in a vector database differ from keyword search in a regular one?
exercises.hint: Think about the query "how to arrange a trip abroad" and a document with the words "business trip to Germany" — do the words match?

exercises.question: You have 40 documents and rare queries. Do you need a vector database?
exercises.hint: Recall the step on limits: at what volume does the database actually start to pay off.

exercises.question: Where does the vector database sit in the RAG chain: before the model or after?
exercises.hint: First we find relevant fragments, then we hand them to the model — who calls whom?

s1.title: Why a vector database is needed
s1.why: Without understanding the purpose it's easy to make a wrong call — putting a heavy tool where it isn't needed, or failing to keep up with growth.
instructions: Picture 50,000 company documents you need to search by meaning, not by exact words.
A regular database (Postgres / MySQL) scans every record — that's seconds per query.
A vector database returns "the 10 closest in meaning" in tens of milliseconds.
Remember the key idea: it finds similar, not an exact word match.
s1.validate: You can state in one sentence what problem a vector database solves and why a regular one isn't enough.
s1.tip: Keep the library image in mind: books shelved by topic — similar ones always nearby.

s2.title: How data gets in
s2.why: The database is useless until meaning fingerprints are loaded into it. Understanding this step removes the magic.
instructions: Each document or fragment is run through a model and turned into an [[node:af-embeddings|embedding]] — a number set that encodes meaning.
That number set is stored in the vector database along with a link to the source text.
Large documents are split into chunks beforehand — so search can find the specific relevant fragment.
Once loaded, the database is ready: meanings sit there waiting for a query.
s2.validate: You can describe the path "text, then number set, then record in the database" in your own words.
s2.tip: A separate model creates the embeddings — the database only stores and searches.

s3.title: How similarity search works
s3.why: This is the heart of a vector database. Grasp the principle and it stops being a black box.
instructions: The user's query is also turned into a number set — the same kind of [[node:af-embeddings|embedding]].
The database compares this set against all the stored ones and looks for the closest in meaning.
This is nearest neighbor — "closest neighbors": the closer the number sets, the closer the meaning.
The response brings back not one but several most-similar fragments (e.g. the top 5).
s3.validate: You can explain "nearest neighbors" without a single formula, using a query-and-documents example.
s3.tip: The database doesn't understand text — it only measures how close the meaning fingerprints are.

s4.title: The role in RAG
s4.why: A vector database rarely works alone — most often it's part of [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]]. Without that context its value is incomplete.
instructions: In [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]], relevant fragments are first found for the question — that's the vector database's job.
The found fragments are passed to the model as context along with the question.
The model answers based on your data, not on general knowledge from training.
So the database handles "find the right thing", and the model handles "phrase the answer".
s4.validate: You can order the RAG steps: question, then search in the database, then pass to model, then answer.
s4.tip: The database finds, the model phrases — different roles, don't mix them up.

s5.title: Popular solutions and when it's needed
s5.why: The choice of tool strongly affects cost and complexity. Better to decide deliberately than by fashion.
instructions: Remember the main names: Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, Chroma, and pgvector (an extension for Postgres).
If the team already has Postgres — pgvector adds vector search simply and cheaply.
Expensive managed services are justified at very large volumes or with strict speed requirements.
It's worth adding a database when you have more than ~1,000 documents or need semantic search over a large base.
s5.validate: You can name 3-4 solutions and say when pgvector is enough and when a managed service is needed.
s5.tip: With Claude, Pinecone, Qdrant, and pgvector come up often — but choose by scale and compliance, not by model compatibility.

s6.title: Limits, mistakes, and a check
s6.why: Understanding the limits saves you from wasted spend and inflated expectations — it's the final filter before deciding.
instructions: At small volumes (dozens of documents) the database isn't needed — keep everything in app memory.
Don't expect a ready answer from the database: it returns similar items; the model shapes the answer.
Don't overpay for a managed solution if pgvector covers your scale.
Remember: search quality depends on embedding quality — garbage in, garbage out.
s6.validate: You can honestly answer "do I need a vector database right now, and which one" with a justification.
s6.tip: First measure scale and query frequency — then pick the tool, not the other way around.

af-rag-basics.title: RAG: how AI answers from your documents
af-rag-basics.subtitle: From question to sourced answer — in 6 steps
af-rag-basics.whatItIs: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is a way to make AI answer not from its head, but from your documents. The AI first finds relevant chunks in your knowledge base, reads them, and only then forms an answer. Like a cheat-sheet at an exam: open the right section first, then answer. For how it's built — [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG architecture]].
af-rag-basics.approach: We go from "why" to "how": first understand the problem RAG solves, then break the pipeline into parts (chunking, then [[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]], then [[node:af-vector-db|vector DB]], then search, then answer), then what drives quality, why RAG beats simply uploading a file, common mistakes, and where to start. Conceptual but practical: every step can be touched in [[node:ai-fundamentals|AI fundamentals]].
outcomes: Explain in plain words what RAG is and why it's needed
Break down the RAG pipeline step by step: chunking, embeddings, vector DB, search, answer
Understand what drives answer quality — chunking and relevance
Tell when you need RAG versus when just uploading a file to chat is enough
Learn the common mistakes and how to check that the system works

applyIn.title: Customer support
applyIn.description: AI answers questions from your knowledge base with a source citation — the customer sees where the answer came from.

applyIn.title: Internal company knowledge
applyIn.description: Employees ask about policies, HR rules, product docs — AI finds and answers from up-to-date documents.

applyIn.title: Personal knowledge archive
applyIn.description: Notes, articles, conversation history — AI searches by meaning and gives an answer instead of making you scroll through everything.

pitfalls: "Just turn on RAG and it works" — naive RAG answers correctly only about half the time, tuning is required
Garbage in: old drafts, duplicates, contradicting versions — AI finds garbage and answers garbage
Bad chunking: chunks too big or cut a thought in half — search finds the wrong pieces
No relevance check: the system returns the first chunks it finds, even off-topic ones
Confusing RAG with fine-tuning — RAG changes nothing in the model, it just feeds in the right documents

exercises.question: Using one example from your work, frame a question that AI without RAG would answer with "I don't know" or invent, but with RAG would answer correctly.
exercises.hint: Pick a question whose answer lives in one of your documents but definitely not in general internet knowledge.

exercises.question: Explain in your own words why splitting documents into chunks affects answer quality.
exercises.hint: Think about what happens if an important thought is cut right in the middle between two chunks.

exercises.question: Decide: for "answer one question about one PDF", do you need RAG or is uploading the file to chat enough? Justify it.
exercises.hint: Compare document volume and query frequency — RAG pays off when there are many documents and repeated questions.

s1.title: Why RAG is needed at all
s1.why: Without understanding "why", RAG looks like needless complexity. AI on its own doesn't know your documents: ask about your refund policy and it'll either say "I don't know" or invent something plausible (hallucination). RAG gives three things: answers from your data, freshness (the base updates without retraining the model), and fewer hallucinations — with a source citation.
instructions: Ask the AI a question whose answer lives only in your documents (e.g. an internal policy)
Notice the reaction: "I don't know" or a plausible invention — that's the problem RAG solves
State the three benefits of RAG: answers from your data, freshness, fewer hallucinations
Write down 2-3 real questions from your work where RAG would help
s1.validate: You can name a concrete question AI answers badly without RAG and explain why RAG would fix it.
s1.tip: RAG is the most common way AI is used in companies. Not "AI writes creative copy" but "AI answers from our knowledge base".

s2.title: How the RAG pipeline works
s2.why: RAG sounds complex, but it's just five steps in a row. Knowing the pipeline, you see where things can break and you speak the same language as your team.
instructions: Step 1 — chunking: documents are split into right-sized pieces (chunks)
Step 2 — each chunk is turned into [[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]] (a set of numbers capturing meaning)
Step 3 — those numbers go into a [[node:af-vector-db|vector DB]] so you can search by meaning
Step 4 — search: the question is also turned into numbers, the system finds chunks close in meaning
Step 5 — answer: the found chunks + the question go to the AI, which forms an answer with a citation
s2.validate: You can list the five pipeline steps from memory and explain what each one does.
s2.tip: Key idea: the AI doesn't "remember" your documents — it freshly searches for the right chunks and reads them before every answer.

s3.title: What drives quality
s3.why: Two RAGs on the same documents can give different answers. Quality comes down to two things: how documents are chunked, and how accurately the system finds relevant pieces.
instructions: Chunking: chunks shouldn't be too big (details drown) or too small (context is lost)
Make sure splitting doesn't cut a thought in half — split by paragraphs or sections
Relevance: verify the system finds exactly the chunks that relate to the question
Add metadata (section, date, source) — it helps filter and rank what's found
In production add re-ranking: reordering the found chunks by accuracy
s3.validate: You can explain why chunks that are too big and too small both hurt quality.
s3.tip: Naive RAG (grab top 3 chunks, then hand to AI) works at 50%. Tuning chunking and relevance raises it to 80-90%.

s4.title: RAG vs just uploading a file to chat
s4.why: Often you don't need RAG — uploading a file to chat is enough. Knowing the boundary keeps you from building a complex system where one action would do.
instructions: Uploading a file to chat: fast and simple, but the AI only sees what fits in one window
RAG: searches a large document base and feeds in only the relevant chunks
Rule: one or two documents and a one-off question — uploading to chat is enough
Rule: many documents, repeated questions, source citations needed — you need RAG
In Claude you can start without a separate service: [[node:cap-files|Files]] for documents, and full RAG for a large base
s4.validate: For two of your tasks you can say where uploading a file suffices and where RAG is needed, and justify the choice.
s4.tip: Don't build RAG for the sake of RAG. If uploading one PDF solves it, do that — it's cheaper and faster.

s5.title: Common mistakes and how to check
s5.why: Most RAG failures aren't about the model — they're about garbage in and bad chunking. Knowing the common mistakes saves weeks of debugging.
instructions: Mistake "garbage in": old drafts, duplicates, contradictions in the base, so AI answers garbage
Mistake "bad chunks": chunks cut a thought or are too large, so search finds the wrong pieces
Check 1: ask 10 real questions and compare answers against what the documents actually say
Check 2: for each answer, look at which chunks the system found — are they on topic?
Cleanliness beats quantity: remove duplicates and stale content before adding more
s5.validate: You've run at least a few test questions and can say where the system errs and why.
s5.tip: If an answer is bad, look first at which chunks were found. In 8 of 10 cases the problem is the retrieved chunks, not the model.

s6.title: Where to start
s6.why: Understanding without action is quickly forgotten. A small working RAG over 5-10 documents teaches more than reading ten articles.
instructions: Gather 5-10 clean, current documents on one topic — no duplicates or drafts
Start simple: upload them via [[node:cap-files|Files]] and ask questions — that's already a mini-RAG
When documents pile up, move to the full pipeline from step 2
Lock in the basics: go through [[node:ai-fundamentals|AI fundamentals]] to understand how the model uses what it finds
Keep a list of questions the system answers badly — that's your improvement plan
s6.validate: You have a working mini-system: you ask a question about your documents and get an answer from them, not from general knowledge.
s6.tip: Start with one narrow topic and 5-10 documents. Expand once you see the basic scenario works.

af-memory-systems.title: AI memory — why it "forgets"
af-memory-systems.subtitle: Context window, memory types, and tricks against AI "amnesia"
af-memory-systems.whatItIs: An AI model has no built-in long-term memory: it only works with what is right now "in front of it" — in the context window. As soon as a conversation ends or the window overflows, everything is forgotten. This course explains why it works this way, what memory types AI systems have, and how to make AI "remember" what matters.
af-memory-systems.approach: We go from cause to solution. First we unpack why the model "forgets" at all and what the context window is in plain words. Then we look at memory types — session, long-term, external. Then how this is implemented in Claude through Memory and projects. And finally — practical tricks and the honest limits of what's possible.
outcomes: Understand why AI has no built-in long-term memory and what "forgot" means
Explain the context window in plain words, no jargon
Distinguish memory types: session, long-term, external
Know how Claude remembers context via Memory and projects
Apply anti-forgetting tricks: summaries, /compact, external documents

applyIn.title: Long work sessions
applyIn.description: When you work with AI on one task for hours and it starts "losing the thread" — you understand the cause and apply summaries and /compact.

applyIn.title: Projects that accumulate context
applyIn.description: When you need AI to remember agreements and work style across conversations — you use projects and Memory.

applyIn.title: Working with large documents
applyIn.description: When there are more documents than fit in the window — you connect external memory via RAG instead of pasting everything into the chat.

pitfalls: Thinking AI "remembers" past conversations on its own — without projects or Memory it starts from scratch every time
Believing it's enough to "just expand the context window" — a bigger window is more expensive, slower, and AI gets lost in the middle
Pasting all the long context into every request instead of a short summary
Not checking what AI actually "remembers" — and being surprised when it relies on stale information
Confusing session memory with long-term: what AI knew in one chat doesn't carry into a new one automatically

exercises.question: You've been discussing a big project with AI for three hours, and it starts forgetting early details. Why does this happen and what do you do?
exercises.hint: Recall the context window and its limited size. Think about summaries and /compact.

exercises.question: You need AI to remember your work-style preferences in every new conversation. Which memory type is needed and how do you do it in Claude?
exercises.hint: This isn't single-session memory. Check the step about Memory and projects.

exercises.question: You have 500 pages of documentation, and it doesn't fit in the window. How do you give AI access to the relevant pieces?
exercises.hint: External memory. Recall the approach where AI searches for the needed fragment rather than holding everything in view.

s1.title: Why the model "forgets"
s1.why: The core misunderstanding: people expect AI to remember like a human. In reality the model has no built-in long-term memory — and that's not a breakage, it's how it works.
instructions: Remember a simple truth: an AI model works only with what was handed to it in this very request. It has no "memory" of yesterday's conversation on its own.
Everything AI "sees" fits into a limited space — the context window. When it fills up, old content gets pushed out by new.
When a conversation closes, the model saves it nowhere. A new chat is a blank slate.
Compare with yourself: you don't hold every word of last week in your head — you remember the gist, the rest is written down somewhere. Without special add-ons AI doesn't even have that.

Remember the takeaway: "AI forgot" almost always means "the needed info didn't make it into the context window or isn't stored externally". More on how AI works — [[node:ai-fundamentals|AI fundamentals]].
s1.validate: You can explain in one sentence why a new AI chat doesn't remember the previous conversation.
s1.tip: "Forgot" isn't about AI's ill will. It's always about where the information is right now: in the window, outside, or nowhere.

s2.title: The context window in plain words
s2.why: The context window is the central concept of the whole memory topic. Without it you can't understand why AI forgets or how to deal with it.
instructions: Picture a desk of limited size. AI can only look at what's lying on that desk right now — that's the context window.
Everything goes on the desk: your question, past messages of this chat, attached documents, instructions. Together they take up space.
When the desk overflows, something has to be removed — usually the oldest. That's why early details "drop out" in a long conversation.
The window is big, but not infinite. And the more is in it, the more expensive the request and the easier it is for AI to "get lost in the middle" — miss what matters amid the noise.
Remember: the goal isn't to "cram the window full" but to put only what's needed for the current task on the desk.
s2.validate: You can explain the context window via the desk metaphor and say what happens when it overflows.
s2.tip: More context ≠ better. A clean, focused "desk" works more accurately than a cluttered one.

s3.title: Types of memory in AI systems
s3.why: "AI memory" isn't one thing. It's several different mechanisms for different jobs. Confusing them is the main cause of problems.
instructions: Session memory: what AI remembers within one conversation, as long as it all fits in the context window. Close the chat — session memory is gone.
Long-term memory: what is specifically saved and pulled into new conversations — for example your preferences or facts about the project.
External memory: a large base of documents outside, from which AI fetches the needed piece on request rather than holding it all in view. That's what [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]] does.
Selection rule: the current conversation — session memory; durable facts about you — long-term; huge documents — external.
Remember: each type solves its own job. Trying to stuff everything into one is the path to overpaying and clutter.
s3.validate: You can name the three memory types and give an example for each of when it fits.
s3.tip: If you ask yourself "should AI remember this always or only in this chat?" — you're already choosing between long-term and session memory.

s4.title: How Claude remembers context
s4.why: Theory becomes useful when you see it in a concrete tool. Claude has built-in ways to give AI long-term and project memory.
instructions: Memory: Claude can save durable facts about you and your work and pull them into new conversations — that's long-term memory. More — [[node:cap-memory|Memory]].
Projects: inside a project Claude keeps shared context and files available across all chats of that project. So conversations stop starting from scratch.
The difference matters: session memory lives in one chat; Memory and projects carry knowledge between chats.
What goes where: personal preferences and stable facts — into Memory; documents and materials of specific work — into project files.
Remember: you decide what Claude should remember long-term. It doesn't happen magically — you set it up.
s4.validate: You can explain the difference between what Claude remembers in one chat and what carries over via Memory and projects.
s4.tip: If you catch yourself repeating the same thing to Claude in every chat — that's a signal to move it into Memory or a project.

s5.title: Tricks against "forgetting"
s5.why: Knowing the cause, you can act. A few simple tricks greatly reduce the "AI forgot everything" effect in real work.
instructions: Summary: when a conversation is long, ask AI to briefly summarize the agreements. A short summary takes little space and keeps the essence.
/compact: in a long session this command compresses the past conversation, freeing space in the window without losing the main points.
External documents: keep important materials in project files or a knowledge base rather than pasting them as a wall into every chat.
Explicit context up front: if a task needs facts, give them at the start of the request — don't rely on AI "remembering" from last time.
Remember the combo: short summary + external documents + Memory cover most "forgetting" problems.
s5.validate: You can name at least three tricks and say which problem each solves.
s5.tip: Before closing an important session, ask for a short summary of decisions — that's your "episodic memory" for next time.

s6.title: Limits and verification
s6.why: To avoid disappointment, it's important to understand the honest limits of AI memory and to be able to check that it really "remembers".
instructions: Remember the limit: even a large context window is finite, and long-term memory holds only what you saved — not everything.
Don't rely on "AI surely remembers". If a fact is critical — give it explicitly or check that it's in Memory or the project.
Verification: ask AI what it remembers about the task. If the answer is inaccurate — the needed context isn't on the "desk" and must be added.
Stale-data danger: long-term memory can hold old facts. Periodically check that AI relies on what's current.

Put it together: the cause of "forgetting" is the context window; the solution is the right memory type (session, long-term via [[node:cap-memory|Memory]], external via [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]]) plus tricks.
s6.validate: You can check what exactly AI remembers about a task and understand where the boundary of its memory lies.
s6.tip: A simple test: ask "what do you remember about my project?". The answer shows what's really in memory versus what you only thought you saved.

af-multimodal.title: Multimodal AI — a model that sees and hears
af-multimodal.subtitle: How AI works not only with text but with images too, and where its limits are
af-multimodal.whatItIs: Ordinary AI used to work only with text. Multimodal AI understands several data types at once in a single request: text together with images (as well as audio and video). You can show the model a screenshot, a photo, a diagram — and it describes what it sees and answers your question.
af-multimodal.approach: We move from concept to practice: first what "multimodality" even means, then how the model "sees" an image in plain terms. Next, what it does well versus poorly, and how to use it in Claude via [[node:cap-vision|Vision]] and [[node:cap-input-modalities|input modalities]]. Finally, the limits and how to verify the result. Conceptual, no code.
outcomes: You understand what "multimodality" means: text and images in one request
You can explain in plain terms how the model "sees" an image
You know which visual tasks AI handles well and which it handles poorly
You can apply it in Claude: show a screenshot, photo, or diagram and ask a question
You see the limits of the technology and verify the answer instead of trusting blindly

applyIn.title: Parsing screenshots and errors
applyIn.description: Show a screenshot of an error or interface and ask "what's wrong here?" instead of retyping the text by hand.

applyIn.title: Reading documents and receipts
applyIn.description: A photo of an invoice, receipt, or table — AI recognizes amounts and dates and transfers the data, saving manual work.

applyIn.title: Understanding diagrams and mockups
applyIn.description: Show a chart from a report or a design mockup — AI describes the trend or helps build a page from the picture.

pitfalls: Thinking "AI sees everything like a human" — in reality there are weak spots
Asking it to read tiny or handwritten text — specialized OCR does this better
Expecting pixel precision: counting objects in a photo exactly is something the model does worse
Loading a busy diagram with a dozen lines and trusting the answer without checking
Using multimodality where the task is purely textual — that's needless overhead

exercises.question: How does multimodal AI differ from ordinary text AI — in one sentence?
exercises.hint: It's about data types: text vs. "text + images and other types in one request".

exercises.question: Name two tasks where the model "sees" well, and two where it does poorly.
exercises.hint: Well: objects in photos, printed text. Poorly: handwriting, exact counting, an overloaded chart.

exercises.question: Someone sent you an error screenshot. How does multimodality save time versus the "old way"?
exercises.hint: No need to retype the error text by hand — you drop in the image and ask right away.

s1.title: What "multimodality" means
s1.why: Without this concept it's easy to confuse multimodal AI with ordinary AI or expect too much. A modality is a data type: text, image, audio, video.
instructions: Remember the simple definition: a "modality" = a data type. Text is one modality, an image is another.
Multimodal AI takes several types at once: for example, the text of your question together with an attached image.
Compare: with ordinary AI you write "translate this article". With multimodal AI you attach a screenshot and write "what's wrong here?".
Recall the related concept in Atlas — [[node:ai-fundamentals|AI fundamentals]] — to see where this topic fits.
s1.validate: You can say in your own words that multimodality is working with text and images (and other types) in a single request.
s1.tip: The word "modality" sounds complex, but it just means a "channel of perception": like a human has sight and hearing.

s2.title: How the model "sees" an image
s2.why: Understanding the mechanics in plain terms removes the magic and helps you predict where the model will fail.
instructions: Imagine the model doesn't "look with eyes" but turns the picture into a set of numbers — features of shape, color, and text in it.
From these features it looks for patterns it was trained on: "this looks like a button", "this is a line of code", "this is a chart".
Text and image land in one shared "understanding" — that's why you can ask about the image in words.
Remember the key point: this is pattern recognition, not exact "reading of pixels".
s2.validate: You can explain that the model converts the picture into features and matches them against what it learned, rather than "seeing" like a human.
s2.tip: Analogy: the model "recognizes" the familiar in a picture rather than measuring it with a ruler.

s3.title: What it does well
s3.why: Knowing the strengths lets you apply AI right where it genuinely saves time.
instructions: Describing an image: "what's in this picture?" — the model confidently lists objects and the scene.
Parsing a screenshot: an interface, an error message, a long stack trace — it finds where the problem is.
Diagrams and charts of medium complexity: it describes the trend and explains what an axis shows.
Printed text in a photo: it recognizes amounts on a receipt, headings, captions.
Try it yourself: show AI a screenshot of any screen and ask it to describe what's visible.
s3.validate: You can name at least three tasks where the model "sees" reliably: description, parsing a screenshot, reading printed text.
s3.tip: The clearer and larger the image, the more accurate the answer — send a good-quality screenshot.

s4.title: What it does poorly
s4.why: Weak spots are a source of silent errors. If you don't know them, it's easy to trust a wrong answer.
instructions: Tiny text: the model may "guess" blurry characters instead of reading them exactly.
Handwritten text: specialized OCR tools handle it better.
Exact counting: "how many people are in the photo?" is a frequent source of errors.
Overloaded diagrams with a dozen lines and labels — high risk of mixing things up.
Pixel precision (coordinates, exact colors) — not a strong point.
s4.validate: You can name at least three cases where the model shouldn't be trusted without checking: tiny/handwritten text, exact counting, complex charts.
s4.tip: If the task falls into a weak zone — don't drop AI entirely, but always double-check the answer.

s5.title: How to use it in Claude
s5.why: Theory without practice is useless. In Claude, multimodality is available right in the chat.
instructions: Attach an image to your message — a screenshot, photo, diagram — and ask your question in words.
In Claude this works through the [[node:cap-vision|Vision]] capability — the model "sees" the attached picture.
The input data types themselves are described as [[node:cap-input-modalities|input modalities]]: exactly what the model can accept as input.
Phrase the question specifically: not "look at the picture" but "find the line with the error" or "extract the amount and date".
Start simple: drop in an error screenshot and ask it to explain what the problem is.
s5.validate: You attached an image in Claude, asked a specific question, and got a meaningful answer about the picture.
s5.tip: One precise question about a picture beats a vague "what do you think?" — the model answers to the request.

s6.title: Limits and verification
s6.why: Mature use = knowing the limit of the technology and building in a check, rather than trusting the answer blindly.
instructions: Remember the main mistake: "multimodal AI sees everything like a human" — that's not true.
Before trusting it, ask yourself: is the task in a strong zone (description, printed text) or a weak one (tiny font, exact counting)?
For important data (amounts, numbers) always check the answer against the original with your own eyes.
Test on your own task types — generic promises that "AI can do everything" don't replace verification.
If the answer is critical — ask the model to show exactly what in the picture it relies on.
s6.validate: You have a habit: before trusting an answer, identify the zone (strong/weak) and re-check important numbers against the original.
s6.tip: The rule is simple: AI speeds you up, but keep the final check of important data for yourself.

af-fine-tuning.title: Fine-tuning vs Prompting — train or explain
af-fine-tuning.subtitle: When to train the model and when a good prompt is enough
af-fine-tuning.whatItIs: A course on two ways to make AI do what you need: **prompting** (explain the task in text) and **fine-tuning** (train the model on your own data). We'll cover the difference, when fine-tuning is truly justified, and why 90% of tasks are solved without it — via [[node:prompting|prompt engineering]] and [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]].
af-fine-tuning.approach: We move from concepts to decision. First a clear line between "train" and "explain", then what fine-tuning is and what it costs, then the ladder for choosing a tool. We finish with common mistakes and a quick "do I even need fine-tuning" check. Conceptual, no code or math.
outcomes: Explain the difference between fine-tuning and prompting in your own words
Understand when fine-tuning is genuinely needed versus wasted spend
Know the choice ladder: prompt, then few-shot, then RAG, then fine-tune
Estimate the real cost and complexity of fine-tuning before you start
Stop confusing "trendy" with "needed" when picking an approach

applyIn.title: Style and tone of replies
