applyIn.description: You need AI to answer in your brand voice. Examples in the prompt first; fine-tune only if the style won't transfer via few-shot.

applyIn.title: Narrow domain with data
applyIn.description: Medicine, law, support with thousands of question-answer pairs. Here fine-tuning may pay off — but check RAG first.

applyIn.title: Cutting production cost
applyIn.description: Fine-tune a small model so it replaces a big one on a narrow task and lowers per-request cost.

pitfalls: Fine-tuning "just in case" from day one — like tuning a car you haven't driven yet
Thinking fine-tuning = "AI gets smarter". It's specialization, not an upgrade
Ignoring tech debt: a new model version makes your old fine-tune obsolete
Fine-tuning where a prompt + RAG would do — a wasted quarter and budget
Skipping prompting and few-shot before reaching for fine-tuning

exercises.question: Your task: AI sorts incoming emails into 5 categories. Do you try fine-tuning or prompting first, and why?
exercises.hint: Think about how many examples it takes to explain 5 categories and whether they fit right inside the prompt.

exercises.question: A team spent a quarter fine-tuning, and a month later a better model shipped. What was the planning mistake?
exercises.hint: Recall what happens to a fine-tuned model when a newer base version is released.

exercises.question: Name the three rungs worth climbing before fine-tuning, in the right order.
exercises.hint: The ladder starts with the cheapest, fastest tool and ends with the most expensive one.

s1.title: The difference: train or explain
s1.why: Without a clear line between prompting and fine-tuning, any tool choice is guesswork.
instructions: Picture a new hire: prompting = give instructions each time, fine-tuning = train for months so they just know.
Write in one line what prompting changes (the instruction text) and what fine-tuning changes (the model itself).
Note: prompting is flexible and instant; fine-tuning is slow and locks behavior into the model's weights.
Tie it to basics: review [[node:ai-fundamentals|how AI works]] to see what changes inside.
s1.validate: You can explain the difference in 30 seconds without the word "neural network".
s1.tip: Simple test: if a decision changes by editing text — that's prompting.

s2.title: What fine-tuning is and when it's truly needed
s2.why: Fine-tuning sounds like magic, but it's a narrow tool with three honest scenarios.
instructions: Define fine-tuning: the model is further trained on thousands of your input-output pairs, changing its behavior.
List the three justified cases: distinct style, narrow domain with thousands of examples, cost cuts via a small model.
Note: in all other cases — prompting + RAG + tools.
Form the rule: if you don't have thousands of quality examples, fine-tuning is premature.
s2.validate: You can name the three scenarios where fine-tuning is justified and why.
s2.tip: No labeled data in the thousands means it's too early for fine-tuning.

s3.title: Why 90% of tasks are solved by prompting and context
s3.why: Most teams underestimate how far a good prompt with examples and pulled-in context gets you.
instructions: Take the task "AI replies in the CEO's voice" and solve it with examples in the prompt — few-shot.
Study [[node:prompting|prompt engineering]]: a clear role, style, and 3-5 examples of the desired answer.
Where knowledge is missing, pull it in via [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]] rather than baking it into the model.
Compare timelines: prompt + RAG = result in a week versus a quarter for fine-tuning.
s3.validate: You understand why prompt + RAG is usually faster and cheaper than fine-tuning.
s3.tip: Run 50 prompt iterations first — then think about fine-tuning.

s4.title: Cost and complexity of fine-tuning
s4.why: The cost of fine-tuning isn't just training money — it's ongoing tech debt.
instructions: Count the direct costs: gathering and labeling thousands of examples, the training itself, infrastructure.
Add the hidden price: a new base model ships, your fine-tune is outdated, retrain from scratch.
Note the quality risk: the model "specializes" and may answer worse outside the training data.
Compare with prompting: switching models takes seconds, retraining a fine-tune takes weeks and money.
s4.validate: You can name at least three cost items of fine-tuning beyond the training itself.
s4.tip: Budget for repeating fine-tuning every time a new model ships.

s5.title: The tool-choice ladder
s5.why: The right order of tools saves months: start with the cheap and fast one.
instructions: Rung 1 — plain prompt: a clear instruction, a role, an output format.
Rung 2 — few-shot: add 3-5 input-output examples right in the prompt ([[node:pr-fewshot|few-shot prompting]]).
Rung 3 — RAG: pull fresh knowledge from your own documents ([[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]]).
Rung 4 — fine-tuning: only if the previous three are exhausted and you have thousands of examples.
Climb up only when the current rung has provably failed.
s5.validate: You can recite the four rungs in the correct order from memory.
s5.tip: Never jump to fine-tuning skipping RAG.

s6.title: Common mistakes and the check
s6.why: The main trap is fine-tuning where a prompt would do; a quick checklist removes it.
instructions: Mistake 1: fine-tuning "just in case" from day one — climb the ladder first.
Mistake 2: expecting fine-tuning to make AI smarter — it only fits it to your data.
Check yourself with three questions: tried prompt and few-shot? tried RAG? have thousands of examples?
If any answer is "no" — fine-tuning is premature, go back to the ladder.
Record the verdict for your task: which tool is sufficient right now.
s6.validate: You ran your real task through the checklist and chose a tool deliberately.
s6.tip: Even one "no" on the checklist means fine-tuning is still too early.

cc-md.title: CLAUDE.md
cc-md.subtitle: The project instructions file Claude Code reads in every conversation
cc-md.whatItIs: CLAUDE.md is a text file in the project root that [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] automatically loads at the start of every conversation. You describe the stack, conventions, important paths, commands, and taboos once — and stop repeating them in each request.
cc-md.approach: This course builds a working CLAUDE.md step by step: why it matters, how to create it via /init or by hand, what to put in it, how the hierarchy works (global, project, local), and how to keep the file short and current. No general prompting — only Claude Code specifics.
outcomes: Understand why CLAUDE.md matters and how much context it saves in every conversation
Can create the file via /init and refine it by hand
Know what to write (conventions, paths, commands, taboos) and what NOT to write
Grasp the hierarchy: global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, project, CLAUDE.local.md, imports
Keep the file short and current, avoiding walls of text and stale rules

applyIn.title: Starting a new project
applyIn.description: Run /init first — Claude inspects the repo and generates a base CLAUDE.md that you then polish.

applyIn.title: Team work
applyIn.description: A project CLAUDE.md in git holds shared conventions for everyone. Keep personal settings in CLAUDE.local.md outside the commit.

applyIn.title: Recurring model mistakes
applyIn.description: If Claude keeps breaking one rule, add it to CLAUDE.md as a taboo — it's then respected automatically in future conversations.

pitfalls: Wall of text: the longer CLAUDE.md gets, the worse the model holds priorities. Keep it short and on point.
Obvious over valuable: the repo name and "it's React" are useless — write rules, conventions, and taboos.
Stale rules: the file lives with the project. Changed your linter or a path? Update CLAUDE.md, or the model works off the old one.
Secrets in the file: CLAUDE.md is often in git. Keys, tokens, passwords never go here — only in CLAUDE.local.md or the environment.
Duplicating README: CLAUDE.md is instructions for Claude, not docs for humans. Don't copy the whole README.

exercises.question: Run /init in an existing project and open the resulting CLAUDE.md. What's obvious (can be removed) and what's a genuinely useful rule?
exercises.hint: Obvious: project name, that it's React. Useful: build/test commands, non-standard paths, naming conventions.

exercises.question: Formulate 3 taboos for your project (what Claude should NOT do) and add them to CLAUDE.md as a separate block.
exercises.hint: Examples: "don't use any in TypeScript", "don't touch migrations without asking", "don't add dependencies without justification".

exercises.question: Create ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md with one personal rule (e.g. response language) and check that it applies in any project.
exercises.hint: The global file applies across all projects; the project CLAUDE.md adds to it rather than replacing it.

s1.title: Why CLAUDE.md matters
s1.why: Without an instructions file, the model re-figures the stack, structure, and rules in every new conversation — the first lost minutes and a risk of breaking your conventions. CLAUDE.md provides that context once and automatically.
instructions: Remember the key point: [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] reads CLAUDE.md at the start of EVERY conversation — without reminders.
It's the project's "character": stack, conventions, important paths, commands, and taboos in one place.
Without the file you repeat the same things in every request — with it you write only the task itself.
CLAUDE.md speeds up not one answer but every one: it's a permanent part of the context.
s1.validate: You can explain in one sentence why repeating conventions in every request is worse than keeping them in CLAUDE.md.
s1.tip: Think of CLAUDE.md as Custom Instructions, but for code and for a specific project.

s2.title: How to create it and where it lives
s2.why: Writing the file from scratch by hand is slow and easy to forget things. The /init command inspects the repo and assembles a draft for you — you just polish it.
instructions: Fastest path: run [[node:cc-cmd-init|/init]] in the project root — Claude scans the code and generates a base CLAUDE.md.
Alternative: create CLAUDE.md manually in the repo root with a plain text editor.
Check the location: the project CLAUDE.md sits in the root (next to package.json / .git).
Open the resulting file and read it — /init often writes extra you should remove.
s2.validate: There's a CLAUDE.md file in the project root, and Claude Code picks it up in a new conversation.
s2.tip: After /init, always re-read the file by hand — auto-generation gives a base, not a final.

s3.title: What to write inside
s3.why: The value of CLAUDE.md isn't in describing the obvious but in what the model can't guess: your commands, non-standard paths, conventions, and explicit prohibitions. That turns the file from a brochure into a working tool.
instructions: Stack and versions — briefly: what's actually used (e.g. React 18 + Vite), if it affects decisions.
Commands: how to build, run tests, lint — exact lines Claude can execute.
Important paths: where the code is, where configs are, where NOT to change anything.
Conventions: naming, style, patterns the team follows.
Taboos: what's NOT allowed — "don't use any", "don't touch migrations without asking".
s3.validate: The file has commands, paths, and at least 2-3 explicit taboos — not just a description of "what this project is".
s3.tip: Simple rule: if Claude can learn it from the code itself — don't write it; if it can't or often gets it wrong — write it.

s4.title: Hierarchy and scope
s4.why: CLAUDE.md comes in several levels, and they stack rather than conflict. Understanding the hierarchy lets you keep personal rules separate from team ones and avoid committing extras.
instructions: Global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md — your personal rules for ALL projects (e.g. response language).
Project CLAUDE.md in the repo root — shared team rules, goes into git.
CLAUDE.local.md — personal settings just for you in this project; add it to .gitignore.
Levels stack: global + project + local apply together.
Imports: long blocks can be moved to separate files and linked from CLAUDE.md.
s4.validate: You understand which rule to put in global, which in project, and which in CLAUDE.local.md.
s4.tip: Secrets, personal paths, and experiments go in CLAUDE.local.md (outside git), not the shared CLAUDE.md.

s5.title: Keep it short and current
s5.why: The longer the file, the worse the model holds priorities, and a stale rule is worse than no rule — it actively harms. A short, fresh CLAUDE.md beats a big, forgotten one.
instructions: Don't put human docs in CLAUDE.md — that's what the README is for.
Don't duplicate the README, changelog, or feature descriptions — only instructions for the model.
Don't store secrets, tokens, or keys — those go in the environment or CLAUDE.local.md.
Clean up regularly: changed a tool or path? Fix the file right away.
If the file grows large — move topics into separate files and link them via imports.
s5.validate: The file fits a manageable size, with no stale items and no copies of the README.
s5.tip: Every couple of weeks, re-read CLAUDE.md as a newcomer: is it all still true?

s6.title: Common mistakes and a check
s6.why: Most CLAUDE.md problems are walls of text and stale rules. A quick check in a live conversation shows whether the file actually works or just sits in the repo.
instructions: Check for a wall of text: if the file scrolls forever — trim it to the essentials.
Check for staleness: is every rule still true? Delete what stopped being true.
Check for obviousness: remove what Claude can already see in the code.
Live test: open a new conversation in [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] and give a task touching your rule — is it respected?
If a rule is ignored — rephrase it shorter and clearer, with no fuzzy wording.
s6.validate: In a new conversation Claude respects your conventions and taboos without reminders in the request itself.
s6.tip: Keep current Claude Code settings and commands handy in the [[node:cc-config|config]] and [[node:cc-install|install]] — CLAUDE.md works together with them.

uc-ai-reporting-launch.title: Launch AI Reporting
uc-ai-reporting-launch.subtitle: A ready scenario: from manual reports to a working weekly report workflow in 2 weeks
uc-ai-reporting-launch.whatItIs: A step-by-step route to move a regular report (weekly/monthly) onto Claude: from a manual draft to a repeatable workflow used by the team. Built on a chain of 105 Atlas nodes — [[node:prompting|Prompting]], [[node:projects|Projects]], [[node:i-claudemd|CLAUDE.md]], [[node:ops-reporting-automation|Reporting Automation]], [[node:sc-data|working with data]].
uc-ai-reporting-launch.approach: Quality first, automation later. AI writes a draft, then a human edits, then measure quality on 5-10 real reports. Only after stable results do you add triggers and scheduling. A two-week cycle: Day 1-3 setup, Day 4-7 iterations, Day 8-14 roll-out.
outcomes: A working weekly report workflow in 2 weeks
Time-to-report cut from 4 hours to 30 minutes
Report consistency up ~90% (single format)
The team can use the workflow and trusts it (NPS survey)
The report format is fixed and reused instead of rebuilt every time

applyIn.title: Operations / business analytics
applyIn.description: Weekly summaries of sales, funnel, and metrics from CRM and analytics with CSV export.

applyIn.title: Management reporting
applyIn.description: Regular reports for leadership: project status, KPIs, concise digests from many sources.

applyIn.title: Team / department updates
applyIn.description: Recurring team summaries where the format is stable and data refreshes each period.

pitfalls: Wanting full automation in the first week — get draft quality right first, then add triggers
Starting without available data: if there is no CRM/analytics export, the workflow stalls
Rewriting the format from scratch each time instead of fixing it in [[node:i-claudemd|CLAUDE.md]]
Rolling out to the team before 5-10 successful manual iterations — no trust, no feedback
Not measuring results: without time-to-report and NPS metrics you cannot prove value

exercises.question: Which of your reports fits the first launch and why exactly that one?
exercises.hint: Look for a regular report taking ≥3 hours per week, with available data and a stable format.

exercises.question: What fields and structure should the final report have so they can be described in CLAUDE.md?
exercises.hint: Take 1-2 past reports and list the sections, metrics, and tone — that is your future format.

exercises.question: How will you know the workflow is ready to roll out to the team?
exercises.hint: Use the criterion: 5-10 real reports in a row with acceptable draft quality.

s1.title: When the scenario is needed and what you get
s1.why: Without a clear trigger and expected result, the team drowns in "start reading everything". This step confirms the scenario applies at all and locks in a measurable outcome.
instructions: Check the trigger: there is a regular report (weekly/monthly) taking ≥3 hours per week
Check data: it is available via CRM/analytics export (CSV, etc.)
Check buy-in: the team agrees to try a new workflow
Lock target metrics: time-to-report from 4h to 30min, consistency +90%, NPS survey
State the outcome in one phrase: "a working weekly report workflow in 2 weeks"
s1.validate: You have one concrete candidate report, access to its data, and recorded target metrics.
s1.tip: If the trigger or the data is missing, do not launch yet — it saves you two weeks.

s2.title: Preparation: data, access, context
s2.why: Report quality is capped by input quality. This step prepares the data and a shared workspace so iterations run without stopping to ask "where do the numbers come from".
instructions: Gather data sources and confirm export works (see [[node:sc-data|working with CSV data]])
Create a shared "Weekly Reports" workspace for the team via [[node:projects|Projects]]
If the report needs CRM context, learn how to feed it to Claude ([[node:af-rag-basics|RAG basics]])
Take 1-2 past reports as a reference for format and tone
Agree on who owns the workflow and who edits drafts
s2.validate: Data exports cleanly, the workspace exists, reference reports are at hand.
s2.tip: Start with a single data source — do not try to connect everything at once.

s3.title: First draft: prompt and format
s3.why: This is the heart of the scenario: teach Claude to write the report in the right format. Manually at first, to see real quality and find what to improve.
instructions: Write a system prompt for the report (see [[node:prompting|Prompting]] and [[node:b-system|system prompt]])
Describe the report format — sections, metrics, tone — in the workspace [[node:i-claudemd|CLAUDE.md]]
Feed real data for one period and get a first draft
Compare the draft against the reference report and note the gaps
Record what the AI does well and what you have to fix by hand
s3.validate: You have a first coherent draft, and the format lives in CLAUDE.md and is reused.
s3.tip: Do not chase perfection on the first try — the goal is a working starting point.

s4.title: Iterate on real reports
s4.why: One draft proves nothing. Stable quality only shows on a series of real reports — this is where the workflow matures into something repeatable.
instructions: Run 5-10 real reports as: AI draft, then human edits, then log the edits
After each iteration refine the prompt and format in [[node:i-claudemd|CLAUDE.md]]
Shape the stages into a repeatable process following [[node:ops-reporting-automation|Reporting Automation]]
Measure editing time — it should drop from iteration to iteration
Collect frequent edits into a checklist so the prompt covers them upfront
s4.validate: 5-10 reports in a row produce an acceptable draft, and manual editing steadily decreases.
s4.tip: If editing is still heavy after 10 iterations, the issue is the data or the format, not Claude.

s5.title: Quality check and risks
s5.why: Before going to the team you must confirm the report is accurate and reproducible — one wrong number would undermine trust in the whole workflow.
instructions: Reconcile the draft's numbers against the source data — check for factual errors
Test stability: the same data yields a comparable result
Record the measured time-to-report and compare with the 30-minute target
Define which parts require mandatory human review
Describe the risk zones (sources with dirty data, sensitive metrics)
s5.validate: Quality is confirmed by the check, metrics are met, mandatory-review spots are known.
s5.tip: Add full automation only after this step — never before.

s6.title: Roll-out and scaling
s6.why: Value appears when the whole team uses the workflow, not just one author. The final step is the roll-out, gathering feedback, and cementing the practice.
instructions: Run the team roll-out: show the workflow and the shared workspace [[node:projects|Projects]]
Collect feedback and run an NPS survey (likelihood to recommend, 0-10)
Add automation — triggers and scheduling — following [[node:ops-reporting-automation|Reporting Automation]]
Assign an owner who maintains the prompt and format in [[node:i-claudemd|CLAUDE.md]]
Readiness checklist: format in CLAUDE.md, 5-10 successful iterations, metrics met, team trained, owner assigned
s6.validate: The team uses the workflow, NPS is collected, automation is added, the checklist is closed.
s6.tip: Once one report is dialed in, the same path repeats easily for the next — the format already exists.

uc-ai-process-automation.title: Automate a Recurring Process
uc-ai-process-automation.subtitle: From an operations process your team does by hand every week to a production workflow on Skills and Hooks with quality checks
uc-ai-process-automation.whatItIs: A structured path to automating one specific recurring process via AI: from choosing a good candidate to a production-ready workflow with [[node:skills|Skills]] and automatic triggers. Not "we tried Claude and liked it", but a systematic approach with metrics and quality gates.
uc-ai-process-automation.approach: First pick and stabilize a process that runs at least 5 times a week with clear inputs/outputs. Then document it as-is and identify the steps AI can realistically take over. Build the automation core — a reusable Skill plus external integrations if needed — and add triggers. Always embed quality gates with human review, test on historical data, and only then roll out to production with monitoring and a scaling plan.
outcomes: An automated workflow for a specific process, ready for daily use in 2-3 weeks
70-90% time savings on the routine steps of the process
Error rate below 5% thanks to quality gates and human review
A reusable Skill you can apply to similar processes
Clear before/after metrics to prove the value to your team and leadership

applyIn.title: Incoming request handling
applyIn.description: Classifying, enriching, and routing tickets or requests that arrive by the dozen each day in a single template.

applyIn.title: Producing regular documents
applyIn.description: Weekly reports, summaries, client emails — where the format is stable and manual variability gets in the way.

applyIn.title: Routine data operations
applyIn.description: Moving, reconciling, normalizing data between systems via [[node:mcp|MCP]] integrations when the steps repeat and are well described.

pitfalls: Automating a process that isn't stabilized yet — the workflow will break with every change
Skipping quality gates: without human review, automation produces trash at scale
Picking a process that is too complex or too rare — no savings, and maintenance eats your time
Testing only on "convenient" examples and ignoring edge cases from historical data
Rolling out to production without monitoring — errors pile up unnoticed and team trust drops

exercises.question: Find one process in your team that runs ≥5 times a week with clear inputs and outputs. Describe its steps and mark which ones AI could take over.
exercises.hint: A good candidate: stable format, clear result, measurable time. If the process still changes every week, stabilize it first.

exercises.question: For the chosen process, design 3 quality gates — points where the result is checked before moving on. Where is a human strictly required?
exercises.hint: Think about irreversible actions: sending to a client, changing data, financial operations. Cover those with human review first.

exercises.question: Define a before/after success metric for your automation: how much time is spent now and what target error rate is acceptable.
exercises.hint: A practical benchmark: 70-90% time savings and an error rate below 5%. Capture the baseline BEFORE launch, or you have nothing to prove value with.

s1.title: When you need it and the target outcome
s1.why: Without the right candidate, automation either won't pay off or will keep breaking. This step decides whether to start at all.
instructions: Check candidate criteria: the process runs ≥5 times a week with clear inputs and outputs
Confirm that result variability in manual execution is a real problem for the team
Verify technical feasibility: do you have access to the needed triggers and integrations
State the expected outcome in metrics: 70-90% time savings, error rate <5%
Look at [[node:ops-process-automation|Process Automation]] as the target structure with quality gates
s1.validate: You have one specific process and a written goal in measurable before/after metrics.
s1.tip: If torn between two processes, take the one that repeats more often and changes less. Frequency × stability = payoff.

s2.title: Preparation: document the process as-is
s2.why: You can't automate what isn't described. The as-is document shows which steps AI can take over and which must stay with a human.
instructions: Write out the process step by step as it runs today (Week 1)
For each step note: inputs, action, result, who/what is responsible
Mark the AI-replaceable steps — where Claude can produce a stable result from clear rules
Collect a set of historical examples for future tests (real cases, including edge cases)
Make sure the process is stable — if it still changes, lock it down first
s2.validate: You have a step-by-step map of the process, marked AI steps, and a set of historical examples for tests.
s2.tip: Edge and "awkward" cases from history are worth more than a dozen typical ones — that's exactly where the workflow breaks in production.

s3.title: Execution: the automation core — a Skill
s3.why: A reusable Skill is the instruction Claude applies the same way every time. It turns a one-off prompt into a systematic process.
instructions: Build the workflow core as a Skill via [[node:s-create|Creating a Skill]] — describe the goal, steps, and output format
Lean on [[node:skills|Skills]] so the Skill is self-contained and reusable
Work out the core workflow prompt following [[node:prompting|Prompting]] rules
Run the Skill on the historical examples from step 2 and compare with the real results (Week 2)
Tune the prompt to a stable output on both typical and edge cases
s3.validate: The Skill produces the expected result on historical examples, including some of the edge cases.
s3.tip: Don't try to cover everything with one giant prompt. A clear Skill with a defined output format is more reliable than a wall of instructions.

s4.title: Execution: integrations and triggers
s4.why: The Skill handles "what to do", while integrations and triggers handle "where the data comes from" and "when to run". Without them, automation stays a manual button.
instructions: If external systems are needed, connect them via [[node:mcp|MCP]] (data sources, team tools)
Set up automatic triggers via [[node:cc-hooks|Claude Code Hooks]] — by event, schedule, or incoming request
Wire the chain: trigger, then data via MCP, then Skill, then result
Run the full path end-to-end on test data, not just the Skill itself
Record which steps stay manual and why (part of the quality gates)
s4.validate: The full path from trigger to result runs on test data with no manual intervention on the automatic steps.
s4.tip: Start with one trigger and minimal integrations. Extra connections complicate debugging and widen the surface for errors.

s5.title: Quality checks and risks
s5.why: Quality gates are the main defense against "automated trash". Without checks, errors pile up at scale and destroy team trust.
instructions: Embed quality gates: points where the result is checked before moving on
For irreversible actions (sending to a client, changing data, money) keep a mandatory human review
Measure the actual error rate on historical data and compare with the <5% target
Test edge cases separately — they reveal the weak spots of the workflow
Describe a rollback plan: what to do if automation produces a wrong result
s5.validate: The error rate is within target, risky steps have human review, and there is a rollback plan.
s5.tip: A quality gate isn't a slowdown — it's insurance: better to route 100% of results through review the first week than fix your reputation later.

s6.title: Rollout, scaling, and checklist
s6.why: A production launch without monitoring and a scaling plan turns a working prototype into an unmanaged risk. This step locks in the value.
instructions: Roll the workflow out to production with monitoring of results and error rate (Week 3)
Capture the after metrics and compare with the baseline from step 1 — prove the savings to the team
Decide whether to expand the approach: stage transition from stage 1 to stage 2 (first automation) or from stage 2 to stage 3 (scaling)
Find similar processes that reuse the same Skill and add them to the queue
Run the checklist: candidate fits / process documented / Skill stable / triggers and MCP work / quality gates in place / monitoring on
s6.validate: The workflow runs in production, the after metrics confirm the value, and the checklist is fully passed.
s6.tip: Write up the case: process, metrics, gotchas. It's both proof of value and a template for the next automation from the [[node:use-cases|Use Cases]].

uc-ai-decision-support.title: AI Support for Operational Decisions
uc-ai-decision-support.subtitle: From "let us discuss in Slack" to a structured decision process with AI analysis in 3-4 weeks
uc-ai-decision-support.whatItIs: This course shows how to bring AI into your team's operational decisions — not as "the decider", but as a tool for structuring and pattern matching. You will build a working decision process where AI prepares trade-off analysis and surfaces past cases, while the human makes the call and owns accountability.
uc-ai-decision-support.approach: Operations teams make 5-10 decisions a week under load: lots of reactive, little learning. This approach adds discipline without bureaucracy — a lightweight template, AI analysis via [[node:prompting|structured prompting]], and a decision log in [[node:projects|Projects]]. Start with a pilot of 3-5 decisions, then refine and roll out with a retrospective.
outcomes: A working decision process with AI support in 3-4 weeks
Reactive decisions drop by 50-70%
A learning loop is established: retrospective with AI pattern matching over decision history
A "Decision Log" with outcome tracking for future retrospectives
The team clearly understands AI's boundaries: where it adds value, and where accountability stays with the human

applyIn.title: Hiring and recruiting
applyIn.description: Hire vs no-hire decisions with trade-off analysis: AI structures the arguments for and against, the human weighs context and decides.

applyIn.title: Vendor and tool selection
applyIn.description: Vendor selection by matching criteria and pricing: AI assembles data into one structure and surfaces similar past choices from the log.

applyIn.title: Process changes
applyIn.description: Process change decisions: AI pattern-matches against past changes ("we decided this a year ago"), reducing repeat mistakes.

pitfalls: Using AI as "the decider". AI is good at structuring and pattern matching, but context and accountability belong to the human.
Ignoring documentation. Tracking outcomes matters more than the AI output itself: no log means no learning loop.
Overloading the process with bureaucracy. A heavy template kills adoption — keep it light.
Putting every decision into the process at once. Start with major decisions that need trade-off; leave the small stuff as is.
Trusting AI output without checking the data. Weak inputs lead to confident-sounding but wrong analysis.

exercises.question: List 5 decisions your team made last month. Which required trade-off analysis and would fit AI support, and which would not?
exercises.hint: Candidates: hires, vendors, process changes. Non-candidates: obvious operational actions with no alternatives.

exercises.question: Take one past decision the team later regretted. What data and arguments would AI have helped structure beforehand?
exercises.hint: Think about what was known at the time but never pulled into one picture.

exercises.question: State a boundary: which decision would you NOT trust AI to even structure? Why?
exercises.hint: Look for decisions tied to hidden context, people, or ethics — that is where AI is blind.

s1.title: Define when the scenario is needed and the target outcome
s1.why: Without a clear scope, AI support turns into bureaucracy for every decision. First decide which decisions to include at all.
instructions: Collect the types of decisions your team made over a month (hires, vendors, processes).
Mark those that require trade-off analysis — these are candidates for AI support.
Define the expected outcome: a working process in 3-4 weeks, reactive decisions down 50-70%.
Fix the goal: structuring and a learning loop, not handing decisions to AI.
s1.validate: You have a short list (3-5 types) of decisions where AI support adds value.
s1.tip: If a decision is obvious and has no alternatives, it does not belong in this process.

s2.title: Prepare the data and context for analysis
s2.why: AI analysis quality equals input data quality. Weak input leads to a confident-sounding but wrong conclusion.
instructions: For each decision type, define what data is needed (numbers, criteria, constraints).
Learn to feed data to AI via [[node:prompting|structured prompting]] — facts separate from the question.
Set up a "Decision Log" workspace in [[node:projects|Projects]] for history and context.
Collect 2-3 past decisions as a reference for future pattern matching.
s2.validate: For the pilot decision, you can quickly assemble a clean set of data and context.
s2.tip: Separate "facts" from "the question for AI" — it sharply improves structuring quality.

s3.title: Step 1: structure trade-off analysis with chain-of-thought
s3.why: The key to value is making AI reason step by step and lay out arguments for and against, rather than spitting out a ready answer.
instructions: Build a prompt template on [[node:prompting|prompting principles]]: context, then data, then task, then output format.
Ask AI to expand its chain-of-thought: criteria, options, pros/cons of each.
Fix the output format: a trade-off table plus AI's explicit assumptions.
Run it on 1 simple pilot decision and assess how useful the structure is.
s3.validate: AI produces a readable trade-off breakdown with explicit assumptions, not a single "answer".
s3.tip: Always ask AI to name its assumptions — that reveals where it might be wrong.

s4.title: Step 2: add pattern matching over decision history
s4.why: The core operations pain is "we decided this a year ago and forgot". History in the log turns past decisions into a learning loop.
instructions: Give AI access to the "Decision Log" in [[node:projects|Projects]] as context.
Ask AI to find similar past decisions and their outcomes before a new conclusion.
For each new decision, record: context, options, choice, expected outcome.
After 1-2 cycles, verify AI actually surfaces relevant past cases.
s4.validate: On a new decision, AI references similar past cases from the log.
s4.tip: Record not just the choice but the expected outcome — otherwise the retrospective has no teeth.

s5.title: Quality and risk check: the human decides, not AI
s5.why: AI is good at structuring and pattern matching, but context and accountability belong to the human. Without this barrier the process is dangerous.
instructions: Set the rule: AI output is an input for discussion, not a decision.
Check AI's assumptions and the data its analysis was built on.
Flag decisions where hidden context/ethics/people make AI blind — there it only structures.
Pin down who is accountable for each decision (a human, not the model).
s5.validate: The team understands: the final decision and accountability always rest with the human.
s5.tip: If AI sounds too confident, treat it as a signal to re-check the input data.

s6.title: Rollout and the rollout checklist
s6.why: The pilot proves value; rollout with a retrospective turns it into a durable team process.
instructions: Week 1: pilot on 3-5 simple decisions.
Week 2-3: refine the template and verify quality on real cases.
Week 4: roll out to all major decisions + the first retrospective with AI pattern matching.
Checklist: lightweight template, log in [[node:projects|Projects]], the "human decides" rule, outcome tracking.
s6.validate: The process works across all major decisions, reactive decisions have dropped, the first retrospective is done.
s6.tip: Keep the template light: heavy bureaucracy kills adoption faster than poor AI output.

uc-ai-content-ops-launch.title: Launch AI Content Operations
uc-ai-content-ops-launch.subtitle: From generic AI texts to a content machine with brand voice in 2 weeks
uc-ai-content-ops-launch.whatItIs: A step-by-step scenario that turns scattered AI use across a team into a working content pipeline with a recognizable brand voice. Not "AI writes faster" but "AI writes the way we write" — systematically, with quality checks and rollout to the team.
uc-ai-content-ops-launch.approach: The core of the scenario is brand voice. First you capture the brand voice and templates (preparation), then you build the two key pipeline steps (brief-to-draft and review-to-edit), and only then scale to the team. Without voice work the pipeline just produces generic texts faster — so voice setup is ~30% of the effort and must not be skipped.
outcomes: You understand when the scenario fits and the concrete result it delivers (time-to-publish, consistency, volume)
A documented brand voice as a reusable doc and system prompt
A working pipeline: brief, then draft, then review, then publish with clear roles at each step
A quality and tone check that separates "sounds like us" from "sounds like AI"
A rollout checklist the team uses to scale the process without losing quality

applyIn.title: Marketing team with inconsistent AI
applyIn.description: The team already uses AI ad-hoc but texts sound different. The scenario brings everyone to one voice and predictable quality.

applyIn.title: Blog and regular content >10 pieces/month
applyIn.description: Once volume grows, hand-editing every draft does not scale. A pipeline with voice cuts time-to-publish dramatically.

applyIn.title: Launching a new content stream
applyIn.description: A new product or section needs a voice from scratch. The scenario gives the frame: voice, templates, review — before chaos accumulates.

pitfalls: Building the pipeline without voice work — you get generic texts faster, but still generic
Treating brand voice as "a couple of adjectives" instead of concrete attributes with "do / don't" examples
Skipping the tone review — speed goes up but AI style leaks into published pieces
Rolling out to the whole team at once without test pieces and voice-prompt iteration
Not measuring results — without time-to-publish and consistency you cannot tell if it improved

exercises.question: Assemble a brand voice doc: 5 voice attributes, each with a "do / don't" pair using real phrases from your brand.
exercises.hint: Pull wording from your best published pieces, not from your head. Voice is what already works.

exercises.question: Run one piece through the full pipeline (brief, then draft, then review, then publish) and time each step.
exercises.hint: The before measurement is your baseline. Without it you cannot prove time-to-publish dropped.

exercises.question: Give a colleague 3 texts: 2 of your published ones and 1 AI draft without voice. Can they tell which is which?
exercises.hint: If the AI text is easy to spot, the voice is still weak — add specifics to the system prompt.

s1.title: Decide when the scenario is needed and lock the target result
s1.why: The scenario pays off only under certain conditions. Launching a pipeline "just in case" without volume and without editor buy-in wastes time and yields no measurable effect.
instructions: Check the triggers: team already uses AI ad-hoc, quality is inconsistent, volume >10 pieces/month, editor/content lead buy-in exists.
Record baseline metrics: current time from draft to publish, share of pieces "on brand voice", monthly volume.
State the target result: e.g. time-to-publish from 2 days to 4h, brand consistency from 60% to 90%, volume +200%.
If even one trigger is missing (no volume or no buy-in) — postpone the scenario, otherwise the pipeline will not stick.
s1.validate: You have 3 baseline numbers and 3 target numbers — something to compare against in 2 weeks.
s1.tip: This scenario is the path from Foundation to Transformation. If basic prompting still wobbles, start with [[node:prompting|writing briefs]].

s2.title: Preparation: brand voice and templates
s2.why: Brand voice is the core of the whole scenario (about 30% of the effort). Without an explicitly described voice any pipeline produces generic texts, just faster.
instructions: Audit existing content: pick 5-10 best pieces and write down voice attributes (tone, vocabulary, sentence length, what the brand never says).
Capture the brand voice as a [[node:b-system|system prompt]] and mirror it with profile-level [[node:instructions|custom instructions]] for everyday chats.
Create a [[node:projects|"Blog" Project]] and put voice files, "do / don't" examples and brief templates into it.
For the team workspace add a [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] with voice rules if you work in Claude Code.
s2.validate: You have a voice doc + a Project with voice files; on a test phrase Claude answers in the right tone without long briefing.
s2.tip: A voice attribute without a "do / don't" example is useless. Claude learns from contrast, not from adjectives.

s3.title: Key step 1: brief, then draft
s3.why: This is the pipeline input. Draft quality is 80% determined by brief quality — no editing will rescue a weak input.
instructions: Lock a brief template: topic, goal, audience, key points, format, length, what NOT to write.
Generate the draft inside the "Blog" Project so voice files are pulled in automatically.
Run 3-5 test pieces and iteratively fix the voice prompt where Claude drifts off tone.
Lock the final draft prompt as part of the Project — it is a reusable asset.
s3.validate: On a new brief the draft comes out on brand voice with minimal edits and no manual re-briefing.
s3.tip: If drafts vary in quality, the problem is in the brief, not in Claude. Standardize the input first.

s4.title: Key step 2: review, then edit
s4.why: This is the pipeline output control. Without an explicit review step AI style leaks into published pieces and the whole speed gain is wasted.
instructions: Describe the review step as part of a sequential pipeline — see the [[node:sys-linear-chain|linear chain]] (brief, then draft, then review, then publish).
Give Claude an editor role: check brand voice fit, facts, structure and return a list of edits, not a silent rewrite.
Introduce a tone checklist: "sounds like us?", no clichés or AI markers, banned phrasings respected.
Run 2-3 pieces through the draft-then-review pair and compare the result against the voice doc.
s4.validate: After the review step a piece passes the tone checklist and edits from a human editor are minimal.
s4.tip: Review ≠ re-generation. Ask for a list of edits with reasons — that shows you where the voice breaks systematically.

s5.title: Quality and tone check at scale
s5.why: One good article is luck. Before handing the pipeline to the team you must confirm quality and tone are stable across a series of pieces.
instructions: Build a set of 5 varied pieces (different topics/formats) and run the whole pipeline end to end.
Rate each against the tone checklist and compare with the baseline metrics from step 1.
Blind test: give a colleague a mix of published and AI pieces — if the AI ones are spotted, strengthen the voice prompt.
Record typical tone failures and add counterexamples to the Project and voice doc.
s5.validate: Across 5 different pieces consistency stays at the target level; the blind test does not reveal the AI texts.
s5.tip: Measure, do not "feel". Consistency 90% is a concrete share of pieces passing the checklist, not an impression.

s6.title: Rollout, scale and a team handoff checklist
s6.why: The scenario delivers value only when the team uses it, not a single person. The final step turns the work into a repeatable process.
instructions: Describe the finished process as [[node:mk-content-ops|content operations]] with roles and metrics; for separate deep voice tuning use [[node:mk-brand-voice|brand voice tuning]].
Share the Project, brief templates and voice doc with the whole team; assign a voice owner who keeps it updated.
Run the rollout: a short walkthrough + 1-2 joint runs so the team can repeat it without you.
Turn on measurement: track time-to-publish, consistency and volume weekly for the first 2 weeks.
Go through the handoff checklist: voice doc current, Project shared, pipeline steps documented, metrics tracked, owner assigned.
s6.validate: At least one colleague runs a piece through the whole pipeline on their own, and weekly metrics confirm the gains.
s6.tip: Assign a voice owner. Without one the voice doc goes stale within a month and the pipeline quietly slides back to generic.

uc-ai-support-tier1.title: Launch AI Tier-1 Support
uc-ai-support-tier1.subtitle: From "all by hand" to "AI closes 40% of tickets" in 4 weeks
uc-ai-support-tier1.whatItIs: A how-to course on rolling out AI first-line support (Tier-1 — simple, repetitive questions) step by step in a real team. This is not "buy a bot" but a structured path: knowledge base first, then AI, then quality control and human escalation. One of the highest-ROI AI projects in support.
uc-ai-support-tier1.approach: The order of steps is strict and deliberate: the knowledge base (KB) comes first, because AI answers only as well as the KB it retrieves from (RAG). First we prepare the ground, then assemble the AI scenario, then embed quality control and safe escalation, and only then roll out to live traffic via a pilot and metrics. See the pattern in [[node:ai-native-customer-support|AI-native customer support]] and [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG basics]].
outcomes: A working AI Tier-1 with deflection (share of tickets closed by AI without a human) around 40%
Median response time on AI tickets drops from 4 hours to 2 minutes
CSAT (customer satisfaction score, 1-5) does not drop relative to baseline
Clear boundaries: what AI answers itself versus what it escalates to a human
A repeatable process for expanding from 1 ticket category to 3-5

applyIn.title: High volume of typical questions
applyIn.description: Tier-1 generates >100 tickets per week, and most are repeating questions with known answers in the knowledge base.

applyIn.title: Something to compare against
applyIn.description: A baseline CSAT and response time "before AI" exists, otherwise you cannot prove the rollout actually helped rather than hurt.

applyIn.title: Willing to invest 3-4 weeks
applyIn.description: There is buy-in from the CS lead and product team, and 3-4 weeks can be allocated to KB prep, setup and a pilot.

pitfalls: Launching AI Tier-1 without KB prep — KB ops are 50% of the work, and without them AI answers generic or wrong
Using an outdated or poorly structured KB — AI retrieves garbage and confidently returns a wrong answer
Skipping escalation setup — AI starts "choking" complex tickets instead of handing them to a human, and CSAT collapses
Rolling out to all categories at once instead of a single-category pilot — you cannot see where quality breaks
Not setting up quality control (random sample review) — answer degradation goes unnoticed until a wave of complaints

exercises.question: You have 250 Tier-1 tickets per week, but the knowledge base is two years old and articles were written by different people with no consistent structure. Where do you start — bot setup or the KB?
exercises.hint: Recall the order rule: AI answers only as well as the KB. What happens to retrieval if article structure is poor?

exercises.question: The pilot shows 40% deflection, but CSAT on AI tickets is 0.4 below baseline. What do you check first?
exercises.hint: Think about AI boundaries and escalation: maybe AI is taking on tickets it should have handed to a human.

exercises.question: Which single metric do you show the CS lead to prove the pilot's value in week one?
exercises.hint: The metric must reflect savings (deflection) yet not mask a quality drop — which is why it is always read alongside CSAT.

s1.title: Understand when the scenario fits and what success looks like
s1.why: Without a clear launch criterion and a measurable goal, the project becomes "let's try a bot" and quietly dies. First confirm you truly have a Tier-1 task and define what counts as success.
instructions: Check the volume threshold: Tier-1 generates more than 100 tickets per week — otherwise manual work is cheaper than automation
Record the baseline: current CSAT and median response time "before AI" — this is your reference point
State the goal in numbers: 40% deflection, response time from 4h to 2min, CSAT no lower than baseline
Get buy-in from the CS lead and the product team (product is needed for KB access)
s1.validate: You have a one-pager: ticket volume, baseline metrics, target numbers, and agreement from both teams.
s1.tip: If baseline metrics are missing — collect them for a week before starting. Without a reference point you cannot prove impact.

s2.title: Prepare the knowledge base and set AI boundaries
s2.why: This is 50% of all the work. AI retrieves answers from the KB (the RAG mechanism), so a bad KB means confidently wrong answers. Here we also decide which questions AI answers itself and which go to a human.
instructions: Audit existing KB articles: drop outdated ones, merge duplicates, bring them to a consistent structure
Re-chunk long articles into atomic pieces — so retrieval fetches the exact answer, not "a whole article about everything"
Using [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG basics]], verify the KB is retrieval-ready: clear headings, facts not marketing
Define boundaries: a list of categories where AI answers itself, and stop-topics (billing, legal, complaints) that always go to a human
s2.validate: The KB is cleaned and structured, and there is an explicit "AI answers" / "human only" list.
s2.tip: Take 20 real recent tickets and check by hand whether the KB yields a correct answer. If it doesn't, AI won't either.

s3.title: Assemble the AI ticket-answering scenario
s3.why: The key step: the answering AI is born here. The system prompt sets tone, format and rules, and the connected KB provides the facts. Without a careful prompt, AI answers generic and off-brand.
instructions: Write the support bot system prompt: role, tone of voice, answer format, the rule "if you don't know — escalate, don't invent"
Create a dedicated workspace (Project) and connect the cleaned KB from step 2
Require a source citation from the KB in the prompt — so the answer is verifiable and does not hallucinate
Run 15-20 typical questions and refine the prompt until answers are accurate and on-brand
s3.validate: On typical questions AI answers correctly, in the right tone, with a KB citation, and on stop-topics it proposes escalation itself.
s3.tip: The rule "better to honestly say I don't know and escalate than to invent" matters more than a nice tone — it protects CSAT.

s4.title: Embed quality control and human escalation
s4.why: AI without safe human handoff is dangerous: it will "choke" complex tickets and drag satisfaction down. And without sampled review, answer degradation stays invisible until a wave of complaints.
instructions: Set up escalation routing: on which signals a ticket goes to a human (stop-topic, low confidence, explicit customer request)
Make handoff seamless: the human gets the ticket with full conversation context, not from scratch
Launch random sample review: a random selection of AI answers is checked by a human for correctness
Create a simple answer-scoring checklist: accuracy, tone, source citation, appropriateness of escalation
s4.validate: Any doubtful ticket goes to a human with context, and a portion of AI answers is regularly reviewed against the checklist.
s4.tip: At launch, set the escalation threshold aggressively: better to hand a human too much than to break trust with a wrong answer.

s5.title: Pilot on one category and measure metrics
s5.why: Rolling out to everything at once hides where quality breaks. A single-category pilot gives a clean signal: does the KB + AI + escalation chain work on real traffic?
instructions: Pick one high-volume, low-risk ticket category (for example, "how to reset a password")
Launch AI on that category and measure deflection and CSAT every day
Compare AI-ticket CSAT to baseline — a drop is a signal to fix the prompt or boundaries, not to scale
Collect failing cases from review and return to steps 2-3 to refine the KB and prompt
s5.validate: On the pilot category deflection climbs toward 40% while CSAT holds at baseline.
s5.tip: Don't scale until CSAT has stabilized: rising deflection alongside falling CSAT is a loss, not a success.

s6.title: Rollout, metrics and readiness checklist
s6.why: After a successful pilot you need to expand coverage without losing quality and lock in the process, so the rollout is repeatable rather than a one-time feat.
instructions: Expand AI to 3-5 categories one at a time, repeating the deflection and CSAT measurement each time
Lock in a dashboard with three metrics: deflection rate, median response time, CSAT vs baseline
Make quality review a regular ritual (for example, a weekly sample), not a one-off
Run the readiness checklist: KB current, boundaries set, escalation works, metrics on the dashboard, review on the calendar
s6.validate: AI steadily closes ~40% of Tier-1 across several categories, metrics are visible on a dashboard, and the process is documented and repeatable.
s6.tip: Assign a KB owner: an aging knowledge base is the main cause of slow AI-support degradation months later.

uc-ai-discovery-launch.title: Launch AI Discovery in Your Product
uc-ai-discovery-launch.subtitle: From manual research to an AI-powered discovery pipeline in 2 weeks
uc-ai-discovery-launch.whatItIs: A step-by-step scenario that turns scattered interviews and feedback into a working AI-discovery pipeline. You organize the research repository, set up RAG-based synthesis, and embed it into your product process with validation. This is an applied route from the [[node:use-cases|Use Cases]] set, built on the [[node:pd-discovery-research|Discovery Research]] practice.
uc-ai-discovery-launch.approach: We move by the principle "input first, then synthesis, then process". First we clean up the data (without structured input AI is useless), then we set up two key synthesis steps — theme extraction and conclusion framing — then we verify the conclusions on familiar interviews, and only then embed the pipeline into the team's regular work. Each step produces a verifiable result, not "setup for the sake of setup".
outcomes: The research repository is organized: all interviews and feedback in one place, accessible to AI
Working synthesis: from data to structured themes in ≤2 hours per topic instead of days of manual work
100% research coverage — AI reads the whole corpus, not just the 30% you reach manually
Conclusions are verified and backed by source links, trustworthy for decision-making
The pipeline is embedded in the product process and scales to new feedback flow without manual synthesis

applyIn.title: Product team with accumulated research
applyIn.description: ≥30 interviews or ≥100 feedback items left unprocessed — the scenario turns the archive into a source of insight.

applyIn.title: Slow discovery-to-ship cycle
applyIn.description: When data synthesis is the bottleneck and decisions stall, the pipeline cuts time-to-insight down to hours.

applyIn.title: Building an [[node:ai-native-product|AI-native product]]
applyIn.description: When the team makes AI part of the work itself rather than a one-off experiment, discovery becomes the first reproducible loop.

pitfalls: Running synthesis without structured input: if interviews are scattered across Notion, Google Docs and Slack, AI won't find them
Underestimating data prep — organizing the repository takes ~30% of the whole scenario and cannot be skipped
Trusting conclusions without verification: synthesis without source-checking produces plausible but wrong themes
Stopping at interviews and not extending the pipeline to ongoing feedback — then the system goes stale within a month
Setting up the pipeline solo and not training other PMs — the knowledge stays with one person and doesn't stick

exercises.question: Where do your interviews and feedback live right now, and why won't AI find them in their current state?
exercises.hint: List every storage location. If there's more than one and no single repository — that's your Day 1 work.

exercises.question: How will you know an AI conclusion is correct rather than a plausible fabrication?
exercises.hint: Think about source links: every theme should point to specific interview quotes.

exercises.question: What happens to the pipeline in a month if you set it up only on old interviews?
exercises.hint: Think about the flow of new feedback — whether a separate step for ongoing data is needed.

s1.title: Understand when the scenario is needed and lock in the outcome
s1.why: The scenario pays off only with real data volume and leadership support. Without that, you automate emptiness.
instructions: Check the entry threshold: ≥30 interviews or ≥100 feedback items without structured processing
Confirm the discovery-to-ship cycle is truly slow because of synthesis, not other causes
Get buy-in from the Head of Product — without it the pipeline won't stick in the process
Lock in target metrics: time-to-insight ≤2 hours per topic, 100% research coverage
s1.validate: You have a written scenario goal and the product leader's agreement.
s1.tip: If you have less data than the threshold, the scenario is premature — accumulate research first or the setup won't pay off.

s2.title: Prepare the input: gather research into a single repository
s2.why: Without structured input AI won't find the data — the main reason the scenario fails. Prep takes ~30% of the total time.
instructions: Gather all interviews and feedback from Notion, Google Docs, Slack into one place
Create a [[node:projects|Project]] "Discovery Workspace" and upload the research files there
Normalize the files: clear names, date, source
Set up the RAG foundation ([[node:af-rag-basics|RAG basics]]) so AI can search the whole corpus
s2.validate: All research materials sit in one repository and are searchable via AI.
s2.tip: Don't try to process the whole backlog at once — 5-10 interviews are enough for debugging.

s3.title: Key synthesis step #1: theme extraction
s3.why: Theme extraction is the foundation of discovery. The quality of themes determines how useful all later conclusions will be.
instructions: Frame a synthesis prompt for extracting recurring themes (based on [[node:prompting|Prompting]])
Run it on 5-10 test interviews from the repository
Require each theme to reference specific quotes from sources
Compare the result against what you know about those interviews manually
s3.validate: AI produces a structured list of themes with source links, and the themes are recognizable.
s3.tip: Ask for themes with frequency and examples, not "general conclusions" — they're easier to verify.

s4.title: Key synthesis step #2: connect context and frame conclusions
s4.why: Themes alone aren't conclusions. Context must be passed correctly between steps so synthesis doesn't lose the thread.
instructions: Set up context passing between synthesis steps ([[node:sys-context-passing|Context Passing]])
Turn themes into product conclusions: problem, frequency, who is affected
Embed PM validation gates — points where a human checks the conclusion before use
Assemble the whole process into a reproducible [[node:pd-discovery-research|Discovery Research]] workflow
s4.validate: Themes yield clear conclusions stating the problem and its scale, passing through PM review.
s4.tip: Context is easily lost on large corpora — pass only the condensed essence between steps, not raw text.

s5.title: Verify the reliability of conclusions
s5.why: AI produces plausible but sometimes false themes. Without verification the team will decide based on a fabrication.
instructions: Take 5-10 interviews you know well and check AI conclusions against reality
Confirm each theme is backed by references to specific quotes
Note discrepancies and refine the synthesis prompts based on validation feedback
Document the working prompt patterns that produce reliable results
s5.validate: Conclusions match your manual understanding of familiar interviews, discrepancies resolved.
s5.tip: If AI "invented" a theme with no quotes — that's a signal to refine the prompt, not to ignore the error.

s6.title: Embed into the process and extend to ongoing feedback
s6.why: One-off synthesis goes stale. The scenario's value is a regular pipeline embedded in the team's work.
instructions: Scale synthesis to the full research backlog
Extend the pipeline to ongoing feedback ([[node:pd-feedback-synthesis|Feedback Synthesis]]), not just interviews
Train other PMs to run the pipeline themselves
Lock in a checklist: repository updated, then synthesis run, then conclusions pass validation, then decision
s6.validate: The pipeline runs on a regular data flow, several PMs use it, and a process checklist exists.
s6.tip: Assign an owner for maintaining the repository — without fresh data the pipeline quickly loses value.

uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.title: Enterprise AI Transformation Roadmap
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.subtitle: How to build a roadmap that moves a company from ad-hoc pilots to AI-native operations in 12 months
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.whatItIs: This is the highest-level scenario in the [[node:use-cases|Use Cases catalog]] — for CEOs, CIOs, and Heads of AI. The roadmap describes a company's full path from "doing AI pilots ad-hoc" to "AI-native company-wide operations": enterprise strategy, then tactical department roll-outs, then org-wide change with governance and ROI measurement. Horizon: 6-12 months of work.
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.approach: A roadmap is built not as a feature list but as a sequence of phases. First you decide whether transformation is even needed and what the target outcome is, then you honestly assess organizational readiness. Next comes prioritization of initiatives (which directions and in what order), launching pilots with quick wins, establishing governance and risk management, and only then scaling across the whole company. Key principle: directions are launched sequentially (one per quarter), not all at once.
outcomes: A 12-month roadmap document broken down by quarters with clear gates between phases
A prioritized list of tactical directions with rationale for the launch order
A governance framework and risk register in place before scaling begins, not after an incident
A set of metrics and a target ROI agreed with the executive team before the first pilot
A scaling-readiness checklist: what must be complete before expanding to a new direction

applyIn.title: Board and executive team
applyIn.description: The roadmap becomes the single document where the board sees where money goes, the expected ROI, and which risks are under control.

applyIn.title: Center of Excellence (CoE)
applyIn.description: A team of 3-5 people uses the roadmap as an operational plan: what to launch this quarter, what to measure, what to carry into the next.

applyIn.title: Department heads
applyIn.description: Each direction owner sees when their department enters the transformation and which quick wins are expected from the first pilot.

pitfalls: Launching all 4 tactical directions in parallel in Q1 — a recipe for chaos and team burnout
Starting pilots without an enterprise strategy and governance — incidents will later halt the whole program
Choosing the first direction because it is "trendy" rather than by ROI and data readiness
Failing to fix metrics before launch — six months in, there is nothing to prove the effect to the board
Assuming Stage 4 (full AI-native maturity) is reachable in 12 months — realistically it is from Stage 1 to Stage 3, with Stage 4 another 12-18 months

exercises.question: Your company is launching an AI transformation. You have executive buy-in and an 18-month budget. Where do you start in Q1 — with strategy and the CoE, or straight into two pilots?
exercises.hint: Recall the phase logic: pilots without strategy and governance are vulnerable to the first incident. Q1 is the foundation (strategy, CoE, governance) plus selecting the first directions — not launching them all.

exercises.question: You need to pick the first tactical direction for a pilot. Tier-1 support gives fast ROI, while marketing gives strategic impact. How do you decide?
exercises.hint: In a roadmap you usually take the direction with the highest and fastest ROI first (often Support tier-1) to get a quick win that funds the next phases. Strategic directions go second.

exercises.question: Six months in, the board asks what the transformation delivered. What should you have prepared at the very start to answer with numbers?
exercises.hint: Metrics and target ROI are fixed BEFORE the first pilot. Without baseline measurements you cannot show the uplift — this is built into the governance/measurement phase, not added retroactively.

s1.title: Define when a roadmap is needed and what the target outcome is
s1.why: A roadmap makes sense only when the company commits to transformation strategically, not by running isolated pilots. Without a clear goal and executive buy-in, any plan falls apart midway.
instructions: Check the preconditions: is there executive buy-in and a resource commitment ($M+ budget) for 12-24 months
State the target outcome: e.g., "company at Stage 3 AI-native operations in 12 months"
Define top-level target metrics: number of tactical directions, documented ROI, share of AI-proficient team
Make it explicit that this is a path from Stage 1 to Stage 3 in 12 months, with Stage 4 in the next 12-18 months (managing board expectations)
s1.validate: You have a one-page description of the roadmap goal with a measurable target state and confirmed executive buy-in.
s1.tip: If there is no executive buy-in or a 12+ month budget, this is not a roadmap but a single pilot. Do not launch a transformation without a commitment from the top.

s2.title: Run an organizational readiness audit
s2.why: You cannot prioritize initiatives without knowing the starting point. The audit shows which stage the company is at and where the bottlenecks are — data, skills, infrastructure.
instructions: Assess the current maturity stage: ad-hoc pilots, isolated teams, or some existing systematization
Check data and infrastructure readiness for each potential direction
Assess the team's AI proficiency and where upskilling is needed (talent strategy)
Record the presence or absence of a CoE, governance, and change-management processes
s2.validate: You have a readiness map: current stage, strong and weak zones across data, skills, and processes.
s2.tip: Honesty beats optimism. An inflated readiness estimate leads to choosing directions that fail due to poor data.

s3.title: Prioritize tactical initiatives and set the launch order
s3.why: The main transformation mistake is launching everything at once. Prioritization by ROI and readiness sets a sequence where each previous direction teaches the organization the next.
instructions: Build a list of candidate directions from the [[node:ai-native-enterprise|AI-native enterprise]] (support, operations, product, marketing)
Score each on two axes: size and speed of ROI, data/team readiness
Assign the order: 1 direction in Q1, the 2nd in Q2, the 3rd in Q3, the 4th in Q4
Take the fastest-ROI direction first (often Support tier-1), and the most strategic one second (Product or Marketing)
s3.validate: You have an ordered list of 4 directions with a rationale for the order based on ROI and readiness.
s3.tip: Each previous direction is a lesson for the organization. Sequential rollout is not about caution but about accumulating competence.

s4.title: Launch pilots and lock in quick wins
s4.why: A quick win in the first pilot proves value, funds the next phases, and creates momentum for company-wide change management.
instructions: Alongside the foundation from the [[node:en-transformation-strategy|enterprise transformation strategy]], form the CoE team (3-5 people)
Launch tactical pilot #1 on the highest-ROI direction, limiting scope to a narrow scenario
Launch pilot #2 on a strategic direction, start the change program and the AI upskilling roll-out
Document quick wins in money/time and use them as the argument for the next phase
s4.validate: Two pilots are launched, and there is at least one documented quick win with numbers.
s4.tip: Narrow the pilot scope aggressively. A tight scenario with a clear metric delivers a win faster than "AI for the whole department".

s5.title: Establish management, risks, and governance
s5.why: Without governance and a risk register, the first incident (leak, hallucination, reputation) will halt the whole program. Management must run ahead of scaling, not chase it.
instructions: Implement a governance framework: who makes decisions, which AI usage policies are mandatory
Set up a formal risk register: privacy, security, output quality, regulation
Set up ROI measurement: a baseline before the pilot and regular measurement over the first 6 months
Task the CoE with spreading best practices org-wide so directions do not repeat each other's mistakes
s5.validate: A governance framework, risk register, and ROI measurement system with a recorded baseline are in operation.
s5.tip: Governance is not bureaucracy but insurance. One uncontrolled public incident can freeze the entire transformation budget.

s6.title: Plan scaling and pass the checklist
s6.why: Scaling means adding new directions and moving toward maturity. A readiness checklist ensures you expand on a healthy foundation rather than replicating chaos.
instructions: Add directions #3 and #4 sequentially, building on the learnings from previous quarters
Run a strategy refresh: rebuild the roadmap based on actual results
Prepare an annual board report: ROI, new capabilities, risk status
Pass the expansion-readiness checklist: is ROI documented, does governance work, is the team 80%+ trained, are there no open critical risks
s6.validate: All 4 directions are launched, there is an annual board report, and the readiness checklist for the next maturity phase is passed.
s6.tip: Do not expand to a new direction until the previous one has passed the checklist. Skipping the readiness gate is the main reason transformations stall at Stage 2.

uc-ai-rag-launch.title: Launch a RAG System
uc-ai-rag-launch.subtitle: From "AI doesn't know our documents" to a working pipeline with citations in 6 steps
uc-ai-rag-launch.whatItIs: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is a pattern where the LLM retrieves relevant fragments from your knowledge base before answering, and responds strictly from them with [[node:cap-citations|citations]]. This course goes from deciding "do we need RAG" to a production pipeline: corpus prep, indexing, answer assembly, quality evaluation, and shipping to prod. It's the technical foundation of most AI projects in [[node:use-cases|use-cases]].
uc-ai-rag-launch.approach: We move from simple to reliable, but do NOT stop at Naive RAG. First we fix why RAG is needed and what we measure. Then we build the pipeline in layers: corpus, then embeddings + vector DB, then answer assembly with citations, then evaluation, then prod. At each step we check quality on real questions, not "by eye". The production minimum is chunking with overlap, hybrid search, and re-ranking — otherwise users will see "the AI says wrong things".
outcomes: You know when RAG is needed and when a plain prompt or fine-tuning is enough
A pipeline is built: corpus, then embeddings, then vector DB, then retrieval, then answer with citations
Every answer is backed by source links (citation rate 100%)
There is a measurable quality metric: retrieval relevance and hallucination level
The system ships to production via a checklist: latency, monitoring, corpus updates

applyIn.title: Support and internal knowledge base
applyIn.description: AI answers staff and customers from your policies and ticket history, not from the model's general knowledge — with a link to the exact document.

applyIn.title: Document work and compliance
applyIn.description: Finding answers across contracts, policies, regulations. Citations are critical: a reviewer must see where a fact comes from.

applyIn.title: Product docs and onboarding
applyIn.description: A user asks in natural language, RAG retrieves the exact docs fragment and answers from it instead of making them read the whole page.

pitfalls: Naive RAG in production: query, then vector, then top-K, then LLM yields 50-60% accuracy. You need re-ranking, hybrid search, chunk overlap, metadata filtering
Bad chunking: chunks too large blur relevance, too small lose context. Ignoring overlap loses meaning at boundaries
No quality evaluation: shipping "by eye" without measuring retrieval relevance and hallucinations — the system breaks silently
Answers without citations: users can't verify a fact and don't trust the system; you lose RAG's key edge over a bare LLM
Forgetting corpus updates: the index goes stale, RAG answers from old documents and presents outdated facts as truth

exercises.question: For your scenario: RAG, fine-tuning, or just a prompt with context? Justify the choice.
exercises.hint: RAG — when knowledge changes often and citations are needed. Fine-tuning — when style/format changes, not facts. Prompt with context — when there are few documents and they fit the window.

exercises.question: Take 10 real user questions and for each define which corpus fragment MUST land in the answer. This is your retrieval evaluation gold set.
exercises.hint: Without a gold question-answer set you can't measure relevance. Start with 10-20 pairs — enough for a first quality check.

exercises.question: Design chunking for one type of your documents: chunk size, overlap, which metadata to attach.
exercises.hint: Base it on document structure (paragraphs/sections), not a blind fixed character count. Metadata (source, date, section) is needed for filtering and citations.

s1.title: Decide: do you need RAG and what do you measure
s1.why: RAG is the most common production pattern, but not universal. Without a clear "why" and a metric, you'll build a pipeline you can't evaluate or improve.
instructions: State the problem: where exactly the LLM "doesn't know our facts" (documents, KB, history)
Check alternatives: is a prompt with context enough, or is fine-tuning needed — see [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG basics]]
Fix target metrics: answer accuracy, citation rate, latency per query
Describe the baseline: current accuracy without RAG (usually ~30%)
Define the application direction (Operations/Marketing/Support/Product/Enterprise)
s1.validate: You have a one-sentence "why RAG" and 3 measurable metrics with target values.
s1.tip: If knowledge barely changes and fits the context, you may not need RAG — a prompt is enough.

s2.title: Prepare the corpus: document chunking
s2.why: Retrieval quality is capped by chunk quality. Bad chunking is a ceiling on the whole system's accuracy that no re-ranking can fix.
instructions: Collect a pilot set of documents of one type (not the whole corpus at once)
Pick a chunking strategy: by semantic blocks (paragraphs/sections), not blindly by characters
Set chunk overlap so meaning isn't lost at fragment boundaries
Attach metadata to each chunk: source, date, section — for filtering and citations
Clean noise: navigation, footers, duplicates
s2.validate: Pilot documents are split into chunks with overlap and metadata; manually checking 5-10 chunks shows coherent meaning.
s2.tip: Start with pilot data, not the whole corpus — you'll spot chunking issues faster and redo them cheaper.

s3.title: Indexing: embeddings + vector DB
s3.why: Embeddings turn chunks into vectors for semantic similarity search. The vector DB stores them and enables fast retrieval — the heart of the pipeline.
instructions: Choose an embedding model fit for your documents' language and domain
Choose a vector DB: pgvector / Pinecone / Weaviate for your scale and stack
Run pilot chunks through embeddings and load vectors with metadata into the DB
Set up hybrid search (keyword + semantic), not vector search alone
Check retrieval on the gold questions from the exercise: do the right chunks land in top-K
s3.validate: For gold questions, the right chunk consistently lands in the top-K retrieval results.
s3.tip: Hybrid search covers pure vectors' weakness on exact terms, codes, and names — it almost always lifts relevance.

s4.title: Assemble the answer with citations
s4.why: Retrieval found fragments — but the answer must rely strictly on them and link to the source. Without [[node:cap-citations|citations]], users can't verify facts and don't trust the system.
instructions: Assemble the pipeline per [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG architecture]]: at least Advanced RAG, not Naive
Add re-ranking: re-sort top-K by relevance before passing to the LLM
Pass the retrieved context to the LLM with instruction to answer ONLY from it
Enable [[node:cap-citations|citations]]: every fact linked to a source from metadata
Add "I don't know" behavior when retrieval has no answer — instead of inventing one
s4.validate: On test questions the answer relies on retrieved fragments, includes citations, and honestly says "no data" when there is none.
s4.tip: Re-ranking is the cheapest quality lever: even a simple re-ranker noticeably lifts the relevance of top results.

s5.title: Evaluate quality: relevance and hallucinations
s5.why: Shipping "by eye" means the system breaks silently. You need numbers: how well retrieval fetches the right thing and how well answers stick to facts.
instructions: Run the gold question-answer set from the exercise through the pipeline
Measure retrieval relevance: does the right chunk land in top-K
Measure hallucination level: are there facts in answers without source backing
Check citation rate: does every answer link to a real fragment
Find weak spots and return to chunking (s2) or retrieval (s3) surgically
s5.validate: There is a metrics table over gold questions; accuracy approaches target (85%+), hallucinations are rare.
