pitfalls: One chunk_size for the whole corpus — a PDF contract and an FAQ need different treatment.
Splitting with no overlap — a boundary fact is lost between two vectors, neither is relevant.
Splitting structured blocks — a table or code block torn into pieces becomes meaningless.
Chunks without metadata — no citations and no filtering by tenant/language/date.
Changing strategy without a full re-index — old and new vectors of different sizes give unstable recall.

exercises.question: Take one of your documents (an article or markdown doc) and split it with a recursive splitter at chunk_size=256 and 512. Eyeball 3-4 chunks of each variant.
exercises.hint: Watch the boundaries: where is a fact cut in half? That is the argument for overlap.

exercises.question: Build a mini eval set of 5-10 questions against the corpus and measure recall@5 for two chunk_size values. Record which wins.
exercises.hint: If both are <70%, the problem isn't the size — it's overlap or blocks being split.

exercises.question: Find a document in your corpus with a table or code block and check whether the splitter tore it apart.
exercises.hint: If it did, that's a candidate for a document-aware strategy that protects blocks.

s1.title: Why chunking decides RAG quality
s1.why: Bad chunking breaks everything downstream, yet it gets fixed last — people swap the model first, even though chunk size is the culprit 60-70% of the time.
instructions: Learn the mechanics: a too-large chunk, then the embedding dilutes into an "average meaning" vector, top-N pulls in garbage.
A too-small chunk, then context is lost and the model has no idea what the fragment is about.
Tie this to [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG architecture]]: chunking sits before embedding and decides what is retrievable at all.
Adopt the rule: when someone says "RAG answers poorly," check chunking first, not the model.
s1.validate: You can explain in your own words why both a too-large and a too-small chunk hurt retrieval.
s1.tip: Keep the 60-70% figure in mind: that's the share of diagnoses rooted in chunking. It saves hours of "model tuning."

s2.title: The four splitting strategies
s2.why: Without understanding the differences you'll default to fixed-size — the simplest and most context-losing strategy.
instructions: Fixed-size: N tokens (usually 256-512) with 10-20% overlap. Simple and fast, but tears context at boundaries.
Recursive splitter (LangChain RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter): splits by paragraph, then sentence, then word until a piece fits. The best default for prose.
Semantic chunking: adjacent sentences are compared by embedding similarity, the boundary lands where similarity drops (topic shift). Costlier to ingest, more precise retrieval.
Document-aware: respects structure (markdown headings, HTML tags, code blocks). A chunk is a logical section, not an arbitrary window.
Remember the role of overlap: it preserves a fact that straddles two chunks.
s2.validate: You can name all four strategies and, in a word, each one's main trade-off (speed / context / cost / structure).
s2.tip: Overlap isn't a separate strategy but a parameter layered on fixed-size and recursive. 10-20% is the working range.

s3.title: How to choose a strategy by content
s3.why: The choice follows content type, not fashion: the wrong strategy bakes in weak retrieval that model tuning won't cure.
instructions: Prose / articles / docs, then recursive splitter, chunk_size 256-512. Fast and sufficient.
Mixed format (code + text), then document-aware with per-block-type splitting.
Long structured documents (contracts, research papers), then semantic chunking.
Tabular / structured data, then row-based splitting, not text-based.
FAQ-style content, then smaller chunk_size (128-256), technical docs, then larger (512-1024).
s3.validate: For three of your content types you can name a strategy and an approximate chunk_size with justification.
s3.tip: If you're torn between two options, that's a signal to A/B test, not to guess. An eval set answers more precisely than intuition.

s4.title: Example: a mixed corpus in practice
s4.why: A real corpus is almost always mixed (docs + Slack + PDF), and one strategy for everything is the most common mistake.
instructions: Markdown docs: recursive splitter with separators on headings (\n## , \n### ), chunk_size=512, overlap=80, length measured in tokens (tiktoken).
Slack threads: preserve message boundaries — don't split an individual message into pieces.
PDF contracts: SemanticChunker with a percentile breakpoint — it cuts on topic shifts.
Add universal metadata to every chunk: source_id, source_type, section, lang, updated_at, tenant_id.
Connect to the broader topic of [[node:ai-data-systems|AI data systems]]: chunking is one layer of the data infrastructure.
s4.validate: You have a plan: which strategy for which source and which metadata fields go on every chunk.
s4.tip: Bake metadata in from day one. Adding it later means re-indexing the whole corpus.

s5.title: Limits and risks: too large / too small
s5.why: Over- and under-chunking symptoms are easily mistaken for a "dumb model" — reading the signs saves a diagnostic cycle.
instructions: Under-chunking signs (too small): one document occupies 8 of the top-10, context is fragmented, the answer cites text mid-sentence.
Over-/large-chunking signs: retrieved chunks answer "almost your question," the embedding is diluted, irrelevant noise appears in results.
Cost risk: semantic chunking is 2-5x more expensive to ingest due to extra embedding calls for boundary detection.
Staleness risk: a doc is removed at the source but its chunks stay in the index — tied to [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG basics]] and pipeline refresh.
If recall is <70% on the eval set — A/B chunk_size (256/512/1024) and overlap (10%/20%) usually gains +10-15% without swapping the model.
s5.validate: Given a retrieval symptom you can say which way to turn chunk_size and estimate the cost of the semantic variant.
s5.tip: Don't confuse semantic chunking's expense with its necessity: for prose, recursive is almost always enough.

s6.title: Checklist and validation before indexing
s6.why: Most chunking mistakes are fixable only by a full re-index — it's cheaper to catch them on a checklist before launch.
instructions: Strategy chosen by source_type, not one for the whole corpus.
Overlap set (at least 10%) for fixed-size and recursive.
Structured blocks (tables, code) are kept intact.
Every chunk carries metadata: source_id, source_type, section, lang, updated_at, tenant_id.
An eval set exists and recall@5 is measured; on a strategy change a full re-index is planned, not a partial one.
s6.validate: All five checklist items are ticked and you have a baseline recall before going to production.
s6.tip: Keep this checklist next to the ingestion code — it outlives team and model changes.

sys-hybrid-search.title: Hybrid search: sparse + dense
sys-hybrid-search.subtitle: Keywords and meaning together — more accurate than either alone
sys-hybrid-search.whatItIs:
Hybrid search combines two signals: **sparse** (BM25 — exact words, names, versions, error codes) and **dense** ([[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]] — meaning, paraphrases, concepts). Each compensates for the other's weakness: dense loses exact terms, BM25 does not get "cancel sub" = "subscription termination". Together they give +10-25% recall@10 on typical RAG benchmarks vs pure dense.

This course is about the retrieval layer of [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG architecture]]: how to fuse two methods (RRF or weighted sum), when to add reranking, and how not to break everything without measuring quality.
sys-hybrid-search.approach: Do not believe that "dense is modern, BM25 is obsolete." They are not replacements — they are two different signals. Turn on hybrid with evaluation: first an eval set of 50-200 queries with ground truth, then measure recall@10 before and after. Without measurement you cannot tell whether hybrid helped or chunking broke.
outcomes: Understand that sparse and dense catch different query types and why you need both
Can fuse results via RRF (by rank) or weighted sum (by score with normalization)
Know when to add reranking and why only on the top 50-100, not the whole corpus
Can pick a setup: built-in hybrid (Weaviate, Qdrant) or pgvector + BM25 by hand
Can measure the gain via recall@10 / precision@5 and avoid turning hybrid on blindly

applyIn.title: Search over technical documentation
applyIn.description: Model names, versions, API methods, error codes — BM25 catches exact matches, dense catches paraphrased questions.

applyIn.title: Multilingual knowledge base
applyIn.description: Embeddings link query and document across languages, BM25 keeps exact terms and identifiers.

applyIn.title: Production RAG with short queries
applyIn.description: Users type keywords ("pgvector hnsw m parameter") — here the sparse signal is critical for quality.

pitfalls: Dense-only "because it is modern": a query "sonnet-4-5-20250929 deprecation" gets paraphrased to "model retirement" and loses the exact match — BM25 captures it.
Weighted sum without normalization: BM25 scores 0-15, cosine 0-1, the sum is dominated by BM25. Normalize (min-max) or use RRF (rank-based).
Reranking the whole corpus: a cross-encoder on 1M documents = $1000+ per query. Rerank only the top 50-100 after the first stage.
Hybrid without evaluation: you turn it on, recall does not grow, and the cause is unknown. Always use an eval set before/after, measure recall@10 and precision@5.
Ignoring filters: hybrid without `WHERE tenant_id = X` mixes tenant data. Search and metadata filters are orthogonal — you need both.

exercises.question: Take 10 real queries to your base. Split them into "exact" (names, versions, codes) and "semantic" (paraphrases, questions). Which method would win on each?
exercises.hint: Exact terms -> sparse (BM25). Paraphrases and concepts -> dense. A mix in the corpus -> you need hybrid.

exercises.question: Explain in plain terms why a weighted sum with BM25=12 and cosine=0.7 without normalization gives a bad result.
exercises.hint: Add the numbers directly: 12 vs 0.7. BM25 fully overrides the dense signal — α stops meaning anything.

exercises.question: You have recall@10 = 78% on dense-only. You turn on hybrid — it becomes 80%. Should you add a reranker, and what to check first?
exercises.hint: A small gain (< 5%) signals the problem may be in chunking, not search. Check document chunking first.

s1.title: Why hybrid: keywords + meaning
s1.why: A single signal always misses part of the queries. Dense loses exact terms, BM25 misses paraphrases. Hybrid closes both gaps at once.
instructions: Write down 2 failure cases for dense: exact terms (model names, error codes, person names) and rare words (out-of-vocabulary for the embedder).
Write down 2 failure cases for BM25: paraphrases ("cancel sub" vs "subscription termination") and conceptual queries.
Fix the benchmark number: hybrid gains +10-25% recall@10 vs pure dense on typical RAG benchmarks.
Tie it to [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG architecture]]: hybrid is the retrieval layer, before answer generation.
s1.validate: You can explain with two examples which query dense fails and which BM25 fails.
s1.tip: BM25 is what Google did for 20 years before neural search. "Old" does not mean "useless": on exact terms it beats embeddings.

s2.title: Sparse vs dense in plain terms
s2.why: To fuse two methods you must understand what each one measures and why their scores are not directly comparable.
instructions: Sparse (BM25): matches exact tokens, accounts for word frequency and rarity. Scores in roughly 0-15, not normalized.
Dense ([[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]]): query and document become vectors, closeness = cosine similarity in 0-1.
Key difference: BM25 sees letters and words, dense sees meaning. "MCP" and "Model Context Protocol" are different strings for BM25, close points for dense.
Remember the asymmetry: dense blurs exact-token matches that BM25 takes literally.
s2.validate: You can state the score ranges of BM25 and cosine, and why they cannot be added directly.
s2.tip: You will need this in the fusion step: the incomparability of scores is exactly why RRF is often simpler and more robust than weighted sum.

s3.title: How to fuse: fusion and re-rank
s3.why: Two result lists must merge into one ranking. The fusion method directly affects quality and how much tuning you will need.
instructions: RRF (Reciprocal Rank Fusion): each method returns top-N, ranks merge by `score = Σ 1/(k + rank_i)`, k=60. Works on ranks, not scores — no normalization needed.
Weighted sum: `final_score = α × dense_score + (1-α) × sparse_score`, α≈0.5 as a start. You must normalize scores (min-max), otherwise BM25 dominates.
Default start is RRF: simpler, no weights to tune, robust to different score scales.
Reranking (optional, +5-15% precision@5): feed the top 50-100 to a cross-encoder (Cohere Rerank, BGE-reranker), keep the top 5-10.
A cross-encoder reads query+document together — more accurate than the bi-encoder embedding, but more expensive and slower.
s3.validate: You can write RRF from memory and explain why weighted sum needs normalization while RRF does not.
s3.tip: The reranker is the most expensive part of the pipeline ($0.001/query with Cohere). So it goes last and works only over the already selected 50-100, not the whole corpus.

s4.title: How to apply in practice
s4.why: Architecture must land on a concrete stack. The choice depends on whether you have built-in hybrid or assemble it by hand.
instructions: Built-in hybrid: Weaviate, Qdrant (with FastEmbed), Elasticsearch + dense — hybrid out of the box, less code.
pgvector + BM25 by hand: `tsvector` for sparse + `pgvector` for dense, RRF in a SQL CTE — if you are already on Postgres.
Run BM25 and dense **in parallel**: latency ≈ max(times) ≈ 80-150ms, not the sum.
Add a reranker by budget: Cohere Rerank ($1/1k, 100-200ms, top quality) or BGE-reranker (self-host, free, slightly weaker). Total p95 ≈ 200-400ms.
This is part of the [[node:ai-data-systems|data systems]] and [[node:systems|systems]] around Claude — relevance retrieval before generation.
s4.validate: You have a chosen setup (built-in or pgvector) and a clear latency budget with and without reranker.
s4.tip: BM25 costs cents (CPU), a dense query is $0.00001. The real money goes to the reranker — enable it only if eval shows a precision@5 gain.

s5.title: Limits and risks
s5.why: Hybrid is not always a win. On some cases it adds nothing, and implementation mistakes silently break both quality and data safety.
instructions: When dense-only is enough: long natural-language questions, narrow domain with a fine-tuned embedder, < 10k documents (hybrid gain is small).
When hybrid is essential: technical content (names, versions, error codes), multilingual data, short keyword queries, recall < 80% on dense-only.
Risk #1 — weighted sum without normalization: BM25 overrides dense. Use RRF or normalize.
Risk #2 — reranker on the whole corpus: $1000+ per query. Top 50-100 only.
Risk #3 — ignoring filters: hybrid without `WHERE tenant_id = X` mixes tenant data. Search and metadata filters are both needed.
s5.validate: You can name a case where hybrid is not needed and three implementation mistakes that silently break the result.
s5.tip: The reranker landscape moves fast: Cohere is the 2026-05 baseline, but check current alternatives before choosing.

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: Hybrid without evaluation is faith, not engineering. An eval set turns "feels better" into measurable recall@10 and precision@5.
instructions: Build an eval set: 50-200 real helpful queries with ground truth (which document is correct).
Measure the baseline: recall@10 on dense-only.
Turn on hybrid (RRF), measure recall@10 again. Target norm > 85%.
If using a reranker — measure precision@5 after it (target > 70%) and p95 latency (< 400ms).
If the gain is < 5% — do not celebrate and do not blame search: check chunking, the problem is likely in document splitting.
s6.validate: You have recall@10 numbers before/after and a decision: hybrid helped, or the problem is in another RAG layer.
s6.tip: A/B without vs with hybrid on the same eval set is the only honest way to prove the gain. Without numbers any "it got better" is an illusion.

sys-document-pipelines.title: Document ingestion pipelines
sys-document-pipelines.subtitle: ETL for documents that feed RAG: from source to a vector in the index
sys-document-pipelines.whatItIs: A document ingestion pipeline is a continuously running conveyor that pulls documents from sources (Notion, Confluence, Drive, GitHub, Zendesk), parses, normalizes, deduplicates, chunks, computes embeddings, and writes them into a [[node:sys-rag-architecture|vector store]]. Not a one-off script but a service with incremental sync, deletion handling, retries, and monitoring.
sys-document-pipelines.approach: We follow the real lifecycle of a document: first understand why a continuous pipeline is needed (rather than a one-shot script), then walk the full chain extraction, then cleanup, then chunking, then embeddings, then index, add incremental updates and deletion handling, build a minimal event-driven architecture, examine the limits and risks (garbage in, duplicates, drift), and close with a checklist of metrics.
outcomes: You understand why RAG degrades within weeks without a pipeline and how incremental sync differs from a nightly full re-sync
You know every stage of the chain: extraction, normalization, dedup, chunking, embedding, upsert — and what each one does
You can design incremental updates via webhooks + polling fallback and handle deletions correctly
You see the typical risks — garbage in, duplicates, no embedding version-tracking — and know how to close them
You have a metrics checklist (ingestion lag, parse-failure rate, dedup rate, deletion latency) to check pipeline health

applyIn.title: Production RAG over a corporate knowledge base
applyIn.description: Confluence + Zendesk + GitHub Wiki, where documents change daily and the index must reflect the current state without manual runs.

applyIn.title: A support bot with compliance requirements
applyIn.description: A deleted or stale document must not be cited: you need hard delete, tombstones, and a GDPR audit log.

applyIn.title: Migrating or switching the embedding model
applyIn.description: When the vectorization model changes and you need version-tracking so the index doesn't end up half on old and half on new vectors.

pitfalls: Nightly full re-sync as the only strategy: for 100k+ docs that's hours of compute and a stale index 23 hours a day — you need incremental + weekly full
Not handling deletions: a doc removed at the source stays in the index, then answers linking to a 404 and a privacy issue
Parsing without error handling: one corrupted PDF breaks the whole batch — per-document try/except and a dead-letter queue are mandatory
No deduplication: the same FAQ from 3 sources returns 3 identical hits and erodes trust
Embeddings without version-tracking: after a model swap half the index is on old vectors, half on new, then search degrades

exercises.question: You have 200k Confluence docs and ~500 change per day. Why is a nightly full re-sync a poor strategy, and what should you pick instead?
exercises.hint: Compare cost and freshness: how many compute hours 200k docs take and how long per day the index is stale. Think webhook-driven incremental + a rare full re-sync as catch-up.

exercises.question: A document was deleted at the source. Describe what must happen in the pipeline so it stops being cited, and the difference between soft and hard delete.
exercises.hint: A deletion signal (webhook or periodic diff), then an action in the [[node:sys-rag-architecture|vector store]]. Soft delete = tombstone + filter, hard delete = DELETE + audit for compliance.

exercises.question: RAG recall has slowly dropped for a month with no obvious cause. Which pipeline metrics do you check first?
exercises.hint: Drift often = the pipeline silently broke. Look at ingestion lag, parse-failure rate, connector status, embedding version-tracking, and dedup rate.

s1.title: Why you need a continuous pipeline
s1.why: Without understanding why a one-shot script fails in production, it's easy to build a demo that degrades within weeks. This step sets up the whole motivation of the course.
instructions: Examine three ways RAG degrades without a pipeline: new docs never reach the index, deleted ones answer like ghosts, updated ones return stale info
Articulate the difference: one-shot ingestion works for the demo, production needs incremental sync, deletion propagation, retries on flaky sources, and monitoring
List 4 signals of a broken pipeline: outdated info, citing a deleted document, duplicates in results, recall dropping with no cause (drift)
Place the pipeline in the system: it's the ingestion layer inside [[node:ai-data-systems|data systems]] under the [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG architecture]]
s1.validate: You can explain with one example exactly how a RAG answer becomes wrong if the pipeline stops for a week.
s1.tip: Plan the pipeline the moment RAG ships to production — "we'll add it later" almost never arrives.

s2.title: The chain: extraction, then cleanup, then chunking, then embeddings, then index
s2.why: Each stage solves its own task, and an error at an early stage (garbage parsing) poisons everything downstream. You need to see the whole conveyor.
instructions: Extraction: parse by type — PDF (PyMuPDF, Unstructured), HTML (BeautifulSoup, trafilatura), Office (python-docx), Markdown
Normalization: Unicode NFC, strip boilerplate (nav, footer), language detection, fix encoding
Deduplication: full-text hash + near-dup detection (MinHash / SimHash) for versioned copies of one document
Chunking, then embeddings: split by the source's strategy (see [[node:sys-chunking-strategies|chunking strategies]]), then compute vectors in batches
Upsert to the index: write chunks with embeddings into the [[node:sys-rag-architecture|vector store]] along with metadata (source, doc_id, model version)
s2.validate: For each of the 5 stages you can name its input, output, and one characteristic failure mode.
s2.tip: Garbage in, garbage out: normalization quality directly determines search quality — don't skimp on stripping boilerplate.

s3.title: Incremental updates and deletion handling
s3.why: This is the heart of a production pipeline: incremental sync keeps the index fresh without full re-indexing, and deletion handling closes privacy/compliance gaps.
instructions: Webhook-driven (preferred): Notion, Linear, GitHub fire events, then enqueue, then process, source-to-index latency 1-10 minutes
Polling fallback for sources without webhooks: cursor by `updated_at` + diff, interval 5 min — 1 h depending on volume
Weekly full re-sync as catch-up for missed events and to fight data drift — expensive but mandatory
Deletion: soft delete (tombstone + filter `is_deleted = false`) for speed, hard delete (DELETE from the index) for GDPR with a mandatory audit
The mechanics of syncing sources are covered in [[node:sys-data-sync|data sync]]
s3.validate: You can draw the path of one update and one deletion from source to index with latency annotated.
s3.tip: Periodic reconciliation (diff against the source) catches deletions the webhook missed — without it your tombstones will be incomplete.

s4.title: How to build the pipeline (event-driven skeleton)
s4.why: Theory without a minimal skeleton doesn't run. Here we assemble the event-driven architecture that can scale.
instructions: Connectors publish events to a queue: `{source, doc_id, action: upsert|delete}` (e.g. via SQS)
Worker on `delete`: removes chunks by filter `{source, doc_id}` from the index and writes to audit_log
Worker on `upsert`: fetch, then parse, then normalize, then compare the text sha256 with the previous hash, skip if equal
On change: chunk by source strategy, then embed_batch, then delete the document's old chunks, then upsert new ones, then save the new hash
Parse failures and exhausted retries go to a dead-letter queue with an alert when failure rate > 1%
s4.validate: You have a working loop where reprocessing an unchanged document writes nothing to the index (idempotent via hash).
s4.tip: Hashing the text before chunking is the cheapest way to avoid recomputing embeddings for unchanged documents.

s5.title: Limits and risks: garbage in, duplicates, drift
s5.why: Pipelines break quietly: a connector dies, embeddings split across versions, duplicates pile up. You need to know the limits and close the risks ahead of time.
instructions: Garbage in: one corrupted PDF must not kill the batch — per-document try/except + dead-letter queue, alert above 1% failures
Duplicates: exact hash match, then drop; MinHash similarity > 0.95, then keep the newer one, mark as duplicate (normal dedup rate 5-15%)
Embedding versions: track `embedding_model_version` in metadata + a migration plan, otherwise half the index sits on the old model
Drift: weekly full re-sync + an alert on ingestion lag so a dead connector doesn't freeze the index unnoticed
Retries on flaky sources — exponential backoff so you don't slam into the source's rate limits
s5.validate: For each of the 4 risks (garbage, duplicates, embedding versions, drift) you can name a concrete defense mechanism.
s5.tip: The sneakiest risk is no embedding version-tracking: the problem isn't visible right away and shows up as search degradation weeks later.

s6.title: Checklist and pipeline health check
s6.why: A pipeline without metrics is a black box. The final step turns everything above into an observable system you can actually verify.
instructions: Freshness metric: ingestion lag (norm < 5 min from source to index)
Parsing reliability metric: parse-failure rate (< 1%), alert when exceeded
Dedup metric: dedup rate (norm 5-15%) — a sharp rise signals a new duplicating source
Deletion metric: deletion latency and matching the tombstone count with deletions at the source
Final run: update a document at the source and confirm the new RAG answer reflects the change within the SLA
s6.validate: You have a dashboard or list of 4+ metrics and can tell within a minute whether the pipeline is healthy.
s6.tip: Tie an alert not only to errors but to "silence": zero ingestion while sources are alive is a sign of a dead connector.

sys-multi-agent-patterns.title: Multi-Agent: 4 patterns of teamwork
sys-multi-agent-patterns.subtitle: When you need multiple agents and how to pick a pattern: supervisor-worker, parallel, pipeline, debate
sys-multi-agent-patterns.whatItIs: A course on how several AI agents work together instead of one. We break down the 4 core coordination patterns — supervisor-worker (boss + helpers), parallel fan-out, pipeline, and debate/critique — and learn to choose the right one for a task without creating needless complexity.
sys-multi-agent-patterns.approach: We move from the question "do you even need multiple agents" to a breakdown of each pattern, then to the selection rule, a live example, and the limits (cost, coordination). One principle: one main pattern per task, everything else is a tool inside it. We build on [[node:ai-orchestration|agent orchestration]] and [[node:systems|AI systems]].
outcomes: Tell the 4 multi-agent patterns apart and understand the purpose of each
Decide when a task truly needs multiple agents versus when one is enough
Pick a pattern by the task signal (splittability, differing viewpoints, iterative quality, external data)
Assess the cost of a scheme: call expense, coordination complexity, looping risk
Assemble a working multi-agent workflow from a checklist without mixing patterns

applyIn.title: Content and copy
applyIn.description: Landing pages, email campaigns, articles — the debate/critic pattern lifts a draft from "okay" to "almost done" in a couple of iterations.

applyIn.title: Large-scale data analysis
applyIn.description: 100 interviews, 5 competitors, a stack of documents — supervisor-worker and parallel split the work into independent chunks and assemble the result.

applyIn.title: Support and routing
applyIn.description: Classifying a request and routing it to a specialized agent — pipeline and supervisor-worker handle routine tickets predictably.

pitfalls: Mixing several patterns in one system — many parallel agents, expensive, impossible to tell what broke
Reflection/debate with no iteration limit — agents loop forever, set a cap of 2-3 rounds
Using debate for simple tasks — two agents arguing over the obvious is a waste of money
Jumping straight to a complex scheme instead of debugging one simple pattern over 5-10 tasks
Using multiple agents where one would do — extra cost and coordination with no quality gain

exercises.question: Your task: analyze 80 survey responses and extract common themes. Which pattern do you pick and why?
exercises.hint: Think about whether the task splits into independent chunks and who assembles the result. See [[node:sys-parallel-fan-out|parallel fan-out]].

exercises.question: A team wants "AI writes, then AI critiques, then rewrites, then critiques again..." with no limits. What's the risk and how do you close it?
exercises.hint: This is the reflection/debate pattern. What happens without a cap on the number of rounds?

exercises.question: Name one task signal for each of the 4 patterns in a single word or phrase.
exercises.hint: Splittability, differing viewpoints, iterative quality, external data — map them to supervisor-worker, debate, reflection, tool-using.

s1.title: When do you even need multiple agents
s1.why: Multi-agent always means more calls and more coordination. Before building a team of agents, make sure one agent genuinely can't do the job. Otherwise you pay for complexity with no gain.
instructions: State the task and ask: can one agent do this in a single pass at acceptable quality?
Check the 4 "team needed" signals: the task splits into independent chunks; differing viewpoints matter; quality improves with iteration; external data/tools are required
If none of the signals fire — stay with one agent, don't overcomplicate
If at least one fires — note which: it points to the pattern in step 3
s1.validate: You have a clear answer of "yes, multiple agents needed" with a concrete signal, or "no, one is enough".
s1.tip: The cost and complexity of multi-agent are justified by saving your time and raising quality — but not always. When in doubt, start with one agent.

s2.title: Breaking down the 4 patterns
s2.why: Without knowing the patterns, every project reinvents the wheel. With them, naming the scheme is enough for the team to know what to build. It's a shared vocabulary for agent coordination.
instructions: Supervisor-worker: a boss agent splits the task, specialist helpers do the parts, the boss assembles the result. See [[node:sys-supervisor-worker|supervisor-worker]]
Parallel (fan-out): one task is broken into identical chunks, agents process them in parallel, results are merged. See [[node:sys-parallel-fan-out|parallel fan-out]]
Pipeline: agents are lined up in a conveyor — one's output is the next one's input (classify, then process, then format)
Debate/discussion: several agents produce different options or critique each other, a separate agent picks the best or merges the strengths
For each pattern, write one word for its purpose: splittability / scale / stages / quality-through-comparison
s2.validate: You can describe each of the 4 patterns in your own words and name what it's for.
s2.tip: Tool-using (an agent with tools) is often embedded inside any pattern — it's not a separate team but an agent's ability to pull external data.

s3.title: How to choose a pattern
s3.why: The wrong pattern makes a system expensive, slow and undebuggable. The right one makes it predictable and cheap to maintain. The choice flows from the task signal, not from trends.
instructions: Take the signal you found in step 1 and map it to a pattern
Task splits into different subtasks, then supervisor-worker; splits into identical chunks at scale, then parallel
Task passes through clear stages in sequence, then pipeline; needs differing viewpoints or iterative quality, then debate
Pick EXACTLY one main scheme. If you need more, add a second as a small tool inside the first, not as parallel work
Cross-check against orchestration principles: [[node:ai-orchestration|agent orchestration]]
s3.validate: You have one main pattern chosen for the task, justified by the signal, with no mixing of schemes.
s3.tip: If a task sounds like "both" — it almost always means one pattern on the outside and a second as a nested step, not two parallel systems.

s4.title: Example: walking through a working workflow
s4.why: A pattern only clicks on a concrete scenario. Running one example end to end cements how agents hand work off to each other.
instructions: Take a support task: an incoming request must be classified and routed to the right specialist — this is pipeline + supervisor-worker
Step 1: a coordinator agent receives the message and determines the type (password / billing / bug / complaint)
Step 2: routes to a specialized worker — each has its own data and instructions; complex cases and complaints, then a human
Step 3: the worker does its part and returns the answer; the coordinator formats it and sends it to the customer
Trace where control passes between agents — that's the handoff protocol. See [[node:sys-handoff-protocols|handoff protocols]]
s4.validate: You can sketch the example flow step by step and show the point where one agent hands work to another.
s4.tip: When classification breaks, debug the coordinator, not the whole system — that's the power of explicit role separation.

s5.title: Limits and risks: cost and coordination
s5.why: Several agents make more calls than one and require coordination. Ignore the limits and multi-agent becomes an expensive system you can't debug.
instructions: Estimate cost: each agent = separate calls; a team of 4 costs noticeably more than one
Set an iteration limit for debate/reflection (2-3 rounds), or agents loop for hours
Check observability: can you tell which agent failed without dissecting the whole system
Weigh the gain against the cost: quality rose from "okay" to "slight tweak", edit time dropped 1.5-2x — does that cover the higher cost
If coordination is harder than the task itself — simplify the scheme or go back to one agent
s5.validate: You have a cost estimate for the scheme, an iteration cap, and an answer on whether the system is debuggable.
s5.tip: Starting rule: begin with the simplest pattern (often tool-using or supervisor-worker), debug it over 5-10 tasks, then add complexity.

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: A final pass over the checklist catches the main mistakes before launch: mixed patterns, missing limits, needless complexity. It's insurance before the system goes live.
instructions: The task signal is identified, and it genuinely requires multiple agents (one wouldn't do)
Exactly one main pattern is chosen; nested schemes only as a tool inside, not in parallel
An iteration cap is set for debate/reflection
Cost is estimated and justified by the gain in quality/time
The system is debuggable: it's clear which agent owns what and where control passes. Related to agents: [[node:agents|agents]]
s6.validate: Every checklist item is ticked, and you can explain why you chose this scheme and where its limits are.
s6.tip: If even one item is "no" — don't launch. The failure usually hides in mixed patterns or a missing iteration limit.

sys-supervisor-worker.title: Supervisor-worker pattern
sys-supervisor-worker.subtitle: One orchestrator delegates subtasks to specialized agents
sys-supervisor-worker.whatItIs: Supervisor-worker is a [[node:sys-multi-agent-patterns|multi-agent]] architecture where one **supervisor** accepts a task, splits it into parts, and delegates them to domain-specific **worker agents**. Each worker is narrow: its own system prompt and 2-5 tools. The supervisor never does specialized work itself — it only decomposes, routes, and synthesizes the final answer. It is a form of [[node:ai-orchestration|orchestration]] with strictly separated roles.
sys-supervisor-worker.approach: Don't build a do-everything agent. Start with a supervisor that executes nothing itself plus 2-3 workers with clean boundaries. Routing goes through [[node:sys-branching-logic|branching logic]], task passing through a structured [[node:sys-handoff-protocols|handoff]]. Test each worker in isolation first, then wire the loop and measure the bottleneck — the supervisor itself.
outcomes: Know when supervisor-worker is justified vs. when prompt chaining or fan-out suffices
Designed a supervisor: decompose, then delegate, then synthesize, with no specialized execution
Defined 2-3 workers with non-overlapping boundaries and narrow tool sets
Built the loop: plan, then sequential worker calls, then synthesis with an audit trail
Set the limits: max-depth, max-workers-per-turn, latency and cost control

applyIn.title: Research agent
applyIn.description: The supervisor delegates: web research, then data analysis, then writing the brief. Each stage is a separate worker with its own tools.

applyIn.title: Customer ops
applyIn.description: CRM lookup, ticket creation, email draft — three workers; the supervisor assembles the customer reply.

applyIn.title: Code assistant
applyIn.description: File search, test runs, code generation, linting. Natively implemented via [[node:cc-subagents|Claude Code sub-agents]].

pitfalls: The supervisor does worker tasks itself — the prompt bloats and orchestration focus is lost. Rule: delegate and synthesize only.
Workers with overlapping duties — the supervisor can't decide whom to call, duplicate calls, 2x cost. Draw clear domain/action boundaries.
Infinite recursive delegation — a worker becomes a supervisor with no limit. Hard max-depth = 2, usually 1.
Passing between workers as raw text with no schema — format drifts ~10% of the time. Use a structured [[node:sys-handoff-protocols|handoff]] only.
Supervisor-worker on a simple task — the overhead isn't justified. One type of task = one agent with the right tools.

exercises.question: Take the task "build a B2B brief on a company" (financials + leadership + news + fit score). Lay out which workers you need and where the boundaries between them are.
exercises.hint: 4 workers with non-overlapping sources. If two workers fetch the same data, the boundaries are wrong.

exercises.question: For the same workers, estimate the latency of a sequential loop (~3s per call) and decide: is the pattern fit for interactive UX or do you need [[node:sys-parallel-fan-out|fan-out]]?
exercises.hint: Sequential latency = the sum of all calls. 4 × 3s = 12s — that's a lot for interactive.

exercises.question: Find a task in your project where you currently use one big agent with 10+ tools. Decide whether to split it into supervisor-worker and justify it.
exercises.hint: The test is 3+ different kinds of expertise AND steps that can't be rigidly fixed. Otherwise [[node:sys-prompt-chaining|prompt chaining]] is enough.

s1.title: What the pattern is and when to use it
s1.why: One agent with 20 tools and a 5000-token prompt confuses which tool to call and loses focus. Supervisor-worker is divide-and-conquer, but it isn't always justified — distinguishing it from neighboring patterns matters.
instructions: Memorize the essence: the supervisor decomposes and synthesizes; workers execute narrow tasks.
Check the applicability test: the task needs 3+ different kinds of expertise AND the steps can't be fixed up front.
Rule out alternatives: one type of task, then one agent; rigid sequence, then [[node:sys-prompt-chaining|prompt chaining]]; parallel identical tasks, then [[node:sys-parallel-fan-out|fan-out]].
Fix in mind that the supervisor is a sequential dispatcher, not parallel.
s1.validate: You can state in one sentence why it's supervisor-worker and not chaining/fan-out/a single agent.
s1.tip: If the task's steps are always the same and run in order, it isn't supervisor-worker — it's a chain.

s2.title: The supervisor's role
s2.why: The supervisor is the orchestration brain. If it starts executing tasks itself, the prompt bloats and routing quality drops. Its job is strictly three actions: decompose, delegate, assemble.
instructions: Pick a stronger model: Sonnet/Opus — the supervisor reasons, it doesn't pinch tokens.
Describe in the system prompt (~1-2k tokens) the available workers and when to call which — this is [[node:sys-branching-logic|routing logic]].
Forbid the supervisor from doing specialized work: its tools are worker invocations (3-7), not subject-matter tools.
Add a synthesis mode: the supervisor aggregates worker outputs into the final answer.
s2.validate: The supervisor prompt contains no subject-matter tool — only delegation and synthesis.
s2.tip: A good supervisor reads like a dispatcher: "given X, then call workers A and B, then assemble the answer", with no "how" to do the subtask.

s3.title: The workers' role
s3.why: Workers are executors. Their strength is narrowness: short prompt, few tools, high accuracy on their domain. Fuzzy or overlapping workers break routing and double the cost.
instructions: Split responsibility by domain or action so the boundaries don't overlap.
Give each worker its own system prompt (500-1500 tokens) and 2-5 tools, no more.
Match the model to the task: simple lookup, then Haiku, reasoning/analysis, then Sonnet.
Give each worker its own eval set so you can test it in isolation (see [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|evals]]).
s3.validate: For any subtask it's unambiguous which single worker owns it.
s3.tip: If two workers fetch from the same data source, that's a signal to merge them or redraw the boundaries.

s4.title: How to wire the loop
s4.why: Wiring turns the supervisor and workers into a working system: plan, then calls, then synthesis. Without an audit trail you can't debug "why is the result weak."
instructions: Step 1: the supervisor returns a delegation plan from the input (which workers and with what input).
Step 2: call the workers from the plan sequentially, collecting results into a shared dict.
Step 3: pass results between workers and back via a structured [[node:sys-handoff-protocols|handoff]], not raw text.
Step 4: the supervisor in synthesis mode builds the final answer; return it together with the full trail (plan + results) for [[node:sys-logging-patterns|logging]].
s4.validate: For a single request you can reconstruct: the plan, each worker call, retries, and the final synthesis.
s4.tip: Passing between workers is always by schema — otherwise the format drifts about 10% of the time.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks: the supervisor bottleneck
s5.why: The supervisor is a sequential dispatcher, so it's also the bottleneck: latency accumulates, recursive delegation risks an infinite loop, and each extra worker adds cost.
instructions: Set a hard max-depth = 2 (usually 1): the supervisor doesn't call workers that are themselves supervisors.
Cap max workers per turn at 3-5; if there are more, switch to [[node:sys-parallel-fan-out|fan-out]].
Compute latency: sequential = the sum of all worker calls (4 × 3s = 12s) — assess whether it fits interactive UX.
Budget the cost: supervisor reasoning + executions ≈ 1.5-2.5x one big agent, but quality is higher.
Add metrics ([[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]]): delegation depth, worker success rate, retries per worker.
s5.validate: The system explicitly states max-depth, the per-turn worker cap, and the metrics you watch for degradation.
s5.tip: When latency grows and order isn't required, move the most independent workers into a parallel fan-out.

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: Before shipping you must confirm that roles are separated, boundaries are clean, limits are set, and the system is debuggable. This step closes all the pattern's typical mistakes.
instructions: Supervisor: does no specialized work, only decompose/delegate/synthesize — check the prompt.
Workers: boundaries don't overlap, each has a narrow tool set and its own eval.
Limits: max-depth and max-workers-per-turn are set; recursion is impossible.
Handoff: task and result passing is structured, not raw text.
Observability: there's a full trail and metrics ([[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]]) for debugging.
s6.validate: All five checklist items are ticked, and you can explain why your supervisor-worker beats one big agent on this task.
s6.tip: If even one item is "no," it's a future production incident. Close it before shipping, not after.

sys-parallel-fan-out.title: Parallel fan-out (map-reduce)
sys-parallel-fan-out.subtitle: Split a task into independent chunks, process them in parallel, assemble the result
sys-parallel-fan-out.whatItIs: Map-reduce for AI: one large task is split into N independent subtasks (map), each processed in parallel by a separate model call, then the results are aggregated into a single answer (reduce). Canonical scenarios: corpus processing, multi-source research, multi-judge eval, variant generation. The pattern lives inside [[node:ai-orchestration|orchestration]] and relies on [[node:systems|production-systems]] discipline.
sys-parallel-fan-out.approach: The course goes from deciding whether you even need fan-out to a working map -> reduce pipeline with partial-failure handling. First we verify subtask independence, then build the map phase with a concurrency limiter, choose a reduce strategy, walk through a real example over 50 conversations, draw the boundaries (cost, duplicates, assembly), and close with a checklist that verifies coverage.
outcomes: Tell tasks where fan-out actually speeds things up from sequential chains where it is useless or harmful
Build a map phase with a concurrency limiter (semaphore) and exponential-backoff retries
Pick a reduce strategy — synthesis call, programmatic merge, or voting/averaging — by task type
Handle partial failures via a success threshold (80%) instead of all-or-nothing
Understand the economics: when to switch to the Message Batches API for a 50% discount and a separate limit pool

applyIn.title: Corpus processing
applyIn.description: 100+ pages, conversations, or tickets need summarize / classify / extract. Map is an independent call per item; reduce synthesizes the themes.

applyIn.title: Multi-source research and analytics
applyIn.description: 5-20 sources analyzed in parallel, then aggregated into one brief. Cheaper and faster than reading everything in one long context.

applyIn.title: Multi-judge evaluation
applyIn.description: Several critics score one output in parallel, results averaged. Diversity of perspective with no latency growth.

pitfalls: Running the map phase without a concurrency limiter: 100 simultaneous calls -> 429 storm -> retry amplification -> real throughput worse than sequential. A semaphore is mandatory.
Going sequential where subtasks are independent: a chain of 5 summaries takes 15s instead of 3s. Analyze dependencies explicitly.
Aggregating via plain concat with no synthesis call: 100 summaries glued into a document is a 'mix,' not insight.
All-or-nothing on failures: one crashed worker drops the whole job and loses the work of 99 successful ones. Use a success threshold.
Paying 100% for batch workloads: nightly classification, eval suites, bulk extraction belong in the Message Batches API (50% cheaper, separate limit pool).

exercises.question: You have 200 customer reviews; you need the theme and sentiment of each, then the top 10 pain points. Where is map and where is reduce here, and why is this not a sequential task?
exercises.hint: Extracting from one review does not depend on the others — that is map. The top 10 needs all themes at once — that is reduce. Subtask independence is the fan-out criterion.

exercises.question: You launched 100 parallel calls and got an avalanche of 429 errors; throughput dropped below sequential. What did you forget to add, and how do you fix it?
exercises.hint: A concurrency limiter (semaphore around 10) + retry with exponential backoff. See [[node:sys-rate-limiting|rate limiting]].

exercises.question: Out of 50 map calls, 6 failed. Should you fail the whole job? What rule applies?
exercises.hint: 44/50 = 88% > 80% threshold -> continue, note missing items in coverage. All-or-nothing would discard 44 good results.

s1.title: When you need fan-out: the independence check
s1.why: Fan-out only speeds things up if subtasks are truly independent. If B depends on A's result, there is nothing to parallelize — you get a race or garbage. A wrong call here breaks the whole pipeline.
instructions: Frame the task as a set of subtasks and draw the dependencies between them with arrows
Mark subtasks that can run knowing nothing about the others' results — those are map candidates
Check the scale: one small request does not justify orchestration overhead — fan-out pays off from ~10 items
If there are sequential chains (B after A), pull them outside fan-out; parallelize only the independent layer
s1.validate: You can name concrete subtasks, none of which reads another's output, and there are more than ~10 of them.
s1.tip: Independence test: if you shuffle the execution order of the subtasks, does the result change? No -> you can parallelize.

s2.title: Map phase: parallel processing with a limiter
s2.why: Map is N independent model calls. Without a concurrency limiter they drown the tier in 429s; with the right semaphore and backoff you get a near-free 10x speedup.
instructions: Set up an asyncio.Semaphore (or equivalent) with a sane cap — typically 10 concurrent calls
Wrap each worker in try/except and return an ok/failed status instead of crashing the whole batch
Add retry with exponential backoff for 429 and transient errors
Pick a cheap fast model (Haiku) for map — the volume of work here is large
Store the item's id/index in the result so you can restore order later
s2.validate: A run over 20-30 items causes no 429 flood, and each result carries an id and an ok/failed status.
s2.tip: The parallelism cap depends on tier ([[node:pl-rate|rate limits]]) — start at 10 and raise it while watching for 429s.

s3.title: Reduce phase: choosing the assembly strategy
s3.why: Reduce turns scattered partial results into one meaningful answer. The wrong strategy (just glue them) yields a 'mix' instead of insight. The strategy is chosen by task type.
instructions: Synthesis call — a separate strong-model call (Sonnet) that synthesizes all map results into a coherent answer: best quality, +1 LLM call
Programmatic merge — dedup, sort, top-N in code with no model: cheap, for structured outputs
Voting / averaging — for evaluation and classification: average several critics' scores
Before reduce, sort results by id/index — otherwise random order breaks reproducibility
s3.validate: For your task one reduce strategy is chosen and you can explain why the other two do not fit.
s3.tip: If the output is an insight in text — almost always a synthesis call. If a number or a list — programmatic merge.

s4.title: End-to-end example: 50 conversations -> themes and pains
s4.why: Tying map and reduce into one working pipeline with failure handling is the point of the course. A real example shows how the chunks fit together.
instructions: MAP: asyncio.gather over 50 conversations, each extract_themes under semaphore(10), Haiku, returns {conv_id, themes, status}
Check coverage: succeeded / total; if < 80%, fail the job, otherwise continue
REDUCE: collect all themes from the successes, sort them, one Sonnet call with a synthesize prompt
Return the report together with coverage (e.g. 47/50) so completeness is visible
For 1000+ items rewrite map onto the Message Batches API — submit, fetch in 1-2h
s4.validate: The pipeline returns a synthesized report and a coverage metric; a few worker failures do not bring down the whole run.
s4.tip: Coverage in the output is cheap trust insurance: the reader instantly sees how much data the conclusion rests on.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks: cost, duplicates, assembly
s5.why: Fan-out is not magic: 100 parallel calls cost 100x in tokens. Without understanding the economics and failure modes the pattern turns into an expensive, fragile construct.
instructions: Cost: wall time drops but cost grows linearly with the number of calls — budget ahead, see [[node:sys-cost-management|cost management]]
Batches: for non-realtime workloads switch to the Message Batches API — 50% discount, separate limit pool, latency 5min-24h
Duplicates and order: parallel results arrive out of order — sort by id; dedup themes during reduce
Partial failures: set a success threshold (80-90%), log gaps, do not drop the whole job for one worker
Applicability boundary: under a tight cost budget or sequential dependencies fan-out is not needed — see [[node:sys-multi-agent-patterns|multi-agent patterns]] for more complex coordination
s5.validate: You can state the run's cost, the failure threshold, and the condition for switching to Batches for your task.
s5.tip: Rule: realtime and interactive -> plain parallelism; anything that can wait hours -> Batches API for the 50% saving.

s6.title: Checklist and pipeline verification
s6.why: A final pass catches the classic traps (no limiter, bare concat, all-or-nothing) before they get expensive in production.
instructions: Independence: map subtasks do not read each other's outputs — confirmed
Limiter: a semaphore and exponential-backoff retry on 429 are in place
Reduce: a strategy is chosen (synthesis / merge / voting), not a bare concat
Failures: a success threshold is set, gaps are logged, order is restored by id
Economics: cost is calculated, and for batch workloads the Message Batches API is considered
s6.validate: All five checklist items are closed, and a test run on a slice of the data gives correct coverage with no 429 storm.
s6.tip: Run the pipeline on 10% of the data as a smoke test before the full run — cheaper to find a problem on 5 items than on 5000.

sys-handoff-protocols.title: Hand tasks between agents without losing context
sys-handoff-protocols.subtitle: Structured handoff instead of passing the whole transcript
sys-handoff-protocols.whatItIs:
A handoff protocol is a formal way to transfer a task and its state from one agent to another. Without it, agent-to-agent work turns into a mess of tangled contexts: one agent ships its entire 50k-token transcript to the next, which burns half its context just reading it — more expensive, slower, unfocused.

There are two base formats. Transcript handoff: the receiver sees the sender's full conversation with every tool call — simple, nothing lost, but context bloats. Structured handoff: the sender explicitly builds a compact package {task, context, completed_steps, constraints, success_criteria} and the receiver reads only that. In practice the best option is a hybrid: a structured package plus references to artifacts for optional drill-down. This is a base building block of any [[node:ai-orchestration|agent orchestration]] and [[node:systems|agentic systems]].
sys-handoff-protocols.approach: Never pass the transcript "as is" — over 5 handoffs it grows to 100k tokens. Build a compact structured package and pass references to artifacts (ticket ID, document ID), not the values. Every handoff must carry the task, what is already done, the constraints, and a done-criterion — otherwise the receiver either redoes work or hallucinates.
outcomes: You understand why a formal handoff protocol beats forwarding the whole conversation
You know the 5 mandatory components of a handoff package: task, context, state, constraints, success_criteria
You can assemble a structured handoff message the receiver reads in seconds
You see the boundaries and risks: lost context, infinite A-to-B-to-A loops, private data leaking into logs
You have a checklist to validate a handoff before shipping it to production

applyIn.title: Supervisor-worker system
applyIn.description: A coordinator hands subtasks to workers — each dispatch and result collection goes through a structured package, see [[node:sys-supervisor-worker|supervisor-worker]].

applyIn.title: Sequential agent pipeline
applyIn.description: research agent, then writer agent, then editor agent: each passes a compact package with references to artifacts, not its whole context.

applyIn.title: Human-in-the-loop
applyIn.description: An agent prepares a result, then a human reviews, then the agent continues. Without an explicit package the human cannot tell what is done or where to stop.

pitfalls: Passing the full transcript: over 5 handoffs context grows to 100k tokens, cost 5x, focus 0.2x.
Handoff without success_criteria — the receiver does not know when to stop and either over-works or under-delivers.
Losing trace_id across handoffs: logs fall apart and debugging handoff failures takes far longer.
Putting PII and secrets straight into the package: they land in every agent's logs — pass references (IDs) and resolve values inside a trusted boundary.
Handoff without max-hops: A-to-B-to-A-to-B turns into infinite ping-pong. You need a hard hop limit (3–5) and escalation on overflow.

exercises.question: Take any multi-agent scenario of yours and write down exactly what one agent passes to another. Reduce it to {task, context, completed_steps, constraints, success_criteria} — what stayed in context, and what became artifact references?
exercises.hint: If context holds more than a couple of paragraphs, almost all of it should become an artifact reference, not text in the package.

exercises.question: Simulate a failure: remove completed_steps from the handoff and watch what the receiver does. Then remove success_criteria. Which of the two omissions is more dangerous in your scenario?
exercises.hint: Without completed_steps the receiver repeats work; without success_criteria it never knows when to stop. Compare the cost of each error.

exercises.question: Add max-hops and trace_id to your protocol. Replay a chain of three handoffs and check: can you reconstruct the full task history from a single trace_id?
exercises.hint: If logs from different agents cannot be stitched by one identifier, trace_id is being lost somewhere in the handoff.

s1.title: Why a formal handoff is needed
s1.why: With a single agent no handoff is needed. But the moment two or more agents split a task, implicit transfer breaks in two ways: either the sender ships everything (context and cost explode) or it ships "continue" with no context (the receiver asks back or hallucinates). The protocol removes both extremes.
instructions: Find every point in your scenario where one agent hands work to another: supervisor-to-worker, agent-to-agent in a pipeline, agent-to-human-to-agent.
For each point answer: what is passed today — the whole conversation, a short phrase, or nothing?
Estimate the cost: multiply the size of the passed context by the number of handoffs in a typical task.
State the problem in words: "the receiver redoes work", "context bloats", "constraints get lost".
s1.validate: You can name every handoff point in your scenario and say what goes wrong there without a protocol.
s1.tip: Signal a handoff is broken: the receiving agent repeats the sender's work or loses important constraints. You spot it instantly in duplicated tool calls.

s2.title: What to pass: the 5 package components
s2.why: Passing "everything" or "nothing" are two extremes. The working middle is five mandatory components. They give the receiver exactly enough to continue without questions and without redoing work.
instructions: Task — what specifically must be done (one clear goal statement, not vague).
Context — only the relevant background, not the whole transcript: a short summary plus artifact IDs.
State (completed_steps) — what is already done and what remains, so the receiver does not start over.
Constraints — limits: budget, deadline, tone, forbidden actions, caps.
Success criteria — how to know the task is done and it is safe to stop.
s2.validate: For your task you filled all five fields, and context holds nothing that could be replaced by an artifact reference.
s2.tip: Pass references, not values: a ticket ID instead of the full ticket, an artifact_id instead of the document. The receiver pulls the full content inside a trusted boundary if needed.

s3.title: Structure of the handoff message
s3.why: When the package format is the same for every agent, transfer becomes predictable: equal cost, equal quality, and failures stay localized. The standard schema is a machine-readable object with routing and observability metadata.
instructions: Add routing metadata: from_agent, to_agent — who hands to whom.
Add trace_id — an end-to-end task identifier to stitch logs across all agents.
Fill the body: task, context (with artifact_id instead of data), completed_steps, constraints, success_criteria, open_questions.
Put artifacts in a separate block as references/IDs, not as embedded text.
Wire observability: each handoff is its own log record with package size and timing, see [[node:sys-context-passing|context passing]].
s3.validate: You have a single JSON schema for the package that every agent builds, and it includes trace_id and success_criteria.
s3.tip: If the transcript is still over ~20k tokens, compress it: extract key facts with a separate LLM call and pass the compressed version plus a reference to the raw transcript.

s4.title: How to apply it in practice
s4.why: A schema is useless until it is wired into the transfer code. The goal of this step is to assemble a real handoff in a typical scenario (e.g. customer support: triage-to-specialist-to-escalation) and validate it against metrics.
instructions: Describe the package as a data structure (dataclass / typed dict) with the fields from steps 2–3.
In the sending agent: after work, build the package — a summary instead of raw context, artifact IDs instead of values.
In the receiving agent: add to the prompt explicitly "do not redo anything in completed_steps; stop on success_criteria".
Let the receiver pull the full artifact by reference only when it is actually needed.
Hook up metrics: package size, handoff success rate, rework rate.
s4.validate: Running one task through the chain yields a package < 5k tokens, the receiver does not duplicate the sender's work, and metrics are recorded.
s4.tip: Production baseline: package size < 5k tokens, success rate > 95%, rework near zero. Going past these is a reason to fix the protocol, not the agents.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks
s5.why: A handoff protocol introduces its own failure classes: context loss on compression, infinite loops between agents, private data leaking into logs. Close them up front or they surface in production.
instructions: Context loss: when compressing a transcript, always keep a reference to the raw artifact so details can be recovered.
Loops: introduce a hard max-hops (3–5) and on overflow escalate (to a human or supervisor) instead of another round.
Privacy: never put PII/secrets in the package — references only; resolve values inside a trusted boundary.
Observability: verify trace_id is not lost on any handoff — otherwise debugging failures grows by an order of magnitude.
Degradation: decide what the receiver does with an incomplete package — ask, escalate, or work with what it has.
s5.validate: For each risk (context, loops, privacy, trace_id) you have a concrete protection mechanism, not a "hope it won't happen".
s5.tip: The A-to-B-to-A-to-B loop is the most common hidden failure. A hop counter in the trace plus a hard cap is cheaper than any post-hoc log dig.

s6.title: Checklist and validation
s6.why: Before letting a multi-agent chain run, walk the protocol through a checklist. This is the final filter that catches the most expensive mistakes before they reach production.
instructions: The package contains all 5 components: task, context, completed_steps, constraints, success_criteria.
trace_id is end-to-end, max-hops is set, escalation on overflow is configured.
The package holds only artifact references — no PII/secrets and no raw values.
The receiver prompt explicitly forbids repeating completed_steps and sets the stop on success_criteria.
Metrics (package size, success rate, rework) are logged and land on a dashboard.
s6.validate: Every checklist item is ticked, and a test task passes the chain with no rework, no loops, and no context overflow.
s6.tip: Make the checklist part of the scenario's CI check: then a broken handoff never reaches production silently.

sys-tool-orchestration.title: Tool orchestration
sys-tool-orchestration.subtitle: How an agent reliably selects, calls, and combines tools
sys-tool-orchestration.whatItIs: Tool orchestration is managing how one model works with a set of tools: which tool to call, in what order, what to run in parallel, how to handle results and errors. It is the layer between [[node:cap-tools|the ability to call tools]] and a real agent that has 3, 10, or 20 of them. Without orchestration the model confuses similar tools, does everything sequentially, and loops on failed calls.
sys-tool-orchestration.approach: We move from mechanics to reliability. First we understand what physically happens during tool use / function calling (the model requests a call, your code executes it, the result is returned). Then we learn to write descriptions so selection is unambiguous. Next: parallel vs sequential and dependencies between calls. Then handling results and errors in a structured format. After that, boundaries and risks (wrong selection, loops, tool budget). Finally, a checklist and a check on a real tool set.
outcomes: You understand the tool-use cycle: model requests a call, then code executes, then result returned, then next turn
You write tool descriptions so the model picks the right one in >95% of cases
You run independent tools in parallel and cut latency several-fold
You return errors in a structured form so the model chooses retry / fallback / skip deliberately
You set a tool budget and know how to detect wrong selection and loops

applyIn.title: Support agent with multiple sources
applyIn.description: The bot pulls from CRM, email history, and calendar. Independent calls run in parallel, latency drops from 6s to 2s.

applyIn.title: Research assistant with web and internal DB
applyIn.description: Slow web_search sits next to a fast internal DB. Orchestration decides what to parallelize and what depends on a prior result.

applyIn.title: Internal tool with 15+ tools
applyIn.description: With a large set the key is distinct descriptions and a tool budget, otherwise the model gets confused and spams calls.

pitfalls: Vague descriptions: `search_data` and `query_db` are indistinguishable, then the model picks randomly, up to 30% wrong calls
No parallel hint: without it the model goes sequential ~70% of the time even on independent tools
Dependent tools without explicit order: get_user, then get_orders with no hint causes ordering errors
No tool budget: the model loops and calls one tool dozens of times, then cost and latency
Raw errors fed back: "500 Internal Server Error" instead of structured, then unpredictable retry or failure

exercises.question: An agent has two tools: search_docs and search_kb. Complaint: the model mixes them up. What do you fix first?
exercises.hint: The problem is not the execution code but how the model distinguishes tools. Look at the field it bases the decision on.

exercises.question: A request makes 4 tool calls, all independent, and latency equals their summed time. How do you cut it?
exercises.hint: Claude can call several tools in one turn. What is missing in the system prompt to make it do so?

exercises.question: A tool sometimes fails with a rate limit. What error-result format helps the model behave predictably?
exercises.hint: Compare "500 Internal Server Error" with an object carrying error_code, retry_after, should_retry.

s1.title: What tool orchestration is
s1.why: Before tuning selection and parallelism you must see the cycle: the model does not execute tools itself — it requests a call, your code executes it, the result goes back. Orchestration manages this cycle when there are many tools.
instructions: Memorize the tool use / function calling cycle: the model returns tool_use, then your code executes, then the result returns as tool_result, then the model takes the next turn
Distinguish orchestration from the bare ability to call tools (see [[node:cap-tools|tool use]]) — orchestration is about selection, order, and resilience across a set of tools
Tie it to the layer above: orchestration is part of building [[node:systems|systems from Claude]] and [[node:ai-orchestration|AI orchestration]]
List your current tool set and note how many there are and which ones resemble each other
s1.validate: You can plainly explain when the model requests a call and who actually executes it.
s1.tip: Orchestration starts to matter from 3 tools — with one or two you can live without it.

s2.title: Describe tools for reliable selection
s2.why: The model selects a tool by its description. Vague or overlapping descriptions cause up to 30% wrong calls — the most common and cheapest-to-fix defect.
instructions: In every description state three things: what it does, when to use, when NOT
Disambiguate similar tools explicitly: "Do NOT use for searching users by email — use search_users for that"
Make input schemas precise — required fields, types, no free text where an enum works
Audit the set for overlap: if two tools can be described by the same phrase, that is future confusion
s2.validate: For any pair of similar tools, the description explicitly says when not to use each.
s2.tip: Test: read only the descriptions, without the names — could you yourself pick the right tool for a task without error?

s3.title: Sequential and parallel calls
s3.why: Claude natively can call several independent tools in one turn. Without a hint it goes sequential ~70% of the time, and latency adds up instead of being the maximum.
instructions: Add an explicit hint to the system prompt: "When tools are independent, call them in parallel in a single turn"
For dependent calls describe the order: "fetch user_id first, then use it for orders" — the model must infer the dependency graph from descriptions
In code, execute parallel tool_use calls concurrently (e.g., collect all calls in one turn and run them at once)
Estimate the gain: 3 independent tools at 2s each are 2s in parallel vs 6s sequential
s3.validate: On independent tools the agent does one parallel turn instead of several sequential ones.
s3.tip: A dependency is when one tool's input comes from another's output. Everything else is a candidate for parallel.

s4.title: Handling results and errors
s4.why: The model decides retry / fallback / skip based on what you return. Raw error text leaves it guessing; a structured result gives it grounds for a deliberate decision.
instructions: Return results structured (JSON), not raw text — easier for the model to extract what it needs
Make errors explicit objects: { error_code, retry_after, should_retry } instead of "500 Internal Server Error"
State a failure policy in the system prompt: "If a tool fails twice, skip it and note in response"
Distinguish transient errors (rate limit, then retry) from permanent ones (no permission, then skip and report)
s4.validate: When a tool fails the model behaves predictably: it retries, routes around, or reports — it does not hang.
s4.tip: should_retry: true|false in the error response saves the model from guessing and from extra calls.

s5.title: Boundaries and risks
s5.why: Without guardrails orchestration degrades into wrong selection, loops, and tool spamming — dozens of calls to one tool that burn money and time.
instructions: Set a tool budget: a hard limit on total calls per request (usually 5–15), a safeguard against loops from [[node:sys-loop-patterns|loop patterns]]
Scope tool permissions narrowly: broad permissions are both a security risk and a source of confusion (see [[node:sys-auth-patterns|auth patterns]])
Watch for trouble signals: the model skips a required call, latency = sum, 30+ calls per request
For external tools prefer [[node:mcp|MCP]] — standard schemas, auth, and error semantics out of the box
s5.validate: The code has a hard cap on tool calls, and you know which metrics catch wrong selection.
s5.tip: A tool budget is not about saving money but about protection: one looping tool with no cap easily runs a request for minutes and dollars.

s6.title: Checklist and verification
s6.why: Orchestration counts as working not by "it seems to answer" but by measurable metrics of selection, parallelism, and resilience. The final pass closes the gap between "configured" and "works in production".
instructions: Run the checklist: distinct descriptions (when/when NOT), parallel hint, declared dependencies, structured errors, tool budget
Capture metrics via [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]]: tool-call success rate (>95%), parallel-call ratio, retries per tool, tools-per-request distribution
Run 5–10 real requests and verify: correct tool, parallel where possible, correct reaction to a deliberately triggered error
Record orchestration as part of your agent [[node:m-patterns|patterns]], not a one-off setup
s6.validate: On a test set of requests selection is correct, independent calls run in parallel, errors are handled, the budget is not exceeded.
s6.tip: The key health metric is tool-call success rate >95%. If it is lower, the descriptions (step 2) are almost always to blame.

sys-escalation-paths.title: Escalation to a human: when AI calls for help
sys-escalation-paths.subtitle: How to design handoffs so AI handles the routine itself and passes the hard cases on with ready context
sys-escalation-paths.whatItIs: Escalation is the moment AI says "a human is needed here" and hands the task off. It's not an admission of defeat but part of the [[node:ai-human-collaboration|AI + Human]] system design: AI closes 70-80% of tasks itself and passes the hard ones to a human pre-warmed — with gathered context, attempted solutions, and a recommendation. This course teaches you to design escalation triggers, format the handoff, and keep the balance without calling a human for every little thing.
sys-escalation-paths.approach: We move from meaning to mechanics. First we cover why escalation is needed at all and how a bad one differs from a good one. Then we design triggers — by task type and keywords, not by AI "confidence". We learn to format a handoff with a summary, apply it to a real scenario, examine the boundaries (over- and under-escalation), and assemble a checklist with validation. The running example is e-commerce support.
outcomes: You understand the difference between a bad escalation ("you figure it out") and a good one (with context and a recommendation)
You can design explicit escalation triggers by task type and keywords rather than by confidence
You format the handoff with a ready summary so the agent spends minutes, not hours
You distinguish over-escalation (calling for every little thing) from under-escalation (torturing the customer) and keep the balance
You have a checklist to launch escalation in your own system

applyIn.title: Customer support
applyIn.description: AI answers typical questions and passes complaints, refunds, and mentions of lawsuits to an agent with the conversation history.

applyIn.title: Handling requests and deals
applyIn.description: AI runs standard requests but escalates deals above a money threshold to a manager with calculation and recommendation.

applyIn.title: Internal AI assistants
applyIn.description: An AI helper on the team handles the routine but hands non-standard or risky requests to a responsible person with gathered context.

pitfalls: Escalating by AI "confidence" (confidence < 80%, then call a human): AI is almost always confident, so it either doesn't escalate or does so randomly
Passing a "bare" task without context: the agent re-discovers what AI already knew
Over-escalation: AI calls a human for every little thing, people get overloaded, the point of AI is lost
Under-escalation: AI endlessly repeats failing attempts and annoys the customer instead of calling a human
No retry threshold: AI doesn't count its failed attempts and gets stuck in a loop

exercises.question: Why is escalating by AI "confidence" (confidence < 80%) a bad trigger, and what should replace it?
exercises.hint: Recall how often AI is "confident" even when wrong. Think about what in a task is explainable and noticeable in advance.

exercises.question: Describe what AI should pass to the agent when escalating a complaint so the decision takes 2 minutes, not 20.
exercises.hint: Who the customer is, what the task is, what AI already tried, the recommendation, and a link to the history.

exercises.question: How can one system suffer from over- and under-escalation at the same time across different task categories?
exercises.hint: Think about what happens when rules are set crudely: somewhere the threshold is too low, somewhere it's missing entirely.

s1.title: Why escalate to a human
s1.why: Without escalation AI breaks in two extremes: it either dumbly repeats failing attempts and annoys the customer, or gives up at the first hurdle — then why have it at all. Escalation is part of the [[node:ai-human-collaboration|AI + Human]] design, not an emergency button.
instructions: State the goal: AI does 70-80% of the work itself and hands the hard 20-30% to a human pre-warmed
Write down the difference: bad escalation — "AI couldn't do it, you figure it out"; good — "couldn't do this specific thing, I gathered context, tried these options, recommend looking here"
Note that good escalation raises trust for everyone: customers, agents, management
Set your benchmark: the human should open the task and immediately get what's going on
s1.validate: You can explain with one example how "AI gave up" differs from "AI handed off the task pre-warmed".
s1.tip: Escalation isn't an AI failure but a sign of a mature system. Systems without escalation are more dangerous than ones that call a human on time.

s2.title: Escalation triggers: what fires the handoff
s2.why: The main mistake is escalating by AI "confidence". AI is almost always confident, so such a trigger either doesn't fire or fires randomly. Explainable triggers — by task type and keywords — work predictably. This is adjacent to [[node:sys-confidence-thresholds|confidence thresholds]] but is not replaced by them.
instructions: Build a keyword trigger list: "complaint", "cancellation", "refund", "lawsuit"
Add a retry threshold: AI failed twice in a row, then escalation
Add risk and amount thresholds: deal above a money threshold, then human
Mark task categories as "always human" (legal, medical, disputed)
Always honor the customer's explicit "get me a human" — it's an unconditional trigger
s2.validate: You have a list of 3-5 explicit, explainable triggers, and none of them sound like "if AI is unsure".
s2.tip: A good trigger can be explained in words to management and the customer. "Confidence < 80%" can't be; "mentioned a refund" can.

s3.title: How to format the handoff to a human
s3.why: The second common mistake is passing a "bare" task to the human without context. The agent spends time figuring out what AI already knew. A ready summary turns "an hour to figure out" into "5 minutes to make a call". This intersects with [[node:sys-approval-flows|approval flows]] when the human also approves the action.
