instructions: Type /permissions to open the allow and deny rule management.
Add a specific allow rule, e.g. 'Bash(npm run *)'.
Make sure you don't use broad patterns like 'Bash(*)'.
Save and run an allowed command — Claude executes it without asking.
s2.validate: An allowed tool runs without confirmation while others still ask.
s2.tip: Example: /permissions, then allow 'Bash(npm run *)', then npm scripts run without asking every time.

s3.title: Keybindings: /keybindings
s3.why: Convenient keybindings speed up daily work and remove small friction like an awkward submit.
instructions: Type /keybindings to open or create the keybindings config file.
Find the submit-message action and bind it to, e.g., Cmd+Enter.
Save the file and return to the chat.
Test the new combination in real input.
s3.validate: The assigned combination works as expected (e.g. Cmd+Enter submits the message).
s3.tip: Only change keys that actually bother you — leave the rest at their defaults.

s4.title: Settings panel and natural-language config: /config and /update-config
s4.why: These two commands are the main entry to general settings: one shows an overview, the other lets you edit settings.json with a plain description.
instructions: Type /config to open the settings panel and see current parameters in one place.
Review the available options without changing them right away.
Type /update-config and describe the desired settings.json change in plain words.
Verify the change was applied as you described.
s4.validate: /config shows the current settings, and /update-config correctly edits settings.json from your description.
s4.tip: /config is to look, /update-config is to change. Don't mix up these roles.

s5.title: Privacy, sandbox, and environment: /privacy-settings, /sandbox, /remote-env
s5.why: These commands govern execution safety and data sharing — configure them deliberately, especially in sensitive projects.
instructions: Type /privacy-settings to view and, if needed, update privacy settings.
Type /sandbox to configure the sandbox for tool execution in an isolated environment.
Type /remote-env to set the default remote environment if you work remotely.
Change only what you're sure about; leave the rest at defaults.
s5.validate: You understand what each of the three commands does and changed settings only deliberately.
s5.tip: Sandbox and privacy affect security — don't toggle them at random.

s6.title: Mistakes and verifying the setup
s6.why: A final check catches the most common mistakes — overly broad permissions, command confusion, and unsafe settings.
instructions: Check your /permissions rules: no broad patterns like 'Bash(*)'.
Make sure you're not confusing /config (overview) and /update-config (editing).
Use /help to confirm you're using real group commands, not invented ones.
Run an allowed tool and confirm there are no extra approval prompts.
s6.validate: Permissions are specific, commands are used for their intended purpose, there are no extra confirmations, and sensitive settings are deliberate.
s6.tip: If unsure about a rule, make it narrower, not broader. Safety beats a couple of extra confirmations.

cc-grp-integrations.title: Slash Commands: Integrations
cc-grp-integrations.subtitle: Connecting Claude Code to your IDE, MCP, GitHub, Slack, browser, and plugins
cc-grp-integrations.whatItIs: The Integrations slash-command group embeds Claude Code into your real development workflow. These are /mcp, /ide, /chrome, /hooks, /plugin, /reload-plugins, /agents, /install-github-app, /install-slack-app, and /web-setup. Each one owns a connection point: the IDE, MCP servers, the browser, tool events, plugins, agents, and external services.
cc-grp-integrations.approach: We move from overview to practice. First we view the whole group via /help, then break the commands down by purpose: editor connection (/ide, /chrome), data via /mcp, extension via /plugin, /reload-plugins, /agents, and /hooks, and reaching external services (/install-github-app, /install-slack-app, /web-setup). We finish with common mistakes and verifying that an integration is actually active.
outcomes: You know which commands belong to integrations and what each one does
You connect Claude Code to your IDE via /ide and to data via /mcp
You manage plugins and agents via /plugin, /reload-plugins, /agents
You set up external services: /install-github-app, /install-slack-app, /web-setup
You can verify an integration is active and diagnose it when it isn't

applyIn.title: Working in the IDE
applyIn.description: After installing the VS Code extension you run /ide, and Claude automatically sees your open files and diagnostics right in the editor.

applyIn.title: Connecting data and APIs
applyIn.description: Via /mcp you add MCP servers for access to a database or external API, so Claude works with your real data sources.

applyIn.title: Team automation
applyIn.description: Via /install-github-app and /install-slack-app you bring Claude into GitHub Actions and Slack so the whole team uses it in shared workflows.

pitfalls: Not calling /reload-plugins after adding a plugin — it won't activate until the next session
Calling /ide before installing the IDE extension — there's no integration, so the command does nothing
Confusing /mcp (managing servers) with /hooks (tool events) — they are different connection points
Assuming /install-github-app sets everything up instantly — it launches a wizard you must finish
Not checking status after connecting and assuming the integration works by default

exercises.question: You want Claude to see your open files and errors right inside VS Code. What steps and which command?
exercises.hint: First the IDE extension, then the integrations command that shows status and activates the link.

exercises.question: You added a new plugin, but Claude doesn't 'see' it. What did you forget?
exercises.hint: The group has a dedicated command that activates pending plugin changes without restarting the session.

exercises.question: Your team needs to invoke Claude in a GitHub pull request and a Slack channel. Which two setup commands do you run?
exercises.hint: Both start with /install-...

s1.title: What the Integrations group is
s1.why: Before connecting anything, you need to understand the group's makeup and purpose: integrations embed Claude Code into your full workflow — IDE, GitHub, Slack, browser — instead of running alongside it.
instructions: Start Claude Code and type /help to see the list of all commands
Find the integration group commands: /mcp, /ide, /chrome, /hooks, /plugin, /reload-plugins, /agents, /install-github-app, /install-slack-app, /web-setup
Read the short description next to each — note which is for the editor, which for data, which for external services
Remember the core idea: Claude works inside your tools, not next to them
s1.validate: You can name at least 6 commands in the group and say what each one connects.
s1.tip: /help is your map: integration commands always appear there with the up-to-date description for your version.

s2.title: Editor connection: /ide and /chrome
s2.why: The most common integration is the editor. /ide links Claude Code to VS Code or JetBrains, and /chrome manages Claude in Chrome settings. This lets Claude see context where you actually work.
instructions: Install the Claude extension in VS Code or JetBrains (done inside the editor itself)
In Claude Code run /ide — the command shows integration status and activates the link
Confirm Claude sees your open files and inline diagnostics
If you work in the browser, run /chrome for Claude in Chrome (beta) settings
s2.validate: After /ide the status shows an active integration, and Claude references your open file without you giving the path.
s2.tip: /ide requires the IDE extension to be installed first — without it there's nothing for the command to connect.

s3.title: Connecting data: /mcp
s3.why: /mcp manages MCP servers: add, remove, and list them. Through MCP Claude gains access to databases and external APIs — it's the main way to give it your real data sources.
instructions: Run /mcp to see the list of already connected MCP servers
Via /mcp add the server you need — for example, access to a database or external API
Check that the server appears in the list and is marked active
Ask Claude to reach the connected source and confirm it answers with real data
s3.validate: In the /mcp output your server is visible and active, and Claude successfully retrieves data from it.
s3.tip: Connect only the MCP servers you need: extra ones grow the context and tool list with no benefit.

s4.title: Extending capabilities: /plugin, /reload-plugins, /agents, /hooks
s4.why: These commands extend Claude Code's behavior. /plugin manages plugins, /reload-plugins activates their changes, /agents manages agent configurations, and /hooks shows hook configurations for tool events (pre/post-execution).
instructions: Run /plugin to view and configure plugins
After adding or changing a plugin, always run /reload-plugins — otherwise the changes won't apply
Use /agents to view and configure agent setups
Run /hooks to see which hooks fire before and after tools
s4.validate: After /reload-plugins the new plugin is available in the current session, and /hooks shows your configured hooks.
s4.tip: The most common mistake is forgetting /reload-plugins: without it a new plugin only activates in the next session.

s5.title: External services: /install-github-app, /install-slack-app, /web-setup
s5.why: These commands take Claude beyond your local machine. /install-github-app sets up Claude GitHub Actions, /install-slack-app installs Claude in Slack, and /web-setup sets up Claude Code on the web — so the whole team works with Claude in shared services.
instructions: Run /install-github-app and finish the wizard to connect Claude to GitHub Actions
Run /install-slack-app to install the Claude app in Slack
Run /web-setup to set up Claude Code on the web
After each command go through to the final confirmation — the wizard doesn't finish on its own
s5.validate: The GitHub app responds in a pull request, the Slack app is installed in the workspace, and web access is set up.
s5.tip: These commands launch setup wizards — skipping any step leaves the integration incomplete.

s6.title: Mistakes and verification
s6.why: Integrations often 'don't work' not because of a bug but because of a skipped step. A final check saves time: you confirm each connection is actually active.
instructions: After adding a plugin, confirm you called /reload-plugins and that it's active
Before /ide make sure the editor extension is installed, otherwise there's no integration
Via /mcp check that the servers you need are listed and active, not just added
For /install-github-app and /install-slack-app confirm the wizard was completed
If something didn't connect — go back to /help and compare the command's description with what you did
s6.validate: Each needed integration is explicitly confirmed active (via /ide status, /mcp list, the GitHub/Slack app's action), not assumed to work.
s6.tip: Rule: after any integration command, check status immediately — don't assume everything connected by default.

cc-grp-automation.title: Automation and AI tasks in Claude Code
cc-grp-automation.subtitle: The group of slash commands that turn Claude into an autonomous background worker
cc-grp-automation.whatItIs: The "Automation and AI tasks" command group is a set of Claude Code slash commands (/plan, /tasks, /background, /loop, /schedule, /batch, /goal, /autofix-pr, /ultraplan, /ultrareview) that turn Claude from a chat assistant into an autonomous worker. They run work in the background, on a schedule, or in parallel — while you focus elsewhere.
cc-grp-automation.approach: We go from simple to advanced: first understand what the group is and where to see its list (/help), then break down the commands in pairs by role — background and parallelism, schedules and loops, goals and web agents. We finish with safe-automation rules and verifying that tasks actually complete.
outcomes: Understand which commands belong to the automation group and where to find the list
Launch background and parallel tasks via /background, /tasks and /batch
Set up recurring and scheduled runs via /loop and /schedule
Set goals and review PRs autonomously via /goal, /autofix-pr, /ultrareview
Avoid common automation mistakes — such as running /batch without /plan first

applyIn.title: Large-scale refactor
applyIn.description: Split a uniform change across dozens of files with /batch — parallel agents, each opening its own PR.

applyIn.title: Nightly automation
applyIn.description: Use /schedule to run a remote agent on a schedule: nightly checks, reports, dependency updates.

applyIn.title: Release quality control
applyIn.description: Before a major release, run /ultrareview for deep bug finding and /autofix-pr to auto-fix PR issues.

pitfalls: Running /batch without /plan first — parallel agents start working from an unapproved plan
Using /ultrareview on every small PR — it's a paid command ($5-20), overkill for routine work
An uncontrolled /loop with no stop condition — the command runs forever and burns resources
Not knowing the current group lineup — the command list changes, always verify via /help
Confusing /loop (local recurring interval) with /schedule (remote agent on cron) — different tools

exercises.question: You need to add JSDoc comments to all functions in a large src/ folder. Which command fits, and what must you do before it?
exercises.hint: Think about parallelism across dozens of files. And recall the key safety rule from the node about /plan.

exercises.question: You need to run a dependency check every night without your involvement. Which command do you pick and how does it differ from /loop?
exercises.hint: Schedule and remote agent versus local recurring interval.

exercises.question: How do you quickly find the full current list of automation commands in your version of Claude Code?
exercises.hint: One built-in command shows all available slash commands.

s1.title: What the group is and where its list lives
s1.why: Before automating, understand the tool's boundaries: which commands belong to the group and how Claude shifts from conversationalist to background-task executor.
instructions: Grasp the group's idea: automation commands run work in the background, on a schedule, or in parallel while you focus elsewhere.
Open the full command list via /help — it shows the current set of slash commands for your version.
Find the automation commands in the list: /plan, /tasks, /background, /loop, /schedule, /batch, /goal, /autofix-pr, /ultraplan, /ultrareview.
Note that some commands run locally and some (e.g. /ultraplan, /ultrareview) run on the web and are paid.
s1.validate: You can name at least 5 commands from the group and explain in one sentence how an autonomous worker differs from a chat assistant.
s1.tip: The group's lineup evolves with Claude Code — /help always shows what is actually available now.

s2.title: Background tasks: /background and /tasks
s2.why: The foundation of automation is sending work to the background and tracking it. Without this, the other commands lose their point.
instructions: Use /background to continue the current session in the background and free up your chat for other work.
Open /tasks — this lists and manages background tasks: you see what's running and what's done.
Through /tasks, monitor status and, if needed, stop or return to a task.
Remember the pairing: /background sends to the background, /tasks controls what runs there.
s2.validate: You launched a task in the background via /background and found it in the /tasks list.
s2.tip: Background doesn't mean "forget": check /tasks so background agents don't run pointlessly.

s3.title: Parallelism and planning: /batch and /plan
s3.why: Large uniform changes are faster with dozens of parallel agents. But parallelism is dangerous without an approved plan.
instructions: First call /plan — plan mode — so Claude drafts the change plan before executing it.
Approve the plan: this is the key safety rule before any parallel run.
Run /batch for a large-scale change — it spreads work across 5-30 parallel agents, each opening its own PR.
Example: /batch 'add JSDoc to all functions in src/', then 20 agents, each taking its file group.
s3.validate: You understand why /batch always follows an approved /plan, and you can describe what parallel agents return (a PR per file group).
s3.tip: The clearer the plan, the fewer divergences between parallel agents — a plan saves time sorting results.

s4.title: Schedules and loops: /schedule and /loop
s4.why: Many tasks repeat. /loop and /schedule remove the routine: runs on an interval or on a schedule without your involvement.
instructions: Use /loop to run a command on an interval — for recurring local tasks.
Use /schedule to create scheduled remote agent routines — e.g. nightly automation.
Draw a clear line: /loop is a local recurring interval, /schedule is a remote agent on a schedule (cron).
For /loop, keep a stop condition in mind so the loop doesn't run forever.
s4.validate: You can pick the right command for the task: "repeat locally", then /loop; "nightly remote", then /schedule.
s4.tip: Nightly automation via /schedule is the most underrated scenario: checks and reports get done while you sleep.

s5.title: Goals and web agents: /goal, /autofix-pr, /ultraplan, /ultrareview
s5.why: The highest tier of automation is setting a goal and driving the task to completion, while offloading heavy reviews to web agents.
instructions: Use /goal to set a completion condition and keep working until the goal is met.
Use /autofix-pr to monitor a PR and automatically fix issues found.
To align on a large plan, use /ultraplan — the plan draft is prepared on the web for editing and approval.
Before a major release, run /ultrareview — deep bug finding on the web (paid, $5-20).
s5.validate: You can state which of these commands are paid and run on the web (/ultraplan, /ultrareview) and which set the work mode (/goal, /autofix-pr).
s5.tip: /ultrareview saves money when run selectively — before a release, not on every small PR.

s6.title: Automation mistakes and verification
s6.why: An autonomous worker is dangerous without discipline: parallelism without a plan, endless loops, and needless paid runs quickly turn benefit into harm.
instructions: Top rule: never run /batch without a prior, approved /plan.
Don't overuse paid commands: /ultrareview is only for important checks, not routine.
For /loop, always keep a stop condition so the command doesn't spin pointlessly.
Regularly verify the current command list via /help — the group's lineup changes.
Verify results: open /tasks to confirm background tasks completed correctly.
s6.validate: You can list at least 3 common automation mistakes and, for each, name how to avoid it.
s6.tip: The discipline of "plan, then run, then verify via /tasks" makes automation reliable rather than risky.

cc-grp-quality.title: Code quality and review
cc-grp-quality.subtitle: The Claude Code slash-command group for checking code quality and security before shipping
cc-grp-quality.whatItIs: A group of Claude Code commands that act as quality gates: /review analyzes a pull request, /security-review hunts for vulnerabilities, /simplify strips out over-engineering, /diff shows uncommitted changes, /debug enables session diagnostics, and /fewer-permission-prompts reduces permission interruptions. Claude catches what linters miss: logic errors, security issues, and over-engineering.
cc-grp-quality.approach: We move from the big picture to specifics: first understand why the group exists as a whole, then walk through the commands one or two per step on real code, then wire the checks into your working cycle (before merge, before deploy, after a long session), and finish with common mistakes and a self-check. Each command is practiced on your own uncommitted change, with /help kept handy as a reference.
outcomes: Know which command does what: PR review, security, simplification, viewing changes, diagnostics
Run /review and read its output by severity (Critical / Warning / Info)
Run /security-review before deploy and understand the vulnerability report
Wire quality checks into a steady cycle: before merge, before deploy, after a session
Avoid treating review as a rubber stamp and confirm results with a self-check

applyIn.title: Before merging a pull request
applyIn.description: Run /review before merging the branch — Claude lists issues by severity, and you fix Critical items before the code reaches the main branch.

applyIn.title: Before deploying to production
applyIn.description: Run /security-review over the branch changes to catch risks like SQL injection or leaked secrets before they reach users.

applyIn.title: After a long development session
applyIn.description: Use /simplify so Claude finds the duplication and over-engineering that piled up during the session and suggests cleaner code.

pitfalls: Using /review as a rubber stamp — read the output carefully, especially Critical items
Running /security-review only at the end of a big release instead of regularly before every deploy
Confusing /simplify (quality cleanup) with bug hunting — /simplify does not find logic errors, /review does
Skipping /diff before review and not knowing exactly which changes go into the check
Forgetting /help and guessing command flags instead of reading the built-in reference

exercises.question: You have an uncommitted change on a branch. Which command gives you a structured breakdown by severity before merging?
exercises.hint: It's the core PR-review command of the group; output is split into Critical / Warning / Info.

exercises.question: Before deploy you must confirm the changes carry no security risks. Which command is it, and how does its output differ from a normal review?
exercises.hint: The command is specifically about security; it looks for vulnerabilities like injections and leaked secrets, not general quality.

exercises.question: How do you find the exact list and purpose of the group's commands right inside Claude Code, without guessing from memory?
exercises.hint: The built-in reference command, shared by all slash commands.

s1.title: What the group is and why it exists
s1.why: Before running commands, understand their shared role: they are quality gates before shipping. Without that picture it's easy to treat review as a formality and skip critical issues.
instructions: Open Claude Code in a project with uncommitted changes or an active branch
Run /help and locate the group commands: /review, /security-review, /simplify, /diff, /debug, /fewer-permission-prompts
Read the short description of each command in the /help output
Phrase the group's role for yourself: catch what linters miss — logic, security, complexity
s1.validate: You can name all six group commands and say which is for review, which for security, and which for simplification.
s1.tip: /help is your first source of truth about the commands: it shows the current set without guesswork.

s2.title: /review — structured review of changes
s2.why: /review is the group's central command. It analyzes changes and lists issues by severity, making review repeatable and independent of your mood and fatigue.
instructions: First run /diff to see which uncommitted changes will go into the review
Run /review
Read the output by level: Critical, Warning, Info
Start with Critical items — for example, a SQL injection risk — and decide what to fix immediately
Mark Info items as future improvements if they don't block the merge
s2.validate: You got a list of issues split by severity and understand which items are Critical versus recommendations.
s2.tip: Example output: Critical (SQL injection risk), Warning (no error handling), Info (rename for clarity).

s3.title: /security-review — security check before deploy
s3.why: A general review doesn't replace a dedicated security check. /security-review deliberately hunts for vulnerabilities in the branch changes to catch them before the code reaches users.
instructions: Make sure the changes going to deploy are on the current branch
Run /security-review
Read the vulnerability report — watch for injections, leaked secrets, unsafe input handling
Compare its focus with a regular /review: here the priority is security, not general quality
Fix the identified risks before deploy
s3.validate: You ran the security check and can explain how its report differs from /review output.
s3.tip: Run /security-review regularly before every deploy, not just at the end of a big release.

s4.title: /simplify and /diff — code cleanliness and change control
s4.why: After a long session, code accumulates duplication and over-engineering. /simplify cleans up quality, and /diff gives a clear picture of exactly what you're changing and sending into review.
instructions: Run /diff to see the full list of uncommitted changes
Run /simplify so Claude finds reusable pieces and over-engineering
Read the suggestions and apply the ones that improve the code without losing clarity
Remember the split: /simplify is about quality, not bug hunting; /review handles logic
Run /diff again after the edits to see the final state
s4.validate: You received simplification suggestions from /simplify and can see via /diff how the code changed.
s4.tip: Use /simplify at the end of a long session — that's when extra complexity piles up.

s5.title: /debug and /fewer-permission-prompts — diagnostics and fewer interruptions
s5.why: Two helper commands remove friction: /debug helps you understand what went wrong in a session, and /fewer-permission-prompts cuts the stream of permission requests so quality checks run without constant pauses.
instructions: If a session behaves oddly, run /debug to enable debug logging for diagnostics
Study the extra detail that appears in the output once diagnostics are on
Run /fewer-permission-prompts — it scans transcripts and builds an allowlist of frequent safe actions
Review the proposed allowlist before accepting: only allow what is genuinely safe
Run /review or /simplify again and notice there are fewer permission interruptions
s5.validate: You understand when /debug is needed and ran /fewer-permission-prompts after deliberately reviewing the proposed permission list.
s5.tip: Don't allow everything via /fewer-permission-prompts — add only verified read-only actions to the allowlist.

s6.title: Common mistakes and a self-check of the cycle
s6.why: The commands only pay off when wired into a steady cycle and not turned into a formality. The final step cements the habit and helps you check yourself.
instructions: Fix your cycle: /diff, then /review before merge, /security-review before deploy, /simplify after a session
Check you don't use /review formally: re-read the Critical items of your last review
Make sure /security-review runs regularly, not once per release
If unsure about flags or the command set — open /help instead of guessing
Write yourself a short checklist of the commands and when to apply each
s6.validate: You have a clear personal quality-check cycle and can name the main mistake of each command and how to avoid it.
s6.tip: The group's main mistake is treating review as a stamp. The value is in actually reading and fixing the Critical items.

cc-grp-help.title: Help, learning and account in Claude Code
cc-grp-help.subtitle: The group of slash commands that help you learn, diagnose problems and manage your account — without leaving the CLI
cc-grp-help.whatItIs: This is the set of utility slash commands in Claude Code covering three jobs: onboarding and learning (/help, /powerup, /release-notes, /skills, /team-onboarding), help mid-task (/btw, /insights), and managing your account and installation health (/login, /logout, /feedback, /doctor, /mobile). They all run straight from the input line without leaving your current task.
cc-grp-help.approach: First understand what the group is for, then work through the commands in logical pairs: learning, help mid-task, skills and team onboarding, account, diagnostics. At each step you try a command live and learn to read its output. The base entry point is always /help: it shows the current list of what's actually available in your version.
outcomes: Know which slash commands handle help, learning and account
Can ask a side question with /btw without losing the main task's context
Can diagnose installation issues yourself with /doctor
Understand how to sign in and out of your account (/login, /logout)
Know where to find new features and the list of skills (/release-notes, /skills)

applyIn.title: Starting work on a new project
applyIn.description: Run /powerup for interactive lessons and /help to refresh the list of available commands before diving in.

applyIn.title: A question mid-task
applyIn.description: In the middle of a refactor, use /btw to ask a quick clarification without breaking your main line of work.

applyIn.title: Something broke
applyIn.description: The CLI behaves strangely — run /doctor, which catches 90% of common installation issues instantly.

pitfalls: Not running /doctor when the CLI behaves strangely — it fixes most common issues right away
Interrupting your main task with a plain question instead of a lightweight /btw, losing context
Ignoring /insights — analyzing session patterns shows where your time goes
Forgetting /release-notes and missing new features, working the old way
Not signing out with /logout on a shared or borrowed device, leaving the account active

exercises.question: You're mid-way through a big task and want to quickly clarify what a pattern does without interrupting your work. Which command do you use and why?
exercises.hint: Look for the command for a side question without interrupting the main task.

exercises.question: The CLI started behaving strangely after an update. Which command do you start the diagnosis with?
exercises.hint: This command checks installation health and catches up to 90% of common issues.

exercises.question: How do you find the full, current list of commands in your specific version of Claude Code?
exercises.hint: The most basic command of the group, the entry point to help.

s1.title: What this command group is
s1.why: Before dissecting individual commands, it's important to see the whole group: that it covers three different jobs — learning, help mid-task and account — and why they're grouped together.
instructions: Remember the group's three areas: learning (/help, /powerup, /release-notes, /skills, /team-onboarding), help mid-task (/btw, /insights), account and health (/login, /logout, /feedback, /doctor, /mobile)
Open the Claude Code input line and type / — you'll see the list of available commands
Find the commands from this group in the list and note which ones you know and which you don't
Remember that the entry point to all help is the /help command
s1.validate: You can name the group's three areas and at least one command in each.
s1.tip: Don't try to memorize every command — it's enough to know that /help always shows the current list.

s2.title: Learning: /help and /powerup
s2.why: These are the two main commands for getting into Claude Code: /help gives you a map of all commands, and /powerup teaches features through short interactive lessons.
instructions: Run /help and review the full list of available commands
Find the commands we'll cover next in the /help output to confirm they exist in your version
Run /powerup and complete one interactive lesson on Claude Code features
Note what the lesson taught you — this is how continuous learning works
s2.validate: After /help you see the full command list, and after /powerup you completed at least one lesson.
s2.tip: /powerup is handy at the start of work — a couple of minutes of lessons saves hours of trial-and-error on features.

s3.title: Help mid-task: /btw and /insights
s3.why: These are the group's underused gems: /btw lets you ask a side question without interrupting the main task, and /insights shows your session patterns weekly.
instructions: In the middle of any task, type /btw and ask a short question, for example about an unfamiliar pattern
Confirm that Claude answered briefly and the main task continued without losing context
Run /insights and look at the analysis of your session patterns
Make a habit of running /insights weekly to analyze where your time goes
s3.validate: You asked a question via /btw without interrupting the task and opened /insights at least once.
s3.tip: /btw alone saves dozens of context-breaking interruptions per day — it's the fastest way to clarify a small thing.

s4.title: Skills and onboarding: /skills, /team-onboarding, /release-notes
s4.why: These commands help you see available skills, quickly get a team up to speed, and keep track of new Claude Code features.
instructions: Run /skills and look at the list of available installed skills
Run /release-notes and see what's new in Claude Code
Run /team-onboarding to generate a guide for onboarding your team
Compare the skills list from /skills with what was there before — that's how you spot new capabilities
s4.validate: You saw the skills list via /skills, learned what's new via /release-notes, and generated an onboarding guide.
s4.tip: Check /release-notes periodically — otherwise you'll keep working the old way, unaware of new features.

s5.title: Account: /login, /logout, /mobile
s5.why: These commands manage your access: signing in and out of your account, plus linking the mobile app via a QR code.
instructions: Run /login if you need to sign in, or confirm you're already signed in
Remember the /logout command — it's useful on a shared or borrowed device
Run /mobile to get a QR code for the mobile app
Scan the QR code with your phone if you want to link the mobile app
s5.validate: You understand how to sign in and out, and you got a QR code via /mobile.
s5.tip: On a shared computer, always end your session with /logout so the account doesn't stay active.

s6.title: Diagnostics and mistakes: /doctor and /feedback
s6.why: The final step reinforces the group's main rule: whenever the CLI behaves strangely you run /doctor first, and you send notable issues to Anthropic via /feedback.
instructions: Run /doctor and read the report on your installation's health
Remember the main rule: when the CLI behaves strangely, run /doctor first — it catches 90% of common issues instantly
If you found a problem or have an idea — send it to Anthropic via /feedback
Repeat to yourself: /help is the command map, /btw is a quick question, /doctor is diagnostics
s6.validate: You ran /doctor, read its report, and know how to send /feedback.
s6.tip: The main mistake is not running /doctor when things break. Make it your first reflex, not a last resort.

skill-md.title: SKILL.md
skill-md.subtitle: The skill's recipe file: what's inside and how to write it so Claude activates it at the right time
skill-md.whatItIs: SKILL.md is a text recipe file, the only required file in any [[node:skills|Skill]]. It tells Claude WHAT the skill does, WHEN to activate it, and WHICH steps to follow. Claude reads SKILL.md as an instruction and follows it the same way every time, no improvisation. No SKILL.md, no Skill.
skill-md.approach: We go from structure to meaning. First we cover why the file exists and what parts it consists of. Then each part separately: name, description as a precise activation trigger, the step-by-step instruction body, and supporting files next to it. At the end — what most often breaks activation and how to verify the file actually works.
outcomes: Understand why SKILL.md is the only required file and how Claude uses it
Know the required parts: name and description, and what each is responsible for
Write a description as a precise trigger: WHAT it does + WHEN to activate
Format the instruction body step by step so the skill runs the same way
Check a finished SKILL.md and catch typical activation mistakes

applyIn.title: Repeating process
applyIn.description: Any task you explain to Claude a second time gets turned into a SKILL.md — and from then on runs the same way without repeated instructions.

applyIn.title: Team standards
applyIn.description: SKILL.md fixes 'how we do things': task formatting, reviews, releases. The file is a single source of truth for everyone.

applyIn.title: Complex multi-step operation
applyIn.description: When an exact sequence of steps matters and nothing can be skipped, the SKILL.md body holds the order of actions for you.

pitfalls: A one-phrase description like 'helps with tasks' — Claude won't know when to activate the skill and will use it on everything or never
The description states only WHAT but not WHEN — there's no trigger, so the skill doesn't fire at the right moment
The instruction body is written in paragraphs instead of clear steps — Claude loses the order and skips actions
Supporting files are scattered instead of sitting next to SKILL.md — the skill can't find templates and examples
The file is not named SKILL.md (case, typo) — the Skill simply doesn't exist for Claude

exercises.question: A description reads: 'A skill for working with text.' Why won't Claude be able to activate it correctly?
exercises.hint: A description must say WHAT it does and WHEN to activate. Find what's missing here: which text exactly, at what moment, in response to which user request?

exercises.question: You need to turn a 5-step process into a Skill. Which parts of SKILL.md are required, and what goes into the body?
exercises.hint: name and description are required. The 5 steps themselves are the instruction body. Consider whether you need supporting files alongside.

exercises.question: A skill fires on EVERY user request, even off-topic ones. What do you fix first?
exercises.hint: The problem is almost always in the description: the trigger is too broad. Narrow the WHEN — add specific activation conditions.

smd-1.title: What SKILL.md is and why it's needed
smd-1.why: Until it's clear that SKILL.md is an instruction Claude reads and executes, it's easy to mistake it for an ordinary note. Everything else depends on this.
instructions: Remember: SKILL.md is the only required file in a [[node:skills|Skill]]. No file, no Skill
Claude reads it as an instruction and follows it the same way every time, no improvisation
The file answers three questions: WHAT the skill does, WHEN to activate it, WHICH steps to follow
Main effect: one good SKILL.md replaces 20 repeated explanations of the same process
smd-1.validate: You can explain in your own words why there's no skill without SKILL.md and why the file matters more than a one-time chat explanation.
smd-1.tip: Think of SKILL.md as a recipe for a cook who follows it exactly — so the recipe must be complete.

smd-2.title: Required parts: name and description
smd-2.why: These two parts are how Claude even decides the skill exists and whether to run it. Without them, the instruction body is useless.
instructions: name — the skill's short name: what kind of recipe this is
description — the main part: WHAT the skill does and WHEN to activate it
The description is what drives the [[node:s-trigger|activation trigger]] — the moment Claude turns the skill on
Remember the pairing: name answers 'what it's called', description — 'what it does and when it fires'
smd-2.validate: For your skill you can state the name in one line and describe what goes into the description (both WHAT and WHEN).
smd-2.tip: If name and description blur together — name is the recipe title, description is 'when to cook this dish'.

smd-3.title: The instruction body: steps, what to do
smd-3.why: Activation is half the job. Once the skill fires, Claude must know the exact sequence of actions, or the result will differ every time.
instructions: After name and description comes the body — the step-by-step instructions themselves
Write in steps, not a solid paragraph: '1. Clarify… 2. Request… 3. Format…'
Each step is one clear action, no ambiguity
Example of a minimal body: '## Steps — 1. Clarify which system the task is for. 2. Request acceptance criteria. 3. Format: Goal / What to do / Acceptance criteria'
smd-3.validate: Your skill's body reads as a numbered list of actions, and you can run the process from it without guessing anything.
smd-3.tip: Body quality check: hand it to someone unfamiliar with the topic. If they execute it without questions, the steps are clear enough.

smd-4.title: Supporting files alongside
smd-4.why: Sometimes the instruction alone isn't enough: you need templates, examples, checklists. If they sit nearby, the skill finds and uses them.
instructions: Besides SKILL.md, the skill folder can hold [[node:s-files|supporting files]]: templates, examples, output samples
Put them in the same folder as SKILL.md — alongside, not scattered
Reference them in the SKILL.md body so Claude knows when to reach for them
Don't bloat SKILL.md itself: move long samples into separate files alongside
smd-4.validate: You understand what goes into SKILL.md itself versus into supporting files alongside, and why keep them in one folder.
smd-4.tip: Simple rule: the instruction goes in SKILL.md, the material for the instruction (templates, examples) goes in files alongside.

smd-5.title: A good description = a precise trigger
smd-5.why: The most common skill breakage is not the body but the description. If the trigger is vague, the skill fires at the wrong time or not at all.
instructions: A good description contains both WHAT it does and WHEN to activate — both together
WHEN is a concrete condition: on which user request, in what situation to turn the skill on
Bad: 'helps with tasks'. Good: 'Use when the user asks to create a task or user story'
The more precise the activation condition, the less often the [[node:s-trigger|trigger]] fires out of place
smd-5.validate: Your description explicitly names the activation situation so it's clear which requests turn the skill on and which don't.
smd-5.tip: Trigger test: come up with 3 requests the skill MUST fire on and 3 it must NOT. A good description distinguishes them.

smd-6.title: Common mistakes and verification
smd-6.why: A finished SKILL.md is easy to ship with a silent error that makes the skill quietly fail. A final check catches it before the skill lets you down.
instructions: Check the description: does it have BOTH what it does AND when to activate — without WHEN the skill doesn't fire
Check the file name: exactly SKILL.md, no typos or wrong case — otherwise the [[node:s-create|skill doesn't exist]]
Check the body: it's clear steps, not a solid paragraph
Run the trigger mentally against real requests: it fires where needed and stays silent where it shouldn't
smd-6.validate: You went through the checklist: file name correct, description has WHAT and WHEN, body is step-by-step, trigger tested on examples.
smd-6.tip: If a skill applies 'to everything' or 'never', it's almost always the description, not the body. Fix the trigger first.

skill-trigger.title: Skill Triggers: how a Skill activates
skill-trigger.subtitle: Two launch mechanisms — auto by intent and explicit call — and how to make a Skill fire exactly when you need it
skill-trigger.whatItIs: A trigger is the condition under which Claude decides to apply a Skill. There are two paths: in [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] Claude reads the Skills list itself and enables the right one based on the request's meaning; in [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] you explicitly type /skillname. The key to the auto-trigger is the description field in [[node:s-md|SKILL.md]].
skill-trigger.approach: We move from mechanism to practice: first how Claude even decides to apply a [[node:skills|Skill]], then the role of the description, the difference between auto-mode and explicit call, the formula for a precise description, diagnosing "why it didn't fire", and a final trigger check.
outcomes: You understand how Claude decides to apply a Skill in auto-mode and on explicit call
You can write a description that fires precisely — no false or missed activations
You distinguish the trigger in claude.ai (by intent) from Claude Code (by /command)
You diagnose why a Skill didn't activate: vague description, conflict, missing /command
You test the trigger on real requests before the Skill goes live

applyIn.title: Creating a new Skill
applyIn.description: When you write SKILL.md, the description is the most important field. Its wording decides whether the Skill turns on by itself or stays silent.

applyIn.title: Debugging "the Skill didn't fire"
applyIn.description: The Skill exists, but Claude ignores it. Knowing the trigger mechanism, you quickly find the cause: a too-general description or a conflict with a neighboring Skill.

applyIn.title: A set of several Skills in one Project
applyIn.description: With several skills in a project, their descriptions must not overlap, so each fires on its own class of requests.

pitfalls: A too-general description ("helps with documents") — the Skill fires on every request, or Claude never understands when to call it
Expecting a /command launch in claude.ai — there is no explicit call there; only the auto-trigger by intent works
Expecting a Skill to turn on by itself in Claude Code — it only activates when you explicitly type /skillname
Two Skills with similar descriptions conflict — Claude picks the wrong one or hesitates
The description states what the Skill does, not when to apply it — a trigger needs "use when…", not "this skill formats…"

exercises.question: You have a Skill that checks text for errors. Write its description so it fires in claude.ai on "proofread this paragraph" but not on any question about text.
exercises.hint: Start with "Use when the user asks to…" and list concrete actions: proofread, check for typos, review grammar — not a generic "works with text".

exercises.question: In Claude Code you wrote a description, but the Skill "won't turn on by itself". What's wrong with the expectation?
exercises.hint: Recall the two mechanisms: in Claude Code the trigger is always explicit — /skillname. Auto-activation by intent is claude.ai behavior.

exercises.question: Two Skills: one "create-slides", another "format-document". On "make this document look nice" Claude gets confused. How do you separate the triggers?
exercises.hint: Make the scopes non-overlapping in the descriptions themselves: specify "slides/presentation" vs "text document/report", drop generic words like "format nicely".

strg-1.title: How Claude decides to apply a Skill
strg-1.why: Without understanding the decision mechanism, you can neither write a working trigger nor diagnose a failure.
instructions: Remember: Claude doesn't "run a program" — it reads the list of available [[node:skills|Skills]] and their descriptions as part of the context
In auto-mode ([[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]]) it matches the meaning of your request against each Skill's description
If a description clearly matches the request's intent — Claude enables that Skill and reads its [[node:s-md|SKILL.md]]
In explicit mode ([[node:claude-code|Claude Code]]) there's no decision by meaning: the trigger is the /skillname command
strg-1.validate: You can state in one sentence what signal makes Claude enable a Skill in each of the two modes.
strg-1.tip: Think of the description as "when to call me", not "what I can do" — Claude decides exactly by this field.

strg-2.title: The role of the description in activation
strg-2.why: In auto-mode the description is the only signal by which Claude decides to apply a Skill. It reads the SKILL.md body only after activation.
instructions: Open [[node:s-md|SKILL.md]] and find the description field at the start of the file
Grasp the split: description is for the trigger (when to apply), the body is the instructions (how to execute)
Claude sees the descriptions of all Skills at once, but the body only of the activated one
So an imprecise description = the Skill either won't turn on or turns on at the wrong time — the body can't save it
strg-2.validate: You can explain why a great SKILL.md body doesn't compensate for a bad description.
strg-2.tip: Write the description aimed at someone else's request: what words will the user phrase the task with that needs this Skill.

strg-3.title: Auto-trigger by intent vs explicit call
strg-3.why: The two activation modes work differently; confusing them is a common cause of "the Skill didn't fire".
instructions: [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]]: Claude enables the Skill itself by the request's meaning — the user types no commands
[[node:claude-code|Claude Code]]: activation is explicit — you type /skillname, Claude reads [[node:s-md|SKILL.md]] and follows the steps
In explicit mode the description barely affects the launch — the command decides; the description helps Claude with hints
Remember the rule: claude.ai = magic by intent, Claude Code = full manual control
strg-3.validate: For a specific Skill you can say how it launches in claude.ai and how in Claude Code.
strg-3.tip: If you need a predictable launch with no surprises — that's Claude Code with an explicit /command. If you want the skill to plug in by itself — that's claude.ai.

strg-4.title: How to phrase a description so it fires precisely
strg-4.why: A precise description is the difference between a Skill that fires exactly when needed and one that stays silent or barges in everywhere.
instructions: Start with "Use when the user asks to…" — describe the condition of application, not the function
List concrete signal-actions (create a presentation, prepare slides), not broad categories ("working with documents")
Add the request vocabulary: what phrasings the user will describe the task with
Keep the scope narrow and non-overlapping with other Skills — one Skill = one class of requests
Check: from the description alone it's clear when to call the Skill and when not to
strg-4.validate: Your description starts with "use when", contains concrete actions, and doesn't overlap with other Skills.
strg-4.tip: Formula: "Use when [request signal] — [concrete actions]". Example: "Use when user asks to create a presentation or prepare slides".

strg-5.title: Why it doesn't fire: vague description and conflict
strg-5.why: Most trigger failures come down to two causes; able to tell them apart, you fix the Skill in a minute.
instructions: Cause 1 — vague description: "helps with documents" matches any request, so Claude can't find the moment
Cause 2 — conflict: two Skills with close descriptions, Claude picks the wrong one or hesitates
Cause 3 (Claude Code): you expected auto-activation but didn't type /skillname — here the trigger is explicit only
Diagnosis: read the description aloud as "when to call me" — if it fits everything, it's vague
To resolve a conflict — make the scopes explicitly different in both descriptions
strg-5.validate: For a broken Skill you can name the specific cause: vagueness, conflict, or missing /command.
strg-5.tip: Vagueness test: if the description fits 3+ unrelated requests — it's too general, narrow it.

strg-6.title: Trigger testing and common mistakes
strg-6.why: The trigger must be tested on real requests before the Skill goes live — otherwise the failure surfaces at the worst moment.
instructions: Compose 3-4 test requests: ones the Skill SHOULD fire on, and similar ones it should NOT
In [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] run them and check the Skill turns on exactly on the right ones
In [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] confirm that /skillname reads [[node:s-md|SKILL.md]] and follows the steps
If it fires on the extra ones — narrow the description; if it misses the right ones — add signal-phrasings
Avoid common mistakes: a general description, expecting a /command in claude.ai, expecting auto-mode in Claude Code
strg-6.validate: The Skill turns on for every "should" request and stays silent for every "shouldn't" — in both modes.
strg-6.tip: Test negative requests too: a Skill that fires in the wrong place is as disruptive as one that stays silent.

skill-files.title: Skill helper files
skill-files.subtitle: Templates, checklists, schemas and scripts next to SKILL.md
skill-files.whatItIs: A Skill folder is more than SKILL.md. Alongside it you can keep helper files: report templates, checklists, JSON schemas, ready-made scripts. Claude reads them as part of the instruction and fills them in with user data. A long template moves out of SKILL.md into a separate file — the main file stays short, and the output format becomes guaranteed.
skill-files.approach: We go from motivation to practice: why helper files are needed at all, what types exist, how SKILL.md references them, a working example (report template + JSON schema), keeping the folder tidy, and closing out the common mistakes with a check. We build on the [[node:skills|Skills]] node and the [[node:s-md|SKILL.md]] and [[node:s-create|Creating a Skill]] skills.
outcomes: You understand why to move templates and lists out of SKILL.md into separate files
You tell apart the types of helper files: templates, checklists, schemas, scripts
You can reference a file from SKILL.md so that Claude reads and applies it
You can assemble a "template + JSON schema" pair for structured output
You keep the Skill folder organized and lightweight, free of extra and heavy files

applyIn.title: Regular reports
applyIn.description: A Skill with a report template produces the same format every time — headings, sections and order don't drift from run to run.

applyIn.title: Structured output
applyIn.description: A JSON schema next to the Skill defines the exact shape of the data: Claude returns an answer another program can read directly without manual fixes.

applyIn.title: Repeatable checks
applyIn.description: A checklist in a separate file guarantees the Skill walks through every review item each time instead of recalling them on the fly.

pitfalls: Stuffing a 50-line template straight into SKILL.md — the file bloats and Claude follows the instruction less reliably
Keeping heavy or binary files in the Skill folder — they bloat the context and aren't needed for the work
Creating a file but forgetting to reference it from SKILL.md — Claude never learns about it
Duplicating one template across several Skills instead of linking to a shared file
Naming files chaotically (file1.md, tmp.json) — later it's unclear what does what

exercises.question: A Skill generates a weekly report, and its SKILL.md has grown to 80 lines because of an inline template. What do you move into a separate file, and how do you reference it?
exercises.hint: The report template goes in templates/report.md. In SKILL.md keep a short instruction: "Fill templates/report.md with user data".

exercises.question: You need the Skill to always return data in a strict shape for another program. What helper file do you add, and why?
exercises.hint: A JSON schema: it fixes the set of fields and their types, making the output machine-readable without manual fixes.

exercises.question: The Skill folder holds report.md, tmp.json, file1.md and a 5 MB image. What's wrong here?
exercises.hint: The heavy/binary file is unnecessary, and tmp.json and file1.md say nothing about their purpose — tidy up and keep only what's needed.

sfl-1.title: Why helper files in the Skill folder
sfl-1.why: If the whole template and every question list live inside SKILL.md, the file quickly becomes unreadable and Claude follows the instruction less reliably. Moving long parts outside keeps the main file short and the output format stable.
instructions: Open any of your Skills and look at SKILL.md: does it contain a long inline template or a list of 10+ items
Grasp the principle: the main file is the "what to do" instruction, while long content (template, checklist, schema) is a separate file the instruction points to
Remember the payoff: a Skill with a template gives a guaranteed format every time, not "whatever comes out"
Tie it to the basics: helper files are part of how [[node:skills|Skills]] are built, not a separate entity
sfl-1.validate: You can explain in one sentence why a long template is better kept outside SKILL.md.
sfl-1.tip: Simple rule: SKILL.md answers "what to do", helper files answer "in what shape".

sfl-2.title: What types of files exist
sfl-2.why: Different tasks call for different helper files. Knowing the standard set, you quickly see exactly what to move outside for your task.
instructions: Templates (templates/): an output stub with sections — report, letter, brief
Checklists: a list of items the Skill walks through during a check or review
Schemas (JSON schemas): the exact shape of structured data — which fields and of what types
Scripts: ready-made code the Skill runs for a repeatable operation
Figure out for your Skill which of these types would cover its weak spot
sfl-2.validate: For your task you name at least one suitable file type and explain what it gives.
sfl-2.tip: A template governs the shape of text, a JSON schema the shape of data. They're different tools — don't mix them up.

sfl-3.title: How SKILL.md references files
sfl-3.why: A file next to the Skill doesn't work on its own — Claude must get the instruction to read it. Without a reference from SKILL.md, a helper file just sits there as dead weight.
instructions: In SKILL.md state the relative path to the file: for example, templates/report.md
Give an explicit action instruction: "Fill templates/report.md with user data" or "Check the result against checklist.md"
Keep the path relative to the Skill folder — that way the link survives a move
Make sure the file name in the reference exactly matches the real name on disk
Build on the main-file conventions from the [[node:s-md|SKILL.md]] skill
sfl-3.validate: Your SKILL.md has a line with a path to the file and an action verb (fill/check/use).
sfl-3.tip: The verb is decisive: "templates/report.md" with no action may be ignored, "fill templates/report.md" won't be.

sfl-4.title: Example: report template + JSON schema
sfl-4.why: A two-file pair is the most common working case: the template sets a human-readable shape, the JSON schema a strict machine shape. The example shows how both references coexist in one SKILL.md.
instructions: Assemble the structure: skills/report/ with SKILL.md, templates/report.md and schema.json
In templates/report.md set the template sections: Goal / Findings / Recommendations
In schema.json describe the structured-output fields and their types (e.g. goal — string, findings — list)
In SKILL.md add two instructions: "Fill templates/report.md with user data" and "Return data strictly per schema.json"
Cross-check with the Skill build order from the [[node:s-create|Creating a Skill]] skill
sfl-4.validate: You have a Skill where SKILL.md references both the template and the JSON schema, and both files sit in the folder.
sfl-4.tip: The template is for human eyes, the JSON schema for another program. One Skill happily produces both outputs.

sfl-5.title: Organizing the Skill folder
sfl-5.why: Once you have more than two files, without order the folder turns into a dump and it's unclear what does what. A clear structure and names save time on every return to the Skill.
instructions: Group same-type files into subfolders: templates in templates/, schemas alongside or in a separate folder
Give telling names: report.md, review-checklist.md, output-schema.json — not file1.md or tmp.json
Keep one template needed by several Skills in one place and reference it, don't copy it
Delete drafts and temporary files — only what SKILL.md actually references stays in the folder
sfl-5.validate: The file names in the folder immediately reveal their purpose, and every file is mentioned in SKILL.md.
sfl-5.tip: Order check: if a file's name doesn't hint at why it exists, rename it right now.

sfl-6.title: Mistakes and final check
sfl-6.why: Heavy, extra or unlinked files quietly break a Skill: they bloat the context or simply go unused. A final pass through the common mistakes catches this before the Skill goes live.
instructions: Check that SKILL.md has no inline long template — it should be moved to a separate file
Make sure the folder has no heavy or binary files: only light text, schemas and needed scripts
Walk through each file: is it definitely referenced from SKILL.md? No reference — delete it or add one
Run the Skill on real data and verify the output matches the template and schema
If the format drifts, look for the cause in an inaccurate reference or a file-name mismatch
sfl-6.validate: The Skill runs, output follows the template and schema strictly, and the folder has no unreferenced or needless files.
sfl-6.tip: The main red flag is a file that sits in the folder but is mentioned nowhere. Either reference it or remove it.

skill-ready.title: Ready-made Skills
skill-ready.subtitle: Anthropic's catalog: add a skill in one click
skill-ready.whatItIs: Ready-made Skills are add-ons Anthropic has already written and tested: pptx (presentations), xlsx (spreadsheets), pdf (document analysis), docx (Word files), skill-creator (build your own). The catalog lives in [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]]: Project Settings, then Skills, then Browse. They're added with one click and work right away.
skill-ready.approach: Don't write your own Skill until you've checked the catalog. First open Browse, pick the right ready-made one, enable it, and confirm Claude actually activates it on your task. Only if nothing fits should you move on to [[node:s-create|building your own]]. This course walks the full cycle: find, choose, enable, verify, tune, and avoid the common traps.
outcomes: Know where the ready-made Skills catalog is and what's in it
Can pick a Skill for a specific task instead of guessing
Can confirm a Skill actually activated, not just shows as enabled
Understand how a ready-made Skill behaves in a project and how to tune it
Stop wasting time reinventing what already exists in one click

applyIn.title: Presentations from text
applyIn.description: Enable pptx, hand Claude your text, get a finished .pptx from a template without opening PowerPoint.

applyIn.title: Parsing PDFs and documents
applyIn.description: The pdf Skill pulls the gist, tables and key figures from a long document with no manual copying.

applyIn.title: Working with spreadsheets
applyIn.description: xlsx builds and edits Excel files — formulas, pivots, formatting — from a task described in words.

pitfalls: Writing your own Skill for PDF, Excel or slides without opening Browse — losing half an hour where a one-click solution exists
Assuming enabled = active: a Skill only fires when the task matches its purpose
Enabling everything 'just in case' — extra Skills confuse Claude's choice of tool
Not reading a Skill's description before enabling, then being surprised it does the wrong thing
Trusting any source: install Anthropic's Skills, and verify what third-party ones actually do

exercises.question: You need to turn a long report into a presentation. Which ready-made Skill do you use and where do you find it?
exercises.hint: Presentations = .pptx. Catalog: Project Settings, then Skills, then Browse.

exercises.question: You enabled a Skill, but Claude seems to ignore it. How do you check it actually activated?
exercises.hint: Give a task that directly matches the Skill's purpose and see whether Claude follows its steps/template in the answer.

exercises.question: Browse has no ready-made Skill for your task. What's next?
exercises.hint: Move on to [[node:s-create|building your own Skill]] — but only after confirming none exists.

srd-1.title: What ready-made Skills are and where to get them
srd-1.why: Before doing anything by hand or writing your own Skill, you need to know: half the routine is already covered by Anthropic's ready-made skills.
instructions: Open [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] and go into a project.
Navigate: Project Settings, then Skills, then Browse.
Look through the Anthropic-built Skills: pptx, xlsx, pdf, docx, skill-creator.
Read each description — what it does and which task it's for.
srd-1.validate: You can see the Browse catalog and name at least 3 ready-made Skills and their purpose.
srd-1.tip: The catalog is your first stop before any file-related task. Browse first, everything else after.

srd-2.title: How to choose the right Skill
srd-2.why: Guessing leads to a Skill that either doesn't fire or does the wrong thing. A Skill is matched to the type of task.
instructions: State the task in one sentence: 'need a presentation', 'parse a PDF', 'build a table'.
Match the output type to the Skill's purpose: .pptx for pptx, .xlsx for xlsx, PDF analysis for pdf, Word for docx.
Open the chosen Skill's description and confirm it covers exactly your case.
If none fits — note that: next stop is [[node:s-create|your own Skill]].
srd-2.validate: You've picked one specific Skill for your task and can explain why that one.
srd-2.tip: A Skill's purpose is the output format, not the topic. 'A presentation about finance' is pptx, not a 'finance' Skill.

srd-3.title: Enable it and verify it activates
srd-3.why: An enabled Skill isn't a working one — it only fires when the task matches its purpose. You need to verify this in practice.
instructions: In Browse, click add on the chosen Skill — it turns on for the project.
Give Claude a task that directly matches the Skill's purpose (e.g. 'Create a presentation from this text: …').
Check the answer: Claude should follow the Skill's steps and produce the right file/format.
If the Skill didn't fire — rephrase the task so it clearly demands its output.
srd-3.validate: You gave a test task and got a result that shows the Skill at work (the right file or format).
srd-3.tip: If Claude ignores the Skill, it's almost always the wording: the task doesn't 'sound' like its profile.

srd-4.title: Tune it to your needs
srd-4.why: A ready-made Skill is the baseline. You steer its behavior toward your standards (template, tone, structure) through the project and your wording.
instructions: Spell out your requirements in the task: brand style, slide structure, the table columns you need.
Use project instructions so you don't restate recurring requirements every time.
Run the Skill again and compare the result against the standard you want.
Save the winning phrasing as a ready prompt for reuse.
srd-4.validate: The Skill's output matches your standard, not the default template.
srd-4.tip: You don't rewrite a ready-made Skill — you steer it through project context and a precise request.

srd-5.title: Updates and trusting the source
srd-5.why: Skills get updated, and you can install ones beyond Anthropic's. The source decides whether you can trust what a Skill does with your data.
instructions: Prioritize Anthropic's Skills in Browse — they're officially written and tested.
Before enabling a third-party Skill, read its description: what it does and what it accesses.
Check Browse periodically — the list and capabilities of ready-made Skills keep growing.
If a Skill behaves differently after an update — re-verify it on the test task from step 3.
srd-5.validate: You can explain why you trust an enabled Skill and know where it came from.
srd-5.tip: Unknown source = read the description first, enable second. Anthropic Skills are the safest start.

srd-6.title: Mistakes and the final check
srd-6.why: The common traps with ready-made Skills are predictable — knowing them upfront saves time and spares you junk output.
instructions: Check: are you writing your own Skill where a ready-made one exists in Browse?
Make sure only the needed Skill is enabled, not a dozen 'just in case'.
Re-read the enabled Skill's description — does it do exactly what you expect?
Run a control task and compare the result against what it should be.
If nothing ready-made fits — deliberately move to [[node:s-create|building your own]] or the [[node:skills|Skills]] overview.
srd-6.validate: The ready-made Skill is chosen deliberately, only the needed one is enabled, tested on a task, and gives the expected result.
srd-6.tip: The rule is simple: Browse first, verify activation, and only then — your own Skill.

skill-create.title: Build your own Skill
skill-create.subtitle: Turn a repeating process into a /skill command with /skill-creator
skill-create.whatItIs: A Skill is a packaged instruction that Claude picks up by its description and applies automatically. In [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] you build one with /skill-creator: you answer a few questions and it produces a SKILL.md file with a name, description, and steps. This course goes from deciding "is a Skill even worth it" to a working, tested command.
skill-create.approach: We follow the logic of the Skill itself: first confirm the task is genuinely repeatable, then run /skill-creator, precisely describe WHAT and WHEN (name/description) — that drives activation, write the body steps, add supporting files, and finally test activation on a real request and fix the misses.
outcomes: Tell a Skill-worthy task from a one-off using the "≥ 3 times" rule
Run /skill-creator and walk through its questions without getting stuck
Write a description that makes the Skill fire at the right moment
Write the body steps and attach supporting files
Test activation and refine the Skill based on the result

applyIn.title: Recurring text audits
applyIn.description: A Skill with fixed review criteria — you type /audit and Claude applies the same checklist to any text.

applyIn.title: Task and report formatting
applyIn.description: A single brief or report template in a Skill — you don't explain the format each time, the command shapes the output for you.

applyIn.title: Team processes
applyIn.description: One Skill in a Project sets a shared standard — everyone gets the same result from one command.

pitfalls: Building a Skill "just in case" with no real repeating need — it never pays off and clutters the Project.
A vague description ("help with text") — Claude can't tell WHEN to fire the Skill, so it doesn't.
Cramming three different tasks into one Skill — three narrow Skills beat one "do-everything" Skill.
Writing the steps but never testing activation on a live request.
Loading bulky data straight into SKILL.md instead of moving it to a supporting file.

exercises.question: Name a process from your work that repeats ≥ 3 times a week and that you re-explain to Claude every time. Does it qualify for a Skill?
exercises.hint: A good candidate has the same steps and output format across different inputs.

exercises.question: Write a one-sentence description for that Skill: WHAT it does and WHEN it should fire.
exercises.hint: A strong description names the trigger situation, not just the function: "when text needs checking against checklist X."

exercises.question: Which chunk of data in your Skill should live in a separate supporting file rather than in SKILL.md?
exercises.hint: Long lists, templates, references — anything that bloats the main file and rarely changes in substance.

scr-1.title: Decide whether you need a Skill
scr-1.why: A Skill only pays off on a repeatable task. "Just in case" it isn't worth it — it takes up space and interferes with other Skills firing.
instructions: Take a task you give Claude regularly.
Apply the "≥ 3 times a week" rule: if rarer, it's a one-off, not a Skill.
Confirm the steps and output format stay the same across different inputs.
If yes on all points — the task is ready to become a Skill.
scr-1.validate: You have a concrete process that repeats ≥ 3 times and that you re-explain to Claude every time.
scr-1.tip: Unsure — compare with the [[node:skills|Skills]] node: a Skill replaces re-explaining "how exactly to do it".

scr-2.title: Run /skill-creator
scr-2.why: /skill-creator is a built-in helper: it asks the right questions and assembles a valid SKILL.md so you don't write the structure by hand.
instructions: Open the right Project in [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]].
Type /skill-creator in the chat.
Wait until it starts asking questions about the future Skill.
Answer to the point — based on the process from step 1.
scr-2.validate: /skill-creator launched and asked its first question (the Skill's name or purpose).
scr-2.tip: Keep the step-1 process description handy — answering its questions will go faster.

scr-3.title: Describe WHAT and WHEN (name/description)
scr-3.why: Claude decides whether to fire the Skill from its description field. A vague description = the Skill won't fire at the right moment.
instructions: Give the Skill a short, clear name in kebab-case (e.g. text-audit).
In the description state WHAT the Skill does in one phrase.
Add the trigger situation WHEN to fire it — specific words and request context.
Avoid generic wording like "help with text".
scr-3.validate: The description carries both the function and the firing condition — it's clear when the Skill should activate.
scr-3.tip: File structure details are in the [[node:s-md|SKILL.md]] node; firing principles are in [[node:s-trigger|triggers]].

scr-4.title: Write the body steps
scr-4.why: The Skill body is the instruction Claude follows to do the task. Clear steps give a repeatable result instead of improvisation.
instructions: Break the process into sequential steps, as you'd do it by hand.
For each step, state the action and the expected result.
Pin down the output format if it matters (report structure, checklist).
Cut the noise — keep only what the task actually needs.
scr-4.validate: The SKILL.md body describes the process step by step, and the task can be done from it without extra explanation.
scr-4.tip: Lean on the body structure in the [[node:s-md|SKILL.md]] node — step headings beat a "wall of text".

scr-5.title: Add supporting files
scr-5.why: Templates, references, and long data shouldn't bloat SKILL.md. Moved-out files keep the main file light and readable.
instructions: Single out data that doesn't change in substance: templates, checklists, examples.
Place them as separate files next to SKILL.md.
In the Skill body, reference these files instead of pasting the full content.
Keep only the instruction and logic in SKILL.md.
scr-5.validate: Bulky data is moved into separate files, and SKILL.md stays compact and references them.
scr-5.tip: What exactly to move out and how to structure it — see the [[node:s-files|supporting files]] node.

scr-6.title: Test activation and refine
scr-6.why: A Skill untested on a live request may not fire or may give the wrong result. The test reveals real misses in the description and steps.
instructions: Give a real request that the Skill should fire on by itself.
Check that it activated without an explicit command call.
Compare the result with the expected format from step 4.
If it didn't fire — sharpen the description (step 3); if the result is wrong — fix the steps (step 4).
Repeat the test until activation and output are stable.
scr-6.validate: The Skill fires on a real request on its own and returns the result in the right format.
scr-6.tip: A common mistake is blaming the steps when the description is at fault. Check firing first ([[node:s-trigger|triggers]]), then quality.

skill-vs-subagents.title: Skill ≠ Sub-agent: when to use which
skill-vs-subagents.subtitle: A recipe for 'what to do' versus a separate executor with its own context
skill-vs-subagents.whatItIs: A short breakdown of two distinct mechanisms that are easy to confuse. A [[node:skills|Skill]] is a recipe for WHAT to do: a set of steps Claude follows inside the current chat, with no context or tools of its own. A Sub-agent (see [[node:cc-subagents|Sub-agents]]) is a separate executor with its own context window and access to tools (files, terminal, network), launched from [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] for isolated tasks. This course teaches you to pick one for a given task.
skill-vs-subagents.approach: We move from the core distinction to the practice of choosing. First we separate the concepts (recipe vs executor), then we map the boundaries: when a Skill is enough, when you need a Sub-agent, how they combine, and where people get confused. The finale is a selection algorithm for the task at hand, with a check. Each step rests on one distinction, with no repetition or filler.
outcomes: Explain the distinction in one sentence: Skill = WHAT to do, Sub-agent = a separate executor with its own context
See when a task fits a Skill and external tools aren't needed
Recognize the signs that require a Sub-agent: context isolation, tools, parallelism, long-running work
Combine both: a Sub-agent does the work, relying on a Skill as its procedure
Pick the mechanism for a task in seconds and verify the choice against a checklist

applyIn.title: Repeatable formatting
applyIn.description: A template procedure with no external tools (formatting a task, report, commit) is a Skill. Claude follows the steps right in the chat, instantly.

applyIn.title: Isolated research
applyIn.description: Walking repo files, gathering data, finding outdated dependencies is a Sub-agent: its own context window and tool access, without cluttering the main chat.

applyIn.title: Complex pipeline
applyIn.description: A large task split into parallel branches, where each Sub-agent follows its own Skill recipe — a combination of both mechanisms.

pitfalls: A Sub-agent for a template task is overkill: it takes longer to launch and burns context where a Skill would do in seconds
A Skill for long research with files will hit the main chat's context limit, forcing a redo
Assuming a Skill has its own context and tools — it doesn't, it runs inside the current chat and depends on its window
Confusing 'separate executor' with 'different model' — a Sub-agent is context and tool isolation, not a model swap
Choosing the mechanism by habit rather than by task — always check against the signs of isolation and tools

exercises.question: Task: every time you're asked to write a release note, format it using a fixed template, no file reading. Skill or Sub-agent?
exercises.hint: Ask: does the task repeat? Are external tools needed? If the steps fit a recipe and no tools are involved — it's a Skill.

exercises.question: Task: walk through 200 repo files and collect a list of TODOs. What do you pick and why?
exercises.hint: Long file-reading work clutters the main chat. You need context isolation and tool access — signs of a Sub-agent.

exercises.question: Can you use both at once? Give an example of the combination.
exercises.hint: A Sub-agent is an executor. Give it a Skill as a procedure: it works in its own context, following your recipe for WHAT to do.

svs-1.title: The core distinction: recipe vs executor
svs-1.why: Without a clear boundary between 'what to do' and 'who does it', every later decision is a guess. This is the foundation of the choice.
instructions: Memorize the formula: a [[node:skills|Skill]] = a recipe for WHAT to do, Claude follows the steps inside the current chat
Memorize the second: a Sub-agent = a separate executor with its own context window and tools (files, terminal, network)
Note the key point: a Skill has no context of its own — it depends on the current chat's window
Note the second key point: a Sub-agent is launched from [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] for isolated tasks
svs-1.validate: You can explain the distinction in one sentence without confusing 'recipe' and 'executor'.
svs-1.tip: Analogy: a Skill is an instruction on paper, a Sub-agent is a separate worker you can hand that instruction to.

svs-2.title: When a Skill is enough
svs-2.why: Most repeatable tasks don't need isolation — and a Skill solves them in seconds, with no overhead.
instructions: Check the repeatability sign: the task recurs regularly and fits into fixed steps
