Downloads is a temporary zone: downloaded, used, then deleted or moved
Once a week, quickly tidy both places
If something valuable ended up in Downloads — send it to ~/projects/
fs-organize-disk-5.validate: The Desktop doesn't look like a dump of dozens of files with spaces in their names.
fs-organize-disk-5.tip: The rule is simple: the Desktop is a desk, not a cabinet. Only the current task belongs on the desk.

fs-organize-disk-6.title: Set up a backup or sync
fs-organize-disk-6.why: A disk can fail, a laptop can be lost. Without a copy the whole tidy system vanishes in a second. A backup turns order into reliability.
instructions: Simple option: put ~/projects/ inside a cloud folder (iCloud, Google Drive, Dropbox)
System option on Mac: turn on Time Machine with an external drive
Check that sync really runs: create a test file and confirm it appears in the cloud
Decide once and forget — the backup should work on its own
fs-organize-disk-6.validate: You can honestly answer: "if the disk dies tomorrow, my projects won't be lost".
fs-organize-disk-6.tip: The best backup is one you don't have to think about. Automatic sync beats manual copying that you'll forget to do.

course-fs-navigate.title: Navigate and look around
course-fs-navigate.subtitle: Basic terminal navigation: pwd, ls, cd — three commands that handle 95% of tasks
course-fs-navigate.whatItIs: A short hands-on course on moving between folders in the terminal. You'll learn how to find out where you are (`pwd`), see what's in a folder (`ls`), and step in and out of folders (`cd`). That's the whole vocabulary you need to bring [[node:cc-install|Claude Code]] into the right project folder.
course-fs-navigate.approach: We learn by doing, not by theory: each step is one command you type right into your own terminal and watch the result. First "where am I", then "what's around me", then "how to move". At the end you put it all together and walk yourself to a project folder ready to launch.
outcomes: Open the terminal without being scared of the empty window
Instantly know which folder you're currently in
See the contents of any folder with one command
Freely step into folders and climb back out
Bring the terminal to your project folder before launching Claude Code

applyIn.title: Before every Claude Code session
applyIn.description: Claude Code works in the folder where you launched it. First you move into the project folder, then launch — otherwise it digs around in the wrong files.

applyIn.title: Installing tools and dependencies
applyIn.description: Install commands act on the current folder. Check `pwd`, make sure you're in the right place, and only then install.

applyIn.title: Figuring out "where did my files go"
applyIn.description: If a file ended up "who knows where" — `pwd` and `ls` show where you actually were in five seconds.

pitfalls: Running commands without checking `pwd` first — then wondering why everything was created in the wrong folder.
Confusing `cd ..` (go up one level) with `cd .` (stay put) — the number of dots matters exactly.
Getting the folder name wrong: the terminal distinguishes upper and lower case — `Projects` and `projects` are different folders.
Writing a path with spaces without quotes: `cd My Folder` breaks, you need `cd "My Folder"`.
Thinking `ls` showed nothing because of an error — when really the folder is simply empty.

exercises.question: You opened the terminal and don't know which folder you ended up in. What command tells you?
exercises.hint: Three letters, stands for "print working directory".

exercises.question: You're in the project folder but need to go up to the parent folder. What do you type?
exercises.hint: `cd` plus two dots. Two dots always mean "one level up".

exercises.question: You're in the home folder, there's a projects folder next to you, and atlas inside it. How do you enter atlas with one command?
exercises.hint: You can build a path with a slash: `cd projects/atlas`.

fs-navigate-1.title: Open the terminal
fs-navigate-1.why: The terminal is a window where you type text commands and the computer runs them. Without it, navigating folders isn't possible.
instructions: On Mac: press Cmd+Space, type "Terminal" and press Enter.
On Windows: open the Start menu, type "PowerShell" and launch it.
On Linux: usually Ctrl+Alt+T or search "Terminal" in the app menu.
A window with a blinking cursor and a prompt line appeared — you're ready.
fs-navigate-1.validate: You see a window with a text line you can type into. The cursor is blinking.
fs-navigate-1.tip: Don't close this window until the end of the course — every step happens right here.

fs-navigate-2.title: Find out where you are — pwd
fs-navigate-2.why: Every command runs in the "current" folder. Before doing anything, it's always useful to know exactly where you are.
instructions: Type `pwd` and press Enter.
The terminal prints the full path, e.g. `/Users/name` or `C:\Users\name`.
That's your current folder — all commands run from here right now.
fs-navigate-2.validate: You see a path line starting with a slash (Mac/Linux) or a drive letter (Windows).
fs-navigate-2.tip: Whenever you doubt "where am I anyway?" — `pwd` first. It's free and breaks nothing.

fs-navigate-3.title: Look around — ls
fs-navigate-3.why: To move into a folder, you need its exact name. `ls` shows the list of what's next to you.
instructions: Type `ls` (on Mac/Linux) or `dir` (on Windows) and press Enter.
The terminal lists the folders and files in the current folder.
Find familiar names in the list — for example Desktop, Documents, projects.
If the list is empty — the folder is just empty, that's not an error.
fs-navigate-3.validate: You see a list of folder and file names (or an empty line if the folder is empty).
fs-navigate-3.tip: Folder names often stand out by color or a trailing slash — those are your targets for `cd`.

fs-navigate-4.title: Step into a folder — cd
fs-navigate-4.why: `cd` (change directory) moves you inside a folder. That's how you approach the right place step by step.
instructions: Pick any folder from the `ls` list, for example Desktop.
Type `cd Desktop` (exactly the same case as in the list) and press Enter.
Type `pwd` again — the path got longer, the folder name was added at the end.
Type `ls` once more — now you see the contents of the new folder.
fs-navigate-4.validate: After `cd`, the `pwd` command shows a path with the folder name added at the end.
fs-navigate-4.tip: Type the first letters of the folder name and press Tab — the terminal completes the rest and saves you from typos.

fs-navigate-5.title: Step back out — cd ..
fs-navigate-5.why: Sometimes you went too deep or into the wrong place. Two dots mean "the folder one level up" and take you back.
instructions: While inside a folder, type `cd ..` and press Enter.
Check the result with `pwd` — the path is shorter by one name.
To go up two levels at once, type `cd ../..`.
To instantly return to your home folder, just type `cd` and Enter.
fs-navigate-5.validate: After `cd ..`, the path in `pwd` is shorter than before — you went up one level.
fs-navigate-5.tip: Lost after several moves? Type `cd` with nothing — you'll return to your home folder and start fresh.

fs-navigate-6.title: Reach the project folder
fs-navigate-6.why: The final goal of navigation is to bring the terminal into the project folder so [[node:cc-install|Claude Code]] works with your files. How to organize the folders themselves is in [[node:fs-organize-disk|keeping your disk tidy]].
instructions: Using `ls` and `cd`, walk to your project folder (e.g. `cd projects/atlas`).
Type `pwd` — confirm the path leads exactly to the right folder.
Type `ls` — you should see the project files (src, package.json, CLAUDE.md, etc.).
Now the terminal is in the right place — from here you can launch Claude Code or [[node:fs-install-node|install Node.js]].
fs-navigate-6.validate: `pwd` shows the path to the project folder, and `ls` shows that project's files.
fs-navigate-6.tip: Write down the command to reach your project (`cd ~/projects/atlas`) — handy to copy before every session so you don't wander again.

course-fs-install-node.title: Install Node.js
course-fs-install-node.subtitle: Set up the npm "engine" from scratch — and verify it works
course-fs-install-node.whatItIs: Node.js is the program that runs npm commands on your computer. npm is how you install [[node:cc-install|Claude Code]] and most developer tools. Without Node.js, the `npm install` command simply doesn't exist on your system. Installation takes a couple of minutes and is done once per machine.
course-fs-install-node.approach: We follow the principle "download LTS, install, verify". LTS is the stable, long-term-support version — that's the one to install (fresh, not ancient). On Mac it's easiest via Homebrew or the official installer; on Windows via the installer from nodejs.org. At the end two short commands `node -v` and `npm -v` confirm everything is in place.
outcomes: You understand why Node.js is needed for Claude Code and npm
You know the difference between LTS and Current and why we pick LTS
You installed Node.js your way (Mac or Windows)
You verified the install with node -v and npm -v
You can recognize and fix common install errors

applyIn.title: Installing Claude Code
applyIn.description: Node.js is a hard requirement before `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`. Without it the Claude Code install won't run.

applyIn.title: Connecting MCP servers
applyIn.description: Many MCP servers install via npx, which is part of Node.js. Node first, then any MCP tool.

applyIn.title: Any npm packages
applyIn.description: After installing, you grab linters, bundlers, and CLI utilities with one command. Node.js unlocks the whole npm ecosystem.

pitfalls: Installing an old version (14.x or 16.x) and hitting "engine not supported" errors. Always grab a fresh LTS.
Downloading Current instead of LTS out of curiosity — LTS is more stable for work, Current can be raw.
Not restarting the terminal after install — the old window doesn't see the new node. Close and reopen it.
On Windows, forgetting the "Add to PATH" checkbox in the installer — then `node -v` returns "command not found".
Installing from random sites instead of nodejs.org — risk of a fake. Use the official source only.

exercises.question: You open a new terminal and `node -v` returns "command not found", even though the installer finished. What's the likely cause?
exercises.hint: Think about PATH and whether the current terminal window sees the new program. What should you do with the window?

exercises.question: On nodejs.org there are two big buttons: LTS and Current. Which one for working with Claude Code, and why?
exercises.hint: One is stable with long support, the other is the newest but may be unstable.

exercises.question: After `node -v` you see v14.18.0. Can you install Claude Code on this?
exercises.hint: Recall the minimum version (18+) and the "engine not supported" error.

fs-install-node-1.title: Why you need Node.js
fs-install-node-1.why: Before installing, it helps to understand exactly what you're installing and why. This saves you from blindly copying commands.
instructions: Remember: Node.js is the "engine" that can run npm and npx commands on your computer.
The `npm install` command appears on your system only together with Node.js — there's no separate npm.
[[node:cc-install|Claude Code]] and MCP servers install via npm, so Node is a mandatory foundation.
You only need to install it once per machine where you'll work.
fs-install-node-1.validate: You can answer in your own words: "Why do I need Node.js?" — because without it npm doesn't work, and neither does Claude Code.
fs-install-node-1.tip: Node.js and npm install together in one installer — you don't need to look for npm separately.

fs-install-node-2.title: Choose the LTS version
fs-install-node-2.why: The wrong version is the most common cause of errors later. Better to pick correctly upfront.
instructions: Open the official site nodejs.org — only this one, no third-party mirrors.
Find two buttons: LTS and Current. You want LTS.
LTS = "Long Term Support" — the stable, long-supported version recommended for work.
Make sure the version number is 18 or higher — that's the minimum for Claude Code.
fs-install-node-2.validate: You understand you're downloading the LTS version with a number of 18+.
fs-install-node-2.tip: If you're torn between LTS and Current, always take LTS. Current is only for experiments.

fs-install-node-3.title: Install on Mac
fs-install-node-3.why: Mac has two convenient paths; pick one. If you're on Windows, skip to step 4.
instructions: Option 1 (if you have Homebrew): open Terminal and type `brew install node`.
Option 2 (no Homebrew): download the .pkg installer from nodejs.org and go through the "Next, Next" wizard.
Wait for it to finish — usually under a minute.
Close the Terminal window and open a new one so the system sees the new program.
fs-install-node-3.validate: The installer finished without red errors, and you opened a fresh terminal window.
fs-install-node-3.tip: Not sure if you have Homebrew? Type `brew -v`. If you get a version, you have it; if an error, use the .pkg.

fs-install-node-4.title: Install on Windows
fs-install-node-4.why: On Windows the key point is adding Node to PATH, otherwise commands won't be found. If you're on Mac, skip to step 5.
instructions: Download the .msi installer (LTS) from nodejs.org.
Run it and go through the wizard with "Next".
Make sure the "Add to PATH" item is enabled — it's usually on by default.
Finish the install and close all open command-line windows.
fs-install-node-4.validate: The install completed, "Add to PATH" was active, and old terminal windows are closed.
fs-install-node-4.tip: After installing, open a new command line (cmd or PowerShell) — the old one doesn't know about node.

fs-install-node-5.title: Verify the install
fs-install-node-5.why: Two short commands confirm that Node.js and npm are in place and visible to the system.
instructions: In a new terminal window, type `node -v` and press Enter.
A version like v20.11.0 should appear (the number may differ, just 18+).
Now type `npm -v` — you'll see the npm version, e.g. 10.2.4.
If both commands show versions, the install succeeded.
fs-install-node-5.validate: Both `node -v` and `npm -v` print a version number without errors.
fs-install-node-5.tip: The npm version is always different from the node version — that's normal, they're two separate programs.

fs-install-node-6.title: Fix common problems
fs-install-node-6.why: If the check failed, it's almost always one of four typical causes. Let's go through them.
instructions: "command not found": close and reopen the terminal, then check again.
If that didn't help — on Windows, reinstall with "Add to PATH" enabled.
Seeing an old version (14.x, 16.x): remove it and install a fresh LTS again.
Ready for the next step? Next you install [[node:cc-install|Claude Code]] with one npm command.
fs-install-node-6.validate: After re-checking, `node -v` shows version 18+ with no errors — you can move on to installing Claude Code.
fs-install-node-6.tip: 90% of problems are solved by "close and reopen the terminal" — try that first.

course-pl-plans.title: Claude Plans: Free, Pro, Max, Team
course-pl-plans.subtitle: What each plan includes, who needs which, and how to avoid overpaying
course-pl-plans.whatItIs: Claude's plan lineup is simple: you pay not for individual features but for **access tier to models + quota volume**. Free is a trial (limited models, low quotas). Pro is for daily individual work with all models. Max gives the same models but much higher Opus limits. Team adds Projects and shared team billing. This course teaches you to read the lineup and match a plan to your real usage rather than the marketing.
course-pl-plans.approach: We start from your actual scenario, not from a price table. First we unpack how plans really differ (models and quotas, not features), then we estimate your weekly Opus and long-session volume, then we map it against the thresholds from Pro to Max and from one seat to Team. We deliberately don't memorize prices — Anthropic changes them 1-2 times a year, so the final step is always "check anthropic.com/pricing".
outcomes: You understand that Pro/Max/Team give identical functionality — the difference is only models and limits
You can estimate your weekly Opus and long-session volume to choose between Pro and Max
You know when Team is justified (≥3 people + shared Projects) and when it's overpayment
You avoid the Free trap — you don't draw conclusions about Claude's power from it
You can upgrade and downgrade deliberately based on actually hitting limits, not blindly

applyIn.title: Personal plan choice
applyIn.description: You work with Claude daily and aren't sure whether Pro is enough or it's time for Max. You count your Opus session volume and decide by threshold, not by feeling.

applyIn.title: Team decision
applyIn.description: Your team of 2-5 people considers Team "for convenience". You check the ≥3 people + genuinely shared Projects criterion, otherwise you keep individual Pro plans.

applyIn.title: Sizing before a demo/pilot
applyIn.description: You're preparing a serious showcase of Claude's capabilities. You don't run it on Free — otherwise you'll hit the quota within an hour and seed the false conclusion "Claude is weak".

pitfalls: Staying on Free "until I figure it out" — limits won't let you figure it out, and you form a false impression of the capabilities
Taking Team when the team is fewer than 3 people — you pay for empty seats
Paying for Pro but only working on Sonnet — then you barely use what differs from Free, while Opus is exactly what justifies the price
Jumping straight to Max "just in case" — without regularly hitting the weekly Opus limit it's paying for empty space
Memorizing exact prices and plan composition — Anthropic revises them 1-2 times a year, the current info is only on the site

exercises.question: You work with Claude 3-5 hours a day: Sonnet for code plus 2-3 long Opus sessions per week. Pro or Max?
exercises.hint: Max is needed only if you *regularly* hit the weekly Opus limit. 2-3 sessions isn't hitting the wall yet. Start with Pro and watch for the moment the Opus limit becomes the bottleneck.

exercises.question: A 2-person team suggests moving to Team for convenience. What to check before deciding?
exercises.hint: The Team criterion is ≥3 people AND real shared work in Projects with unified billing. For two it's overpayment: two individual Pro plans are usually better value.

exercises.question: Why is it risky to judge Claude's "power" after trying it for a couple of hours on Free?
exercises.hint: Free gives limited models and low quotas. A serious load hits the limit within an hour, and the impression forms from cut-down access, not from Opus's real capabilities.

pl-plans-1.title: The core principle: you pay for access and quotas, not features
pl-plans-1.why: Most choice mistakes come from the thought "more expensive = more features". In reality Pro, Max and Team give identical functionality — they differ only in available models and limit size. You need to grasp this before comparing prices.
instructions: Memorize the formula: price = model access tier + quota volume, not a set of unique features
Accept that Pro/Max/Team are functionally equal — moving up gives more limits and models, not new buttons
Connect this with how the models themselves work — see [[node:pl-models|Claude models]]
Drop the mindset "I'll take a pricier plan, it has more features" — that's not the case here
pl-plans-1.validate: You can explain in one sentence how Pro differs from Max without mentioning a single "exclusive feature".
pl-plans-1.tip: If a seller/ad promises "features only on the higher plan" — it's almost always about limits and models, not functionality.

pl-plans-2.title: Unpacking the lineup: Free, Pro, Max, Team
pl-plans-2.why: To choose, you need to hold each plan's purpose in mind. This is the map the rest of the calculation runs on.
instructions: Free — trial: limited models and low quotas, only for first acquaintance
Pro — daily individual work with all models and reasonable limits
Max — the same models, but noticeably raised Opus limits (the plan launched in 2025)
Team — Projects between colleagues plus shared team billing
Note that Enterprise (SSO, audit log, SLA) is a separate story for compliance, not for individual choice
pl-plans-2.validate: You can name from memory the key purpose of Free, Pro, Max and Team in one phrase each.
pl-plans-2.tip: Keep the differences in terms of "models and limits" — this ties into how quotas are counted, see [[node:pl-limits|limits]].

pl-plans-3.title: Estimating your real usage volume
pl-plans-3.why: A plan is matched to fact, not to wish. Without estimating weekly Opus and long-session volume, any choice is guessing.
instructions: Estimate how many hours a day you actually work with Claude
Split the load: what goes to Sonnet (routine, code) and what needs Opus (complex reasoning)
Count how many long Opus sessions per week you need
Note whether you hit the weekly Opus limit — and how often (one-off or regular)
pl-plans-3.validate: You have two numbers: long sessions per week and an approximate count of hitting the Opus limit per week.
pl-plans-3.tip: A reference for individual work — 5-20 long sessions per week usually fit within Pro.

pl-plans-4.title: Choosing between Pro and Max
pl-plans-4.why: This is the most common decision for an individual user. A mistake either way costs money or time waiting for reset.
instructions: By default start with Pro — it covers daily individual work with all models
Move to Max only if you *regularly* hit the weekly Opus limit on Pro
Don't jump to Max "just in case" — hitting the wall once every couple of weeks isn't a reason
If you pay for Pro but only sit on Sonnet — reconsider: you aren't using the main advantage a paid plan is taken for
pl-plans-4.validate: You've chosen Pro or Max and can name a concrete reason (e.g. "I hit Opus 3-4 times a week, so Max").
pl-plans-4.tip: Max pays off through removed friction: if you wait daily for the Opus limit to reset, the lost time is worth more than the price difference.

pl-plans-5.title: When you need Team and when it's overpayment
pl-plans-5.why: Team sounds "more solid", and teams take it prematurely. The criterion is simple and easy to check before paying.
instructions: Take Team only if you are ≥3 people AND you genuinely work in shared Projects
Team's value is shared Projects plus unified team billing, not more models
If there are two of you — stay on individual Pro: Team for two is almost always overpayment
Compare plans by your own set of criteria before deciding — see [[node:pl-compare|plan comparison]]
pl-plans-5.validate: You can say "yes/no" on Team based on two conditions: team size and presence of shared Projects.
pl-plans-5.tip: "Convenience of a shared bill" alone doesn't justify Team if there are no shared Projects — it's just a different way to pay.

pl-plans-6.title: Upgrade, downgrade and checking current prices
pl-plans-6.why: Choosing a plan isn't a one-time decision. Volume changes, and Anthropic revises plan composition and prices 1-2 times a year. The right habit is to move by fact and always check the primary source.
instructions: Agree on triggers with yourself: regularly hitting the limit means upgrade; seats/Opus sitting idle means downgrade
Don't memorize exact prices — they change; keep only the choice logic in mind
Before paying or switching plans, always open anthropic.com/pricing and look at the current composition
Every few months re-check your plan: has volume grown, has a new plan appeared for your case
pl-plans-6.validate: You have a personal rule "when to upgrade and when to downgrade", and you know you only verify prices on the site.
pl-plans-6.tip: Anthropic changes plan composition and prices 1-2 times a year — no memorized table replaces checking anthropic.com/pricing before paying.

course-pl-limits.title: Usage limits: how to live with them
course-pl-limits.subtitle: The 5-hour window, the weekly ceiling, and the habits that keep you from hitting a wall mid-work
course-pl-limits.whatItIs: A practical course on how Claude's limits work: where they come from, how the rolling 5-hour window works (not a calendar reset), why Opus burns through the quota faster than Sonnet, and what to do when you've already hit the limit. No invented numbers — Anthropic doesn't publish them and adjusts by demand, so we teach the principle, not the digits.
course-pl-limits.approach: We go from model to habit. First the mechanics of the two windows (5h + weekly), then reading the indicator and predicting the wall, then saving tactics (right model per task, sprints with breaks), then a plan of action when the limit is reached. Finally — a personal plan for spreading load across the day and week.
outcomes: You understand the difference between the rolling 5-hour window and the weekly ceiling
You read the usage indicator and see the limit approaching in advance
You spread heavy requests across the day instead of hitting a mid-day wall
You pick the model per task: Opus for hard work, Sonnet for routine
You have a clear plan for when the limit is already reached

applyIn.title: A long workday with Claude
applyIn.description: Several heavy sessions in a row — you arrange them so the 5-hour window doesn't wipe out your afternoon.

applyIn.title: A team or intensive week
applyIn.description: Lots of Opus tasks across the week — you watch the weekly ceiling and decide whether you need a higher plan.

applyIn.title: A deadline with no downtime allowed
applyIn.description: You keep a quota buffer in advance and move routine to Sonnet so you don't stall at the critical moment.

pitfalls: Assuming the limit "resets at midnight" — it's rolling, counted from the first message in the window
Staying on Opus for everything — the fastest way to drain the quota; Sonnet handles up to 80% of work
Ignoring the usage indicator in the interface — it warns in advance, not after the fact
Memorizing specific numbers from someone's post — Anthropic changes them by demand, the number goes stale
Dropping the work when you hit the wall instead of switching the model or taking a short pause until the window frees up

exercises.question: You have 4 long Opus sessions of 100k tokens each. You did three in the morning back to back. Should you launch the fourth right away?
exercises.hint: Recall the mechanics: the window is rolling and counted from the first message. Three heavy sessions already sit inside the current 5 hours.

exercises.question: Claude started to "slow down" and a warning appeared. Which of the two windows most likely triggered, and what does that mean for today's plan?
exercises.hint: The 5-hour window triggers more often and within the day; the weekly one if you hit the wall on Opus several times a week.

exercises.question: You're hitting the weekly Opus ceiling for the third time in 7 days. Is this a signal to fix habits or to change the plan?
exercises.hint: First check that routine isn't sitting on Opus. If switching to Sonnet doesn't help — it's a plan conversation.

pl-limits-1.title: Where limits come from and why
pl-limits-1.why: Without the "why", a limit feels like a punishment. In reality it protects shared infrastructure from overload — and it's easier to accept once you see the logic.
instructions: Adopt the frame: a limit isn't a bug or a fine, it's protection of servers from demand overload
Remember the key fact: a limit isn't fixed "N messages" — it depends on context length, model and current load
Accept there are no exact public numbers — Anthropic doesn't publish them and changes them by demand
Conclude: we learn the principle and habits, not the digits — the digits go stale
pl-limits-1.validate: You can explain in one sentence why a limit has no single honest "messages per day" number.
pl-limits-1.tip: If you find an exact limit number online, treat it as a rumor: it's only true for a specific date and plan.

pl-limits-2.title: Two windows: 5 hours and a week
pl-limits-2.why: This is the core of the course. Confusing the rolling and calendar window breaks all planning — that's where the "midnight" and "Monday" myths come from.
instructions: Break down the 5-hour window: it's a rolling span of the last 5 hours, counted from the first message, not from a calendar mark
Break down the weekly window: total volume over 7 days, mainly affecting Opus
Lock in: the window doesn't "reset at midnight" — it frees up gradually as old messages slide past the 5-hour edge
Tie it to models: more on the consumption difference — [[node:pl-models|models and their cost]]
pl-limits-2.validate: You can explain the difference: which window triggers within the day, and which is about total weekly volume.
pl-limits-2.tip: Mental image: the 5-hour window is a "belt" where old messages slide off and free space on their own — not a "tank" emptied once a day.

pl-limits-3.title: Read the indicator and predict the wall
pl-limits-3.why: The limit almost never hits out of nowhere — the interface warns ahead. Those who read the indicator don't lose hours mid-work.
instructions: Find the usage indicator in the interface and get used to glancing at it before a heavy session
Catch early signals: "Claude is slowing down" and a warning about approaching the limit — usually the 5-hour window
Tell the frequency apart: hitting the wall once a day is almost always 5h; several times a week on Opus is the weekly window
Before launching a long task, estimate how much heavy work you've already done in the last 5 hours
pl-limits-3.validate: From the symptom (slowdown / warning / frequency) you can tell which window is near its limit.
pl-limits-3.tip: Make it a rule: one glance at the indicator before a long Opus session. A second that saves hours.

pl-limits-4.title: Saving tactics: right model and sprints
pl-limits-4.why: Most of the quota is eaten by the habit of keeping Opus on everything. A simple task split gives stable productivity without walls.
instructions: Split the tasks: Opus for hard and important, Sonnet for routine and drafts (it handles up to 80% of work)
Remember the consumption gap: Opus eats the quota several times faster than Sonnet
Work in sprints: short intense blocks with breaks instead of a non-stop marathon on the top model
Spread heavy work across the day instead of stacking three giant sessions in a row in the morning
Check the plans and thresholds: [[node:pl-plans|plans and subscriptions]]
pl-limits-4.validate: For a specific to-do list you can say what goes to Sonnet, what stays on Opus, and why.
pl-limits-4.tip: Before each task, a short question: "do I really need Opus here?" Half the time the honest answer is no.

pl-limits-5.title: What to do when the limit is reached
pl-limits-5.why: Hitting the wall isn't the end of work, it's a fork. Without a ready plan you lose 2-3 hours to panic; with one, you lose minutes.
instructions: Don't drop the task: first check if you can switch it to Sonnet, if you hit the wall specifically on Opus
If you hit the 5-hour window — work out when the first message frees up and plan the pause around it
Move the heaviest work to after the window frees up (often that's "in the morning", not "now")
If you hit the weekly ceiling regularly — that's a signal not about tactics but about the plan: time to consider a higher tier
pl-limits-5.validate: You have a step-by-step answer to "limit reached" without downtime or panic.
pl-limits-5.tip: Prepare a mini-list of "tasks without Claude" (planning, review, notes) — it fills the pause while the window frees up.

pl-limits-6.title: A personal load plan for the day and week
pl-limits-6.why: All the knowledge sticks into a habit only through a concrete plan for your rhythm. That turns the course into a skill.
instructions: Describe your typical day: how many heavy sessions, on which model, at what time
Spread the heavy blocks across the day so they don't land in a single 5-hour window
Assign routine to Sonnet, and Opus peaks to moments with a quota buffer
Build a weekly buffer: don't burn all your Opus volume in the first days if you hit the weekly ceiling
Lock in a personal rule of checking the indicator before a long session
pl-limits-6.validate: You have a written plan: what goes to Sonnet, what to Opus, in which windows and with which pauses — for your real schedule.
pl-limits-6.tip: Revisit the plan every couple of weeks: as the nature of tasks changes, so does the split across models and windows.

course-pl-models.title: Models per plan: what's available and when you need the bigger one
course-pl-models.subtitle: Linking each plan to its models, picking a model for the task, and switching deliberately
course-pl-models.whatItIs: A mini-course on which Claude models are available on each plan. Free usually gives Sonnet and Haiku, while Opus unlocks on Pro/Team/Enterprise. The exact model list changes over time, so this course teaches you not to memorize it but to check the current one in the interface and pick a model for the specific task.
course-pl-models.approach: We go from basics to practice: first the link from a plan to its set of models, then reading the current list in [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]], then when you truly need the bigger model, how to switch within a plan, and how to match the choice with your limits. Grounded only in the node's facts, without guessing prices or exact names.
outcomes: You understand why Opus isn't visible on Free — it's a plan limit, not a bug
You can check the current list of available models right in the interface
You pick a model for the task, not 'by habit'
You know when a task justifies moving to the bigger model and when the smaller one is enough
You connect model choice with your plan's limits

applyIn.title: Choosing a plan
applyIn.description: Before paying, you check which models a plan unlocks and don't pay for what you don't need.

applyIn.title: Matching a model to a task
applyIn.description: For a draft or simple question you take the smaller model, for complex reasoning — the bigger one.

applyIn.title: Diagnosing 'I don't see the model I need'
applyIn.description: When a model is unavailable, you quickly see it's the plan and decide whether to change task, model, or plan.

pitfalls: Thinking the absence of Opus on Free is a bug: it's just a plan limit
Memorizing the model list — it changes, always check the current one in the interface
Sticking to one model by habit without checking whether a newer version is better for the task
Using the bigger model for everything and hitting your plan limits faster
Confusing model choice with limits — these are different constraints, see [[node:pl-limits|limits]]

exercises.question: On Free you can't find Opus in the model list. Is this a breakage or normal?
exercises.hint: Recall: Opus unlocks only on Pro/Team/Enterprise.

exercises.question: You need to quickly reword a short text. Which model makes sense and why?
exercises.hint: A simple task doesn't need the most powerful model — save your plan's resource.

exercises.question: Where do you see the exact list of models available to you right now?
exercises.hint: The list changes, check it in the claude.ai interface, not from memory.

pl-models-1.title: The link between plan and set of models
pl-models-1.why: Core idea: models don't open on their own, they come with the plan. Without this you can't understand why something is 'not visible'.
instructions: Remember the principle: each plan unlocks its own set of models
Free usually gives the smaller models — Sonnet and Haiku
The bigger model Opus unlocks on Pro/Team/Enterprise
Compare plan sets in the [[node:pl-plans|Plans]] node
pl-models-1.validate: You can explain in one sentence why Free has no Opus.
pl-models-1.tip: A missing model almost always means 'wrong plan', not an error.

pl-models-2.title: Check the current list in the interface
pl-models-2.why: The exact model list changes over time — memory goes stale, while the interface shows the current state.
instructions: Open [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] under your account
Find the model selector in the chat window
See which models are currently available to you specifically
Note the gap between what you expected and what you see
pl-models-2.validate: You have the real model list of your plan in front of you, not from memory.
pl-models-2.tip: Do this check whenever in doubt — the list updates without warning.

pl-models-3.title: Getting to know the models themselves
pl-models-3.why: To choose deliberately you need to understand how models differ in power and purpose.
instructions: Open the [[node:b-models|Models]] node and study the differences
Note which models count as smaller and which as bigger
Match this with the list you saw in step 2
Write down which model fits your typical tasks
pl-models-3.validate: You can name the strengths of at least two models available to you.
pl-models-3.tip: Don't judge a model by its name — check the description in the models node.

pl-models-4.title: When you really need the bigger model
pl-models-4.why: The bigger model isn't always better: for simple tasks it's overkill and burns your plan's resource faster.
instructions: Split tasks into simple and complex by the amount of reasoning
For drafts and short answers pick the smaller model
For complex analysis and long reasoning — the bigger one
Ask yourself: what do I lose if I take the smaller model?
pl-models-4.validate: For your current task you justifiably picked the smaller or bigger model.
pl-models-4.tip: In doubt — start with the smaller one and move up only when quality falls short.

pl-models-5.title: Switching models within a plan
pl-models-5.why: Within one plan several models are often available — being able to switch saves resource and time.
instructions: Find the model selector in the chat window
Switch to another available model and assess the answer
Compare quality and speed on the same task
Pick the model that gives the needed result at lower cost
pl-models-5.validate: You deliberately changed the model and see the difference in result.
pl-models-5.tip: A habit of one model holds you back — test new versions on your tasks.

pl-models-6.title: Link with limits and the final choice
pl-models-6.why: Model choice and plan limits are connected: the bigger model spends resource faster, and it's important to keep that in mind.
instructions: Open the [[node:pl-limits|Limits]] node and understand your plan's bounds
Match how often you use the bigger model with the limit
Build a personal rule: which model for which task
If you lack models or limit, weigh moving to a higher plan via [[node:pl-plans|Plans]]
pl-models-6.validate: You have a simple rule for choosing a model that accounts for plan limits.
pl-models-6.tip: First optimize your model choice, and only then think about changing the plan.

course-pl-platforms.title: Where Claude works: pick the platform for the task
course-pl-platforms.subtitle: Web, Desktop, Mobile, Code and API — what each offers and when to use it
course-pl-platforms.whatItIs: Claude isn't "one website" but a family of channels: web ([[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]]), mobile apps (iOS/Android), desktop ([[node:pl-desktop|Mac/Windows]]), [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] in the terminal, VS Code/JetBrains extensions, and an API to embed into a product. All of them sit under one account: subscription and chat history are shared.
course-pl-platforms.approach: We start from the task, not from habit. First we go through each platform — what it's for and where it shines. Then we learn to pick a channel for a concrete scenario: chat on the go, working with documents, development, automation, embedding. Finally — one shared account and a quick selection cheat sheet via the [[node:pl-compare|platform comparison]].
outcomes: You know every Claude channel and the strength of each
You pick a platform for a task in seconds, not by trial and error
You understand when web loses to Desktop or Claude Code
You use one account and shared history across all devices
You stop wasting time on the "wrong" platform for routine tasks

applyIn.title: Everyday development
applyIn.description: Working with code, project files and the terminal — [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] or an IDE extension instead of copy-pasting into a browser.

applyIn.title: Chat and ideas on the go
applyIn.description: A quick question, dictation, a photo from your phone — the mobile app; the same history as on your computer.

applyIn.title: Embedding into a product
applyIn.description: Claude inside your own service or automation script — via the API, not via the interface.

pitfalls: Staying only in [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] when the task is about code — you lose access to files and the terminal
Thinking you need separate subscriptions for separate platforms — there's one account
Reaching for the API where a ready-made app would do — needless development
Ignoring Desktop with its access to files and apps on your computer
Choosing a platform by habit rather than by task type

exercises.question: You need to compare two PDF contracts in 5 minutes from your phone while traveling. Which channel?
exercises.hint: Mobility matters more than power; attachments work in the app.

exercises.question: You want Claude to edit files in your repository and run tests itself. What to choose?
exercises.hint: You need filesystem and terminal access, not a chat window.

exercises.question: You want to embed Claude's answers into your web service for clients. Interface or API?
exercises.hint: A ready interface is for a human at the screen; programmatic integration needs something else.

pl-platforms-1.title: Web (claude.ai): the base for everything
pl-platforms-1.why: Web is the entry point: nothing to install, works on any device, and this is where your history and subscription live.
instructions: Open [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] and sign in
Run a simple chat: a question, text to analyze, an image or PDF as an attachment
Find the sidebar with history — all conversations are stored here
Note the strength: zero install, access from anywhere
pl-platforms-1.validate: You sent a request with an attachment and later found it in history.
pl-platforms-1.tip: For chat, text and documents the web is almost always enough — only level up when you hit a limit.

pl-platforms-2.title: Mobile: Claude on the go
pl-platforms-2.why: The phone covers "here and now" scenarios: dictate, photograph, ask while traveling — with the same history.
instructions: Install the Claude app from the App Store or Google Play
Sign in with the same account — web conversations sync automatically
Try voice input and a camera photo as an attachment
Remember: mobile is strong on mobility, not on workload
pl-platforms-2.validate: A chat started on the phone shows up on the computer, and vice versa.
pl-platforms-2.tip: The phone is for quickly getting into a task; finish heavy work on a computer.

pl-platforms-3.title: Desktop: access to files and apps
pl-platforms-3.why: The desktop app lives right in your system: it sees local files and connects to apps on your computer — a plain browser window can't.
instructions: Install the [[node:pl-desktop|app for Mac or Windows]] and sign in
Compare with web: the same chat convenience, plus working with local files
Open the quick-launch window with a hotkey — Claude is always at hand
Figure out where it wins: documents on disk, local tools
pl-platforms-3.validate: You launched the Desktop app and gave it a file from your computer.
pl-platforms-3.tip: If you constantly drag files off your disk — Desktop saves the most clicks.

pl-platforms-4.title: Claude Code and IDE extensions: for development
pl-platforms-4.why: Code needs access to the whole project: files, terminal, tests. That's what [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] in the terminal and VS Code/JetBrains extensions give — a browser chat loses here.
instructions: Install [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] or the extension for your IDE
Run it in the project folder — Claude sees the file structure
Give it a task that edits code and runs tests in one flow
Compare with web: this is real repo work, not copy-paste
pl-platforms-4.validate: Claude read the project files and made an edit without manual copying.
pl-platforms-4.tip: A coding task means Claude Code or an IDE extension right away — don't waste time on browser chat.

pl-platforms-5.title: API: embedding into a product and automation
pl-platforms-5.why: When Claude is needed not by a human at the screen but by a program — in your service, script, mailing — you connect via the API, not the interface.
instructions: Understand the boundary: interfaces (web/desktop/mobile) are for humans, the API is for code
Typical API scenarios: handling requests, generation inside your app, batch jobs
Weigh the development cost: the API pays off when a ready app isn't enough
Don't reach for the API where a plain chat solves the task
pl-platforms-5.validate: You can explain with an example when you need the API and when an app suffices.
pl-platforms-5.tip: Test the idea in chat first — move to the API only when you need automation or embedding.

pl-platforms-6.title: One account and picking the channel per task
pl-platforms-6.why: All platforms run under one account with shared history and subscription. What's left is to lock in the skill: see a task — instantly know the channel.
instructions: Check that you signed in with one account everywhere — history is in sync
Boil it down to a rule: chat/docs use web; on the go use mobile; local files use desktop; code use Claude Code; embedding use API
Open the [[node:pl-compare|platform comparison]] and check your cheat sheet
Run a couple of your real tasks through this rule
pl-platforms-6.validate: For three of your tasks you named the platform in seconds and justified the choice.
pl-platforms-6.tip: Torn between two channels — open the [[node:pl-compare|platform comparison]] and pick by the strength.

course-pl-rate.title: Rate limits API: TPM, RPM and tiers
course-pl-rate.subtitle: How to keep growth from turning prod into a 429 cascade
course-pl-rate.whatItIs: The Anthropic API caps load with three metrics: RPM (requests per minute), TPM (input+output tokens per minute) and a daily token limit. The actual numbers depend on your account tier (from Tier 1 to Tier 4), which grows automatically with cumulative spend. On excess the API returns 429 Too Many Requests with a retry-after header. This course teaches you to design integrations so spikes and batch loads don't take the service down. API context lives in [[node:pl-api|Platform: API]] and [[tutorial:api-basics|API basics]].
course-pl-rate.approach: We go from the limit model to practice: first what RPM/TPM/daily actually count and how tiers work, then reading 429 and retry-after, building retry with exponential backoff and jitter, budgeting an 80% buffer, moving offline load to the Message Batches API, and finally planning a tier upgrade against forecast traffic. Every step is a working technique, not theory.
outcomes: You understand RPM vs TPM vs daily limit and which one you'll hit first
You read 429 and the retry-after header instead of retrying blindly
You implement retry with exponential backoff and jitter without killing your own limit
You budget a buffer and use the Message Batches API for batch loads
You forecast the needed tier from TPM and file an upgrade request ahead of time

applyIn.title: Production chat under load
applyIn.description: Real users create uneven traffic — backoff and a buffer keep the service stable on spikes without 429.

applyIn.title: Batch processing (evals, classification)
applyIn.description: Tens of thousands of requests in a window: compute TPM, move it to the Message Batches API for the discount and a separate limit.

applyIn.title: Growth and budget planning
applyIn.description: Traffic forecast, then required tier, then an upgrade request ahead of time, so a viral launch doesn't get stuck on Tier 1.

pitfalls: Ignoring 429 without backoff — blind retries kill your own limit and create an error cascade
Not reading the retry-after header — you retry before the limit has cleared
Retry without jitter — all workers retry in sync and hit the limit again (thundering herd)
Not budgeting a buffer (running at 100% of the limit) — any spike breaks instantly
Not knowing about the Message Batches API — losing the 50% discount and a separate limit on offline load

exercises.question: A nightly batch of 50k classifications, ~800 tokens per request, a 2-hour window. What TPM is needed and will it hit RPM?
exercises.hint: TPM = 50000 × 800 / 120 minutes. Separately estimate RPM = 50000 / 120. Compare both to your tier limits and consider whether the Message Batches API fits better.

exercises.question: The API returned 429 with retry-after: 30. How should a client behave with three workers?
exercises.hint: Wait at least retry-after seconds, then exponential backoff + random jitter per worker so they don't retry simultaneously.

exercises.question: The service runs steadily at 95% of the TPM limit. Why is that dangerous and what do you do?
exercises.hint: Any surge pushes past 100% and triggers 429. You need a ~80% buffer and an upgrade request before you hit the wall.

pl-rate-1.title: Break down the three metrics: RPM, TPM, daily
pl-rate-1.why: You can't design protection without knowing which limit you'll hit first. TPM and RPM constrain differently, and the bottleneck depends on your load profile.
instructions: Write the definitions: RPM — requests per minute, TPM — sum of input+output tokens per minute, daily — tokens per 24 hours
Estimate your profile: many small requests hit RPM, few large ones hit TPM
Open docs.anthropic.com/en/api/rate-limits and copy the current numbers for your tier (Anthropic revises them)
Note that output tokens also count toward TPM — long answers burn the limit faster
pl-rate-1.validate: You can name which of the three metrics is the bottleneck for your load and quote your tier's numbers.
pl-rate-1.tip: TPM counts input + output together. A large max_tokens reserves answer budget up front — factor it into the math.

pl-rate-2.title: Learn to read 429 and retry-after
pl-rate-2.why: 429 isn't an app error, it's a 'wait' signal. The retry-after header says exactly how long. Blind retries without it kill the limit and extend downtime.
instructions: Catch the 429 status separately from other 4xx/5xx in code
Read the retry-after header — it's the seconds until the next safe attempt
Log which limit fired so you understand the real bottleneck
Never retry the request before retry-after has elapsed
pl-rate-2.validate: On 429 the client waits exactly retry-after seconds before the first retry and logs it.
pl-rate-2.tip: If retry-after is missing — use your base backoff delay as a fallback, but never retry instantly.

pl-rate-3.title: Build retry with backoff and jitter
pl-rate-3.why: Fixed or synchronous retries create a thundering herd: all workers hit the API at once and get 429 again. Exponential backoff with jitter spreads the load out.
instructions: Base delay grows exponentially: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s by attempt number
Add random jitter to each delay so workers don't synchronize
Respect retry-after: take the max of retry-after and the computed backoff
Cap the attempts (e.g. 5) and after exhaustion do graceful degradation, not an infinite loop
pl-rate-3.validate: Under synthetic 429s the retries spread out in time, there are no synchronized bursts, and there's an attempt cap.
pl-rate-3.tip: Many Anthropic SDKs already retry out of the box — check the client settings before writing your own loop.

pl-rate-4.title: Budget a buffer and a queue
pl-rate-4.why: Running at 100% of the limit leaves no headroom for spikes — any surge yields 429. An 80% buffer and a queue smooth uneven traffic before it hits the ceiling.
instructions: Target no more than ~80% of the tier's TPM/RPM, leaving 20% for surges
Put a queue or rate-limiter on your side so you don't send more than the tier can take
Add graceful degradation: when the queue fills, answer the user clearly instead of crashing
Monitor the actual percentage of limit used, not just the error count
pl-rate-4.validate: Under a load test the service holds ~80% of the limit and doesn't return 429 to users on expected spikes.
pl-rate-4.tip: A local rate-limiter is cheaper than catching 429 from the API: you save requests and keep predictable latency.

pl-rate-5.title: Move offline load to the Message Batches API
pl-rate-5.why: Batch jobs (evals, classification) don't need an instant answer. The Message Batches API gives a separate limit and a ~50% discount — running them through the regular synchronous limit is wasteful.
instructions: Separate loads that don't need a real-time answer from interactive ones
Route them through the Message Batches API — it has its own limit that doesn't compete with online RPM/TPM
Recompute the budget: batch is usually ~50% cheaper than regular requests
Plan a processing window around the async nature of batch, not an instant SLA
pl-rate-5.validate: Offline load goes through the Batches API, freeing the main TPM limit for interactive traffic.
pl-rate-5.tip: Moving evals and background classification to batch often immediately removes half the 429s on your main limit.

pl-rate-6.title: Forecast the tier and file the request early
pl-rate-6.why: Tier grows automatically with spend, but a traffic jump (viral launch, big batch) can outpace the auto-upgrade. Filing early closes the gap between forecast and current limit.
instructions: Compute the required TPM/RPM for the forecast: peak requests × avg tokens / window
Compare with the current tier's limits and find the gap
If there's a gap — file a tier upgrade request ahead of time, don't wait for 429 in prod
Combine measures: buffer + backoff + batch + the right tier, not a single trick
pl-rate-6.validate: You have a target TPM number, an understanding of the needed tier, and an upgrade plan before the load launches.
pl-rate-6.tip: Tier rises with cumulative spend — steady regular traffic grows it on its own, but for a one-off spike ask in advance.

course-pl-compare.title: Claude.ai vs Claude Code vs API: when to use which
course-pl-compare.subtitle: Three ways to work with Claude — chat, terminal agent, programmatic access — and how to pick by task
course-pl-compare.whatItIs: A practical breakdown of the three main access channels to Claude. [[node:pl-web-setup|Claude.ai]] — browser chat for interactive tasks. [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] — a terminal agent that reads and edits files in your project itself. API — programmatic access for embedding Claude into your product and batch processing. The course teaches you to pick a channel by the nature of the task and to combine them in a single workflow.
course-pl-compare.approach: We start from the nature of each channel, not from habit. First we cover the strengths of each of the three on its own, then we build a task-to-channel map, then we learn to switch mid-work and combine channels. Each step ends with a check on your own real task, so the choice sticks as a skill rather than theory.
outcomes: You understand the nature of each channel: chat for dialogue, agent for files, API for integration
You pick a channel for a task in seconds, not by trial and error
You don't pay for API where chat is enough, and don't struggle in chat where an agent is needed
You can switch channels when a task changes character right in the middle of work
You combine channels in one project: research in chat, then edits by the agent, then automation via API

applyIn.title: Daily work with text and ideas
applyIn.description: Drafts, document analysis, brainstorming, one-off questions — all faster and cheaper in Claude.ai chat, with no setup and no paying per token.

applyIn.title: Development and repository work
applyIn.description: Refactoring, reading dozens of files, running tests, project-wide edits — this is Claude Code territory, which sees files directly.

applyIn.title: Product and automation
applyIn.description: Embedding Claude into your app, processing a thousand records in a batch, building a repeatable pipeline — only via API with programmatic control.

pitfalls: Living only in Claude.ai when the task is about files — manual copy-paste back and forth instead of direct agent work
Reaching for the API for a one-off question "because I'm a developer" — you lose the ready interface and pay for what is free in chat
Using Claude Code for plain dialogue without files — needless overhead where chat would suffice
Not noticing the task changed character: research grew into code editing, yet you're still copying answers out of chat
Thinking you must pick one channel forever — in reality strong teams use all three and switch as needed

exercises.question: Take 5 of your real tasks from last week and label each by channel: chat, agent, or API. Justify the choice in one sentence.
exercises.hint: Ask yourself: does the task touch project files? Do you need to repeat it programmatically many times? If both are 'no' — it's chat.

exercises.question: Find a task you do in chat that actually calls for another channel. Describe how it would go faster in Claude Code or via API.
exercises.hint: Candidates are tasks where you repeatedly copy text between Claude.ai and a code editor or spreadsheet.

exercises.question: Design a 3-stage process for one large task so that each stage runs in its own channel.
exercises.hint: A typical chain: discuss the approach in chat, then make edits with the agent, then run it in a batch via API.

pl-compare-1.title: Three channels: one model, three ways in
pl-compare-1.why: Newcomers confuse the channels because they think these are 'different Claudes'. In fact the model is the same — what differs is the way in and what the channel can do hands-on.
instructions: Memorize the formula: Claude.ai = browser dialogue, Claude Code = terminal agent with file access, API = programmatic call from code
Open the channel overview in [[node:pl-platforms|Claude platforms]] to see them side by side
For each channel write one anchor word: chat / files / integration
Lock it in: the model inside is the same; the difference is the interface and the channel's capabilities
pl-compare-1.validate: You can name the three channels and, for each, one word describing its essence.
pl-compare-1.tip: Don't cling to 'I'm a developer, so API'. You pick a channel by the task, not by your profession.

pl-compare-2.title: Claude.ai — the power of interactive dialogue
pl-compare-2.why: Chat is the most underrated channel among techies and the most intuitive for newcomers. It wins where start speed, dialogue, and a ready interface matter.
instructions: Open [[node:pl-web-setup|Claude.ai]] and frame a one-off question or document analysis
Note its strengths: zero setup, instant start, easy to hold a dialogue and refine
Remember the boundary: chat does not edit files in your project and does not repeat a task programmatically
Conclude: anything that begins and ends inside a conversation belongs here
pl-compare-2.validate: You completed one real task in chat and can explain why it needed no other channel.
pl-compare-2.tip: Drafts, brainstorming, explanations, a one-off text audit — almost always cheaper and faster in chat.

pl-compare-3.title: Claude Code — the agent that works with files
pl-compare-3.why: As soon as a task touches real project files, chat turns into endless copy-paste. Here you need an agent that sees the files directly.
instructions: Study [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] as a channel: a terminal agent with access to files and commands
Note its strengths: reads dozens of files, makes project-wide edits, runs tests itself
Compare with chat: what would take 30 copy-pastes in Claude.ai, the agent does in a single pass
Remember the boundary: for plain dialogue without files the agent is needless overhead
pl-compare-3.validate: You understand the signal that moves a task out of chat into Claude Code: it touches project files.
pl-compare-3.tip: Beacon rule: if you catch yourself copying code between chat and the editor — that's the cue to move to Claude Code.

pl-compare-4.title: API — programmatic access for integration and batches
pl-compare-4.why: When a task must be repeated programmatically or Claude must be embedded into a product, neither chat nor agent fits — you need programmatic control through code.
instructions: Study [[node:pl-api|Claude API]] as a channel: calling the model from your own code
Note its strengths: embedding into a product, batch-processing thousands of records, repeatable pipelines
Remember the cost of flexibility: it needs code and setup, with no ready interface like chat has
Conclude: API is for what must work without a human at the keyboard every time
pl-compare-4.validate: You can name a task from your practice that genuinely requires the API and explain why.
pl-compare-4.tip: Don't use the API for a one-off question. Programmatic access pays off only with repetition or embedding.

pl-compare-5.title: Decision map: from task to channel
pl-compare-5.why: Knowing the three channels isn't enough — the skill is picking in seconds. That takes a simple decision scheme, not deliberation every time.
instructions: Build a tree from two questions: does the task touch project files? does it need to be repeated programmatically?
No files and no repetition means Claude.ai. Files involved means Claude Code. Programmatic repetition/embedding means API
Run 5 of your real tasks through the scheme and check that the choice is obvious
Note the edge cases and justify them in one sentence
pl-compare-5.validate: For any new task you pick a channel in a couple of seconds from two questions, without long deliberation.
pl-compare-5.tip: The right channel is 2-5× faster and 2-3× cheaper for the same task. A channel mistake hits both time and money.

pl-compare-6.title: Combining channels in one process
pl-compare-6.why: Strong teams don't pick a channel forever — they switch mid-work when the task changes character. That is what a mature workflow looks like.
instructions: Take one large task and break it into stages: research, then edits, then automation
Assign each stage its channel: discuss the approach in [[node:pl-web-setup|Claude.ai]], then make edits in [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]], then run a batch via [[node:pl-api|API]]
Rehearse the switch: learn to notice the moment dialogue has grown into file work
Cross-check against the overview in [[node:pl-platforms|Claude platforms]] that nothing was missed
pl-compare-6.validate: You designed a 3-stage process where each runs in its own channel, and you understand the switching triggers.
pl-compare-6.tip: The core skill is not loyalty to one channel but sensitivity to the moment the task changed character and it's time to change tools.

course-pl-web-setup.title: Setting up Claude.ai from scratch
course-pl-web-setup.subtitle: From sign-up to your first meaningful chat in 15 minutes
course-pl-web-setup.whatItIs: A hands-on start for beginners: create a Claude.ai account, pick the right plan, fill in your profile and instructions for Claude, learn the interface, and run a first productive chat. After this course you have a working account that knows who you are and how to answer you.
course-pl-web-setup.approach: We follow the real order of a first day: log in, choose a plan, configure the settings that save time in every future chat, and only at the end — the conversation itself. Each step ends with a check that it worked.
outcomes: A working Claude.ai account with a verified email
A deliberate choice between the free and paid plan
A filled-in profile and instructions that Claude applies in every chat
Confident navigation: chats, history, projects, settings
A first completed dialogue with a clear result

applyIn.title: Daily text work
applyIn.description: Emails, drafts, summaries of long documents — Claude already knows your role and tone, no briefing needed.

applyIn.title: Learning and exploring topics
applyIn.description: Ask questions about a new field and Claude explains at the level you set in your instructions.

applyIn.title: Repetitive tasks
applyIn.description: A profile set up once saves you from re-explaining context in every new chat.

pitfalls: Skipping privacy settings — by default your data may go toward model training; opt out in Settings, then Privacy.
Buying a paid plan immediately without trying the free one — free limits are often enough to start.
Leaving the profile empty and then wondering why Claude answers impersonally.
Writing vague instructions like 'answer well' instead of being specific about role, language, and format.
Confusing a new chat with continuing an old one — old context gets lost or, conversely, gets in the way.

exercises.question: How does the free plan differ from the paid one, and how do you know which you need?
exercises.hint: Compare the message limit and access to the stronger model with how often and how complex your tasks will be.

exercises.question: What exactly should you write in the 'About me' section so Claude answers more precisely?
exercises.hint: Role/profession, main tasks, preferred language, and level of detail — short and to the point.

exercises.question: How do you check that your instructions are actually being applied?
exercises.hint: Open a new chat and ask a typical question without explanations — see whether Claude respects the set tone and format.

pl-web-setup-1.title: Create an account and log in
pl-web-setup-1.why: Without an account there's no chat history, no settings, no projects. It's the foundation for everything else.
instructions: Open claude.ai in your browser.
Click 'Sign up' and register via email or a Google account.
Confirm your address via the link in the email if you signed up by email.
Log in and accept the terms of use.
pl-web-setup-1.validate: You see the main screen with a message input field and an empty chat history.
pl-web-setup-1.tip: Use an email you have permanent access to — important notifications and password resets go there.

pl-web-setup-2.title: Choose the right plan
pl-web-setup-2.why: The plan defines your limits and access to stronger models. A deliberate choice saves money and frustration.
instructions: Start with the free plan — it's enough to see whether Claude suits you.
Notice whether you hit the message limit during the day.
If your tasks are frequent and complex — consider a paid plan in the pricing section.
Compare web access with other options in [[node:pl-platforms|Claude platforms]] and tiers in [[node:pl-plans|plans and subscriptions]].
pl-web-setup-2.validate: You know which plan you're currently on and understand its limits.
pl-web-setup-2.tip: Don't pay upfront. Work a week on the free plan — real usage shows whether you need an upgrade.

pl-web-setup-3.title: Fill in your profile
pl-web-setup-3.why: A profile with name and language is the basis of personalization. Claude starts addressing you and speaking the right language.
instructions: Open Settings (the profile or gear icon).
Enter the name Claude should use to address you.
Choose your preferred answer language.
Check privacy settings — opt out of data use for training if needed.
pl-web-setup-3.validate: In a new chat Claude addresses you by name and answers in the chosen language.
pl-web-setup-3.tip: The privacy section is easy to miss — check it right away; by default data may be used for model training.

pl-web-setup-4.title: Set up instructions for Claude
pl-web-setup-4.why: Instructions are a one-time brief applied in every chat. Without them you repeat the context again and again.
instructions: Find the [[node:instructions|Custom Instructions]] section in settings.
In 'About me' describe your role, tasks, and language: short and specific.
In 'How to respond' set the tone and format: e.g., 'bullet points, no fluff'.
For recurring situations, explore [[node:i-global|global instructions]].
Save your changes.
pl-web-setup-4.validate: A new chat respects the set tone and format without extra explanation from you.
pl-web-setup-4.tip: Write instructions like a brief for a new colleague: 'who I am', 'what matters to me', 'how to respond' — specifics beat generalities.

pl-web-setup-5.title: Learn the interface
pl-web-setup-5.why: Knowing where history, new chat, and projects are turns Claude from a toy into a working tool.
instructions: Find the 'New chat' button — each new task in its own chat.
Open the history panel on the left: all past conversations are saved.
Find the Projects section — a place to group chats by topic.
Remember where Settings is, to quickly change profile and instructions.
pl-web-setup-5.validate: You can open a new chat, find an old one, and reach settings in a couple of clicks.
pl-web-setup-5.tip: Keep tasks in separate chats — history stays readable and one topic's context doesn't interfere with another.

pl-web-setup-6.title: Run your first chat
pl-web-setup-6.why: Settings are only verified in practice. A first meaningful dialogue locks in everything you've done.
instructions: Open a new chat and give it a real task from your work.
Phrase the request in plain words — the instructions already set the context.
Evaluate the answer: did Claude account for your role, language, and format.
If needed, refine the request and ask for a redo.
pl-web-setup-6.validate: You got a useful answer and see that Claude applies the settings you configured earlier.
pl-web-setup-6.tip: If the answer is off — don't rewrite everything; just say what to fix: it's faster and more precise.

course-pl-integrations.title: Claude Integrations: Connectors and Connections
course-pl-integrations.subtitle: How to link Claude to your apps and connect only what you actually need
course-pl-integrations.whatItIs: Integrations are how you give Claude access to external apps without copying content by hand. A connector is a ready-made bridge between Claude and a service (Google Drive, GitHub, Microsoft 365, Slack). Under the hood many connectors run on the MCP protocol — a single standard Claude uses to talk to external sources. This course explains what connectors are, how they differ from MCP, how access security works, and how to choose connections deliberately.
course-pl-integrations.approach: We move from concept to practice: first why integrations matter and what they give you; then how built-in connectors work (Google, M365, Slack, GitHub scenarios); then MCP as the mechanism beneath connectors; then the permission model and security; and finally how to deliberately choose what to connect so you don't bloat your access surface.
outcomes: Understand the difference between a connector (a ready connection) and MCP (the protocol it runs on)
Know which built-in integrations exist and what each can do (read vs act)
Can connect a connector and grant exactly the permissions a task needs
Assess access risk: what a connector sees, what it can do, who owns the data
Choose connections deliberately — on a least-necessary-access basis

applyIn.title: Email and documents
applyIn.description: Connect Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace and ask Claude about your emails, files, and meetings without switching tabs.

applyIn.title: Team communication
applyIn.description: Through the Slack connector, Claude finds past decisions and meeting summaries in message history instead of manual scrolling.

applyIn.title: Development and repositories
applyIn.description: Through an MCP connector to GitHub, Claude reads code, issues, and pull requests to answer in the context of a real project.

pitfalls: Expecting actions from read-only connectors: M365 and Google only read for now — they won't send an email or create a document
Not granting the needed permissions during setup (e.g., the Chrome extension) — then Claude can't see content and 'misses' the point
Connecting everything 'just in case' — every extra connector widens the access surface to your data
Confusing connector and MCP: a connector is a specific connection, MCP is the standard it communicates over
Ignoring who owns the data and where it's stored — especially for work and corporate accounts

exercises.question: How does a connector differ from MCP? Explain using a Google Drive connection as an example.
exercises.hint: A connector is a ready bridge to a specific service; MCP is the common protocol-language Claude and the service exchange data over. A Drive connector can run on top of MCP.

exercises.question: You need Claude to answer about last week's emails. Which connector do you pick and what permissions are required?
exercises.hint: M365 or Google — both give email access. Think: you only need read access to mail, not the whole account. Grant the minimum necessary.

exercises.question: Why is connecting all integrations at once a bad idea from a security standpoint?
exercises.hint: Each connection is a new channel of access to your data. The more there are, the more can go wrong. Connect per task.

pl-integrations-1.title: Why integrations matter
pl-integrations-1.why: Without integrations you manually copy context between apps and Claude. Integrations remove that friction — Claude sees what you're already working in.
instructions: Recall the last task where you copied text from email or a document into Claude — that friction is what integrations remove
Remember the core idea: integration = Claude gets context from an app directly, no copy-paste
Open [[node:m-what|what Claude is]] to understand the base product integrations layer onto
Name 1-2 routines you'd like to automate through connections
pl-integrations-1.validate: You can name a concrete task from your work where an integration would remove manual context transfer.
pl-integrations-1.tip: Integrations pay off where data changes often: email, calendar, chats. For a one-off file it's simpler to attach it manually.

pl-integrations-2.title: What a connector is and which exist
pl-integrations-2.why: A connector is a ready-made connection to a specific service. Knowing the map of built-in connectors tells you what you can connect and what each does.
instructions: Remember the definition: a connector is a 'bridge' between Claude and an external app

Review the built-ins: Microsoft 365 (read mail, docs, meetings), Google Workspace (Drive, Gmail, Calendar), Slack (search messages and meeting summaries), Chrome extension (read pages and act in the browser)
Note the key distinction: some connectors only read, others can act (Chrome — navigation and form filling)
Find the connections menu in Claude (the '+' icon or connectors section) and look at what's available on your plan
pl-integrations-2.validate: For each of the four connectors you can say in one phrase what it connects and whether it reads or acts.
pl-integrations-2.tip: The Chrome extension and some capabilities are paid-plan and beta only — check your plan before setting up.

pl-integrations-3.title: MCP as the mechanism beneath connectors
pl-integrations-3.why: Many connectors run on the MCP protocol — a single connection standard. Understanding MCP shows you how to add sources beyond the built-in list.
instructions: Grasp the essence: MCP is the common 'language' Claude uses to reach external tools and data
Draw the analogy: a connector is a specific connection, MCP is the standard it's built on (like a socket and a voltage standard)
Open [[node:mcp|MCP]] and read how the protocol lets you connect your own sources that aren't in the ready list
Note the practical takeaway: via MCP you can connect, for example, GitHub, a database, or an internal team service
pl-integrations-3.validate: You can explain why MCP matters: it gives a standard way to connect any source, not just pre-built ones.
pl-integrations-3.tip: Not every connector appears as 'MCP' in the UI — but understanding the protocol helps you assess any third-party connection.

pl-integrations-4.title: Permissions and access security
pl-integrations-4.why: A connection is a grant of access to your data. Permissions define what a connector sees and can do. Without understanding this it's easy to give too much.
instructions: When connecting, read the permissions screen carefully: what exactly is requested (read-only mail or the whole account)
Remember the least-necessary-access principle: grant exactly what the task needs, no more
Distinguish reading from actions: a read-only connector won't send mail or change a file — that's both a limit and a safeguard
Open [[node:m-security|security]] and check the access rules for work and corporate accounts
Verify who owns the data and where it's stored, especially if the account is work, not personal
pl-integrations-4.validate: Before connecting you can state what data the connector will see, what it can do, and why that's enough for the task.
pl-integrations-4.tip: If the permissions screen asks for more than your task needs — that's a signal to stop and double-check.

pl-integrations-5.title: Connecting a connector in practice
pl-integrations-5.why: Theory sticks with one real connection. Going through the 'choose — permit — verify' cycle gives you a working skill, not just understanding.
instructions: Pick one connector for a concrete task (e.g., M365 for email questions)
Open the connections menu in Claude and start setting up the chosen connector
On the permissions screen grant only what the task needs and confirm the connection
Test it with a context query: 'Summarize last week's emails about project X and list open action items'
Confirm Claude is actually reading the source rather than answering generically
pl-integrations-5.validate: The connector is connected and Claude answers the question drawing on real data from the connected app.
pl-integrations-5.tip: Start with a read-only connector (M365 or Google) — the safest way to try integrations without risking unwanted actions.

pl-integrations-6.title: What to connect deliberately
pl-integrations-6.why: The final skill is connection hygiene. Every connector widens your access surface, so connect per task, not 'just in case'.
instructions: Make a short list: which apps Claude actually needs in your work every week
For each decide: is reading enough or do you need actions — and connect the minimum
Disconnect connectors that are no longer needed: extra access is extra risk
Open [[node:m-ready|readiness to work]] and check your set of connections against real work scenarios
Build the habit of periodically reviewing your active connectors and their permissions
pl-integrations-6.validate: You have a deliberate set of a few needed connectors and can justify why each one is connected.
pl-integrations-6.tip: The rule is simple: connect for a specific recurring task. No task — no connection.

course-pl-privacy.title: Data privacy in Claude
course-pl-privacy.subtitle: What's stored, whether your data trains models, and how to control it
course-pl-privacy.whatItIs: A practical breakdown of what Anthropic does with your conversations: what gets stored, whether your data is used to train models, how a consumer plan differs from API and business plans, and which privacy settings are available. By default, Free/Pro/Team conversations aren't used for training, but details depend on your plan and change over time — so this course teaches you not to memorize the policy but to find and verify the current one.
