course-pl-privacy.approach: We move from a threat model to concrete actions: first understand what data exists and where, then tackle training and storage, then the difference between modes (consumer vs API/business), and finish with a 'what not to send' checklist and a real check of the settings in your own account. No memorized policy wording — just the skill of verifying it.
outcomes: You understand exactly what's saved from your chats and for how long
You know whether your data is used for training and how to turn it off
You distinguish privacy across consumer plan, API, and business/Enterprise
You have a personal 'do not send' checklist for your context
You can find and verify the current policy instead of relying on hearsay

applyIn.title: Working with client documents
applyIn.description: Before uploading a contract, NDA material, or client database, you quickly assess whether it's allowed under the policy and your plan.

applyIn.title: Team and compliance
applyIn.description: You explain plan differences to colleagues and configure the work account to meet company requirements.

applyIn.title: Personal and sensitive data
applyIn.description: You decide which personal data, passwords, medical or financial information can be sent — and which never should be.

pitfalls: Assuming 'no training by default' equals 'nothing is stored' — these are different things
Confusing consumer-plan privacy with API: guarantees and settings differ
Relying on an old article or screenshot instead of the current official policy
Sending sensitive data 'to try it out' without checking the plan and settings first
Forgetting that enabled memory or history is a separate storage layer with its own risks

exercises.question: In which mode are your conversations more likely NOT to be used for training by default — the regular Claude chat app or via API/business plan?
exercises.hint: Recall the consumer vs API difference. In both, training is limited by default, but API/business has stricter formal guarantees and contracts — think about where that's documented.

exercises.question: Name three types of data you personally should not send to Claude without checking the policy and settings.
exercises.hint: Think in categories: other people's personal data, access secrets, protected IP, or regulated data (medical/financial).

exercises.question: Where will you check the current storage and training policy before uploading a sensitive document?
exercises.hint: Official Anthropic sources, the privacy settings in your own account, and the terms of your specific plan — not forums or retellings.

pl-privacy-1.title: Data map: what exists and where
pl-privacy-1.why: You can't protect what you can't see. First understand the traces your work with Claude leaves: messages, uploaded files, history, memory, metadata.
instructions: Write down what you usually send to Claude: text, files, code, links
Note whether chat history and memory are enabled — these are separate storage layers
Split data into 'yours' and 'others' (client, team, personal)
Mark which of these are sensitive: contracts, personal data, secrets, IP
pl-privacy-1.validate: You have a list of what you send, with sensitivity flagged.
pl-privacy-1.tip: Memory and history are convenience at the cost of storage. If you handle sensitive data, decide consciously whether to enable them.

pl-privacy-2.title: Storage: what's saved and for how long
pl-privacy-2.why: Storage and training are different questions. Data may not be used for training yet still be stored (for history, safety, support). It's important to understand both layers.
instructions: Frame the question as: 'what exactly is stored from my chats and for how long'
Find the answer in Anthropic's official privacy policy, not retellings
Distinguish: messages, files, account history, safety logs
Note that enabled history stays in your account until you delete it
pl-privacy-2.validate: You can say in one sentence what's stored and whether it can be deleted.
pl-privacy-2.tip: Deleting a chat in the interface and the service-side retention period are not the same. Check the policy wording.

pl-privacy-3.title: Training: is your data used and how to turn it off
pl-privacy-3.why: Users' main fear is 'my conversation will end up in the model.' On Free/Pro/Team, conversations aren't used for training by default, but details and settings change and must be verified for your plan.
instructions: Check the current stance: is your plan's data used for training by default
Find the account settings related to data use and model improvement
If such a setting exists, consciously choose your state (on/off)
Record where exactly this setting lives so you can return to it
pl-privacy-3.validate: You know the current state of the training setting in your account and where to change it.
pl-privacy-3.tip: 'No training by default' doesn't mean 'can never be enabled.' Check your own state, not the general rule.

pl-privacy-4.title: Consumer vs API and business
pl-privacy-4.why: Privacy guarantees depend heavily on the mode. The regular chat app, the API, and business/Enterprise are different terms, contracts, and controls. Confusion here leads to wrong decisions.
instructions: Separate three modes: chat app (consumer), developer API, business/Enterprise
For each, note: formal guarantees, contract (DPA), additional control
Remember: business/Enterprise usually has stricter SLAs and compliance options
Match it to your task — which mode fits your data
If you handle regulated data, look toward API/business with a contract
pl-privacy-4.validate: You can explain how business-plan privacy differs from the regular chat.
pl-privacy-4.tip: For serious work with client data, a contract (DPA) matters more than a checkbox in the interface. That's the API/business layer. See [[node:pl-plans|Claude plans]].

pl-privacy-5.title: The 'what not to send' checklist
pl-privacy-5.why: The best protection is not sending what shouldn't leave your control. Even with a perfect policy, some data simply doesn't belong in a third-party service without a separate contract.
instructions: Build a personal stop-list: access secrets (passwords, keys, tokens)
Add other people's personal data without consent and legal basis
Add regulated data: medical, financial, legally protected
Add others' intellectual property and NDA-covered materials
Decide what's acceptable only in a contracted mode and what's never acceptable
pl-privacy-5.validate: You have a short stop-list to consult before sending.
pl-privacy-5.tip: When in doubt, anonymize. Replace real names, numbers, and keys with placeholders. Related to [[node:b-safety|safety]].

pl-privacy-6.title: Checking settings and staying current
pl-privacy-6.why: Policies and settings change. The skill isn't memorizing the 2026 rules but regularly verifying your actual state and the official source.
instructions: Open your account's privacy settings and go through them point by point
Compare the actual state (history, memory, training) with your decision from steps 1–3
Save a link to the official privacy policy as a check point
Set yourself a rule to re-check before every sensitive upload
When changing plan or role, run this check again
pl-privacy-6.validate: Your settings match your decision, and you know where to verify the current policy.
pl-privacy-6.tip: Before uploading something important, a 30-second settings check is cheaper than handling an incident later.

course-a-types.title: Artifact types: code, document, diagram, HTML
course-a-types.subtitle: Pick the right format — so instead of a wall of text you get a live preview you can see at once
course-a-types.whatItIs: An artifact is a separate panel next to the chat where the model assembles the result as a standalone object: an HTML page, a React component, an SVG drawing, a Mermaid diagram, a Markdown document, or just a code file. Each type has its own preview: HTML and React render as a working page, Mermaid and SVG as an image, Markdown as a formatted document, code with syntax highlighting. Choosing the type decides whether you see the finished result live or only text you still have to paste somewhere and run.
course-a-types.approach: We move from the question "what do I want to see in the end" to picking a type. First we go over which types exist and what each gives you in the preview. Then we learn to match the type to the task (prototype to React, diagram to Mermaid, report to Markdown). Then how to explicitly ask for the type you need, how to read the preview, and how not to over-complicate (don't reach for React where HTML is enough). One principle: the format should match how you'll actually use the result.
outcomes: You know the main artifact types and what each shows in the preview
You match a type to a task in seconds: prototype, diagram, document, or code file
You phrase the request so you get exactly the type you need on the first try
You read the preview and know when the result is ready and when it needs work
You don't over-complicate the format or pick a heavy type where a simple one is enough

applyIn.title: Interface prototype
applyIn.description: Need a clickable button, form, or mini-page — ask for HTML or React so you can immediately poke a working prototype in the preview instead of reading a description.

applyIn.title: Explaining a process with a diagram
applyIn.description: A tangled flow or architecture is easier to show as a diagram: ask for a Mermaid flowchart, and the diagram is drawn right in the panel — you see it whole, not as a retelling.

applyIn.title: A ready document or report
applyIn.description: For an article, a guide, or a summary ask for a Markdown document: you get formatted text with headings and lists that you can copy and use right away.

pitfalls: Asking for a React component where plain HTML is enough — adding an unnecessary layer of complexity for no reason
Not specifying the type at all and being surprised that you got a text retelling instead of a diagram
Confusing "code in chat" with "artifact": without an artifact there's no live preview, only text you have to paste manually
Using Markdown for interactivity (buttons, forms) — it isn't clickable, you need HTML or React
Ignoring the preview and copying the result without checking that it actually assembles and looks right

exercises.question: You need to show a colleague how an approval process works: five steps with a branch. Which artifact type do you ask for and how do you phrase the request?
exercises.hint: A process diagram is a chart. Ask for a Mermaid flowchart as an Artifact and say outright that you want to see the diagram in the preview, not as text.

exercises.question: You asked "make a subscribe button" and got a React component, though you needed a simple static page. What's the overkill and how do you rephrase?
exercises.hint: React is extra complexity for static content. Ask for the same result as a plain HTML artifact: the page opens in the preview without the extra wiring.

exercises.question: You need a two-page report with headings, lists, and a table that you'll later paste into a document. Which type do you pick and why not code?
exercises.hint: This is a document, not a program. Ask for a Markdown artifact: you get formatted text with ready structure that copies as is.

a-types-1.title: What an artifact is and why it has a preview
a-types-1.why: Before choosing a type you need to grasp the idea itself: an artifact isn't text in the chat, it's a separate object with a live preview. Without that distinction, choosing a type makes no sense.
instructions: Remember the difference: a normal answer is text in the chat thread; an artifact is a separate panel where the finished result is assembled
Understand the key benefit: an artifact has a preview — the page, image, or document is shown at once, not described in words
Open any past request of yours for code or a diagram and imagine how much easier it would have been to see the result live
Connect the topic to the basics of what artifacts are at all: [[node:artifacts|Artifacts]]
a-types-1.validate: You can explain in one sentence how an artifact differs from a regular text answer.
a-types-1.tip: Simple rule: if you'd rather see the result than read it — it's a candidate for an artifact.

a-types-2.title: Type map: code, HTML, React, SVG, Mermaid, Markdown
a-types-2.why: You can't choose a type without knowing the range. Each type gives its own preview, and understanding this map is the basis of every later decision.
instructions: Remember the six working types: code file (with highlighting), HTML page, React component, SVG drawing, Mermaid diagram, Markdown document
Tie each type to its preview: HTML and React give a working page, SVG and Mermaid give an image, Markdown gives a formatted document, code gives highlighted text
Note the main distinction: HTML and React are interactive (clickable), while Mermaid, SVG, and Markdown are static (they show but don't react to clicks)
Estimate against your own tasks which type would cover each of them
a-types-2.validate: You can name at least four artifact types and say what each shows in the preview.
a-types-2.tip: Interactivity (buttons, forms) uses HTML/React. Image-diagram uses Mermaid/SVG. Text uses Markdown. Three families — navigate by them.

a-types-3.title: Which type for which task
a-types-3.why: The list of types alone is useless without a rule for choosing. The link from task to type is the whole reason to bother understanding artifacts.
instructions: Interface prototype (button, form, mini-page): React if there's state and logic; HTML if the page is static
Process, architecture, or relationship diagram: Mermaid flowchart draws a diagram from a text description
Icon, simple drawing, logo: SVG, a crisp vector image
Article, guide, summary, report: Markdown document with headings and lists
A piece of logic in a specific language without an interface: code file with highlighting
a-types-3.validate: Give yourself three random tasks and for each name a fitting type within a couple of seconds.
a-types-3.tip: Ask yourself: "is this interactivity, an image, or text?" — and the type is almost chosen.

a-types-4.title: How to ask for the type you need in words
a-types-4.why: If you don't name the type explicitly, the model guesses — and often guesses wrong. A direct phrasing of the request guarantees the right format on the first try.
instructions: Name the type right in the request: "as a Mermaid flowchart", "as an HTML page", "as a Markdown document", "React component"
Add the word "Artifact" and a phrase about the preview: "make it an Artifact — I want to see the result at once"
Say how you'll use the result: "to poke at it", "to paste into a document", "to show the diagram" — this helps the model pick the format
If the type is critical — repeat it at the end of the request in one word
See how to phrase the request so an artifact appears at all: [[node:a-trigger|How to trigger an artifact]]
a-types-4.validate: Your request contains an explicit type name and it's clear in what format the result should come.
a-types-4.tip: Not "draw a diagram" but "make a Mermaid flowchart as an Artifact" — specifics remove the guessing.

a-types-5.title: Reading the preview and checking the result
a-types-5.why: An artifact is valuable precisely for its preview. If you don't learn to read it, the whole point is lost — you'll copy blindly something that may not assemble.
instructions: Open the artifact panel and look at the preview, not just the code or text below it
For HTML/React check that the page renders and elements are clickable; for Mermaid/SVG — that the image assembled without errors
For Markdown make sure headings, lists, and tables are formatted as needed
If the preview is empty or has an error — that's a signal the type was chosen wrong or the request needs clarifying
For edits right in the artifact, see: [[node:a-edit|Editing an artifact]]
a-types-5.validate: From the preview you can tell whether the result is ready or needs more work.
a-types-5.tip: An empty or broken preview isn't a mood bug, it's a hint: the format or the request didn't match the task.

a-types-6.title: Don't over-complicate: the minimal sufficient type
a-types-6.why: The main anti-pattern is reaching for a heavy type where a light one is enough. The habit of picking the minimal sufficient format saves effort and keeps the result cleaner.
instructions: Before the request ask: would HTML do instead of React, an SVG image instead of interactivity, Markdown instead of code
Reach for React only when you actually need logic and state; for a static page — HTML
Reach for a code file only if the result is exactly code to paste into a project, not something you want to see in the preview
If you picked the wrong type — don't start over, ask to re-format it into another type and keep refining
Bring the result to where you need it iteratively: [[node:a-iterate|Iterating on an artifact]]
a-types-6.validate: For your last task you picked the simplest type that covers it and can justify the choice.
a-types-6.tip: An extra layer of complexity always costs more: it's easier to add than to later simplify an overloaded artifact.

course-a-trigger.title: When an artifact triggers
course-a-trigger.subtitle: What makes Claude move an answer into an [[node:artifacts|artifact]] and how to control it
course-a-trigger.whatItIs: An artifact is a separate panel next to the chat where Claude places a self-contained result: code, a document, an HTML page, a diagram. Claude decides to move the answer there automatically based on three signals: length (roughly 15–20+ lines), self-containment (the result has value on its own, you'd want to save or open it) and content type (executable code, finished text, markup). This course is about what exactly pulls the trigger, how to ask for an artifact explicitly, and why it sometimes doesn't appear where you expected.
course-a-trigger.approach: We go from mechanics to control. First we break down the three trigger signals on live examples, then learn to force an artifact with an explicit phrasing, then diagnose why it didn't appear, and finally distinguish cases where an artifact isn't needed. Each step is a mini-experiment in a real chat: phrase a request, watch the reaction, draw a conclusion.
outcomes: You understand the three signals Claude uses to decide on an artifact: length, self-containment, content type
You can explicitly ask for an artifact in one phrase, without relying on automation
You diagnose why an answer stayed in chat and rephrase the request
You tell artifact-worthy tasks apart from ones where it only gets in the way
You link the trigger to follow-up work: [[node:a-iterate|editing the artifact]] and [[node:a-types|choosing its type]]

applyIn.title: Interface prototype
applyIn.description: You ask for a page or component — the artifact gives a live preview you can see and play with right away, instead of a wall of code in the chat.

applyIn.title: Document to keep
applyIn.description: A letter, spec, README, policy — something you'll take out of the chat whole. The artifact keeps it as a separate block, easy to copy and edit.

applyIn.title: Script or function
applyIn.description: Working code you'll run on your side. The artifact stores it as a single file instead of breaking it up with paragraphs of explanation.

pitfalls: You expect an artifact, but the request sounds like "explain how to do it" — Claude answers with text in chat, because you asked for an explanation, not a result
Code shorter than ~15 lines almost never goes to an artifact on its own — ask explicitly for short snippets
You don't specify the format — and get in flat chat what you wanted as a separate panel
You assume an artifact is mandatory everywhere — for a quick answer or a discussion it's redundant and slows things down
You say "keep adding" in a new message without referencing the artifact — Claude may start over in chat instead of [[node:a-iterate|editing the existing one]]

exercises.question: You asked "write a short regex for email" and the answer came as chat text, not an artifact. Why?
exercises.hint: Recall the length signal. A one-line regex is not a self-contained 20-line document. What do you add to the request to force an artifact?

exercises.question: Phrase a landing-page request so the artifact with a preview is guaranteed to appear on the first try.
exercises.hint: Combine three levers: the explicit word "artifact", the result type (HTML page), and the goal — "so I can open the preview".

exercises.question: In which of the two cases is an artifact not needed: (a) "explain the difference between map and forEach", (b) "make a comparison table of map and forEach with examples"?
exercises.hint: Ask yourself: is the result self-contained and worth saving — or is it a conversational explanation?

a-trigger-1.title: The three trigger signals
a-trigger-1.why: Before controlling the trigger, you need to know what it reacts to. Claude weighs three things: length, self-containment, and content type. Understanding these signals turns the "magic" into a predictable mechanism.
instructions: Open a new chat and ask: "Write a Python function that computes a factorial" — note whether it went to an artifact or stayed in chat
Then ask: "Now explain in two words what recursion is" — compare where the answer ended up
Note the difference: the first request is self-contained code, the second a short explanation
Phrase for yourself which of the three signals fired in the first case
a-trigger-1.validate: You can name the three signals (length, self-containment, type) and show on your two requests which one fired where.
a-trigger-1.tip: Self-containment is the main signal: "would I want to save this whole?" If yes — it's an artifact candidate.

a-trigger-2.title: Length and self-containment signal
a-trigger-2.why: Length is the most tangible threshold. Roughly 15–20 lines of code or a finished document push Claude toward an artifact. But length works in tandem with self-containment: a long explanation won't go to an artifact, while a short but whole HTML page might.
instructions: Ask "write 5 lines of code to sort a list" — it will most likely stay in chat
Ask "write a full script: reads a CSV, filters rows, saves the result" — the added length and wholeness push it into an artifact
Compare the two answers: what changed besides line count
Lock in the takeaway: it's not just about lines, but about the result becoming a finished whole
a-trigger-2.validate: You understand why a short snippet stays in chat while a finished script goes to an artifact — and can explain the role of self-containment.
a-trigger-2.tip: If the result is "a piece to insert into an explanation", it stays in chat. If it's "a finished thing", it goes to an artifact.

a-trigger-3.title: Asking for an artifact explicitly
a-trigger-3.why: Relying on automation is unreliable: edge cases (short code, ambiguous format) may stay in chat. An explicit request removes the uncertainty and guarantees the result where you need it.
instructions: Take a task that didn't go to an artifact on its own (e.g. a short regex or a small function)
Rephrase: "Format this as an artifact" or "Make an artifact with …"
Strengthen it with a goal: "…so I can open the preview" or "…to copy as one block"
Send it and confirm the answer is now in a separate panel
Save this template phrase for future requests
a-trigger-3.validate: With one phrase you force an artifact even for short code that automation would have left in chat.
a-trigger-3.tip: The words "format as an artifact", "make an artifact", "so I can open the preview" are the most reliable triggers. State the type too: HTML page, document, script.

a-trigger-4.title: Why the artifact didn't appear
a-trigger-4.why: The most common complaint is "I expected an artifact but got text in chat". The cause is almost always the phrasing: the request sounded like a plea to explain, not to make. Being able to diagnose this saves time.
instructions: Write a deliberately "wrong" request: "Explain how to make a business-card page in HTML"
Note: the answer is an explanation in chat, because you asked for an explanation
Rephrase to "make": "Make an artifact — a business-card page in HTML"
Compare the two reactions and write out the verb difference: "explain" vs "make/create"
Check one more cause: the result is too short — add volume or an explicit request
a-trigger-4.validate: Looking at a request that stayed in chat, you name the cause (explanation verb or short length) and fix it by rephrasing.
a-trigger-4.tip: One-question diagnosis: "did I ask to make a thing or to explain a process?" An explanation always stays in chat.

a-trigger-5.title: When an artifact isn't needed
a-trigger-5.why: It's important not only to use the trigger but also not to overuse it. For a short answer, a discussion, or an intermediate step an artifact is redundant — it adds a panel you can't usefully keep and slows the dialogue.
instructions: Make two task lists: "artifact needed" (page, script, document) and "not needed" (explanation, advice, short answer, brainstorm)
Ask for something from the second list — e.g. "suggest three ways to speed up a function" — and confirm no artifact appears, and that's correct
Phrase the criterion: would I want to take this result whole and open/run it separately
Remember: if the answer is part of a conversation, its place is the chat
a-trigger-5.validate: From the task wording you say in advance whether an artifact is needed, and you don't force it where it gets in the way.
a-trigger-5.tip: One-phrase criterion: "is this a thing or a conversation?" A thing — artifact, a conversation — chat.

a-trigger-6.title: The trigger in the work cycle
a-trigger-6.why: Creating an artifact isn't the finale but the start of a cycle: create, then look, then ask for an edit. By linking the trigger to follow-up work, you stop starting from scratch and start iterating on top of what exists.
instructions: Create an artifact with an explicit request (repeat the lever from step 3)
Without opening a new chat, ask for a change: "Change the heading and add a button" — this is the move to [[node:a-iterate|editing the artifact]]
Note: Claude edits the existing artifact rather than spawning a new one in chat
Think about which [[node:a-types|artifact type]] fits your task: code, HTML, document, diagram
Assemble the chain: trigger, then preview, then edit — as a single workflow
a-trigger-6.validate: You run the full cycle: force an artifact, view the result, ask for an edit — and it applies to the same artifact instead of going to chat.
a-trigger-6.tip: To make an edit land in the artifact rather than the chat, reference it: "in the artifact, change…". That keeps Claude [[node:a-iterate|iterating]] instead of starting over.

course-a-iterate.title: Artifact iterations and versions
course-a-iterate.subtitle: Edit boldly: every version is saved, you can revert to any
course-a-iterate.whatItIs: Every change to an [[node:artifacts|Artifact]] creates a new version. The old one doesn't disappear — it stays in history, and you can return to it with one click. This turns editing into a safe experiment: you try options without risking the working result.
course-a-iterate.approach: Think in versions, not edits stacked on top. Phrase each request as one focused step, compare versions against each other rather than from memory, and revert to a previous one the moment a new one turns out worse. Version history is your insurance, not a trash bin.
outcomes: Understand how and when a new artifact version is created
Phrase an edit request precisely so only the intended part changes
Revert to any previous version without losing work
Compare 2-3 versions of one artifact deliberately, not by guesswork
Keep edits focused and avoid destroying the working result with random changes

applyIn.title: Design experiments
applyIn.description: Show 3 hero-section or landing variants as different versions and pick the best by comparison.

applyIn.title: Code refinement
applyIn.description: Change a function step by step: each edit is a version you roll back to if something breaks.

applyIn.title: Text and documents
applyIn.description: Run wording through several tones, keeping previous ones as versions for comparison.

pitfalls: "Everything at once" edits in one request — impossible to tell what changed for the worse
Relying on memory instead of comparing versions — "it felt better" but actually wasn't
Deleting old versions manually before the new one is verified and working
Not reverting in time — stacking edits on top of an already broken result
Losing focus: requesting a new feature and a redesign in one step

exercises.question: You asked to change a button color, but the model also rewrote the whole layout. How do you phrase the request so only the intended part changes?
exercises.hint: Name the single edit target explicitly and add "don't touch anything else".

exercises.question: A new artifact version turned out worse than the previous one. What do you do first — ask "put it back" or roll back to the version?
exercises.hint: Version history is more precise than the model's memory: a rollback guarantees the working state.

exercises.question: You need to compare 3 landing headline variants. How do you organize this through versions?
exercises.hint: One artifact, three sequential versions, switch between them to compare.

a-iterate-1.title: How artifact versioning works
a-iterate-1.why: Without grasping that each edit = a new version, you fear experimenting and lose your safety net.
instructions: Create any simple [[node:artifacts|Artifact]] — for example, a short HTML page.
Ask for a small change and notice: a new version appeared.
Find the version switcher in the artifact interface.
Switch between the current and previous version back and forth.
a-iterate-1.validate: You see at least two versions and can switch between them.
a-iterate-1.tip: A version is created on every change — you don't need to "save" anything manually.

a-iterate-2.title: How to ask for a targeted edit
a-iterate-2.why: A vague request changes extra things. A precise phrasing keeps the edit within one step.
instructions: Name the specific target: "change only the hero-section headline".
Add a constraint: "leave the rest of the layout and styles untouched".
Avoid "and also" — one edit = one request (see [[node:a-edit|editing an artifact]]).
Check the new version: did exactly what you asked change?
a-iterate-2.validate: The new version differs from the previous only in the one requested place.
a-iterate-2.tip: If more changed than needed — roll back and rephrase tighter, don't edit on top.

a-iterate-3.title: Versions as variants to compare
a-iterate-3.why: Side-by-side comparison beats memory: "it felt better" is a common illusion.
instructions: Take one artifact and ask for variant A.
Then ask for variant B as the next version of the same artifact.
Switch between versions A and B, judging by one criterion.
Make a variant C if needed and compare all three.
a-iterate-3.validate: You have 2-3 versions of one artifact and choose between them deliberately.
a-iterate-3.tip: Compare one criterion at a time — otherwise the choice gets blurry.

a-iterate-4.title: Reverting to a previous version
a-iterate-4.why: Rollback is the core insurance of iteration. Without it, every bold edit becomes a risk.
instructions: Deliberately make an edit that worsens the artifact.
Don't ask "put it back" — open the version history.
Pick the previous working version and revert to it.
Confirm the artifact is back in the needed state.
a-iterate-4.validate: You returned to a working version via history, not by rewriting from scratch.
a-iterate-4.tip: A rollback is more precise than asking "put it back": the model may not restore details from memory.

a-iterate-5.title: Keeping a series of edits focused
a-iterate-5.why: Stacking unrelated edits in one version branch quietly destroys the working result.
instructions: State the goal of the series: what exactly should get better.
Make one edit per step, checking the version before the next.
If an edit went off track — roll back at once, don't stack on top.
Don't mix tasks: design and new logic are separate edit series.
a-iterate-5.validate: Each version in the series is a deliberate step toward the goal, not a random change.
a-iterate-5.tip: Reverting in time is cheaper than fixing ten stacked edits.

a-iterate-6.title: Safely finishing iterations
a-iterate-6.why: The final version should be verified, not just last on the list.
instructions: Compare the final version with the best of the intermediate ones.
Verify the final actually works before calling it done.
Don't delete old versions manually until the new one is confirmed.
Note which version is the final one so you don't get confused.
For code, check the iteration practice in [[node:pr-iterate|project iterations]].
a-iterate-6.validate: The final version is chosen by comparison and verified in use, history preserved.
a-iterate-6.tip: "Latest version" and "best version" aren't always the same; comparison decides.

course-a-edit.title: Targeted artifact edits
course-a-edit.subtitle: When to update a part vs rewrite the whole thing
course-a-edit.whatItIs: A targeted edit is a request to change a specific part of an [[node:artifacts|artifact]] (one button, one color, one text block) without touching the rest. Claude updates only that spot, preserving all prior work. The alternative is a full rewrite, where the model regenerates the artifact from scratch. This course teaches you to choose between these modes and phrase an edit so that exactly what you intend changes.
course-a-edit.approach: We work from the update-vs-rewrite contrast: first learn to see the line between them, then phrase a targeted request (what to change, where, what to leave alone), then judge when each is faster and cheaper. Every step uses one concrete artifact: we edit a color, text, a piece of logic, and compare against a full rewrite.
outcomes: Distinguish a targeted part-update from a full rewrite and pick the mode deliberately
Phrase an edit with the formula "what, where, what to leave alone"
Judge when an update is faster and cheaper, and when a rewrite wins
Avoid vague "improve everything" prompts that make the model break finished work
Connect targeted edits to iterative work on an artifact

applyIn.title: Polishing a UI artifact
applyIn.description: Change a button's color, padding, or text in a finished interface without risking the layout of everything else.

applyIn.title: Editing a long document
applyIn.description: Rewrite a single paragraph or heading in a large text while keeping the structure and tone of the rest.

applyIn.title: Fixing a piece of code
applyIn.description: Repair one function or line in a script artifact without regenerating the whole file or losing working parts.

pitfalls: "Improve everything" — the model rewrites half at random and breaks decisions already made
Not stating what NOT to touch — Claude "helpfully" changes neighboring blocks too
A targeted edit where a rewrite is simpler: a dozen tiny edits cost more than one rewrite
A rewrite where an update would do — you lose manual polish and burn extra tokens
A fuzzy anchor like "change the button" when there are several — the model edits the wrong one

exercises.question: You have a 300-line landing-page artifact. You need to change only the main button's color. How do you phrase the edit?
exercises.hint: Name the specific element, the target value, and explicitly say "leave the rest alone."

exercises.question: In a 5-paragraph text, the third paragraph reads dry. When is a targeted edit better, and when should you rewrite the whole text?
exercises.hint: If one paragraph changes and the structure and tone of the rest are fine — it's an update. Rewrite fully only if there are so many edits they touch the whole text.

exercises.question: You gave three small edits in a row, and on the third Claude broke what the first one fixed. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
exercises.hint: Too many accumulated targeted edits dilute context; sometimes it's cheaper to state the desired result and ask to rewrite the section whole.

a-edit-1.title: Update vs rewrite: where's the line
a-edit-1.why: Before phrasing an edit you must see two modes. Update changes part of the artifact and keeps the rest; rewrite regenerates everything. Confusing the modes is the root of most breakage.
instructions: Open any finished [[node:artifacts|artifact]] of medium length (an interface or a document)
Write down: what you want to change in it and what must stay untouched
Estimate the share of change: one element among many means update; almost everything changes means rewrite
State the rule aloud: "small and targeted change — I ask to update a part, not rewrite"
a-edit-1.validate: You can say of any of your requests whether it's an update or a rewrite, and why.
a-edit-1.tip: If less than ~20% of the artifact is affected, a targeted update almost always wins.

a-edit-2.title: The targeted-edit formula
a-edit-2.why: A precise edit rests on three parts: what to change, where exactly, what to leave alone. Without the third part Claude edits the neighbors "while it's at it."
instructions: Name the element specifically: not "the button" but "the CTA button in the header"
State the target value: "primary color, set to #0F172A"
Add a stop boundary: "don't touch the rest", "keep the structure"
Combine into one request: what, where, what to leave alone
Send it and compare: did exactly the named spot change?
a-edit-2.validate: Only the stated part changed; neighboring blocks are untouched.
a-edit-2.tip: "Leave the rest alone" is the cheapest safeguard against stray edits.

a-edit-3.title: Anchoring: which spot exactly
a-edit-3.why: If the artifact has several similar elements, a fuzzy anchor makes the model edit the wrong one. An anchor makes the edit unambiguous.
instructions: Find an element with "twins" in the artifact (several buttons, headings, sections)
Give an anchor: by text ("the button reading Buy"), by position ("the second heading"), by role ("the primary CTA")
If there's no anchor — ask first which elements exist, then refer to the one you need
Phrase the edit with the anchor and check it hit exactly that element
a-edit-3.validate: The edit landed on the right one of several similar elements on the first try.
a-edit-3.tip: Quoting the element's exact text is the most reliable anchor — better than "top/bottom."

a-edit-4.title: When an update is faster and cheaper
a-edit-4.why: A targeted update saves tokens and preserves manual polish. But it isn't always a win — the mode has an efficiency zone.
instructions: Take the edit from step 2 and estimate how much of the artifact actually changes
An update wins when: a small part changes, the rest is already polished, and prior decisions matter
Assess breakage risk: a targeted edit touches neighbors 3-5× less often than "improve everything"
Set yourself a threshold: "editing one or two spots means update"
a-edit-4.validate: You can name three signs that an update beats a rewrite.
a-edit-4.tip: The main saving of an update isn't tokens — it's the manual polish a rewrite would lose.

a-edit-5.title: When a full rewrite wins
a-edit-5.why: Targeted edits have a limit: a dozen small edits in a row dilute context and cost more than one clean rewrite.
instructions: Count how many edits you've already given on one artifact in a row
If there are many and they touch different parts — that's a signal to rewrite the section anew
State the desired result whole ("I want a block like this") and ask to rewrite only it
Compare: rewriting one section is often cleaner than five targeted patches
a-edit-5.validate: You recognize the moment when accumulated edits should be replaced by one rewrite.
a-edit-5.tip: If the third edit breaks what the first one fixed — stop, rewrite the section whole.

a-edit-6.title: Tying into iterative work
a-edit-6.why: Targeted edits are a tool inside [[node:a-iterate|iterative polishing]] of an artifact. Knowing which [[node:a-types|types of artifacts]] you're editing lets you choose the mode deliberately.
instructions: Run one artifact through a cycle: create, then edit targeted 2-3 times, then rewrite the section once edits pile up
Notice the artifact type: text, interface, code — each has its own convenient anchors
Treat edits as a series of deliberate updates, not a stream of "improve more"
Lock in a personal rule for the switch from update to rewrite for future sessions
a-edit-6.validate: You run artifact polishing as an alternation of targeted edits and rare rewrites, without losing finished work.
a-edit-6.tip: Tie targeted edits to iteration: each edit is a deliberate step, not a random "improve."

course-sc-coding.title: Claude for Programming
course-sc-coding.subtitle: How Claude helps you write, explain, debug, and refactor code
course-sc-coding.whatItIs: Claude is one of the strongest coding models. It writes new code, explains existing code, finds and fixes bugs, refactors, and runs migrations. In [[node:scenarios|Claude.ai]] chat you work with pasted code snippets; in [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] it reads and edits your project files directly, sees history, and runs commands.
course-sc-coding.approach: The main rule: give context. Claude is exactly as good as its understanding of your task, stack, and constraints. In chat that means pasting real code and describing the environment; in Claude Code it means pointing to files and keeping a [[node:claude-code|CLAUDE.md]] with project rules. Then you work in iterations: request, then check the output, then refine. Never take code on faith — read it and run it.
outcomes: You know when chat [[node:scenarios|Claude.ai]] is enough and when you need [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] with file access
You can give Claude enough context for code to fit your project on the first or second try
You phrase coding tasks tightly: what, in which file, under which constraints
You check and test generated code instead of accepting it blindly
You use Claude for debugging, refactoring, and explaining unfamiliar code

applyIn.title: New code and prototypes
applyIn.description: Endpoint, component, script, function — from idea to working draft in minutes. Chat for isolated snippets, Claude Code for changes straight into project files.

applyIn.title: Debugging and refactoring
applyIn.description: Paste the error and the code — Claude finds the cause. Ask it to simplify, speed up, or rewrite to a new pattern without changing behavior.

applyIn.title: Understanding others' code
applyIn.description: Unfamiliar codebase, legacy, a complex function — Claude explains what it does and why, and maps the dependencies.

pitfalls: Working in chat where you need [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] — you lose access to files, history, and project context
Skipping context: without stack, versions, and real code Claude guesses and drifts into its own habits
Accepting code blindly — not reading or running it. Claude makes mistakes, especially in edge cases
Asking it to "fix everything at once" instead of iterating — harder to verify and roll back
Not keeping a [[node:claude-code|CLAUDE.md]] in Claude Code — then it ignores your conventions and style

exercises.question: You have a slow SQL query and a timeout error message. How do you phrase the task for Claude to get a useful answer on the first try?
exercises.hint: Give the query itself, the table schema, the data volume, and where it runs. Ask it to explain the cause of the slowness first, then propose options — not an instant "rewrite it".

exercises.question: You want to rewrite an endpoint so it uses transactions and caches the result for 60 seconds. When do you choose chat vs. [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]]?
exercises.hint: One isolated file you paste and return by hand — chat is enough. If the endpoint pulls in several modules that must change together — Claude Code with file access.

exercises.question: Claude returned a function that looks correct. What two steps do you take before accepting it?
exercises.hint: Read the logic with your own eyes (especially edge cases and error handling) and run it — a test or a manual pass with real data.

sc-coding-1.title: Pick the tool: chat or Claude Code
sc-coding-1.why: This choice decides how much context you'll supply by hand. Chat is isolated — you paste and retrieve code yourself. [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] sees files, history, and runs commands.
instructions: For one isolated snippet (function, query, config) — open [[node:scenarios|Claude.ai]] chat
For project work (several files, refactoring, migration) — use [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]]
If the task needs running tests or commands — it's clearly Claude Code
Unsure — start in chat, move to Claude Code once context runs short
sc-coding-1.validate: You can state in one sentence why you chose this tool for the current task.
sc-coding-1.tip: A sign it's time for Claude Code: you're pasting a third file into chat just so it "sees the picture".

sc-coding-2.title: Give context: code, stack, constraints
sc-coding-2.why: Claude is exactly as good as its grasp of the task. Without real code and environment it guesses and drifts into others' habits.
instructions: Paste real code, not a paraphrase. In Claude Code — name the files
State the stack and versions: language, framework, DB, runtime
Spell out constraints: what must not break, the style, which dependencies are forbidden
In Claude Code keep a [[node:claude-code|CLAUDE.md]] with project rules — it picks them up on its own
sc-coding-2.validate: Your request contains code, the stack, and at least one explicit constraint.
sc-coding-2.tip: One sentence about "what must not break" saves more iterations than a paragraph about "what I'd like".

sc-coding-3.title: Phrase the coding task tightly
sc-coding-3.why: A vague request yields vague code. A clear "what, where, under which constraints" sharply raises first-try accuracy.
instructions: Describe the result: what the solution should do and how to tell it works
Name the place: which file, function, layer
List constraints right in the request: transactions, 60s cache, no new dependencies
Ask for one change at a time, not "fix everything at once"
If the task is exploratory — ask for a plan first, then the code
sc-coding-3.validate: Your request makes it clear what counts as success, and it can be verified.
sc-coding-3.tip: Example of a tight phrasing: "Rewrite this endpoint so it uses transactions and caches the result for 60s".

sc-coding-4.title: Check the output: read it and run it
sc-coding-4.why: Claude makes mistakes, especially in edge cases and error handling. Blindly accepted code is the top source of hidden bugs.
instructions: Read the logic with your own eyes: edge cases, error handling, boundary values
Run the code — a test or a manual pass with real data
Compare behavior with the original: a refactor must not change results
Found a problem — hand it back to Claude with the code and the error, don't silently rewrite
sc-coding-4.validate: The code was run and checked on real or near-real data, not just read.
sc-coding-4.tip: In Claude Code, ask it to run the tests itself — it sees the output and proposes the fix.

sc-coding-5.title: Debugging, refactoring, and explaining
sc-coding-5.why: Claude's strength isn't only new code. It quickly finds a bug's cause, safely simplifies code, and explains an unfamiliar codebase.
instructions: For a bug: give the code, the error text, and repro steps — ask for the cause first, then the fix
For a refactor: state the goal (faster, simpler, new pattern) and the requirement to keep behavior
For understanding: paste the function or module and ask it to explain what it does and why
Ask for a dependency map when working through large legacy
sc-coding-5.validate: You got not just working code but an understanding of why it's that way.
sc-coding-5.tip: When debugging, ask separately for the cause — that way you understand the bug instead of just closing it.

sc-coding-6.title: Iteration and project context
sc-coding-6.why: Development is a cycle, not a single request. In [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] history and the [[node:claude-code|CLAUDE.md]] make each next iteration more accurate.
instructions: Work in iterations: request, then check, then refine, not one big dump
Feed check results back to Claude: what worked, what didn't, what the output was
In Claude Code record stable rules and style in the [[node:claude-code|CLAUDE.md]]
Save successful task phrasings — reuse them as templates
sc-coding-6.validate: The next iteration builds on the previous results rather than starting from scratch.
sc-coding-6.tip: A good [[node:claude-code|CLAUDE.md]] is the project's memory: write the conventions once, and Claude keeps them itself.

course-sc-design.title: Claude for Design and UX
course-sc-design.subtitle: From UX copywriting and prototyping to auditing an interface from a screenshot
course-sc-design.whatItIs: A hands-on course on using Claude in design: writing UX copy, building a working prototype in an HTML/React artifact, auditing an interface from a screenshot, and maintaining a design system. Claude is a strong co-designer, especially when it sees the actual layout (via [[node:artifacts|artifacts]] or Figma MCP), but it doesn't replace a designer — it speeds up routine and widens options.
course-sc-design.approach: We follow a real workflow loop: copy, then prototype, then audit, then system. At each step Claude gets maximum context (screenshot, text, brand rules) and produces options you critique and select from. Text without an image is weak input; feed Claude the visual, not a description of the visual.
outcomes: Write UX copy (buttons, errors, empty states) matched to your product's tone and context
Build a clickable prototype right in an HTML/React artifact without leaving the chat
Audit an interface from a screenshot: hierarchy, accessibility, friction points
Define and maintain a mini design system (tokens, components, rules)
Understand the limits: where Claude accelerates and where the call stays human

applyIn.title: UX copywriting
applyIn.description: Rewrite a screen's microcopy to a single tone, fix vague errors and empty states, generate CTA options.

applyIn.title: Fast prototype
applyIn.description: Build an interactive mockup in an artifact to test an idea before drawing it in Figma.

applyIn.title: Audit and review
applyIn.description: Hand over a screenshot and get a breakdown of hierarchy, contrast, touch-target sizes, and friction points.

pitfalls: Design "through text": describing a layout in words instead of a screenshot loses half the context
Accepting the first copy variant without critique — Claude produces plausible but not always vetted text
Confusing an artifact prototype with final design: it's idea validation, not production markup
Ignoring accessibility (contrast, sizes, focus) — it doesn't appear on its own, you must ask explicitly
Expecting Claude to replace a designer: taste, product decisions, and accountability remain yours

exercises.question: Why does a screenshot of the layout give Claude radically more than a text description of the same screen?
exercises.hint: Think about hierarchy, spacing, contrast, and relative placement — which of these simply can't be conveyed precisely in words.

exercises.question: How does an artifact prototype differ from final design, and what job does it do?
exercises.hint: Speed of idea validation vs. polish. What's cheaper to throw away?

exercises.question: What three things must you give Claude for UX copy to hit the product's tone on the first try?
exercises.hint: Tone of voice, screen context, examples of "how we do it here".

sc-design-1.title: UX copywriting: tone, buttons, errors
sc-design-1.why: Microcopy is the cheapest, fastest lever for improving an interface. Claude rewrites it in batches once you set tone and context.
instructions: Describe the product and tone of voice (e.g. "friendly, casual, no jargon")
Provide 2-3 examples of current text and the screen they live on
Ask for 3 options per element: CTA, error message, empty state
Pick the best and ask it to explain why one variant beats another
sc-design-1.validate: You have rewritten microcopy in a consistent tone and a clear criterion for your choice.
sc-design-1.tip: The design:ux-copy skill already knows the analysis structure — invoke it instead of a manual prompt.

sc-design-2.title: Prototype in an artifact (HTML/React)
sc-design-2.why: A clickable prototype validates an idea in minutes, before you spend hours in Figma. The artifact builds it right in the chat.
instructions: Describe the screen: user's task, key blocks, primary action
Ask it to build a React prototype in an artifact with stub data
Click through, name what's wrong, and ask for an iteration — not a full rewrite
Lock the working version as a baseline for the next edits
sc-design-2.validate: The artifact opens an interactive mockup you can walk the main flow through.
sc-design-2.tip: More on the mechanics — [[node:artifacts|artifacts]]: that's the environment where the prototype lives and updates.

sc-design-3.title: Auditing an interface from a screenshot
sc-design-3.why: Claude sees the layout and analyzes it like an expert: hierarchy, contrast, friction points. Without an image this step doesn't work.
instructions: Attach a screenshot of the real screen (not a word description)
Set the audit focus: hierarchy, accessibility, conversion action
Ask for a prioritized list of problems with concrete "what to do"
Cross-check findings against your context — not everything flagged is actually critical
sc-design-3.validate: You have a prioritized list of interface problems with concrete fixes.
sc-design-3.tip: The design:design-critique and design:accessibility-review skills give a ready analysis structure.

sc-design-4.title: Accessibility as a separate pass
sc-design-4.why: Contrast, touch-target sizes, and focus don't appear on their own — they must be checked explicitly. This is often missed at speed.
instructions: Give a screenshot and ask for a WCAG audit: contrast, sizes, keyboard navigation
Clarify color pairs you're unsure about
Get a list of fixes marking what's a blocker vs. an improvement
Apply the blockers to the prototype or layout right away
sc-design-4.validate: Accessibility problems found and prioritized, blockers separated from nice-to-haves.
sc-design-4.tip: Ask for concrete contrast values and pixels — generic "make it accessible" is useless.

sc-design-5.title: Mini design system: tokens and rules
sc-design-5.why: A system keeps the interface consistent as it grows. Claude helps lock down tokens, components, and rules for applying them.
instructions: Gather current colors, fonts, spacing, and buttons into one description
Ask Claude to extract tokens and name them on a single scheme
Fix the rules: when to use which component and variant
Check a new screen against the system
sc-design-5.validate: You have a set of named tokens and rules to check new screens against.
sc-design-5.tip: Tied to content — [[node:ds-content-design|content design]]: text is part of the system too, not just visuals.

sc-design-6.title: Limits: where Claude doesn't replace a designer
sc-design-6.why: Knowing the limits guards against blind trust. Claude speeds up routine, but taste, product decisions, and accountability stay with the human.
instructions: Split the tasks: routine and options — Claude; final choice and strategy — you
Double-check brand nuance and emotion: Claude often smooths them over
Don't hand it decisions with a cost of error without your review
Write down your own checklist of "what I always check by hand"
sc-design-6.validate: You have an explicit boundary: what you delegate to Claude and what you keep.
sc-design-6.tip: The more Claude sees the system (via MCP and [[node:cap-vision|vision]]), the higher the quality — but the call is still yours.

course-sc-research.title: Claude for Research
course-sc-research.subtitle: Collect, verify and synthesize — from raw sources to a cited report
course-sc-research.whatItIs: A workflow where Claude is not a "search box" but an analyst-synthesizer: you feed it sources (articles, transcripts, documents, fresh web data) and it extracts patterns, checks facts and assembles a structured output tied back to sources.
course-sc-research.approach: The course moves from framing a research question and gathering material to synthesis, hallucination-checking and a final report where every claim is backed by a citation. Each step yields a verifiable artifact that feeds the next.
outcomes: Frame a research question with criteria and output format — no fluff
Use web search for fresh data and understand the model's knowledge cutoff
Compress dozens of documents and transcripts into a structured theme synthesis
Check claims for hallucinations and tell fact from the model's guess
Assemble a report where every point is tied to a quote and source

applyIn.title: Product and UX research
applyIn.description: Synthesize 10–20 interviews or surveys into key themes, segments and prioritized problems instead of rereading by hand.

applyIn.title: Market and competitive analysis
applyIn.description: Review competitors, pricing and positioning against clear criteria with fresh web data and links to the original source.

applyIn.title: Literature review and due diligence
applyIn.description: Compress articles, reports and documents into a cited brief for decisions where traceability of every fact matters.

pitfalls: Asking "do a market overview" without criteria or format — you get fluff and generic phrasing
Trusting numbers and dates without checking: the model confidently invents precise figures
Mixing collection and synthesis in one prompt — you lose track of what came from where
Assuming web search refreshes everything: the model may cite stale results
Accepting output without source links — nothing to re-verify and nothing to defend

exercises.question: Turn the vague prompt "study the CRM market" into a research question with criteria and an output format.
exercises.hint: Add a segment, 3–5 comparison axes (price, audience, key feature), a data-freshness horizon and the output table structure.

exercises.question: Give Claude a document with 3 factual claims and ask it to tag each as "in source / inferred / unsupported".
exercises.hint: Require a verbatim supporting quote for every "in source"; a missing quote is a red flag.

exercises.question: Build a mini-synthesis from 4 short transcripts: 3 themes, each with 2 quotes from different respondents.
exercises.hint: First extract quotes as a separate step, then ask to group them into themes — not all at once.

sc-research-1.title: Frame the research question
sc-research-1.why: Without criteria and format Claude returns generic phrasing. A sharp question frames the whole study and makes the output verifiable.
instructions: Frame the question as a decision: what you will do with the answer
Set 3–5 comparison or measurement criteria (axes of analysis)
State the data-freshness horizon and scope boundaries
Describe the exact output format: table, theme list, brief
Browse [[node:scenarios|scenarios]] to pick a close task template
sc-research-1.validate: You have one question statement with criteria, scope and output format — handable to another person without explanation.
sc-research-1.tip: Name what a "good answer" looks like — it cuts the fluff immediately.

sc-research-2.title: Gather fresh data via web search
sc-research-2.why: The model's knowledge has a cutoff. For markets, prices and news you need web search, or the output rests on stale data.
instructions: Enable search and write targeted queries for each criterion from step 1
Ask for the publication date and source of every found fact
Separate what was found in web from what the model knows "from memory"
Save links immediately — you'll need them at the citation step
Check what search can do with [[node:cap-search|web search]]
sc-research-2.validate: A list of facts is collected, each with a source and date; it's clear what is fresh and what is the model's general knowledge.
sc-research-2.tip: One query = one criterion. A broad "tell me about the market" yields shallow results.

sc-research-3.title: Summarize documents and transcripts
sc-research-3.why: Claude's strength is compression. Dozens of pages become manageable points — but only if you separate extraction from generalization.
instructions: Load the sources and ask for a short structured brief per item
Extract verbatim quotes and facts in a separate pass, before generalizing
Keep each point tied to its specific document
Flag contradictions between sources rather than smoothing them over
For long-lived material consider a [[node:b-knowledge|knowledge base]]
sc-research-3.validate: Each source has a brief and a list of extracted quotes with their origin noted.
sc-research-3.tip: First "what was said", then "what it means" — don't merge these two prompts.

sc-research-4.title: Synthesize themes and conclusions
sc-research-4.why: Separate briefs aren't research yet. Value appears when cross-cutting patterns and priorities become visible.
instructions: Ask to group the material from step 3 into 3–7 key themes
For each theme require support from at least two sources
Prioritize themes by the criteria from step 1 (frequency, impact, risk)
Ask to explicitly mark conclusions beyond the data as hypotheses
For deep multi-source synthesis use the design:research-synthesis skill
sc-research-4.validate: There is a list of prioritized themes; each rests on sources with a clear line between fact and hypothesis.
sc-research-4.tip: If a theme stands on one source it's a signal, not a conclusion.

sc-research-5.title: Verify facts and catch hallucinations
sc-research-5.why: The model confidently invents precise figures, dates and quotes. Without a dedicated verification pass the report can't be defended.
instructions: Go through every number, date and name and ask for a supporting quote
Tag claims: "in source / inferred / unsupported"
Any "unsupported" — delete or re-verify in web
Separately check that quotes are verbatim, not paraphrased
Mind the model's limits: a confident tone ≠ accuracy
sc-research-5.validate: Every factual claim is tagged by verification status; no numbers or quotes remain without a source.
sc-research-5.tip: Ask the model to flag what it's least sure of — a cheap detector of weak spots.

sc-research-6.title: Assemble a report with quotes and sources
sc-research-6.why: Research is valuable when every conclusion traces back to a source. Citations make the report defensible and reusable.
instructions: Assemble the final report in the step 1 format: conclusion, themes, rationale
Under each point — a verbatim quote and a source link
Add a limitations section: what's uncovered and where data is weak
Put a list of all sources with dates at the end
Clean reference formatting is supported by [[node:cap-citations|citations and sources]]
sc-research-6.validate: A report is ready where each key point is tied to a quote and source, with a limitations section and a source list.
sc-research-6.tip: A report without a limitations section looks more honest than it is. Name the weak spots yourself.

course-sc-data.title: Claude for data analysis
course-sc-data.subtitle: From table to answer: loading, cleaning, aggregations, charts, and verifying the math
course-sc-data.whatItIs: A hands-on course on working with tables through Claude: load a CSV or Excel file, clean the junk, compute aggregates, find anomalies, plot charts and — most importantly — verify the numbers are real. We rely on [[node:cap-code-exec|Code execution]]: Claude writes and runs code, so it returns actual calculations, not plausible-looking figures.
course-sc-data.approach: Analysis always starts from a concrete question, not from "analyze the data". First load the file and understand its structure, then clean it, then compute and visualize — and verify the result at every step. Claude is an assistant, not an oracle: trust the numbers only after checking them.
outcomes: Load CSV/XLSX and quickly grasp the table's structure: columns, types, missing values
Clean data: duplicates, empty cells, inconsistent date and number formats
Compute aggregates and find anomalies by phrasing the task in plain language
Plot charts through code execution and read them together with Claude
Verify calculations and never trust numbers blindly — catch silent errors

applyIn.title: Sales and revenue
applyIn.description: Find SKUs with drops, seasonality, top customers and explain the pattern — without VLOOKUP or pivot tables.

applyIn.title: Product analytics
applyIn.description: Event or funnel dumps: where users drop off, which cohorts retain, what's anomalous.

applyIn.title: Operational reports
applyIn.description: A recurring table (logistics, support, finance) — a quick "what changed this month" instead of manual formulas.

pitfalls: Asking to "analyze the data" without a question — you'll get a generic description about nothing
Trusting numbers without checking: the model can mishandle aggregation logic silently and confidently
Not noticing that Claude estimated "by eye" without code execution — then the figures are approximate
Skipping cleanup: duplicates and broken date formats distort every aggregate
Loading a huge file whole when a sample or aggregate would do — the model drowns in detail

exercises.question: You loaded a CSV of orders and asked "what's interesting here". Why was the answer vague and how do you fix the request?
exercises.hint: Good analysis starts from a concrete question: metric, breakdown, period. Compare "what's interesting" with "find the top-5 SKUs with a revenue drop >30% in March vs February".

exercises.question: Claude returned "average order value $52". What two things should you do before pasting that number into a report?
exercises.hint: Check the calculation ran through code execution, and ask it to show the formula/code and the number of rows it used. Cross-check with a rough manual estimate.

exercises.question: In the date column some values are 01/03/2026 and some are 2026-03-01. What happens when grouping by month, and what should you do during cleanup?
exercises.hint: Mixed date formats may not parse as dates — some rows drop out or land in the wrong month. During cleanup, normalize the column to a single date type.

sc-data-1.title: Load the table and understand its structure
sc-data-1.why: Before computing anything, you need to see what's in the file: which columns, which types, how many rows, where the gaps are. It's the foundation — without it, analysis is done blind.
instructions: Attach the CSV or XLSX file in the chat (see [[node:cap-files|working with files]])
Ask: "Show the structure: columns, types, row count, sample values, share of missing values per column"
Clarify which columns are key (date, amount, identifier)
If the file is large — ask for a preview of the first rows, not the whole dump
sc-data-1.validate: You have a list of columns with types and a sense of where there are gaps and anomalous values.
sc-data-1.tip: Ask right away "what could be a trap in this data?" — Claude often flags broken formats and outliers upfront.

sc-data-2.title: Clean the data
sc-data-2.why: Duplicates, empty cells and inconsistent date and number formats distort any aggregate. Cleaning is the invisible but decisive step: dirty data yields pretty but false conclusions.
instructions: Ask it to find duplicate rows and decide whether to remove them
Normalize dates to a single format, numbers — free of stray separators and text
Decide what to do with missing values: drop the row, fill, or keep
Lock in the result: "how many rows were there, how many remain, what changed"
sc-data-2.validate: Columns have correct types, dates parse as dates, and the post-cleanup row count makes sense and is explained.
sc-data-2.tip: Ask Claude, via code execution, to show the row count before and after each operation — that's how you see if it silently lost data.

sc-data-3.title: Aggregations and conclusions
sc-data-3.why: This is where the analysis proper begins: sums, averages, groupings, time breakdowns. Claude's strength is phrasing the task in plain language instead of writing formulas by hand.
instructions: Ask a concrete question: metric + breakdown + period (e.g. revenue by SKU for March vs February)
Ask it to group and sort: "top-5 by drop, with percent change"
Ask not only for numbers but a short explanation of the pattern from available columns
Iterate: add breakdowns, narrow the period, change the metric
sc-data-3.validate: You have an aggregate table that directly answers your question, with numbers and a brief conclusion.
sc-data-3.tip: Compare "analyze the data" with "find the top-5 SKUs with a revenue drop >30% in March vs February" — the second yields a result, the first yields fluff.

sc-data-4.title: Charts through code execution
sc-data-4.why: Trends, seasonality and outliers are visible in a chart faster than in a table. Through [[node:cap-code-exec|Code execution]] Claude builds a real chart from real numbers instead of describing it in words.
instructions: Ask for a chart tailored to the question: monthly dynamics, distribution, group comparison
Make sure the chart was built with code, not drawn "by meaning"
Ask to label axes, units and period — otherwise the chart is easy to misread
If there are too many points — ask to aggregate (by weeks/months) before plotting
sc-data-4.validate: You have a chart that answers the question, with labeled axes and clear units.
sc-data-4.tip: One chart — one idea. If it has five lines and three axes, ask to split it into several simple ones.

sc-data-5.title: Verify the math
sc-data-5.why: The model can mishandle aggregation logic silently and confidently: wrong filter, double counting, lost rows. Verification is what separates analysis from a guess.
instructions: Ask it to show the calculation's code/formula and the number of rows it used
Make a rough manual estimate and check the order of magnitude
Check edge cases: empty groups, zeros, negative values
Re-verify one result another way (e.g. a sum via a different grouping)
sc-data-5.validate: Key numbers are confirmed by a second method or manual estimate, with no discrepancies.
sc-data-5.tip: If a number is "too clean" or "too convenient" — that's a reason to recheck, not to celebrate.

sc-data-6.title: Don't trust blindly: conclusions and context
sc-data-6.why: Numbers without context mislead. The final step is to separate fact from interpretation, record assumptions, and not pass correlation off as causation.
instructions: Ask it to split the answer: what strictly follows from the data vs what's a hypothesis
Record assumptions and sample limitations (period, filters, gaps)
Don't accept causal explanations as fact — data shows "what", not always "why"
Preserve reproducibility: the code, the file version, and the questions themselves (see [[node:b-context|context]])
sc-data-6.validate: You have a conclusion where facts are separated from hypotheses, and assumptions and limitations are stated explicitly.
sc-data-6.tip: Ask Claude: "what in this conclusion could be wrong, and what data would refute it?" — the best way to catch self-deception.

course-rp-project.title: The ready-made "Create a Project" prompt
course-rp-project.subtitle: How to assemble a specialized assistant from a template in minutes
course-rp-project.whatItIs: The ready-made "Create a Project" prompt is a starter that tells Claude its role, response format, taboos, and success criteria (KPIs) for a new Project. You plug your task into the placeholders — and the Project works as a domain assistant right away, not as an empty chat.
course-rp-project.approach: The course moves from "why a template at all" to a working cycle: break down the prompt's structure, fill the placeholders for your domain, run it in claude.ai, move the result into the Project's instructions, test it on a real request, and refine. It ends with reusing the template for future Projects.
outcomes: You understand which blocks the "Create a Project" prompt consists of and what each does
You can replace placeholders with your own role, format, taboos, and KPIs
You get ready-made Project instructions and move them into the settings on claude.ai
You test the Project on a real request and fix the weak spots
You reuse a single template for any number of new Projects

applyIn.title: A work assistant for a domain
applyIn.description: Marketing, support, analytics — you assemble a Project with the right role and style in minutes instead of setting up from scratch.

applyIn.title: A team standard
applyIn.description: One prompt template = a unified format for all Projects across the team, with no "bare chats" for anyone.

applyIn.title: A series of similar Projects
applyIn.description: When you need many uniform assistants (per client, per product), you change only the placeholders — the base stays the same.

pitfalls: Copying the prompt as is without plugging in your domain — the Project comes out generic and useless
Leaving placeholders unfilled — Claude gets a starter instead of specifics
Setting the role but forgetting taboos and KPIs — the assistant has no boundaries or success criteria
Not moving the result into the Project's instructions but leaving it in a regular chat — the setup isn't saved
Not testing the Project on a real request — weak wording only surfaces in actual work

exercises.question: Take the "Create a Project" prompt and for your task fill in just three blocks: role, response format, and one taboo. How would those three lines change the assistant's answers?
exercises.hint: The role sets tone and expertise, the format sets output structure, the taboo sets what to avoid. Picture the same question with and without these settings.

exercises.question: Define 2-3 KPIs for your Project — how will you know the assistant is answering well?
exercises.hint: KPIs are measurable quality markers: "always gives an example", "no longer than 5 points", "cites a source". Avoid the vague "answers helpfully".

exercises.question: Figure out how to reuse the same template for a second Project in a different domain. Which blocks change and which stay?
exercises.hint: The structure (role/format/taboos/KPIs) stays, only the placeholder content changes. That's the whole point of a template.

rp-project-1.title: Why a template beats a blank chat
rp-project-1.why: Without a template a Project is just a folder of files, not a specialized assistant. Grasping this keeps you from skipping the setup.
instructions: Open the [[node:ready-prompts|ready-made prompts]] section and find the "Create a Project" prompt
Read it fully, noting the four anchor blocks: role, format, taboos, KPIs
Mentally compare how a regular chat answers versus a Project with a defined role
Write down what assistant you actually need (domain, audience)
rp-project-1.validate: You can say in one sentence why a configured Project beats an empty chat for your task.
rp-project-1.tip: The template saves time exactly on repetition: figure it out once, then just plug in values.

rp-project-2.title: Fill the placeholders for your task
rp-project-2.why: Placeholders are where you write your specifics. Without that the prompt stays a generic starter and gives generic answers.
instructions: Copy the prompt text into a draft
Set the role: who the assistant should be (e.g., "technical text editor")
Define the response format: structure, length, tone
Spell out the taboos: what the assistant must not do
State 2-3 KPIs — measurable criteria of a good answer
rp-project-2.validate: No unfilled placeholder remains in the prompt; everything fits your domain.
rp-project-2.tip: If a field is unclear, write it in your own words; precision matters more than polished phrasing.

rp-project-3.title: Run the prompt in claude.ai
rp-project-3.why: The filled prompt needs to go through Claude to produce ready instruction text for the Project.
instructions: Create a new Project on claude.ai (the [[node:projects|Projects]] section)
Paste the filled prompt into a chat inside the Project
Let Claude produce a draft of the assistant's instructions
Read the result — it should reflect your role, format, taboos, and KPIs
rp-project-3.validate: Claude returned coherent instruction text in which your step-2 settings are recognizable.
rp-project-3.tip: If the result is too generic, go back to the placeholders — some wording is probably still vague.

rp-project-4.title: Move the result into the Project's instructions
rp-project-4.why: A chat answer doesn't save the setup. For the Project to always behave as needed, the text must live in its instructions.
instructions: Open the Project settings and the [[node:p-instructions|Project instructions]] section
Paste the prepared instruction text there
Trim the excess: keep role, format, taboos, and KPIs without fluff
Save the settings
rp-project-4.validate: The Project instructions hold the final text, and a new chat inside the Project already behaves by the set rules.
rp-project-4.tip: Instructions are the Project's persistent memory: what's written there applies in every new chat.

rp-project-5.title: Test on a real request
rp-project-5.why: Weak wording shows only in action. A test on a real task reveals whether the Project holds its role, format, and taboos.
instructions: Ask the Project a question typical of your task
Check the answer against your KPIs: format kept, taboos not broken
Note where the assistant deviated from expectations
If needed, refine the relevant instruction block
rp-project-5.validate: The answer to a real request matches the role, format, and KPIs, with no taboo broken.
rp-project-5.tip: Test with an ordinary working question, not a perfect one — real weak spots surface faster that way.

rp-project-6.title: Reuse the template for new Projects
rp-project-6.why: The template's main value is repeatability. Once the cycle is set, you assemble future Projects far faster.
instructions: Save your filled prompt as a personal starter
For a new Project, change only the placeholder content, keep the structure
Run steps 3-5 for the new Project
Keep a short list of your standard taboos and KPIs so you don't reinvent them
rp-project-6.validate: You can assemble a second Project in another domain by repeating the cycle and changing only the placeholders.
rp-project-6.tip: Over time you'll build a library of ready roles and formats — that is your team standard.

course-rp-artifact.title: Create an Artifact with a Ready-Made Prompt
course-rp-artifact.subtitle: Turn the "Create an Artifact" template into a working interactive prototype in 1-2 iterations
course-rp-artifact.whatItIs: The ready-made "Create an Artifact" prompt is a pre-built request skeleton that already includes requirements for preview, responsiveness, and baseline accessibility. You don't write the prompt from scratch — you fill placeholders with your data: artifact type, audience, device, content. The output is an interactive HTML or React prototype, not a text description.
course-rp-artifact.approach: We move from template to result along a chain: understand why a ready-made prompt helps, then choose the artifact type, then fill placeholders with specifics, then run it and get a preview, then read the prototype and form precise edits, then iterate to the target. Each step narrows uncertainty, so almost no edits remain at the end.
outcomes: You understand why a ready-made prompt beats a from-scratch request and when to use it
