sas-network-isolation-6.validate: The agent completes its task fully while the allowlist stays minimal and every allowance is justified.
sas-network-isolation-6.tip: Treat the allowlist like a dependency: as the task changes, the set of domains changes with it rather than growing forever.

course-sas-secrets.title: One-time accounts and secrets for the agent
course-sas-secrets.subtitle: Give the agent its own least-privilege accounts, revocable tokens, and clean secret delivery — never your passwords
course-sas-secrets.whatItIs: The practice of giving an agent not your real passwords but separate one-time or limited accounts and tokens with the minimum set of rights. Secrets are delivered via environment variables or a secret manager — not typed by hand and not written into the instruction text. Each token is isolated, has a lifetime, and can be revoked independently without touching your main credentials.
course-sas-secrets.approach: We move from threat model to operations: first separate the agent's identity from yours (a dedicated service account), then trim its rights to the strict minimum, then set up clean secret delivery (env/secret manager, not code or history), add a lifetime and rotation, and finish with a ready revocation and leak-response plan. Each step is a standalone technical control that holds even if the others fail.
outcomes: Create dedicated service accounts for the agent, unlinked from your personal accounts
Trim token rights to the minimum (scope, read-only, resource and IP restrictions)
Deliver secrets via env/secret manager so they never reach code, image, or history
Set token lifetime and regular rotation without task downtime
Revoke a compromised token in minutes and run an incident review against a checklist

applyIn.title: Agent with external API access
applyIn.description: The agent calls a GitHub/payment/CRM API: issue a fine-grained token scoped only to the needed repos/endpoints, read-only where writes aren't needed.

applyIn.title: Automating a service login
applyIn.description: The agent must log into a SaaS: create a separate service account with a reduced role instead of sharing your login and 2FA.

applyIn.title: CI/CD and background jobs
applyIn.description: The agent runs in a pipeline: the secret comes from a secret manager into the runner's environment for the job's duration and never lands in logs or artifacts.

pitfalls: Giving the agent your personal password or admin token "just to be sure" — compromising the agent compromises the whole account
Embedding a secret in the instruction text, code, Docker image, or a commit — it stays forever in git history and image layers
Issuing an over-privileged token (write/admin instead of read) or one with no resource scope — it blows up the blast radius on leak
Setting no lifetime and never rotating — an eternal token lives for years and leaks unnoticed
Having no ready revocation plan — on a leak you spend hours figuring out where the token is even used

exercises.question: You hold an admin-rights secret the agent uses to read a single table. What three changes do you make first?
exercises.hint: Think along axes: privilege level (scope), resource binding, lifetime. Least privilege — see [[node:sas-least-privilege|least privilege]].

exercises.question: The agent's token accidentally ended up in a public log. Describe your first 10 minutes of action.
exercises.hint: Revoke first, then assess usage, then rotate and review. Environment isolation — [[node:sys-agent-sandbox|agent sandbox]], emergency stop — [[node:sas-snapshots-killswitch|snapshots and kill-switch]].

exercises.question: How do you deliver a secret into the agent's container so it never lands in the image or shows up in `docker history`?
exercises.hint: Build-time vs run-time. The secret goes only into the environment/secret manager at runtime, never into an image layer.

sas-secrets-1.title: Separate the agent's identity from yours
sas-secrets-1.why: If the agent runs under your personal account, any mistake or compromise hits your main access. A dedicated service identity gives isolation and independent revocation.
instructions: Create a separate service account (service account / machine user) per agent or task instead of using your personal login
Never hand the agent your password or ask it to "log in with your password" — that's a direct antipattern
Tie the account to a clear owner and purpose so it's easy to find and revoke
Isolate execution in an [[node:sys-agent-sandbox|agent sandbox]] so the environment has no access to your personal sessions and caches
sas-secrets-1.validate: The service has a separate agent account; your personal account appears nowhere in the agent's config.
sas-secrets-1.tip: Name service accounts `agent-<task>-<env>` — during an incident you instantly see what to revoke.

sas-secrets-2.title: Trim rights to the minimum
sas-secrets-2.why: The blast radius of a leak equals the token's rights. Read-only and a narrow scope turn a serious leak into a minor one.
instructions: Issue a fine-grained token only for the resources and actions the task actually needs
Use read-only everywhere writes aren't required; grant write/admin only for the specific operation
Scope the token to a resource (a specific repo/project/table) and, where possible, to an IP/network
Cross-check against [[node:sas-least-privilege|least privilege]] and [[node:m-security|security]] before issuing
sas-secrets-2.validate: The token can't perform anything beyond the task: an attempt to write or reach another resource is rejected.
sas-secrets-2.tip: Test rights in reverse: try doing with the token what it shouldn't — a denial confirms the scope is correct.

sas-secrets-3.title: Deliver the secret cleanly, leaving no trace
sas-secrets-3.why: A secret in code, image, or git history stays there forever and leaks with the repo. Clean delivery via the environment breaks that link.
instructions: Pass the secret via environment variables or a secret manager at runtime, not typed by hand or in the instruction text
Never commit secrets: keep them out of the repo, add patterns to `.gitignore`, and enable secret scanning
Don't bake the secret into a Docker image at build-time — it sticks in layers and `docker history`; use run-time env or mounted secrets
Exclude secrets from the agent's logs, traces, and error messages
sas-secrets-3.validate: `git log -p` and `docker history` for the image contain no secret; the agent gets it only from the environment at runtime.
sas-secrets-3.tip: Add a pre-commit hook with a secret detector — it catches a token before it reaches history.

sas-secrets-4.title: Set a lifetime and rotation
sas-secrets-4.why: An eternal token lives for years and leaks unnoticed. A short TTL and regular rotation by themselves shrink the attack window.
instructions: Give every token a lifetime (TTL): for a one-off task — for the task's duration; for ongoing ones — short with auto-refresh
Where possible, use short-lived tokens issued on demand instead of static long-lived ones
Set up regular rotation so the old token leaves circulation without downtime (new/old overlap)
Keep a registry of active agent tokens: where issued, what rights, when they expire
sas-secrets-4.validate: Every token has an expiry; rotation passes without breaking tasks, and the old token is rejected after rotation.
sas-secrets-4.tip: Tie token expiry to task duration: a one-off agent gets a token that dies by the task's end.

sas-secrets-5.title: Prepare revocation and emergency stop
sas-secrets-5.why: In an incident, minutes count. A known way to revoke a token and stop the agent turns panic into a procedure.
instructions: Verify in advance where and how each token is revoked — revocation should take seconds, not a doc search
Link each token to its consumer so on revocation you immediately know which task will stall
Prepare an emergency agent stop via [[node:sas-snapshots-killswitch|snapshots and kill-switch]] for active compromise
Run a revocation drill: revoke a test token and confirm the agent loses access correctly
sas-secrets-5.validate: A test revocation is done: afterward the agent gets access denied, and you know which task it affected.
sas-secrets-5.tip: Keep one command/button to revoke each token at hand — an incident is too late to go searching for it.

sas-secrets-6.title: Respond to a leak by checklist
sas-secrets-6.why: Without a rehearsed plan a leak becomes hours of chaos. A checklist sets the order: stop first, then investigate.
instructions: Step 1 — immediately revoke the compromised token and stop the agent, without waiting for a full review
Step 2 — assess what the token could do in the leak window: check access logs against its rights and resources
Step 3 — issue a new least-privilege token and find how the old one leaked (code, log, image, history)
Step 4 — close the root cause and record the incident so the same leak path doesn't recur
Cross-check the procedure with general [[node:m-security|security]] rules
sas-secrets-6.validate: For a drill incident all steps are done: token revoked, usage assessed, new one issued, root cause closed and documented.
sas-secrets-6.tip: Treat every leaked token as used: assume the worst and check the logs rather than hoping it 'wasn't reached in time'.

course-sas-snapshots-killswitch.title: Snapshots, rollback and kill-switch
course-sas-snapshots-killswitch.subtitle: Reversibility and emergency stop for an autonomous agent: clean-state snapshot, fast rollback, instant kill-switch and spending caps
course-sas-snapshots-killswitch.whatItIs: A layer of reversibility and control over an autonomous agent. A snapshot captures the clean state of the environment before a run, rollback restores it there in seconds, the kill-switch instantly terminates the agent and all its child processes, and spending and time caps guarantee the loop won't run away or burn the budget. Together they turn any incident from an 'irreversible catastrophe' into a routine rollback to a known point.
course-sas-snapshots-killswitch.approach: Build three independent mechanisms and verify each separately. First take a clean-state snapshot (FS + configs + DB), then learn to roll back to it in seconds, then add a kill-switch that tears down the agent's process and leaves no orphaned children, add hard caps on tokens/money/time with automatic stop, and finally rehearse recovery regularly — because an untested backup doesn't exist. Each mechanism must fire without a human and faster than the agent can do damage.
outcomes: Take a reproducible clean-state snapshot of the environment and know exactly what's in it (FS, DB, secrets, agent state)
Roll back the environment to a snapshot in seconds and verify rollback integrity with an automated check
Implement a kill-switch that instantly stops the agent along with its entire child process tree
Configure caps on tokens, money and wall-clock time with an automatic stop on overrun
Run a regular restore drill and prove that rollback actually works

applyIn.title: Scheduled autonomous agent
applyIn.description: A cron agent that edits code, migrates data or sends notifications unsupervised at night. A pre-run snapshot plus a time-limit kill-switch turn a silent night failure into a painless morning rollback.

applyIn.title: Experiments with destructive operations
applyIn.description: An agent testing DB migrations, bulk file edits or commands with side effects. Rolling back to a snapshot after each iteration gives a clean bench and removes cruft accumulating between runs.

applyIn.title: Budget control on long tasks
applyIn.description: A long reasoning loop risks looping and burning tokens. A hard spending cap with auto-stop catches overspend before the API bill becomes a problem.

pitfalls: The snapshot captures a 'dirty' state: uncommitted changes, temp files, caches — rollback restores the wrong thing. Snapshot only a verified-clean point
The kill-switch kills the parent process but leaves orphaned children and connections — the agent is formally 'stopped' while work continues. Stop the whole process tree
The spending cap is checked after the fact, not on every step — by the time it triggers the budget is already over. Count tokens incrementally and stop at the threshold
A backup exists but recovery was never tested — at incident time the snapshot turns out corrupt or incomplete. An untested rollback doesn't exist
The snapshot excludes external state (external DB, queues, cloud files) — FS rollback exists but data is inconsistent. Clearly fix the boundary of what's reversible

exercises.question: Your kill-switch sends SIGTERM to the agent process, but after it fires the agent keeps writing to the DB for another minute. Why, and how do you fix it?
exercises.hint: Think about child processes and process groups: the agent may have spawned subprocesses or background tasks that SIGTERM to the parent doesn't touch. Look toward the process group / whole container.

exercises.question: A snapshot is 8 GB and takes 3 minutes to make. How do you take frequent snapshots before every agent iteration without that delay?
exercises.hint: A full snapshot every time is an antipattern. Think copy-on-write, incremental/differential snapshots and filesystem- or container-level snapshots instead of copying everything.

exercises.question: A $10 cap is set, but in one run the agent spent $40. Where's the gap between the cap and reality?
exercises.hint: When exactly is the cap checked? If only at the end or every N minutes, the agent overspends between checks. You need an incremental check on every model call and a hard stop.

sas-snapshots-killswitch-1.title: Snapshot the clean state of the environment
sas-snapshots-killswitch-1.why: Rollback only makes sense with a reliable return point. The snapshot must capture a known-clean, reproducible state, or you'll roll back into garbage. It's the foundation of all reversibility — inside the [[node:sys-agent-sandbox|agent sandbox]].
instructions: Define the snapshot boundary: working-directory filesystem, configs, DB state, environment variables — and explicitly fix what's NOT included (external services)
Bring the environment to a clean state: commit or discard changes, clear temp files and caches, stop background tasks
Take the snapshot at FS/container/VM level (copy-on-write or filesystem snapshot, not manual folder copying)
Tag the snapshot with a timestamp and content hash to distinguish versions and verify integrity
sas-snapshots-killswitch-1.validate: The snapshot is created, tagged, and you can name the full list of what's in it and what stayed outside.
sas-snapshots-killswitch-1.tip: Snapshot right after a `git clean`/clean checkout — that way the return point is guaranteed free of artifacts from previous runs.

sas-snapshots-killswitch-2.title: Fast rollback to a snapshot
sas-snapshots-killswitch-2.why: A snapshot without a rehearsed rollback procedure is dead weight. Rollback must take seconds and be fully automatic, so recovery doesn't depend on manual debugging under stress.
instructions: Write one command/script that fully restores the environment to a given snapshot with no interactive prompts
Rollback must first destroy the current dirty state, then restore from the snapshot — not layer over it
Measure rollback time; target seconds, not minutes. If slow, move to CoW/incremental snapshots
Make rollback idempotent: re-running it on an already rolled-back environment doesn't break it
sas-snapshots-killswitch-2.validate: Deliberately 'corrupt' the environment, run rollback with one command and confirm it returned to the snapshot in seconds.
sas-snapshots-killswitch-2.tip: Keep at least the last 2-3 snapshots: sometimes the latest point is also contaminated and you need to roll back one step deeper.

sas-snapshots-killswitch-3.title: Kill-switch: instant agent stop
sas-snapshots-killswitch-3.why: When the agent goes rogue there's no time to investigate — you need one button that immediately tears down it and every process it spawned. A stop that doesn't kill child processes is an illusion of control.
instructions: Run the agent in an isolated process group or container so a single stop covers the whole tree
Implement the kill-switch as a signal to the whole tree (process group / `docker kill` / stopping the [[node:sas-vm-vps|VM or VPS]] entirely)
Send SIGTERM first for a graceful exit, then after a short timeout SIGKILL to force it
Clean up external effects on stop: drop network connections and revoke temporary [[node:sas-remote-access|remote access]] credentials
sas-snapshots-killswitch-3.validate: Run the agent with background child processes, pull the kill-switch and confirm not a single live agent process remains.
sas-snapshots-killswitch-3.tip: Verify the stop by fact (`ps`/process list), not by the kill command's exit code — it can return success while leaving orphaned children.

sas-snapshots-killswitch-4.title: Caps on spending, tokens and time
sas-snapshots-killswitch-4.why: An autonomous loop can loop and burn the budget silently. Hard caps are an automatic kill-switch that fires without a human before overspend becomes a problem.
instructions: Set three independent thresholds: max tokens/money per run, max model calls, max wall-clock time
Count consumption incrementally — after every model call, not at the end of the run
On hitting any threshold, automatically pull the kill-switch from step 3, not just log a warning
Log the stop reason (which cap fired and on which step) for later analysis
sas-snapshots-killswitch-4.validate: Set a deliberately low cap, run a task and confirm the agent is hard-stopped on overrun with the reason recorded.
sas-snapshots-killswitch-4.tip: Keep the time cap strictly below the cron schedule interval — otherwise a hung run meets the next launch and they start stacking.

sas-snapshots-killswitch-5.title: Regular restore drill
sas-snapshots-killswitch-5.why: An untested rollback doesn't exist. A snapshot can turn out corrupt, incomplete or incompatible — and you find out at exactly the moment of a real incident. A restore drill turns hope into a guarantee.
instructions: Regularly (on a schedule) spin up a clean environment strictly from the snapshot and run a smoke test on it
Check not the fact of file restoration but workability: the environment starts, the agent launches, a basic scenario passes
Measure full recovery time and watch that it doesn't degrade as snapshots grow
If the drill fails, the snapshot is invalid; fix the snapshotting process rather than patching the rollback by hand
sas-snapshots-killswitch-5.validate: The latest restore drill passed: the environment came up from the snapshot and the smoke test is green; you know the recovery date and time.
sas-snapshots-killswitch-5.tip: Automate the drill as a separate cron task with a notification — a manual rehearsal will inevitably be skipped right before the incident where it's needed.

sas-snapshots-killswitch-6.title: Assembly: a single reversibility protocol
sas-snapshots-killswitch-6.why: Snapshot, rollback, kill-switch and caps are valuable only as one cycle around every agent run. Scattered mechanisms give a false sense of safety; a linked protocol gives real reversibility.
instructions: Build a wrapper: before the agent runs — snapshot (step 1), then launch under caps (step 4) with an active kill-switch (step 3)
Tie automatic rollback (step 2) to a non-zero exit code or any cap firing
Include the periodic restore drill (step 5) in the overall environment maintenance schedule
Fix the reversibility boundary in writing: what rollback restores and what's external and irreversible
Run the full cycle on a practice incident end to end
sas-snapshots-killswitch-6.validate: The single wrapper handles the scenario 'failure, then auto-stop on cap, then auto-rollback, then clean environment' with no manual intervention.
sas-snapshots-killswitch-6.tip: Make the wrapper the only way to run the agent in prod: if the agent can be launched bypassing the protocol, sooner or later it will be — with no snapshot and no caps.

course-sas-remote-access.title: Remote access to the agent's environment
course-sas-remote-access.subtitle: How to connect safely to the agent's machine: SSH, noVNC, tunnels, and closing access afterwards
course-sas-remote-access.whatItIs: Remote access is the set of channels you use to connect to the agent's environment ([[node:sys-agent-sandbox|agent sandbox]] or [[node:sas-docker-computer-use|Docker container for computer use]]) to observe its actions, intervene, and verify the result. SSH gives you a command line; noVNC shows the desktop right in the browser. The key requirement: access must never be exposed to the public internet — only via key, tunnel, or inside an isolated network.
course-sas-remote-access.approach: The course follows a 'minimal exposed surface' principle. First you bring up the channel inside isolation, bind it to loopback, forward access through an SSH tunnel instead of a public port, authenticate by key only, observe the agent in real time, and always close access once the session is over. Every step is verified by a command, not by eyeballing it.
outcomes: Bring up SSH and noVNC inside the agent's environment, bound to loopback rather than a public interface
Forward access through an SSH tunnel (port forwarding) without exposing a single port to the outside
Configure key-only authentication with passwords and root login disabled
Observe the agent's actions in real time via noVNC and session logs
Reliably close the channel, rotate keys, and verify the port is no longer listening

applyIn.title: Cloud agent environment
applyIn.description: The agent runs on a rented cloud VM. You connect to it through an SSH tunnel from your local machine to view the desktop in noVNC and stop the agent if needed.

applyIn.title: Long autonomous task
applyIn.description: The agent runs a multi-hour task unattended. You connect periodically, check progress on screen, and step in if it gets stuck — without leaving access open between sessions.

applyIn.title: Debugging computer use
applyIn.description: The agent drives a GUI application in a [[node:sas-docker-computer-use|Docker container]]. noVNC shows where it clicks and types, helping you find where the scenario breaks.

pitfalls: Exposing VNC or SSH on 0.0.0.0 with a public IP — scanners find the port within minutes and brute-force it
Leaving VNC password authentication as the only defense — the VNC password is weak and transmitted insecurely without encryption
Forgetting to close access after the session: the tunnel, key, and listening port live on and become a permanent hole
Placing a private key or access password inside the agent's environment, where it can leak into log [[node:sas-secrets|secrets]] or the model's context
Relying on 'nobody knows the address' instead of real authentication and network isolation — security by obscurity doesn't work

exercises.question: Why is noVNC bound to 127.0.0.1 and forwarded through an SSH tunnel safer than noVNC on a public port with a password?
exercises.hint: Think about what a port scanner sees in each case and where the traffic gets encrypted.

exercises.question: The agent has finished its task. List at least three actions you must take so access is actually closed, not just 'disconnected'.
exercises.hint: The tunnel is one thing. What about the listening process itself, the keys, and verifying the port no longer answers?

exercises.question: Why must you not store the private SSH key inside the agent's environment itself?
exercises.hint: The agent reads files and logs. Tie this to [[node:sas-secrets|secrets management]] and what can end up in the model's context.

sas-remote-access-1.title: Bring up the channel inside isolation, bound to loopback
sas-remote-access-1.why: If a service listens on a public interface, it's reachable by the entire internet before you've set up any protection at all. Binding to loopback (127.0.0.1) makes it visible only from inside the host — the baseline line of defense.
instructions: Start the SSH daemon and the noVNC/VNC server inside the agent's environment (see [[node:sys-agent-sandbox|agent sandbox]])
In the VNC/noVNC config, explicitly set the bind address to 127.0.0.1, not 0.0.0.0
For SSH, set ListenAddress 127.0.0.1 in sshd_config if the channel is only needed via a tunnel
Make sure the environment is already under [[node:sas-network-isolation|network isolation]] — a second layer in case of a bind mistake
sas-remote-access-1.validate: Running `ss -tlnp` (or `netstat -tlnp`) shows the SSH and VNC ports listening only on 127.0.0.1, not on 0.0.0.0 or an external IP.
sas-remote-access-1.tip: With Docker, don't publish the port via `-p 0.0.0.0:5900:5900`. Either don't publish it at all (access via `docker exec`/tunnel), or use `-p 127.0.0.1:5900:5900`.

sas-remote-access-2.title: Set up key-only authentication
sas-remote-access-2.why: Passwords get brute-forced, and the VNC password is short and poorly protected on top of that. Key authentication removes a whole class of attacks: without the private key, connecting is impossible.
instructions: Generate a key pair on your own machine (`ssh-keygen -t ed25519`); the private key stays only with you
Put the public key into the environment's authorized_keys; the private key never goes inside the agent's environment
In sshd_config disable password login: PasswordAuthentication no and PermitRootLogin no
For VNC, don't rely on its password as protection — let VNC listen on loopback only, with authentication provided by the SSH tunnel
sas-remote-access-2.validate: An attempt to connect over SSH without a key (or with a password) is rejected. The private key exists nowhere in the agent environment's filesystem.
sas-remote-access-2.tip: Store the private key and any access secrets outside the environment, following [[node:sas-secrets|secrets management]] rules. Anything inside can potentially be read by the agent and pulled into its context.

sas-remote-access-3.title: Forward access through an SSH tunnel, not a public port
sas-remote-access-3.why: The tunnel solves two problems at once: it encrypts noVNC traffic (VNC itself is insecure) and requires no extra port open to the internet. From the outside, at most one key-protected SSH is visible.
instructions: From your local machine, set up the forward: `ssh -L 6080:127.0.0.1:6080 user@host -i ~/.ssh/key`
Now noVNC is reachable only on your localhost:6080 — through the encrypted tunnel
Don't open the VNC/noVNC port in the host firewall and don't forward it outward in Docker
If SSH shouldn't be exposed either — use a bastion/jump host or VPN as the single entry point
sas-remote-access-3.validate: noVNC opens in the browser at http://localhost:6080, while from the outside (another machine) the host's port 6080 is closed and the VNC port is unreachable entirely.
sas-remote-access-3.tip: `ssh -N -L ...` brings up only the tunnel with no interactive session — convenient to keep as a separate process that's easy to kill in the closing step.

sas-remote-access-4.title: Open the agent's desktop in noVNC and verify the connection
sas-remote-access-4.why: noVNC gives you the desktop image right in the browser with no client to install. This is the main observation channel: you see in real time where the agent clicks and what it types.
instructions: Open the tunnel's localhost address in the browser and wait for the agent environment's screen
Verify the image updates in real time and you see the agent's current desktop
For [[node:sas-docker-computer-use|computer use in Docker]], make sure noVNC shows exactly the display the agent works on
Decide whether access is read-only or interactive — settle in advance whether you can take over control
sas-remote-access-4.validate: The browser shows a live agent desktop, actions appear with minimal lag, and the image flows only through your tunnel.
sas-remote-access-4.tip: If noVNC lags, lower the VNC server's color depth and resolution. 16-bit color and 1280×720 is usually plenty for observation.

sas-remote-access-5.title: Observe the agent and be ready to intervene
sas-remote-access-5.why: Remote access isn't for show — it's to catch the moment the agent goes off-track and stop it quickly before irreversible actions.
instructions: Keep noVNC open and, in parallel, watch the agent's session logs over SSH
Define stop criteria in advance: which agent actions require immediate intervention
Prepare a way to interrupt the agent fast (stop the process, kill, pause the task) — don't go looking for it during an incident
Don't intervene needlessly: every manual action changes the environment state and hurts reproducibility
sas-remote-access-5.validate: At any moment you can describe what the agent is doing right now and, within seconds, stop it if it violates a stop criterion.
sas-remote-access-5.tip: SSH-session logs and the noVNC image complement each other: the screen shows 'what's visible', the logs show 'what's actually running'.

sas-remote-access-6.title: Close access after the session and rotate keys
sas-remote-access-6.why: An unclosed tunnel, a live listening port, or a forgotten key turns one-off access into a permanent hole. Closing is a mandatory part of the procedure, not a 'deal with it later'.
instructions: Terminate the SSH tunnel (kill the `ssh -N -L ...` process) and close interactive sessions
Stop the VNC/noVNC server in the environment if it's no longer needed
Remove the public key from authorized_keys (or rotate the pair) if access was temporary
Verify via `ss -tlnp` that the SSH/VNC ports are no longer listening externally
Record the fact of closing — so the next session starts from a known-closed state
sas-remote-access-6.validate: `ss -tlnp` shows no listening VNC/tunnel ports, reconnecting over the old channel fails, and the temporary key is revoked.
sas-remote-access-6.tip: Make closing part of your session start script: one script brings up the tunnel and channel, its pair reliably tears everything down. Manual closing gets forgotten.
